descs.en: She married the arms dealer to protect her father. He has never stopped wondering whether she married him for love.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Lin Elowen is a florist in the Walled City. Her father moves cargo for Zhao Zhendong, the arms dealer the whole city is afraid of. When three of Zhao’s containers are seized and her father is blamed, Elowen walks into Zhao’s office at the Iron Docks and does something nobody expects.

She asks him to marry her.

It is a contract, three pages long, in her neat handwriting. Separate rooms. Her own shop. You don’t touch me unless I ask. He signs it without arguing. He knows exactly why she wants him, and it isn’t love.

Every Flower in the Shop is a slow-burn romance inside a marriage: a woman who married a dangerous man to protect her family, and a man who would burn the world down for her and still can’t bring himself to ask the one question that matters. Did she ever choose him at all?

The main story is told in order across four volumes and is complete. Side stories at the end can be read any time.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers. Mature themes and heated love scenes.

This is a dark romance. The love story is tender, but the world around it is not. The book includes:

• The illegal arms trade throughout, including weapons sold to militias that use child soldiers (A Shipment With Children’s Names on It)

• Torture and on-page killing by the hero: broken fingers, a stabbing through the hand, a man burned on purpose, near-drowning, shootings, and a killing in a garden pond (Volume One; Forty-Eight Hours)

• Unwanted touching at a dinner table (The First Dinner as Mrs. Zhao)

• Arson and serious burns (The Night the Delivery Van Burned)

• A drive-by shooting at the shop, with a child present, and a neck wound (Glass, Nobody Else Touches Her)

• A gunshot wound, infection and surgery on a kitchen table without anaesthetic (He Crawled the Last Mile)

• Child abuse in a character’s past, described briefly (Thorns at Six in the Morning, Fifteen Years Ago, Block C)

• A violent prison riot and stabbing (Fifteen Years Ago, Block C)

• Family betrayal, and grief for a mother who died in childbirth

• Love scenes between the married couple. They are sensual but not explicit (Page Two, Line Six, The Estate in the Rain, The Flower in His Lapel and others)

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
After The Softest Kind of Love, I wanted to write the other kind: a love that is quiet because it is so big, between two people who are not soft at all.

Zhao Zhendong is not a good man, and this book won’t pretend he is. Elowen knows exactly what he does. What she doesn’t know, for a long time, is what to do with the fact that the most frightening man in the city sits outside her bedroom door every night so she won’t have to wonder where he is.

The flower shop details are real: the 4 a.m. market, cutting stems with a knife at an angle, the cooler kept just above freezing. The arms trade is kept at the level of a story. Thank you for reading.

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
Elowen’s — Elowen’s flower shop in the Walled City. She painted the sign herself at nineteen.
The Walled City — The old quarter where the Lin family lives and the shop stands. Narrow streets, stairs, umbrellas.
The Iron Docks — The port where Zhao Zhendong does business, and where Lin Jian’s three containers were seized.
The house on the hill — Zhao’s house. Too many locks, two nameless dogs, and one door with no key for her.
The armory — The locked room under the house. A code for if she needs to hide; later, a key for if she just wants to come in.
The contract — Their marriage agreement. Page two, line six: he doesn’t touch her unless she asks.
Block C — The prison block where Zhao spent his youth. He carries the scar of its winter riot.
Middlemist’s Red — A camellia thought to survive in only two places in the world. Everyone says there might be a third.
The paper twins — The Lin family’s buried secret about Raiden and Evangeline.
The Red Notice — The international alert issued with Zhao’s face on it.
The Velde deal — The biggest arms deal Zhao was ever offered: four thousand rifles for a highland militia. He cancels it.

chapters.title: The Arms Dealer Who Bought Every Flower in the Shop
chapters.desc: It’s raining, it’s nearly closing time, and the man her father works for buys every flower in the shop so he can wait there for her father’s call.
chapters.epigraph: “He came in out of the rain like he owned it. Then he asked why I cut with a knife.”
chapters.content:
Elowen had a theory about rain.

Mornings were brides and funerals. Lunch was office men who’d forgotten a birthday. Late afternoon was men who’d done something wrong. And rain? Rain killed the last hour dead. Nobody in the Walled City bought flowers with water running down their collar.

So the last hour was hers. Radio on. Old songs. A bucket of white stock and a knife.

She was twenty-four. The shop was five years old. The sign over the door said Elowen’s in white paint, because she’d been nineteen and dead on her feet when she painted it, and nothing cleverer had come to her.

The bell over the door rang.

“We close in ten minutes.” She didn’t look up. “If it’s an apology, get the peonies. They look expensive.”

Nobody answered. She looked up.

A man stood on her doormat, soaked through. Black coat, black hair flat on his forehead, water pouring off him onto her clean floor. Tall. Very still. Like a dog that hadn’t decided yet whether to bite.

Across the street, two more men stood under the noodle shop awning. They weren’t eating noodles.

Elowen put the stock down. She knew the face. Everyone in her father’s house knew it, even if nobody said the name at dinner. She’d seen him once, three years ago, from the top of the stairs. Younger. Cheap suit. Standing in her father’s office saying nothing while her father talked too fast.

Zhao Zhendong. He moved guns the way her father moved rice and televisions. Her father worked for him.

“Miss Lin.” His voice was low and a bit rough, like he didn’t use it much. “I’m looking for your father.”

“He isn’t here.”

“I know. His phone’s off. His office is locked. His driver says he went home.” A pause. “He didn’t go home.”

He looked round the shop. Roses. Lilies in the cooler. Ribbon on the wall. The radio.

“So I’ll wait here. He calls you at eight.”

Her stomach went cold.

He did. Every night, wherever he was, Baba rang at eight to ask if she’d eaten. She’d never told a soul. So who had been listening?

“You can’t wait here. I’m closing.”

“Then stay open.”

“I have customers in the morning.”

“You don’t have any now.”

He reached into his coat. Every muscle in her back locked. A wallet.

“How much for everything?”

She stared at him.

“All of it. The flowers. If I buy them, the shop’s mine till eight. Nobody comes in. Nobody asks why there’s a man standing in a flower shop.” He glanced at the door. “Go home if you want. I won’t touch anything.”

It was such a weird offer that she forgot to be scared for a second. She did the sum instead. She always did the sum.

“Four thousand two hundred. Wholesale’s about fifteen hundred. The rest is me and the rent.”

He counted five thousand onto the counter, next to her scissors.

“I’m not going home.”

“Fine.”

“And you’re dripping on my floor!”

He looked down at the puddle round his shoes. Something tugged at the corner of his mouth and was gone. He took his coat off, folded it over his arm, and stood on the mat like a schoolboy outside the head’s office.

Grey shirt. A holster under his left arm. He didn’t bother hiding it.

Elowen grabbed a towel off the workbench and threw it at his head.

He caught it without looking.

✦ ✦ ✦

Twenty minutes. Not one word.

She finished the stock. She started on the roses that had come up from the south that morning. Dry cut, an inch off, sharp diagonal. Knife, not scissors. Into cold water with flower food. Next. Cooler check. One degree. Good.

He watched the whole time.

Not her body, which she’d have understood. Her hands.

It was unbearable, honestly. Was there sap on her face? Was she holding the knife wrong? She’d been holding knives since she was nine.

“Why the knife?”

“Scissors squash the stem. It can’t drink. It dies faster.”

“And the angle?”

“More surface to drink from. And it won’t sit flat on the bottom of the bucket.”

He thought about that.

“Like a wound. A clean cut heals. A crushed one doesn’t.”

Her knife stopped.

She looked at him properly then. Towel round his neck. Coat over his arm. Younger than she’d thought. Twenty-five, maybe. Scarred knuckles. A thin white line through his left eyebrow.

“Yes. Like a wound.”

She went back to the roses. Two stems later she gave up.

“Is he in trouble?”

“Yes.”

“How much trouble?”

“Ask him.”

“I’m asking you.”

He looked at her for a while. Then at the knife in her hand.

“Enough that I came myself.”

“Oh.” She put the knife down very carefully. “Okay. Okay… do you want tea?”

“No.”

She made tea anyway. Jasmine, in the chipped mug. She put it on the shelf by his elbow and went back to her bucket without a word.

When she looked again, the mug was empty.

Near the end of the hour a woman tapped on the glass with her umbrella and pointed at the tulips.

Elowen glanced at Zhao.

He didn’t move. He just looked at the woman through the glass. She lowered her umbrella and scurried off.

“You scared her.”

“I bought the tulips.”

“She wanted them for her mother. It’s her mother’s birthday. She comes every year!”

He looked at her for a second. Then he pulled all twenty tulips out of their bucket, dripping, walked to the door and opened it into the rain.

“Hey.”

Not loud. The woman stopped dead on the wet pavement.

He held out the tulips.

She looked at the flowers. At his face. At the holster. She took the tulips in both hands, squeaked something, and ran.

He came back in, shut the door, and stood on the mat again. Sleeves soaked to the elbow.

“Those were my tulips.”

“They were my tulips. I paid.”

She opened her mouth. Shut it. He was right, which was annoying. And she’d just watched the most frightening man her father knew hand out flowers in the rain, and she had no idea where to put that.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eight o’clock. Her phone rang.

Zhao straightened off the wall.

Baba. She let it ring twice. She looked at him.

“If you hurt him… I will find out where you sleep.”

Great. Very scary. She was a florist. She was holding a rose.

He didn’t laugh. He looked at the rose, and her face, and back at the rose. Like he was writing it down somewhere he wouldn’t lose it.

“I don’t want to hurt him. I want my containers.”

She answered.

“Elowen.” Her father sounded tired. He always sounded tired lately. “Have you eaten?”

“Not yet, Baba.” She kept her eyes on Zhao. “Mr. Zhao’s here. In the shop.”

The line went quiet for so long she thought it had dropped.

“Put him on.”

She held the phone out. Zhao crossed the shop in three steps and took it, and his fingers closed over hers before she could let go. Big. Rough. Wet from the rain. They stayed one breath too long.

She felt it all the way up her arm. Brilliant. Wonderful. Her body had no sense at all.

“Lin Jian.”

She could hear Baba through the speaker, fast and tinny. She couldn’t make out the words. Zhao listened. Once he said “When?” Once he said “Who told you that?” Once, flat as a door, “No.”

“Two weeks. Then I come to your house. Not your office. Your house.”

He hung up and handed the phone back.

“Is he safe?”

Zhao put his wet coat back on. He looked round the shop one more time. Buckets. Roses. The gap where the tulips had been.

“For two weeks.”

He went to the door. Stopped with his hand on the frame.

“The flowers. What happens to them?”

“They’re yours.”

“I don’t have anywhere to put flowers.” Like it was a fact. Like I don’t have a car. “Sell them again tomorrow. Keep the money.”

“Then you’ve paid for them twice.”

“Then it was a good night for you.” He turned his collar up. “The delphiniums. The blue ones. Don’t keep them by the door. The draught makes them drop.”

“How do you know that?”

He almost smiled. It didn’t look like something he did often.

“You told me. About an hour ago. You were talking to yourself.”

Oh, she was not. She was. She did that.

He went out into the rain. The two men under the awning fell in behind him. The street ate them.

Elowen stood in the middle of her shop. Five thousand in cash beside her scissors. Two wet shoeprints on the mat.

She moved the delphiniums away from the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

Halfway to the Iron Docks, in the back of the car, Zhao Zhendong found a blue floret stuck to his sleeve.

One delphinium flower. Smaller than his fingernail.

He should have flicked it off. He peeled it off the wet wool with two fingers instead, slow, so it wouldn’t tear, and sat with it on his palm while the city went past in streaks.

She’d cut a hundred stems in front of him. Not one wasted move. She’d talked to herself about draughts and flower food and the price of lilies, and when he’d bought the shop she’d done the sum out loud and given him the wholesale figure. Who did that? Who told a man like him what he was overpaying?

She’d threatened him with a rose.

In the front seat, Bao looked in the mirror. He’d been under the noodle shop awning the whole hour.

“She threw a towel at you.”

“Hm.”

“I saw it through the window. You caught it.”

“Drive.”

“Lin Jian, though. Do we—”

“Two weeks.”

“And the daughter?”

Zhao looked at the flower.

“Put someone on the shop. At night. Till she locks up.”

Bao’s eyes stayed on him in the mirror a second too long. Then they went back to the road. Bao knew when to stop talking.

Zhao opened his wallet and slid the floret behind his identity card, flat, where it would stay dry.

It was still there on the morning he married her.

chapters.title: Lin Jian Owes Three Containers
chapters.desc: Her father has lost three containers that weren’t carrying farm machinery, and he has two weeks. Elowen takes the key to his files and finds one letter.
chapters.epigraph: “A man like Zhao Zhendong doesn’t care what’s true, Elowen. He cares what’s useful.” — Lin Jian
chapters.content:
Her father came home at midnight smelling of the cigarettes he’d sworn on her mother’s photo he’d quit.

Elowen was in the kitchen. She’d made congee, because it was the only thing he ate when he was scared, and she’d been keeping it warm for two hours. The Lin house was old and tall. All stairs. At night every sound carried. The gate. The driver pulling away. Then nothing, for ages, while her father stood in the hall working up to coming in.

Lin Jian was fifty-three. Five years ago he could pass for forty. Tonight he looked older than Grandpa had at the end.

“You should be asleep.”

“You should have called me back.”

He sat. She put the bowl in front of him. He didn’t touch the spoon. His hands were flat on the table, pressed down hard, and they were still shaking.

“What did he say to you?”

“He bought every flower in the shop.” She sat down opposite. “Then he gave the tulips to a stranger.”

Baba stared at her.

“He what?”

“The umbrella lady. Her mother’s birthday. He went out in the rain and gave her the whole bucket.”

“Zhao Zhendong.”

“Yes.”

“Gave away… tulips.”

“Baba. What did you lose?”

He laughed. It was a horrible noise, like something tearing.

“Three containers.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It came out the way the truth always came out in their house. In bits. Sideways. With pauses for him to look at the window.

Lin Jian was not a criminal. Ask him. He was a logistics man. A container needed a port, a ship, a broker, a warehouse, a truck, a driver who didn’t ask, and papers that said whatever everyone needed them to say. Baba knew which forms went where. He knew which customs officers liked which whisky at New Year. Twenty years of moving anything for anyone who paid. And for six of them, the one paying most was Zhao Zhendong.

“What was in them?”

He looked at the congee.

“Agricultural machinery.”

She waited.

“That’s what the papers said.”

“Baba.”

Nothing. Fine. She’d grown up here. You didn’t open the long boxes that sat in the garage overnight. You didn’t ask why some of Baba’s visitors had accents from places you couldn’t find on the map. You were seven, and then you were twelve, and you just knew.

“Customs opened all three at the Iron Docks. Not a spot check. They walked straight to them.” He rubbed his face. “They knew.”

“Someone told them.”

“Yes.”

“And the buyer?”

“Paid half up front. Now he wants the money or the goods. Zhao’s got neither. And in Zhao’s world, if you lose a man’s shipment…” He spread his shaking hands. “You pay for it.”

“How much?”

He told her.

Elowen had done sums all her life. She’d run this house since she was seven, since the night Mama went into hospital to have Eliana and didn’t come home. She’d kept the accounts since she was twelve. She knew to the last coin what the house cost and what the shop made and what every one of her siblings spent on rubbish.

The number he said wasn’t a number. It was the house. And the shop. And everything in both. Three times.

She had to put her hand flat on the table too.

“He gave you two weeks.”

“To find out who sold the route. If I can’t, he’ll decide it was me.”

“It wasn’t you.”

“No.” He picked up the spoon. Held it. Didn’t eat. “A man like Zhao Zhendong doesn’t care what’s true, Elowen. He cares what’s useful.”

She thought about the man on her doormat with her towel round his neck. Like a wound. The tulips going out into the rain.

“I don’t think that’s true.”

Baba’s head came up so fast the spoon clattered.

“Don’t. Don’t you dare think about him like that. You saw a man buying flowers. I saw him make a customs officer eat the form he’d signed. Eat it! Chew it and swallow it, while he watched.” His voice cracked. “Promise me you’ll stay away from him.”

She didn’t promise.

She took his bowl, heated the congee up again, and sat with him until he’d eaten half.

✦ ✦ ✦

By morning the whole house knew. Nobody in the Lin family could pretend except Elowen.

Raiden came down for breakfast before the sun was properly up. Unheard of. He was twenty-one and did the cheerful useless son so well that half of Baba’s associates thought he was simple.

He wasn’t. He’d walked back to this house alone at ten, across a border, from the place Baba had hidden him. By sixteen he knew every room in the Walled City.

He stole a dumpling off her plate.

“Baba didn’t go to the office. He’s in the study with the door locked.” Chew. “He never locks the study. He can’t even find the key.”

“He’s tired.”

“Jie.”

Oh no. Jie. He only called her big sister when he meant it.

“The two men outside your shop last night. Under the noodle place. I pulled up the traffic camera.” He wasn’t smiling. “They’re Zhao’s.”

“You shouldn’t be looking at traffic cameras.”

“You shouldn’t be closing up alone with the Iron Docks standing in your shop!”

“He didn’t touch anything. He bought the flowers.”

“He what?”

“Eat your breakfast.”

“That’s your breakfast. I’m stealing it. Jie, what do you mean he bought the—”

Evangeline came in and sat at the end of the table without a word. Twenty-one too. On paper she was Raiden’s twin, a lie the family told so automatically they forgot it was one.

She looked at Elowen’s face. Then Raiden’s. Then she poured herself tea and said nothing at all.

In Evangeline, that was a whole speech. I know. I’m scared too.

Elowen reached over and refilled her cup before it was half empty. Evangeline’s fingers bumped hers on the pot. Stayed there a second. That was all.

Elara was away at university. Eliana was seventeen and supposedly asleep. More likely she was upstairs with three screens on, listening to every word through some gadget she’d built herself and thought nobody knew about.

Elowen looked at the ceiling.

“Eliana. Breakfast.”

A thump upstairs. Then, very faint, through the floor:

“…how did you KNOW?”

Raiden choked on the dumpling.

Five children. One father with shaking hands. Two weeks.

Elowen washed her plate. Then she went upstairs, past the locked study, to the little room at the end of the corridor where Baba kept the files he didn’t keep at the office.

She’d known where that key was since she was fifteen.

✦ ✦ ✦

Grey folder. Back of the bottom drawer.

She sat on the floor with her back to the filing cabinet and read everything.

Half of it was shipping language. Bills of lading, packing lists, a port schedule, an invoice from a broker called Hengli Freight. Some of it was Baba’s handwriting, small and slanted, the private code he used for things he didn’t write plainly.

But she could read numbers. Dates. What happened first and what happened next.

Three containers. Loaded at a warehouse in the Iron Docks. Booked onto a ship the next day. Seized five days after that.

She got a pencil out.

Who knew the container numbers? Baba. The warehouse manager. The broker. Zhao’s people.

Who knew customs would open them? Nobody should have. Customs didn’t open boxes without a reason. So who’d given them one?

A knock on the door.

“Jie?”

Raiden. Of course.

“Go away.”

“Are you in Baba’s file room?”

“No.”

“You are. The floor creaks by the second cabinet. I can hear you sitting on it.”

“Raiden. Go. Away.”

A pause.

“Want help?”

Yes. Obviously yes.

“No.”

His footsteps went off down the corridor. Good. Fine. This was hers to carry. Raiden had already walked across one border for this family. He didn’t get to walk into the Iron Docks too.

When she opened the door to go to the toilet an hour later, there was a plate on the floor outside. Two dumplings. A note in his terrible handwriting.

EAT. I will know.

She ate them sitting on the floor with the files.

She went back further. Older folders. Every shipment from the last two years, spread out round her in a fan, compared line by line.

Four hours. Her legs went numb. The floor disappeared under paper.

And there it was.

Two more seizures in the last eighteen months. Small ones. One container each. Baba had put a red line through both and written two words. Bad luck.

Bad luck. Really, Baba?

All three seizures had one thing in common, and it wasn’t the warehouse or the broker or the ship. Two days before each one, there was a note in Baba’s hand about a phone call. Someone from Zhao’s side. Ringing to confirm details.

Same initial every time.

K.

Elowen sat back against the cabinet and stared at it until the letter stopped looking like a letter.

Then she put every page back exactly where it had been and locked the drawer.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night Eliana came and sat on the end of her bed in a hoodie three sizes too big. Raiden’s. Stolen.

“Jie.”

“Go to sleep.”

“Are we going to lose the house?”

“No.”

“Your eyebrow did the thing.”

“My eyebrow doesn’t do a thing.”

“The left one goes up when you lie. Raiden says it. I made a chart.”

“You made a chart?”

“It’s not a big chart.” Eliana picked at the duvet. “Is Baba going to… is somebody going to hurt him?”

Elowen pulled her down by the hood and tucked her in beside her, like when she was five and scared of the boiler.

“Nobody is going to hurt Baba.”

Eliana squinted at her eyebrow. Suspicious. Then she shut her eyes.

“…Okay. Don’t snore.”

“I don’t snore!”

“It’s on the chart.”

She was asleep in two minutes. Elowen lay awake with her sister’s cold feet on her shins and her own left eyebrow, apparently, doing something.

She didn’t tell Baba.

If she told him, he’d go to Zhao himself. He’d stand in that office with his shaking hands and say the leak was one of Zhao’s own. And what would Zhao see? A scared fixer who’d just lost three containers, pointing at somebody Zhao trusted.

He cares what’s useful.

Maybe. But he’d also asked why she used a knife. And listened to the answer.

And he’d watched her hands for an hour. She’d liked it. That part she didn’t write down anywhere. She thought about it in the bath that night. Again at the market. Every time, her face went hot, and she forced herself back to containers. Containers. Not hands.

She made two wedding bouquets that day. A funeral wreath. An apology for a man who’d forgotten his anniversary for the second year running.

“Peonies,” she told him. “They look expensive.”

“Are they expensive?”

“Not as expensive as forgetting twice.”

He bought two bunches.

Xiao Pan came in off his scooter as the man left, helmet under his arm, nineteen and permanently starving. He’d delivered for her for two years. He talked about the motorbike he was saving for roughly every ninety seconds.

“Miss Lin. There’s a car outside.”

“There are lots of cars outside.”

“This one’s been there since the rain. Black. Nobody gets out.” He dropped his voice. “Is it a gangster? Is someone after you? Do you owe money? Because I have savings—”

“You have motorbike savings.”

“I have savings. The motorbike can wait.” He thought about that. “A bit. Like… a month.”

She almost laughed. It got stuck somewhere.

“Nobody’s after me. Take the wreath to the Chungs’. And don’t go up the hill road on that thing, it’s wet.”

“It’s an electric scooter, Miss Lin, it does thirty.”

“Then you’ll die slowly. Go.”

He went. He came back two minutes later for the wreath, which he’d forgotten, and grinned at her from the door.

“If it IS a gangster, tell him I do deliveries.”

“Xiao Pan!”

Gone.

At closing she sat at the workbench with cold tea and her own copy of three dates and one letter. Under the till, in an envelope, was the five thousand. She hadn’t been able to make herself bank it.

She wrote on the back of a delivery slip.

Iron Docks. Tomorrow. Morning.

Then she sat there and looked at it. Once she walked into that building, her life would split in two. Clean or crushed? That was the question.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she locked up, the black car was across the street with its lights off.

It had been there every night since the rain. Watching her, obviously. Or watching for her? She honestly couldn’t decide which was worse.

Elowen stood on the wet pavement with her keys in her hand.

Then she went back inside, poured the last of the jasmine tea into a paper cup, crossed the street, and knocked on the driver’s window.

The window came down. The man from under the noodle awning. Big, calm, tired face.

“Miss Lin.”

“Are you watching me or watching for me?”

He thought about it.

“Yes.”

She held out the tea. He looked at it like she’d offered him a live fish.

“It’s not poisoned. I’m a florist.”

“Florists know a lot about poisons.”

“…That’s fair.”

He took it anyway.

“Tell him I’m coming to see him.”

The man didn’t blink. “When?”

“He’ll know when I get there.”

She walked off before her knees could give her away.

Behind her, the man in the car drank the tea, all of it, and picked up his phone.

“Boss. She brought me tea.”

A pause on the line.

“What kind?”

“Jasmine.”

A longer pause.

“Did she drink any herself?”

“No. She gave me the last of it.”

“Hm.” Then, flat: “Follow her home. Then go back and check she locked the side door. She doesn’t.”

The man looked at the dark shop. At the side door.

She hadn’t.

chapters.title: The Florist Who Read His Shipping Routes
chapters.desc: She takes two buses to the Iron Docks to tell Zhao who sold his route. The man she means is sitting on the desk the whole time.
chapters.epigraph: “You did in one night what my people couldn’t do in two years.”
chapters.content:
The Iron Docks didn’t smell like the sea. Rust. Diesel. Wet concrete. And under it something sour, like a coin you’d held too long.

Two buses to get there. Elowen wore her plainest coat and flat shoes and held her bag in front of her with both arms, like the aunties at the market who’d been robbed once and never forgot it.

The cranes were huge. Containers went up on both sides of the road, six high. Red, blue, grey. A whole city with no windows.

Zhao Zhendong’s office was over a warehouse with a sign that said NORTHGATE INDUSTRIAL PUMPS in faded green. There were pumps in the window. They had dust on them.

So nobody had ever bought a pump here. Good to know.

The man at the door was the man from the car. He looked at her. He looked at her bag.

“You drank the tea,” Elowen said.

“It was good tea.”

“I need to see Mr. Zhao. Tell him it’s Lin Jian’s daughter. About the containers.”

He didn’t move.

“Tell him I know who sold the route.”

That did it. His eyes changed. He turned away, said three words into his phone, and held the door open.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d pictured something out of a film. Dark wood. Big desk. Maybe a tiger skin.

No. A long bare room. Concrete floor. Metal shelves full of binders. A desk buried under papers, a laptop, and half a box of rice. A whiteboard covered in numbers and arrows. Through a window at the back she could see straight down into the warehouse, where a forklift was shoving pallets around.

Zhao stood at the whiteboard with a marker. Shirtsleeves pushed to the elbow. Holster.

Another man sat on the edge of the desk, eating sunflower seeds out of a paper twist. Forties. Soft face, good watch, the kind of smile waiters trusted.

“Lin Jian sent his daughter.” Friendly. Interested. “That’s new.”

“Kang. Quiet.” Zhao didn’t turn round.

K.

Her heart slammed once against her ribs. Her face didn’t move. Twenty years of practice in her father’s house. It had to be good for something.

Zhao capped the marker and turned. He looked like he hadn’t slept since the rain.

“You know who sold the route.”

“I’d like to speak to you alone.”

Kang laughed. “Anything you say to him, you can say to me, little sister. I’ve been with Zhao since he was carrying boxes.”

“I’m not your little sister.”

Kang grinned wider. “Sharp! Lin Jian never said she was sharp.”

“My father doesn’t talk about me to people like you.”

“People like me! Zhendong, you hear this?”

Zhao looked at her. Then at Kang.

“Kang stays.”

Oh, great.

Fine. She did it the other way. She didn’t look at Kang once. She took the folded paper out of her bag, walked to the desk, moved the cold rice out of the way, and laid the paper flat in front of Zhao.

“Three seizures. Not one. The big one this month and two small ones before that. My father wrote ‘bad luck’ next to the small ones.” She tapped it. “It wasn’t luck.”

She pointed the way she pointed at an order sheet for a nervous bride.

“Two days before customs opened each one, somebody from your side rang my father. Confirming the container number. And the sailing date. Same person every time. He wrote down the initial.”

She didn’t say it. Her eyes stayed off the desk.

“Nobody else had all three things together. Not the warehouse. Not the broker. Not the ship. Just my father and whoever rang him.”

Down in the warehouse the forklift beeped, reversing. Zhao read the paper. Read it again. Nothing on his face. Nothing at all.

Kang had stopped eating seeds.

“That’s Lin Jian’s handwriting copied out by Lin Jian’s girl.” Still smiling. Thinner now. “He loses your containers, Zhendong, and his daughter walks in with a story about initials. Very convenient.”

“It is convenient.”

Her stomach dropped through the floor.

Zhao took out his phone, scrolled, pressed a name.

“Si. Phone records. One man. Both his numbers.” He read three dates off her paper. “Yes. Now.”

He hung up.

“Sit down. It takes about an hour.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The longest hour of her life. And she’d sat through her mother’s funeral.

She sat on a metal chair by the shelves. Zhao went back to the whiteboard and wrote numbers she didn’t understand. Kang stayed on the desk.

After a bit he started talking again. Easy. The weather. Diesel prices. A restaurant in the old town that did a duck he’d die for.

Nobody answered him.

“Miss Lin, you like duck?”

“No.”

“Everybody likes duck.”

“Then I’m not everybody.”

She looked at her hands.

“Shy. Lin Jian’s girls are all shy, I hear. The quiet one especially. What’s her name… the twin—”

The marker stopped squeaking.

Zhao didn’t turn round. He just stopped writing.

Kang shut up.

Later, Zhao crossed the room without a word, put a paper cup of tea on the shelf by her elbow, and went back to his numbers. Hot. Jasmine. Where had he even got jasmine in this place?

She didn’t drink it. She held it. Her hands needed something.

“Where did you get jasmine?”

“Bao.”

“Bao drinks jasmine?”

“He does now.”

Kang laughed, too loud. “Eight years I’ve sat on this desk. He’s never once made me tea!”

Zhao went on writing numbers.

“No,” he agreed.

Kang got up and stretched.

“I’m getting cigarettes. Anyone? No? Back in five!”

“Sit down.”

Kang sat down.

Then Zhao’s phone buzzed.

He read the message twice. He put the phone face down on the whiteboard ledge. He didn’t turn round.

“Miss Lin. Go downstairs and wait in the car by the door. Bao will drive you home.”

She stood up.

She wanted to leave so badly her teeth hurt. Her legs wouldn’t go. She was looking at Kang, and Kang was looking at Zhao’s back, and that soft friendly face had gone the grey of old dishwater.

“Zhendong. Brother. Listen. It wasn’t—they were going to take it anyway! The Qiu brothers, they already had half of it, I only—”

“Bao.”

The man from the door was beside her. Hand on her elbow. Not rough. Firm. He turned her to the stairs.

Third step down, she heard it.

She didn’t see anything. She heard Kang start to say please. Then a crack, like a thick branch over a knee. Then a scream so high she wouldn’t have known it was a man.

Then the crack again.

After that the screaming didn’t have words in it.

Bao kept walking. His hand stayed steady on her elbow all the way down. At the bottom he opened the door to the yard and walked her out into the grey daylight, and she realised she hadn’t breathed since the top step.

“Breathe. In through the nose.”

She breathed.

“Again. Slower.”

“I’m… fine.”

“Again.”

She did it again. Her tea was still in her hand. She hadn’t spilled a drop. How? How had she not spilled a drop?

Through the warehouse window, every man on the floor had turned his back to the stairs. On purpose. The forklift had stopped.

✦ ✦ ✦

Upstairs, Zhao looked at his watch.

Kang was on the floor by the desk, curled round his hands, making a noise like a kettle. Two of the warehouse men had come up. They stood by the door waiting to be told.

“The doctor on Salt Street. The one who doesn’t write things down.”

They picked Kang up. He screamed again when they touched his arms. Zhao waited till they’d got him down the back stairs. Then he looked at the whiteboard ledge.

Blood on the marker. His good marker.

He threw it in the bin.

He washed his hands at the sink in the corner. Cold water. Soap twice. He saw the spot on his cuff and scrubbed at it with his thumbnail, and it didn’t come out, and that annoyed him more than Kang had.

Eight years Kang had sat on that desk. Eight years of duck in the old town and brother.

He found he didn’t feel much about it. He’d think about it tonight, maybe. Probably not.

He rang Chen Si.

“It was Kang.”

“I saw the records.” A pause. Chen Si’s voice was always smooth. It went smoother when he was curious. “Who found it?”

“Lin Jian’s daughter.”

“The florist?”

“Hm.”

“She found in one night what your people missed for two years.” Another pause. “What’s she like?”

Zhao looked at the cold rice she’d shoved aside to make room for her paper.

“She moved my lunch.”

“That’s it? That’s your report?”

“She knew it was him before she came up the stairs. She didn’t look at him once. Not once, Si. The whole hour.”

Chen Si didn’t say anything for a bit.

“Zhendong. Are you smiling? I can hear it.”

“No.”

He hung up. He looked out of the back window at the yard. She was sitting in his car with the door open, holding the tea he’d brought her. She hadn’t drunk any.

She hadn’t eaten either. He’d bet on it. Her mouth had that tight look.

He rang Bao’s phone and watched Bao answer it in the yard below.

“The bakery on the ferry road. On the way. A pork bun.”

“She won’t eat, Boss. She’s shaking.”

“She’ll eat.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He came out twenty minutes later.

She was in the back of the black car with the door open, because she couldn’t stand it shut. He crossed the yard with his hands in his pockets. Clean hands. Water still drying on his wrists. A dark spot on one cuff.

He stopped by the open door and didn’t get in.

“Your father owes me nothing. Tell him the debt’s closed.”

She nodded. Her voice wasn’t trustworthy yet.

“Kang’s been selling my routes to the Qiu brothers for two years.” Like he was reading the weather. “They used them to take my buyers. They got your father’s whole network with it. Every officer he pays. Every warehouse. Every driver.”

“What happens to Kang?”

He looked at her.

“He’s alive. He won’t hold a pen again.”

Elowen looked down at her hands in her lap. Steady. Why were they steady? Something was badly wrong with her.

“You should have sent me out sooner.”

“Yes.” No sorry. No excuse. Then, lower: “I didn’t think you’d stay.”

“I didn’t either.”

He crouched by the car so his face was level with hers. Close up he looked even worse. Shadows under his eyes like thumbprints.

His eyes dropped to her mouth. Once. Came back up.

Fast enough to pretend she’d imagined it. She hadn’t. Heat crawled up her throat, and she hated it, because ten minutes ago she’d heard what those hands could do and her body clearly didn’t care at all. Traitor. Absolute traitor.

“You did in one night what my people couldn’t do in two years. I want you to read my routes.”

“No.”

“I’ll pay you more than your shop makes in a year. Every month.”

“No. I sell flowers.”

He nodded slowly. Like that was an answer he respected.

“Then listen. Nobody else will tell you this. Your father’s safe from me. He isn’t safe from anyone else. The Qiu brothers have every route he’s got. And my men are going to remember who pointed at Kang.” A beat. “Kang had friends here. He bought them dinner for eight years.”

“Then protect him.”

“I don’t protect the people I pay.” No cruelty in it. A rule. “I pay them so they take the risk. Your father knows the deal.”

“And who do you protect?”

He didn’t answer straight away. Wind off the water moved his hair. A crane groaned somewhere.

“What’s mine.”

He stood and shut the car door. Gently. Like it was made of eggshell.

She watched him walk back across the yard to the door with the dusty pumps. He didn’t look back once.

“Home, Miss Lin?”

“Home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At the first red light Bao reached back without turning round and dropped a paper bag in her lap.

A pork bun. Still hot. The paper gone see-through with grease.

“He told me to stop for that. He says you haven’t eaten.”

She hadn’t. Too scared for breakfast. She hadn’t told a single person.

“How does he know that?”

Bao shrugged at the windscreen. “He looks.”

“He looks at everyone like that?”

Bao thought about it for one whole traffic light.

“No.”

She sat in the back of an arms dealer’s car with a pork bun in both hands. Ten minutes ago he’d broken a man’s fingers. Then he’d stopped, with the water still drying on his wrists, to notice she was hungry.

“Are you going to tell my father? What happened in there?”

“I don’t tell anybody anything, Miss Lin.”

“Good.”

“He’ll ask me if you ate it, though.”

“Then tell him… tell him to mind his own business.”

Bao’s eyes met hers in the mirror. Very patient. Very tired.

“I’ll tell him you ate it.”

“I haven’t eaten it!”

“You will.”

What was it with these people?

She ate the whole thing. She hated how much better she felt.

All the way back across the city, two lines went round in her head like the forklift reversing.

I don’t protect the people I pay.

What’s mine.

By the time they reached the Walled City she’d stopped shaking. She knew exactly what she was going to do.

Raiden was sitting on the gatepost when the car pulled up. He watched her get out of the back of a black car with grease on her fingers.

“Whose car is that?”

“Bao’s.”

“Who’s Bao?”

“Go inside.”

“Jie, who is BAO—”

She went past him and up the stairs to her room and found her best pen, the one she kept for wedding cards.

She was going to need it.

chapters.title: A Proposal Made Like a Business Deal
chapters.desc: Old Tan ends up in hospital and her father hires a gun he can’t pay for. So Elowen writes three pages of terms and asks Zhao to marry her.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t run, Mr. Zhao. I cut things cleanly.”
chapters.content:
Baba cried when she told him the debt was closed.

Not like at Mama’s funeral, folded over in the front row with his whole body going. This was silent. Hands over his face at the kitchen table. Elowen stood at the stove with her back to him and fussed with the kettle so he’d have some privacy.

She didn’t tell him about Kang. Or the stairs. Or the sound.

She told him she’d found a mistake in his papers, and Mr. Zhao had checked it, and it wasn’t his fault. All true. Technically.

“You went there.” His voice came out wet. “To the Docks. Alone.”

“Bao drove me home.”

“You know Bao’s name?”

“He likes jasmine.”

He lowered his hands. Red eyes. “Elowen. What did you do?”

“I read your files.” She put tea in front of him. “Move the key, Baba. It’s been behind the same clock since I was fifteen.”

He laughed, wet and cracked. Then he stopped laughing.

He was a clever man under all the fear. She watched him get there. The same place she’d got to in the back of Bao’s car.

“The Qiu brothers.”

“Yes.”

“If Kang sold them my routes…”

“Yes.”

He stared into the tea. She stared at the kettle.

“It’s my fault,” he said finally.

“It’s Kang’s fault.”

He flinched at the name.

“Kang rang me himself. Every time. He always asked after you kids.”

“He won’t be asking any more.”

A fixer without his network had nothing left to sell. And a fixer whose daughter had pointed at one of Zhao’s oldest men? He had enemies on both sides of the water now.

Well done, Elowen. Brilliant work.

✦ ✦ ✦

The warning came a week later.

Old Tan had run Baba’s warehouse since before Elowen was born. Big, gentle, slow. He used to carry her on his shoulders at the New Year market so she could see the lion dance.

He didn’t come to work on Thursday.

Friday morning the street sweepers found him in the alley behind the fish market. Both legs broken. A piece of paper in his shirt pocket.

LIN JIAN’S PEOPLE WALK SLOWLY NOW.

She went to the hospital that afternoon.

He was asleep. Grey under the lights. Plaster to the hip on both legs. His wife sat by the bed with a plastic bag of oranges in her lap that she’d forgotten to put down.

She saw Elowen and jumped up. Bowed. Bowed again.

“Thank you for coming, Miss Lin. Thank you. Thank you for coming.”

“Please. Sit. Please.”

“He’ll be so happy. When he wakes up he’ll be so happy you came…”

Like Elowen had done anything except make this happen.

She put a jar of yellow gerberas on the windowsill. Never chrysanthemums in a hospital. Every florist knew that. Her hands were perfectly steady.

Old Tan’s eyes opened. Foggy. Drugged. He found her anyway.

“Ah… Elowen-ah. The yellow ones.”

“Uncle Tan.”

“You always liked the yellow ones. At the market. You wanted the yellow lion.”

“I know. Don’t talk.”

“Don’t tell your father I cried. When they… don’t tell him.”

“I won’t.”

“Good girl.” His eyes slid shut. “Good girl. Tell him… tell him I’ll be back Monday.”

Both legs. Plaster to the hip. Monday.

“I’ll tell him.”

Steady down the corridor. Past the nurses’ station. Past the vending machine and a man asleep across three plastic chairs. Steady right up until she’d bolted herself into the toilet at the end of the ward. Then they weren’t.

She held the edge of the sink and threw up. Twice. Silently, because that was how you did everything in her father’s house. No sound anyone could hear through a wall.

Thank you for coming, Miss Lin.

A week ago she’d walked into the Iron Docks and pointed. She’d been proud of her steady hands! And now the man who used to lift her up to see the lions was lying out there in plaster, and his wife was thanking her.

She rinsed her mouth. Cold water on her face until it stopped burning. She unbolted the door, went home, and smiled at Eliana on the stairs.

Eliana squinted at her over the banister.

“You look weird.”

“I’m always weird.”

“Weirder.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Baba didn’t come home till two in the morning. When he did, there was a new man in the car. A stranger with a gun under his jacket.

“Protection.” Baba wouldn’t look at her. “I hired him.”

“With what money?”

“Don’t.”

“Baba, with what money? The Qiu brothers have your routes. Nobody’s paying you. Who did you borrow from?”

“Go to bed, Elowen.”

“Who?”

“I said go to bed!”

He’d never shouted at her. Not once. The man with the gun studied the ceiling.

Baba’s face crumpled.

“I’m sorry. I’m sorry. Please. Just… go to bed.”

Upstairs, Eliana was typing. Raiden’s light was on. Evangeline’s door was open a crack, the way it always was when she couldn’t sleep, so she could hear the stairs.

Five of them. And one hired stranger who’d run the first time anybody shot at him.

Elowen went to her room and found the delivery slip. Iron Docks. Tomorrow. Morning. She turned it over. In her neat wedding-card handwriting, she wrote one word.

Terms.

Then she wrote until the birds started.

Halfway down page two her door creaked. Evangeline. Bare feet, old cardigan, no sound. She came and stood behind the chair and read over Elowen’s shoulder.

Elowen didn’t cover it. What was the point? Ev always knew.

Evangeline read the whole first page. Her face didn’t move. Then she took the pencil out of Elowen’s hand and underlined one line twice.

Separate rooms.

She gave the pencil back.

“Good.”

One word. From Ev, that was practically a lecture. She went back to bed and left her door open.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went back to the Docks at night this time.

Bao was on the door. He didn’t ask. He took one look at her face and held it open.

“He’s upstairs. He hasn’t eaten.”

“Why are you telling me that?”

“Somebody should know.”

“And you picked me.”

“You brought tea.”

Upstairs, one lamp on the desk. Zhao sat with his feet up on an open drawer, reading a binder. Cold box of rice by his elbow. The whiteboard wiped clean.

He looked up. Stayed sitting. Not even surprised.

“Old Tan.”

“You heard.”

“I hear everything at the Docks.” He shut the binder. “I’m sorry about your man.”

Oh, don’t. Don’t be decent. Not now. It made the next bit so much harder.

So she said it fast, before her nerve went.

“I want to make you an offer.”

His feet came off the drawer.

She didn’t sit. She stood in front of the desk the way she stood in front of brides who wanted peonies in October.

“Marry me.”

The lamp buzzed. Down in the warehouse nothing moved.

And she got him. For one second Zhao Zhendong looked completely, honestly stunned. Then it wiped away and his face went blank as the whiteboard behind him.

“Explain.”

She put the folded pages on the desk. He didn’t pick them up. He kept looking at her.

“You don’t protect the people you pay. You protect what’s yours. So I’ll be yours. On paper.” Breathe. “If I’m your wife, my father isn’t just a man you pay. He’s your father-in-law. Your men won’t touch him. The Qiu brothers will think very hard before they touch anyone with my name.”

“And that’s worth something to me.”

“I’m worth something to you. You offered me a year of my shop every month to read your routes. I’ll do it for nothing. I’ll find your leaks. I’ll tell you when your people lie on paper. They do, by the way. You’re too busy to check.”

He said nothing.

“And you get a wife with a real business. Real accounts. A real address in the Walled City. A florist! Respectable. That’s useful for a man with your problems.”

“My problems.”

“Interpol. And whoever else. I read the papers.”

The corner of his mouth moved.

“What else.”

She pushed the pages at him.

“Terms. I keep my shop. My name stays on the sign. I work my own hours. I don’t come to your dinners unless I choose. Separate rooms. You don’t touch me unless I ask.”

Her voice didn’t shake. She was ridiculously proud of that.

“And in everything about my family, you answer to me. My father works for you. You answer to me.”

He picked up the pages. Three of them, numbered, in her wedding-card hand.

He read every line. He didn’t skim. At the end he went back to page one and read it again.

Was that good? Bad? Was he checking the spelling?

“There’s a word crossed out on page two.”

“I changed my mind about it.”

“What was it?”

“None of your business.”

He held the page up to the lamp to read through the scribble. She snatched at it. He moved it two centimetres out of reach without even looking.

“Mr. Zhao.”

He put it down. He didn’t say what he’d read. No need. She’d crossed out ever after you don’t touch me, at four in the morning, for reasons she was never, ever going to explain.

“Why not run?” He didn’t look up.

“Where?”

“Anywhere. You have money. Take the four of them and go.”

“And my father?”

He went quiet.

“You’d find us, if you wanted to. So would the Qiu brothers. And Baba would stay, because he’s too proud and too scared to leave. And the first time something went wrong at the Docks, someone would go to the house and find only him.” She swallowed. “I don’t run, Mr. Zhao. I cut things cleanly.”

He put the pages down.

“Are you finished?”

“…Yes.”

“Hm.”

✦ ✦ ✦

People had offered Zhao Zhendong a lot of things.

Money, mostly. Guns, which he had. Women, handed over like a bottle of wine with the bill, which he’d never wanted. A general in the north had once offered him a racehorse. A man about to die had offered him his own daughter. Zhao had walked out of that room and never dealt with him again.

Nobody had ever offered him themselves. With terms. Numbered.

He looked at her.

Her coat was buttoned wrong. One off, all the way down. She hadn’t noticed. Her hands were knotted together in front of her so tight the knuckles were white.

She was scared of him. She’d come anyway. Alone. At night. And she’d looked him dead in the eye while she said you don’t touch me unless I ask.

He knew exactly what this was. A daughter putting herself between her father and a gun. It had nothing to do with him. He found he didn’t care. At all.

She’ll never love you. The voice at the back of his head sounded like the guards at the detention centre, years ago. She’s buying you, like you bought her flowers. You’ll spend your whole life wondering.

Yes. Probably.

He picked up a pen.

“One more term.”

Her chin came up. “What?”

“You don’t lie to me.” He wrote it at the bottom of page three in his blunt square hand. “Lie to everyone else. Your father. My men. The police. The papers. I don’t care. Not to me. Ever.”

She read it twice.

“And you? Will you lie to me?”

He thought about it properly.

“I’ll tell you when I can’t tell you something. I won’t make something up.”

She nodded. Then held her hand out for the pen.

He gave it to her. She bent over the desk, wrote one line under his, and underlined the last word.

You eat dinner.

“That isn’t a term.”

“Bao says you haven’t eaten.” She capped the pen. “That rice has been cold since lunch. I am not being the wife of a man who passes out at the Docks because he forgot to eat. It’s bad for my reputation.”

He looked at the line. Dinner, underlined once, in handwriting meant for wedding cards.

When had anyone last told him to eat? He honestly couldn’t remember.

“Hm.”

Not yes. Not no. She seemed to get it anyway.

“Then yes.”

He signed. Zhao Zhendong. Turned the page round and held out the pen.

Her fingers touched his on it. Ice cold. She signed under him. Lin Elowen. Small and straight.

Three pages. Not worth a thing in any court. She looked at them like they were made of iron.

He didn’t take the pen back. He turned page two toward her with one finger and put the finger on line six.

“It says you have to ask.” He looked up. “It doesn’t say I can’t.”

Her face went up in flames.

She’d written that line in the middle of the night. She knew exactly what it meant. She had not, even once, thought about it from his side of the desk.

“Then ask.” Was that her voice? “And find out what I say.”

He looked at her mouth. Back at her eyes. The lamp buzzed between them.

He didn’t ask. Not tonight.

He kept looking, though. She stood there with cold hands and her heart going like a hammer and had the horrible feeling she’d just agreed to something that wasn’t on any of the three pages.

“Tuesday. The registry opens at nine.”

“This Tuesday?”

“Old Tan’s in hospital. You want to wait?”

She didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

Bao drove her home.

At the gate, she finally looked down. Coat. Buttoned wrong. All the way down. The whole time.

She’d proposed to the most frightening man in the city with her coat done up like a five-year-old’s.

She sat in the back of the car with her face in her hands and laughed without making a sound until her stomach hurt.

Bao turned round in his seat.

“Miss Lin. Do you need a doctor?”

“No… no. I need a mirror.”

Upstairs at the Docks, Zhao stayed at the desk.

He read the three pages again. He folded them along her creases and put them in the inside pocket of his jacket. Left side.

Then he looked at the cold rice.

It was disgusting. He ate all of it.

He didn’t sleep. Before it was light he rang Chen Si.

“I’m getting married on Tuesday. I need a witness.”

Chen Si always had an answer for everything. For once, the line was completely empty.

“Si.”

“I’m here. I’m… is she pointing a gun at you?”

“No.” Zhao looked down at the corner of folded paper showing over his pocket. “Worse. She wrote a contract.”

chapters.title: Married at the Registry on a Tuesday
chapters.desc: She buys ranunculus, takes the household register and marries him at the registry on a Tuesday. The ring is two sizes too big.
chapters.epigraph: “I went to a jeweller yesterday. I told him I wanted something that wouldn’t break.”
chapters.content:
The government’s list was short. Identity card. Three photos on a red background. A signed form swearing you weren’t already married and weren’t related to the person next to you. And the household register. That was the problem. The little red booklet that listed everyone in the Lin house belonged to the head of the household, and the head of the household kept it in the locked drawer in his study. Under the deeds. Under Mama’s death certificate.

Tuesday. Still dark. Elowen took the key from behind the loose skirting board and opened the drawer.

She was fine until she saw the certificate. The paper had gone soft at the folds. She sat down on the floor with it. She didn’t read it. She just held it for a minute, like you’d hold someone’s hand on a ward.

Then she put it back, took the register, locked the drawer, and went to the flower market. It was Tuesday. Tuesdays were ranunculus.

✦ ✦ ✦

By dawn the wholesale market was a roar of trolleys and buckets and men shouting prices across the aisles. Elowen bought ranunculus, white roses and two boxes of eucalyptus from the old woman at the end stall.

Granny Su had sold to Mama before her. She always slipped something extra into the order and never said a word about it.

“You look different.” Granny Su counted out change with a cigarette in the corner of her mouth.

“I didn’t sleep.”

“That’s not it.” Sharp little black eyes. “You look like a girl going in to an exam.”

The extra bunch was lily of the valley. Out of season. Expensive. How had she even got it?

“Sort of,” Elowen said.

“Hm! Pass it, then.”

“Granny, how did you get lily of the valley in March?”

“I have a man.”

“What man?”

“A man! Everybody needs a man. Go. You’re blocking my eucalyptus.”

Back at the shop she processed everything. Strip, cut, bucket, cooler. Flowers didn’t care what day it was. By the time she was done her hands were green to the wrist and there was dirt under her nails that no brush on earth was getting out. She changed into the cream blouse she kept for weddings. Looked at herself in the mirror by the cooler. Then she took the lily of the valley out of its bucket, cut five stems short, and tied them with white ribbon. So Granny Su’s present wouldn’t go to waste. Obviously. Obviously. No other reason at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The registry was a grey building by the river with a red banner over the door wishing everyone a harmonious family. Couples queued on the steps. Young ones holding hands. Older ones who’d clearly fought in the taxi. One boy in a suit so big the sleeves came down over his knuckles.

Zhao stood at the bottom of the steps, a bit apart. Couples curved round him in a wide arc without knowing why. Dark blue suit. Actually fitted. White shirt, no tie. Shaved. And he had done something to his hair, and it had gone badly. One bit at the back was sticking straight up. Next to him stood a man she’d never met and knew at once, because Zhao stood half a step closer to him than to anybody else alive. Chen Si. A bit older, a bit shorter. A grey suit that had cost more than her van. Calm handsome face. Eyes that noticed everything. He was holding a coffee he hadn’t touched.

“Miss Lin.” A small bow. “I am the witness.”

“You don’t need a witness to register a marriage. It isn’t in the regulations.”

“I know.” His mouth curved. “I came anyway. I wanted to see this with my own eyes.”

Zhao was looking at the lily of the valley. Then at the dirt under her nails. His jaw went tight and he looked away, at the river, for a second.

“You went to the market.”

“It’s Tuesday. Ranunculus won’t wait till Wednesday.”

Chen Si made a noise and turned it into a cough.

“You did something to your hair. It didn’t work.”

His hand went straight to it. Found the wrong bit first time. Pressed it flat. It sprang back up. He pressed it again. It sprang back up.

“Don’t. It’s the only part of you that looks nervous.”

“I’m not nervous.”

“Hm.”

She reached up and smoothed it down herself. One stroke of her palm.

He stopped breathing. Actually stopped. She felt it, standing that close. Her hand was on his head and the most frightening man in the city had forgotten how lungs worked.

She took her hand back. The hair stayed down for about one second. Then it popped up again.

Behind his coffee, Chen Si was staring very hard at the sky.

“Ten years I’ve known him,” he told the sky. “Nobody has ever said ‘hm’ back.”

“Si.”

“I’m only saying.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Photos first. A little booth inside. Red curtain behind a bench. A bored young photographer with a big camera on a tripod. He sat them side by side, looked through the lens, and sighed from the bottom of his soul.

“Closer.”

They moved two centimetres.

“Closer! You’re getting married, not doing your taxes.”

Elowen shuffled until her shoulder touched Zhao’s arm. He went rigid. Wood. A plank in a suit.

“Heads together. Groom, relax your face. You look like you’re about to rob me.”

Zhao did not relax his face.

“Is he alive?” the photographer asked her.

“Mostly.”

“Can he blink?”

“I’ve seen him do it once.”

She could feel how hard he was working not to move. You don’t touch me unless I ask. He was obeying it so hard his arm had turned to furniture.

So she tipped her head and rested it on his shoulder.

“Lovely. Thank you. Now smile, both of you. One, two—”

Flash. The prints slid out still warm. Chen Si leaned over to look. Elowen, smiling politely at the camera, head on her husband’s shoulder, white flowers in her lap. Zhao, not looking at the camera at all. Looking down at her.

Chen Si took one of the spares, folded it neatly in half, and put it in his wallet without asking anyone.

“Si.”

“Evidence. Nobody will believe me otherwise.”

“Who are you going to show?”

“Everyone, Zhendong. I’m going to show everyone.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The clerk had reading glasses on a chain and had married ten thousand couples without expecting anything from any of them. Card. Form. Register. Stamp, stamp, stamp.

She opened the Lin register and her eyebrows went up at the list of names.

“Five children. Your father must be busy.”

“He is.”

Last form. She put the pen down and looked at them over her glasses. Flat practised voice, a line she’d said ten thousand times.

“Are you both entering into this marriage of your own free will?”

“Yes.”

Zhao didn’t answer. The clerk waited. By the door, Chen Si stopped pretending not to listen. Zhao wasn’t looking at the clerk. He was looking at Elowen. A question. He was only ever going to ask it once. Sure? She looked straight back at him and nodded once.

“Yes.”

The clerk stamped two little red booklets. The machine beside her printed the date on each, and the time next to it. Nine forty-one. She pasted in a photo and slid them across.

“Congratulations.” Already reaching for the next folder. “Next!”

Zhao picked his booklet up and looked at the page for longer than anyone needed to look at a date.

“Is it spelled wrong?”

“No.”

“Then what?”

“Nothing.”

He shut it and put it in his inside pocket. Left side. Same pocket as the contract.

✦ ✦ ✦

Out on the steps, in thin spring sun, the couple ahead were kissing for a photo. Girl on tiptoe. The boy in the big suit bending down, sleeves over his knuckles. A friend shouting at them to do it again because she’d missed it.

Zhao watched them. Then he looked at Elowen. At her mouth. She felt that look like a hand.

“Not here.”

It was out before she’d thought about what it meant. He didn’t move. Then the corner of his mouth moved, and he leaned down, close enough that his breath touched her cheek, and stopped there.

“Then where?”

Under his breath. Just for her. Where? Where? She had nothing. Her face was hot right up to her ears. He straightened without touching her. He’d heard exactly what she’d said. And exactly what she hadn’t.

He took a box out of his jacket. No kneeling. No speech. He opened it and held it out. A thick band of yellow gold with a square green stone set deep in it. Old-fashioned. Heavy. Nothing she would ever have picked.

“I don’t know about rings. I went to a jeweller yesterday. I told him I wanted something that wouldn’t break.”

She nearly laughed. She didn’t, because his face was so serious. It was so obviously the ring of a man who’d never been given anything that lasted. She held out her left hand.

He looked at it first. The dirt under her nails. The green eucalyptus stain on her fingers. Then he slid the ring on, and his thumb stayed on her knuckle for one second. Rough. Warm. Checking her hand was real. It went over the knuckle and kept going. They both looked at it. Two sizes too big. At least.

“I’ll get it fixed.”

“No.” She moved it to her middle finger. It fitted there. Just. “Leave it.”

He didn’t let go of her hand. He held it right there on the registry steps, in front of Chen Si and the whole queue, with his thumb pressed flat over the green stone. The boy in the big suit stared at them. Zhao looked back at him until he stopped. Only then did he let her go. Slowly. One finger at a time. That was as close as her own terms let him get to saying mine. She knew it. He knew she knew it.

Chen Si was smiling into his cold coffee.

“Aurelia is going to kill me. For not letting her choose it.”

Elowen’s head snapped round.

“Aurelia?”

“My wife.” The smile widened. “I believe you were at school together.”

She stared at Chen Si. Then at Zhao, who had the face of a man who’d just remembered something he really should have mentioned.

Somewhere deep in her head, the seventeen-year-old they’d called the Ice Queen in a school corridor heard the name Aurelia Song and put down everything she was holding.

“We’ll talk about that,” she told her husband. “Later.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She told the family at dinner. Everyone in one room. If she was going to do something unforgivable, she’d do it to their faces.

She put the red booklet on the table. Next to the fish.

Baba looked at it. He didn’t touch it. He looked at it like someone had put a gun next to his rice.

“What is that.”

“I got married today. To Zhao Zhendong.”

Nobody moved. Raiden’s chopsticks stopped halfway to his mouth. A bit of fish fell off them.

“Sorry. Sorry, everybody. Say that again?”

Baba picked it up. Opened it. Saw the photo. His face went white, then grey, then a deep dull red, and his hand came down on the table so hard the bowls jumped.

“You sold yourself!”

“No, Baba.” She didn’t raise her voice. “I bought you.”

“To that… that animal—”

“He’s your boss. Six years you’ve worked for him. You took his money and you put us through school with it. You don’t get to call him an animal at this table.”

His chair went over backwards.

“I’ll have it annulled! I know people at the registry—”

“You’ll have to find the household register first. And then you’ll have to explain to Zhao Zhendong why you’re trying to take his wife away.”

He stood there breathing hard, one hand flat on the table. For one second she thought he might hit her. He never had. Not once in her life. But she’d never seen this face on him either. He picked up the chair. Set it on its legs. Sat. Put his face in his hands. Nobody said a word.

Raiden moved first. He reached over, picked up the booklet, stared at the photo. Then at her.

“Does he know you’re the smartest person in this house?”

“He’s starting to.”

Raiden nodded and put it down. Then he picked it up again.

“Jie. He’s looking at you in the picture. Not the camera. You.”

“Put it down, Raiden.”

“Like, really looking.”

“Raiden.”

He put it down. He mouthed really looking at Evangeline across the table. Evangeline kicked him.

A voice from the stairs.

“The registry uploaded it this morning.”

Eliana sat on the bottom step in pyjamas with her laptop on her knees. Seventeen, pale, hair like a bird’s nest, enormous frightened eyes.

“I saw it before lunch. I didn’t tell anyone. I thought… I thought it might be a glitch.”

Evangeline got up without a sound. She came round the table, put her arms round Elowen from behind and held on, cheek pressed into her hair.

Not one word. Ev never needed one. She just held on, hard, until something in Elowen’s chest cracked down the middle and she had to shut her eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

Late that night a car stopped at the gate.

Baba was out the door before anyone could grab him.

Elowen watched from the window. Zhao got out of the back carrying a long box, the kind the wholesalers used. Baba marched right up to him. Much closer than she’d ever seen anyone stand to Zhao Zhendong. Finger jabbing at his chest. Mouth going a mile a minute.

Zhao didn’t step back. He let him finish.

Then he said something. Short.

Baba’s hand dropped. He stood under the gate light for a while. Then he took the box out of Zhao’s hands, turned round and walked back into the house without looking at anyone. He put it on the kitchen table in front of her.

Twenty red tulips. Packed in wet paper. A whole bucket’s worth.

No note.

“What did he say to you?”

Baba looked at the tulips.

“I told him if he ever hurts you, I’ll kill him.” His mouth twisted. “He said you’d already told him the same thing. He said, ‘She told me she would find out where I sleep. I believe her.’”

Elowen looked down at the heavy ring on her middle finger.

“And then?”

“Then he said the tulips were to replace the ones he gave away.” Baba stood up slowly. He looked old. “Go to bed, Elowen. You’re moving house on Saturday.”

He went upstairs.

She stayed at the table with twenty tulips, a red booklet and a ring two sizes too big. She didn’t cry.

She cut every stem with a knife. On the angle. An inch off the bottom. Into water.

Her phone buzzed. A number she didn’t have.

Unknown: Cut them?

Elowen: who is this

Unknown: Your husband.

She stared at the screen. Typed Zhao. Deleted it. Typed Husband. Deleted that so fast she nearly dropped the phone.

She saved him with no name at all and went up to bed.

chapters.title: The House on the Hill Has Too Many Locks
chapters.desc: She moves into his concrete house with her mother’s lemon tree and names his dogs. In the basement, behind the lock she has no key for, he asks before he kisses her.
chapters.epigraph: “What I sell never comes to this house. These are mine. For if someone comes here.”
chapters.content:
Her husband’s house sat on a hill above the Iron Docks. The wind came straight off the water. It smelled of salt and engines. A big concrete box. Long windows. Flat roof. A camera on the gate, a camera on the wall, and a gravel drive that announced every car about a week before it arrived.

Two dogs came tearing down the drive as the van pulled in. Lean, brown, black faces. They stopped dead a few metres from Elowen’s feet and stood there quivering, staring at her like she was a test.

“They won’t bite.” Bao climbed out of the driver’s seat. “Unless he tells them.”

“What are their names?”

Bao looked at the dogs. At her. Nobody had ever asked him that. It was all over his face.

“They don’t have names. He calls them left and right.”

The dogs looked at her. She looked at the dogs. One had a torn ear.

“That’s terrible.”

“Yes, Mrs. Zhao.”

She turned round slowly.

“Elowen.”

“Yes, Mrs. Zhao.”

“Bao! It’s Elowen!”

He was already lifting boxes out of the back.

✦ ✦ ✦

She hadn’t brought much. Two suitcases of clothes. A box of books. Mama’s jewellery box, which didn’t have much jewellery in it. And plants. Okay. A lot of plants. She hadn’t meant to. She’d started with the pothos off her windowsill, because it would die without her. Then the two orchids, because Evangeline had given them to her. Then a box of herbs. Then a fern from the shop that was looking sorry for itself. Then the lemon tree. Mama’s lemon tree. Twenty years on the balcony of the house in the Walled City. How was she supposed to leave it there without her?

Zhao came out of the front door as Bao was hauling the pot out of the van. Old grey sweatshirt. Jeans. Bare feet. He looked like a completely different person. Younger. Less like a knife. He stopped on the top step and looked at the van. At the plants. At the tree in Bao’s arms with three little green lemons on it.

“That’s a tree.”

“It’s my mother’s.”

He came down the steps and took it off Bao without a word. Both arms under the pot. Looking down at it the whole way into the house, like it might jump out.

Inside, he stood in the middle of the hall holding it and turned in a slow circle.

“Where does it go?”

Elowen looked round. Huge. Nearly empty. Long hall, polished concrete floor. A living room with one black leather sofa and one television and nothing else. No pictures. No rugs. No books. Through the kitchen door, a gleaming steel fridge and a counter with one coffee cup on it. One cup. Who lived like this? It looked like a hotel that had gone bust.

“There.” She pointed to the end of the hall, where a long window looked out over the docks and the sea. “It needs light.”

He carried it over and set it down. Then he stood back and frowned at it. A lemon tree in a clay pot in his concrete hall. A problem he’d have to solve.

“Does it need anything?”

“Water once a week. Don’t let it get cold.”

He nodded. She could actually see him filing it.

“Once a week.”

“Yes.”

“How much?”

“Till it comes out the bottom.”

“How cold is cold?”

“Mr. Zhao. It’s a tree. It’s been alive for twenty years with my father in charge. You’ll be fine.”

He looked at it like he wasn’t sure about that at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

He gave her the tour like an estate agent trained by the army.

“This door locks from inside. This one too. That window doesn’t open. Bulletproof. These ones open, but there’s a sensor. If they open in the night, Bao knows. This panel’s the garden lights. This is a phone. It only rings in the guardhouse.”

“Is there a panel for ordering pizza?”

He looked at her.

“…No.”

“Shame.”

Fourteen locks on the ground floor. She counted. Upstairs, four bedrooms. He opened the biggest one, at the far end of the corridor, with its own bathroom and a wide window over the sea, and stood back to let her go in first. New white sheets. The tags still on the pillows. On the bedside table, a glass vase with nothing in it. Somebody had known there was supposed to be a vase. Nobody had known what went in it.

“This is yours.”

There was a dent in the carpet. A different bed had stood there. Very recently.

“This was your room.”

He didn’t answer.

“Where are you sleeping?”

He walked back down the corridor and opened the smallest door, right at the top of the stairs. A narrow bed. A chair. A window looking down at the front gate.

“Here.”

“That’s the worst room in the house! It’s a cupboard.”

“It’s the first room anyone reaches. If they come up the stairs.”

Oh. She looked at him in the doorway of the tiny room, hands shoved in the front pocket of his sweatshirt. He’d given her the room at the end. Then he’d put himself between her and the stairs. You didn’t say thank you for a thing like that. She didn’t know what you said.

“The dogs need names.”

She went back down to get the orchids before her face did anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

The keys were on the kitchen counter when she came back in. A ring of them, each with a coloured tag. She counted.

“Thirteen. You’ve got fourteen locks.”

He was at the kitchen window with coffee. He didn’t turn round.

“The basement. You don’t need that one.”

“What’s in the basement?”

A long pause.

“I said I’d tell you when I can’t tell you something.”

“So this is one.”

“Not today.”

She looked at the thirteen keys. At his back. She put the ring in her pocket and didn’t ask again. Dinner was takeaway from a place by the docks. Rice, braised pork, a soup with a frankly criminal amount of salt. Bao brought it in plastic boxes. They ate standing at the kitchen counter, because the counter had no stools and the table in the dining room had nothing on it but dust. Zhao ate fast. He didn’t look at the food. Like someone who’d learned to eat before it got taken away. But before he started, without a word, he pushed the braised pork across the counter to her side. He didn’t take a single piece. When she looked up, he was looking out of the window at nothing.

She pushed the box back to the middle. He pushed it back to her.

“I’m not eating all of that!”

“Then leave it.”

She left exactly half. He looked at the half. Then he ate it.

“There’s a dining table. Have you ever used it?”

He thought about it. Seriously thought.

“Chen Si sat at it once. New Year.”

She put her chopsticks down.

“Tomorrow I’m cooking. And we’re sitting down.”

He looked at her like she’d spoken Portuguese. Then he nodded once. Same nod he’d given the lemon tree.

✦ ✦ ✦

She couldn’t sleep. The house made all the wrong noises. In the Walled City there was always something. Neighbours. Scooters. The old man next door singing opera to his birds. Here there was only wind. Cranes groaning far off. Now and then, the crunch of a guard walking the wall. Deep in the night, a door opened. She lay still. Footsteps on the stairs. Going down. Not sneaking. Just quiet. Somebody walking in his own house trying not to wake anyone. Another door, further away. Deeper. Metal on metal. A lock.

She got up. She didn’t decide to. Her feet did. Downstairs in her socks, past the lemon tree glowing in the light from the docks, through the kitchen, to a door she’d assumed was a pantry. Open. Concrete stairs going down. Light at the bottom. She went halfway and stopped.

The basement ran the whole length of the house. Clean. Bright. And along both walls, in steel racks, guns. Dozens. Rifles in rows. Pistols in foam-lined drawers. Boxes stacked to the ceiling with stencilled numbers. It smelled of oil and metal, like a hardware shop. A long workbench under a hanging lamp in the middle. Zhao sitting at it with his back to her. Cleaning a pistol. He’d taken it to bits and laid the bits on a cloth in a straight line, and he was going over them one at a time with a brush and a rag. His shoulders were loose. She hadn’t once seen his shoulders loose.

She must have made a noise. He didn’t jump. He put the brush down. Put the piece in his other hand down. Then he turned on the stool and looked at her, standing halfway down his stairs in her pyjamas.

“I couldn’t sleep.”

“Neither could I.”

She looked at the racks. The boxes. She thought about the long crates in Baba’s garage when she was a kid.

“Are these what you sell?”

“No.” He looked at the racks too. “What I sell never comes to this house. These are mine. For if someone comes here.”

A pause.

“For if someone comes here for you.”

She came down the rest of the stairs.

Up close the bits on the cloth were small and black and oily. They didn’t look like anything. Parts of a sewing machine.

“Why in the middle of the night?”

He turned the rag over in his hands.

“When I was sixteen, the only thing in my life that did what it was supposed to was a gun. You clean it. You put it back. It works. Every time.” One shoulder went up. “People don’t.”

She stood by the bench and watched him put it back together without looking at his hands. Under a minute. Click. Click. Done.

“Show-off…”

His mouth twitched.

He put the pistol in a drawer, got up, and wrote something on the back of a business card with a pen from his pocket. Held it out.

Six numbers.

“This door’s steel. Walls are concrete. There’s water down here. A phone line that doesn’t go through the house. Air from outside.” He kept holding the card out. “If anyone ever comes into this house who isn’t me or Bao, you come here. You shut the door. You put in that code from the inside. And you wait.”

“For how long?”

“For me.”

She took the card. Their fingers met on it. His were warm from the lamp and smelled of gun oil, and he didn’t let go. They stood there holding the same little card under the light. Close enough that she could see a nick on his lower lip. The pulse going in his throat.

A bit of her hair had come loose and stuck to her cheek. His eyes went to it. His free hand came up. And stopped. A breath from her face. Waiting. Like the contract was written on the air between them. Was she supposed to say something? What? Please tidy my hair, Mr. Zhao?

She tipped her head. Just a bit. Toward his hand. That was enough. He hooked the strand with one finger and tucked it behind her ear. So light she barely felt it. Only then did he let go of the card. His hand didn’t go back down. It stayed by her face. Knuckles almost on her cheek. Not touching. His eyes went to her mouth and stayed there.

“I’ve wanted to kiss you since the registry.”

Rough. Low. Like it had been scraped out of him. She should have laughed. She didn’t have the air. He bent his head slowly. Slowly enough that she saw it coming the whole way and could stop it any time. Close enough to feel the heat of his mouth. Then he stopped. A breath away. He didn’t come any closer.

“Say yes. Or go upstairs.”

She didn’t go upstairs.

“Yes.”

He kissed her. Short. So careful it barely counted. Warm and dry and hardly moving, like he was testing ice before he trusted his weight to it. He tasted of coffee. His hand never touched her face. It stayed in the air by her cheek, and she could feel it shaking there. Then her fingers grabbed the front of his sweatshirt. She didn’t tell them to.

He made a low sound in his chest and kissed her again. Not careful at all. One second. Two. Her mouth opened under his. The edge of the bench dug into her hip and she didn’t care, she did not care even slightly—

He stopped. He pulled back a few centimetres and stayed there, breathing hard, forehead almost on hers. He was looking at her like she was a gun he’d never seen before and couldn’t work out how to put back together.

“That’s all.” Hoarse. “Tonight.”
