She let go of his sweatshirt. Her hand didn’t want to. She looked down. She’d crushed the card in her other fist, six numbers folded in half, so she smoothed it flat on her pyjamas to give her face something to do.

“You said I didn’t need the basement key.”

“You don’t need a key. You need the code.” He turned the lamp off. “I just didn’t want you to have a reason to use it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They went up together. Him behind her. Of course. At the door of the little room he stopped.

“Goodnight, Elowen.”

No Miss Lin. Just her name. He’d kissed her before he’d ever said it. It sounded strange in his mouth. Careful. Like he was carrying it with both arms underneath.

“Goodnight.”

She went down the corridor to the big room and shut the door and sat on the bed with the card in her hand. She listened for his door. It didn’t close. She opened hers a crack. He was still standing in his doorway, hand on the frame, looking down the corridor at her. Not coming. Not going in either. Holding the distance like it weighed something. She shut her door again. Without a sound. She lay down with her heart going like she’d run up the hill.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao had been awake since before five.

Which was why he saw her, from the window of the little room, go out into the garden in his oversized house slippers with a bowl of last night’s pork.

The dogs came flying and stopped short. Trained. They sat. They stared at the bowl like it was the face of god.

She crouched down in front of them. Said something. Pointed at the one with the torn ear. Then the other.

She fed his guard dogs breakfast with her fingers. Both of them licked her hand.

He didn’t go back to bed.

Bao knocked on the open door twenty minutes later.

“Boss. She named them.”

“I saw.”

“Dumpling and Noodle.”

Zhao looked down at the garden. The dogs were lying on her feet now. Both of them. The traitors.

“Which one’s which?”

chapters.title: Breakfast With a Man Who Eats Standing Up
chapters.desc: She makes him sit down to dinner. He takes her van keys and drives her to the market at four, and she kisses him at the shop door without asking.
chapters.epigraph: “My mother always gave my father the belly. He gave it back to her. Every night, for twenty years.”
chapters.content:
On Sunday, Elowen went to war with the dining table. The dust had sunk right into the grain. There were rings from some glass someone had put down years ago and nobody had ever wiped. She found a cloth and a bucket under the sink, still in their plastic. Of course they were. She scrubbed till the wood shone. Then she found six chairs in a cupboard, also in plastic, and took four out. Zhao came down at noon and stopped in the dining room doorway like he’d walked into the wrong house.

“You cleaned it.”

“I said we’d sit down. I meant it.”

“The chairs were wrapped.”

“I know. I unwrapped them. That’s generally how chairs work.”

He looked at the chairs. He didn’t look convinced.

The kitchen was gorgeous and had never once been used. A huge gas stove. A fridge holding beer, eggs and a bottle of chilli sauce. Cupboards full of white plates that had never left their boxes. She sent Bao to the market with a list. He came back with every single thing on it, plus a bag of mandarins she hadn’t asked for. He tipped them into a bowl on the counter, very serious.

“For the house. A house should have fruit.”

“Bao. Did you just buy this house fruit?”

“Somebody had to.”

She cooked all afternoon. Mama’s dishes. Tomato and egg, because everyone can eat tomato and egg. Steamed fish with ginger and spring onion. Green beans fried with garlic. Rice. And pork bone and lotus root soup, which needed three hours and filled the whole concrete box with a smell that brought both dogs to the kitchen door. They sat outside with their noses squashed flat on the glass. At dinner time she put it all on the table and called him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came in and stood next to his chair. He looked at the food. The chair. Her, already sitting with her napkin in her lap. For a second she honestly thought he wasn’t going to do it. Was the chair going to bite him? What did he think was going to happen? He pulled it out. Slowly. He sat.

Bolt upright. Hands flat on the table either side of his bowl. Not touching his chopsticks. He looked exactly like a boy in a school canteen who’d been told off for eating too fast and was now scared to eat at all. Oh, for heaven’s sake. She picked out the best piece of fish, from the belly, and put it in his bowl. He looked at it.

“My mother always gave my father the belly. He gave it back to her. Every night, for twenty years.”

“Who ate it?”

“Nobody. It went cold every night. It drove my grandmother mad.”

He picked up his chopsticks and ate the fish. Slowly. For once.

She tried to make conversation. It was like squeezing water out of a brick.

“How long have you lived here?”

“Three years.”

“Who designed it?”

“A man from the south. He owed me money.”

“Do you have any family?”

He put his chopsticks down.

“No.”

She waited. Was that all? It seemed like that was all. It wasn’t.

“I was adopted. From an orphanage in the north. By a man who wanted someone to carry steel at his yard. He died when I was fourteen. Then I was on my own.” He picked the chopsticks back up. “Then I was somewhere I wasn’t supposed to be, and I met Chen Si. That’s my family.”

So flat. Like reading out a shopping list. What did you even say to that? She looked at the soup pot instead. Still more than half full. She was used to cooking for six.

“I made too much. It’s better the next day anyway. I’ll heat it up tomorrow night.” A pause. “If you’re home.”

He looked up.

“I’ll be home.” He glanced down at the chair under him, like he still had doubts about it. “And I’ll sit at the table.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Monday. Her alarm went off in the black part of the night that only florists and fishermen know about.

Jeans. Old jumper. Market boots. Hair up. She reached into the bowl by the front door, next to Bao’s mandarins, for the van keys. No van keys. She stood in the hall staring at the bowl. Had she left them in the van? She never left them in the van. A noise from the kitchen. Zhao. Fully dressed. Drinking coffee. A second cup beside him, already poured. The van keys dangling from his other hand.

“No.”

“It’s four in the morning. The road to the market goes past the Qiu brothers’ warehouse. You’re not driving it alone.”

“I’ve driven to the market alone every day for five years!”

“You weren’t my wife for five years.” He held out the coffee. “Bao’s asleep. I’ll drive.”

She glared at him. He looked back. Patient. Not moving one centimetre.

“The contract says I work my own hours.”

“It does.” The coffee didn’t move either. “It doesn’t say anything about who drives.”

She opened her mouth to argue. Then she thought about the Qiu brothers’ warehouse. About Old Tan in plaster to the hip. She took the coffee.

“You carry the buckets.”

At the front door he stopped her. Her coat was hanging open. He looked at the zip. He looked at her.

“Can I?”

For a zip? He was asking permission for a zip?

“It’s a zip… fine. Fine!”

He did it up. All the way. Right to her chin, so the collar squashed her cheeks. Then he looked at the result and seemed satisfied.

“It’s cold by the river.”

She couldn’t answer. Her mouth was inside her coat.

✦ ✦ ✦

The wholesale flower market was a long low shed by the river. The shutters rolled up in the dark, and the smell of wet leaves and diesel came pouring out. The car park was jammed with vans. Crossing it, he walked on the side where the vans were reversing. She didn’t notice till the third van. Then she noticed and couldn’t stop noticing. Inside, under bare tube lights, a hundred stalls stood shoulder to shoulder. Roses from the south. Lilies from the hothouses. Chrysanthemums by the thousand. Carnations in every colour that existed and a few that really shouldn’t.

She loved it here. She’d loved it since she was eight and Mama brought her half asleep in a coat and bought her hot soy milk from the man at the door. She walked in fast like always, her list in her head.

The market went quiet behind her. Not completely. The trolleys still rattled. A radio somewhere kept going. But the shouting stopped. Men who’d been fighting over gypsophila went silent and found something fascinating on the floor. She looked back. Zhao was two steps behind her, hands in his pockets, looking at the flowers with polite interest. Doing absolutely nothing.

“You’re frightening everybody.”

“I’m walking.”

“Walk less frighteningly.”

He considered that. Then he took his hands out of his pockets. Somehow that was much worse.

At the end stall, Granny Su looked up from her stool, saw who was behind Elowen, and took the cigarette out of her mouth.

“Granny Su. This is my husband.”

Granny Su looked Zhao up. Then down. Then up again. He stood there and let her. Then she looked at the ring on Elowen’s middle finger.

“Too big. Get it fixed.”

“She won’t let me.”

Granny Su stuck the cigarette back in and pointed it at him like a gun.

“Then you carry. Twenty boxes. The eucalyptus is heavy. Don’t crush the stems.”

Elowen had never in her life seen anybody give Zhao Zhendong an order. She was going to remember this on her deathbed. He picked up the first box with both arms under it. Like it might shatter.

“Not like that! Carry it like you’re carrying it. It’s not made of glass.”

He changed his grip.

“Better.” Grudging. Then, to Elowen, not even lowering her voice: “He’s big. Good. Feed him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Third stall. The rose man. She’d bought from him for two years. He counted out ten bunches, wrapped them, named his price. She reached for her purse.

“That bunch.”

The rose man looked up. Saw who’d spoken. Went white. Zhao reached past her and lifted the fourth bunch off the pile.

“Count it.”

“Sir, I—”

“Count it.”

He counted. His hands were shaking. Eighteen stems. A standard bunch was twenty. Zhao put it down and picked up the next. Eighteen. The next. Nineteen. The next. Nineteen roses missing across ten bunches. Elowen stood there with her purse half open, doing the sum before she could stop herself. Nineteen roses a day. Six days a week. Two years.

“I’m sorry, I’m so sorry, Miss Lin, it was a mistake, the packer, it’s the new packer—” He was babbling at Zhao. Not at her. “I’ll make it right, I’ll give you—”

“Don’t talk to me. Talk to her. She’s the one you were stealing from.”

The man turned to her. Sweat on his top lip. Shaking with terror of somebody who had done nothing but count roses. She thought about the stairs at the Docks. That sound.

“Give me the missing stems. From now on I count every bunch. If it happens again, I buy somewhere else.” A beat. “That’s all.”

He nodded so hard she worried for his neck.

Out of earshot, she rounded on Zhao.

“You didn’t need to do that.”

“He was stealing from you.”

“I would have found out!”

“When?”

She didn’t have an answer.

“That’s why I did it.”

She stopped in the middle of the aisle. A woman pushing a trolley of lilies swung round them in a wide nervous curve.

“If you scare every person who cheats me, nobody in this market will ever talk to me normally again.”

He actually thought about it. She could see him turning it over, like the bits of the pistol on the cloth.

“Then tell me when you want me to stand somewhere else.”

“Now. By the door. With the soy milk man.”

He went and stood by the door with the soy milk man.

When she came out with the rest of her order, he was holding two hot cups, and the soy milk man was telling him all about his son’s university entrance exams. In detail. With hand gestures.

Zhao held a cup out to her.

“He says you’ve had one every market day since you were eight. No sugar. He says your mother used to blow on it for you because you always burned your tongue.”

She stared at him.

“You interrogated the soy milk man.”

“He volunteered. Everyone volunteers.”

She took the cup. It was exactly the right temperature. Not hot. Not cold. Which meant he’d been standing there holding it, waiting for it to get there, for ages. She drank it so she wouldn’t have to say anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the way back, the sky over the river started going grey. She meant to stay awake. She always stayed awake. But the car was warm, and he drove smoothly, no sudden brakes, nothing like Bao. Somewhere on the long road past the Qiu brothers’ dark warehouse her head tipped onto the window.

When she woke up, they were parked outside the shop and his jacket was over her. Tucked in round her shoulders. It smelled of coffee and cold air and something that was just him. She didn’t remember him putting it there. She stayed against the window with her eyes nearly shut. Engine off. Street empty.

He was sitting with both hands on the wheel, staring straight ahead. Except the windscreen was dark enough to be a mirror, and in it she could see where he was really looking. At her. His knuckles were white on the wheel. Like he was holding onto it so he wouldn’t hold onto anything else. Her heart did something stupid.

“You should have woken me.”

“You were asleep.”

That settled it, apparently. He went back to looking at the empty street. How long had he sat there? With the engine off so the noise wouldn’t wake her? In his shirtsleeves, in the cold? When she handed the jacket back their fingers bumped, and his hands were freezing. He nearly smiled. She looked away first. Her face was hot. She got out to open the shop.

He carried the buckets in. He didn’t know where anything went, so he stood in the middle of the shop holding the eucalyptus until she told him. Then he put every box exactly where she pointed. In a perfectly straight line. She made breakfast on the hot plate in the back. Two fried eggs on rice with soy sauce. The only thing she ever had time for on market days. She put one plate on the counter for him.

He picked it up and started eating. Standing. By the door. Unbelievable.

“There’s a stool.”

He looked at the stool behind the counter. Looked at her. Then, without a word, he sat on it, plate on his knees, and ate his fried eggs sitting down in a flower shop at dawn. His shoulders came down from round his ears, a bit at a time.

When he’d finished, he washed the plate in the little sink at the back. Dried it. Put it away in completely the wrong place. She didn’t move it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the door he stopped.

“Tomorrow. Same time.”

“The contract—”

“Says you work your own hours. I know.” He put his hand on the door. “I’m not working. I’m driving.”

He turned to go.

She thought about the car with the engine off. His white knuckles. The basement. How he’d stopped a breath away and waited for her, like waiting cost him blood.

“Come here.”

He came back from the door.

She grabbed a fistful of his shirt, pulled him down the last few centimetres, and kissed him. Quick and hard. Up on her toes between the buckets of eucalyptus.

She didn’t ask. The contract said he had to wait for her. It didn’t say a single word about her waiting for him. She let go. He didn’t move. He stood in the middle of her shop looking down at her like she’d shot him and he was still waiting to find out where.

“Same time,” she said, and turned to the buckets, because her face was on fire and her hands needed a job.

Through the window she watched him get in the car. He didn’t start it. He sat there with his forehead almost on the steering wheel, like he’d run a very long way. He touched his mouth once with the back of his knuckles. Then he started the engine.

✦ ✦ ✦

Next day, when she came down in the dark, he was in the kitchen with two coffees. The day after that there were two new stools at the kitchen counter. Tall. Wooden. With backs. Nobody said a thing about them. That night, when she got in from the shop, he was sitting on one, eating the last of the lotus root soup.

“You’re eating it cold.”

“Hm.”

“There’s a stove! Right there. I showed you the stove.”

He had another spoonful. Sitting down.

chapters.title: Aurelia Song Hears the News
chapters.desc: Aurelia comes to gloat that their husbands are brothers, and leaves with a commission. That night Zhao wants to know which bus the physics boy took.
chapters.epigraph: “My husband is the brain. Yours is the fist. That’s what everyone says.” — Aurelia Chen
chapters.content:
Aurelia Chen—Aurelia Song, as Elowen would always think of her—arrived on a Thursday, just as the lunch rush ended. Of course she did. Aurelia had been timing entrances since she was fifteen. The bell rang. Perfume came in first. Something expensive, with fig in it. Then Aurelia. Cream coat. Enormous sunglasses. Dark hair in a perfect low knot. Heels that had never in their lives touched a wet market floor. She stopped just inside the door and took the sunglasses off. Slowly. She made a whole show of it.

“Lin Elowen. Or should I say Mrs. Zhao.”

Elowen was wiring a corsage. She didn’t put it down.

“Aurelia. Or should I say Mrs. Chen.”

They looked at each other across the shop. Same look as across a school corridor seven years ago, when the rankings went up on the noticeboard and one of them was first and the other was not.

Then Aurelia smiled. Dazzling. Lethal. She walked to the counter and dropped her handbag right on top of Elowen’s order book.

“Darling. I had to see it for myself. You married the muscle.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Final year of school. Two girls everyone talked about. Aurelia Song. Came from Milan at fifteen with a perfect accent and a mother who expected her to be first at everything and said so every night. Loud. Brilliant. Gorgeous. Physically unable to lose. Top of the rankings two years running. The teachers called her the Firebrand.

And Lin Elowen. Quiet. Never put her hand up. Went home at four every day to feed a brother and three sisters. Then in their final year, without looking like she was even trying, she came first. The students called her the Ice Queen. Aurelia never forgave her. Not for the ranking. For how little she’d seemed to try.

And then there was Miles Wei. Advanced physics. The boy who solved problems the teachers couldn’t and didn’t care about rankings, or about either of them. They’d fought over him for eight days in the library. The whole school took sides. Somebody got slapped on the sports field in the rain. At the end of it Miles looked at them both, went pale, and chose physics.

Seven years later, Elowen still thought about that library sometimes. The quiet. The smell of old books. A boy who talked about light.

She was not going to tell Aurelia that. Ever. Under torture.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I didn’t marry the muscle.” Elowen tied off the corsage and boxed it. “I married a businessman.”

“Oh, please.” Aurelia leaned on the counter and looked round the shop with bright greedy eyes. “I know exactly what Zhao Zhendong is. I’ve had him to dinner. He ate a whole fish with his hands, said nothing for two hours, and then fixed our dishwasher.”

She pulled a rose out of the bucket by the till and sniffed it.

“My husband is the brain. Yours is the fist. That’s what everyone says.”

“Does everyone also say your husband launders money through your shop?”

Aurelia’s smile didn’t move. Her eyes did.

“Our boutique is a very successful jewellery label with stores in three cities. If some of our customers are generous, that’s their business.”

“And if some of my customers are frightening, that’s mine.”

A long look.

Then Aurelia laughed. A real one. Short and surprised, like it had been punched out of her.

“God. I’ve missed this. Do you know nobody argues with me any more? I married a Don. People bring me flowers and agree with everything I say. It’s killing me!”

“I can argue with you. It costs extra.”

Aurelia stuck the rose back and pulled out the stool from behind the counter. The stool. Zhao’s egg stool. She sat on it without asking, crossed her legs, and beamed at Elowen with enormous delighted malice.

“I came last Wednesday, you know. The morning after. You had a sign on the door. Back in one hour.”

“I was at the hospital.”

“I don’t wait an hour for anybody, darling.”

“So you waited a week.”

“I waited eight days. I was making it worth it.” She folded her hands on her knee. “Do you understand what you’ve done?”

“I married a man.”

“You married Zhao Zhendong. My husband’s brother.”

“I know. Chen Si was at the registry.”

“Yes, but do you understand?” Aurelia spread her hands. “They’re not friends, Elowen. They’re not partners. They’re brothers. The kind who cut their palms and shake on it. Zhendong comes to us every New Year. Every birthday. Every time somebody shoots at one of them, the other one’s there inside an hour.”

She leaned in.

“Which means every family dinner for the rest of your life. Every holiday. Every wedding. Every funeral. You and me. Same table.”

Elowen had florist’s scissors in her hand. She put them down. Oh no. She had not thought about it like that.

“Every New Year.”

“Every single one.” Aurelia smiled. “Till we die. Probably at the same table as well.”

“You came here to tell me I’m having dinner with you for the rest of my life.”

“I came here to watch your face while I told you.” She tapped her sunglasses on her chin. “Worth the drive.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She stayed two hours.

The first hour was war. Aurelia hated the window display. Elowen hated Aurelia’s jewellery, which was heavy and gold and suspiciously like the ring on Elowen’s own finger. They both noticed. Neither mentioned it.

“Where was the wedding?”

“Registry. Tuesday.”

Aurelia laughed so hard she had to dab under her eyes with one finger so her make-up wouldn’t run.

“A Tuesday. Oh, that’s perfect. That’s so you.”

“Where was yours?”

“Milan. Eleven guests.” A shrug. “My parents found out from a magazine.”

Elowen stopped with her mug halfway to her mouth.

“From a magazine?”

“They didn’t approve of Chen Si.” For one second Aurelia’s face went completely flat. “They don’t approve of anything I didn’t win first.”

Elowen thought of the noticeboard. Of seventeen-year-old Aurelia’s face when she saw the number two by her name. Back then she’d thought it was jealousy. Now? Now it looked a lot like fear.

She didn’t say so. She made jasmine tea instead, in the chipped mugs from behind the counter, and put one in front of Aurelia.

Aurelia looked at the mug. Then at her.

“This is a truce.”

“It’s tea.”

“From you, it’s a truce.” She drank it anyway. Then her eyes dropped to Elowen’s hand. “That ring is too big for you.”

“Everybody says that.”

“Give it to me. Enzo can size it in a day. He’s a genius, he’s eighty, he hates everybody.”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because.”

“Because what?”

“Because it’s fine.”

Aurelia put her mug down very slowly. Her eyes narrowed.

“Oh my god.”

“Don’t.”

“You like him.”

“I married him for my father.”

“You LIKE him! The Ice Queen likes the muscle!”

“Drink your tea, Aurelia.”

“I’m telling Chen Si. I’m telling him tonight…”

Elowen picked up her scissors again. Pointedly. Aurelia only laughed harder.

When she finally stood up and collected her handbag, she paused. Opened it. Pulled out a folded sheet.

“I’m launching a collection next month. The gallery on Harbour Road. Two hundred guests. I need flowers. White, gold, nothing that smells too strong, it fights with the perfume. I’ve had three florists. They were all terrible.”

It was a proper brief. With sketches.

“You came to gloat and you brought a commission.”

“I came to gloat and I need flowers. I can do two things at once.” Sunglasses back on. “And you’re the only florist in this city I can’t bully.”

Elowen read the brief and did the sum. Then she named a price. Three times what she’d have charged anyone else.

Aurelia didn’t even blink.

“Done.”

She walked to the door. Then she turned back with her hand on the frame, and for one second, behind the sunglasses and the perfect knot, Elowen saw a seventeen-year-old in school uniform.

“Elowen. One serious thing. Just once.”

Elowen waited.

“They’re not like other men. Not just dangerous. Other men are dangerous. These two…” She hunted for the words. “When one of them bleeds, the other one does something terrible. And when we bleed, darling, they both do.”

Her hand tightened on the frame.

“Be ready for that. I wasn’t.”

The bell rang behind her. The fig perfume hung around for an hour.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen: your brother’s wife came to the shop

Unknown: Did she hurt you.

Elowen: she ordered flowers

Unknown: Charge her double.

Elowen: triple

A long gap. Three dots. Gone. Three dots again.

Unknown: Good.

She looked at the word for far too long for a person who had customers.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, at the clean table in the house on the hill, she put down her chopsticks.

“You might have told me about Aurelia.”

Zhao looked up from his rice.

“I didn’t know you knew her. I don’t know anything about your school.”

That landed oddly. It was true. He didn’t know where she’d gone to school. What she’d studied. Who her friends were. He knew the dates in Baba’s files, how she cut stems, and that she liked fish belly. That was about it.

“She was first in our year. Then I was.”

He waited.

“And there was a boy.” Why was she saying this? “Miles Wei. He did physics. We both wanted him. He didn’t want either of us. He chose physics.” She pushed a green bean around. “It was so stupid. We were seventeen.”

Zhao put his chopsticks down.

Nothing on his face changed. Nothing she could point at. But the air in the room changed. Like right before a typhoon, when the birds go quiet.

“What was he like?”

Even voice. Very even. Suspiciously even.

She thought about the library.

“Quiet. He talked about light. How it bends.” She smiled a bit without meaning to. “He was the only person at that school who didn’t care whose daughter I was.”

Zhao picked up his chopsticks.

Then he reached across the table, took her fish, and started picking the bones out of it.

Every single one. Fast. Precise. With the focus of a man defusing something. He laid the bones on the side of his own plate in a neat row and put the fish back in front of her completely clean.

She stared at it.

“I can do my own fish.”

“Hm.”

“Mr. Zhao. I’ve been doing my own fish since I was four—”

He went back to his rice. He said the fish was good. He washed his own bowl.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the top of the stairs, outside the little room, he stopped.

“Did he walk you home? The physics boy.”

She turned round. He was looking at the banister. Not her.

“No. He took the other bus.”

“Hm.” A glance at her. His face was so carefully blank she nearly laughed out loud. “Which bus?”

She was not answering that.

She started toward her room.

“I’ll walk you. To your door.” A pause. “If you say yes.”

Ten metres of corridor. In his own house.

“Yes.”

He walked beside her the whole ten metres. Close enough that his sleeve brushed hers twice. At her door he stopped dead, like there was a line painted on the floor.

She turned round in the doorway. He put one hand flat on the frame above her head. Didn’t lean on it. Didn’t say anything. He was looking at her mouth. His jaw was tight. She knew exactly what he was thinking about. A boy who took the other bus. Oh, for god’s sake.

“Yes.”

Before he could even ask.

This time it wasn’t careful. He kissed her against the door frame like he was trying to rub somebody else out of her head. His free hand at her waist, pulling her off the wood and into him. Hard. Hungry. A bit angry.

She felt the frame at her back and his heart going under her palm. She kissed him back just as hard. She was angry too. At what? No idea. And the physics boy had never once kissed her, not once, and she wanted Zhao to know it without her having to say a word.

Her head knocked the frame. Not hard.

He stopped at once. His hand was there in a heartbeat, between her hair and the wood. He stayed like that, breathing, forehead on hers.

“Did he ever—”

“No.”

A breath went out of him. It shook.

He took his hand from the back of her head and stepped back over the line on the floor that wasn’t there.

“Goodnight.” She shut the door before he could see her face.

She lay in bed with her fingers on her mouth. She was never going to think about the physics boy again. It turned out to be easy. She couldn’t think about anything except the door frame.

✦ ✦ ✦

He thought about the physics boy. Deep in the night, in the basement, under the hanging lamp, Zhao took apart a rifle he’d cleaned the night before and cleaned it again. Quiet. Physics. Libraries.

A boy who didn’t care whose daughter she was. A boy she still smiled about, seven years later, without meaning to. Sounded like a clean life. A life with no basement in it. He put the rifle back together. It worked. It always did.

Then he sat with his hands flat on the bench and let himself think it. The physics boy took the other bus. That was his mistake. It was seven years old and Zhao was not going to make it. Her name was next to his in a red booklet. He could still taste her. He’d learn every bus in the city if he had to.

He took out his phone and looked up the school she’d gone to. Then the bus routes from it.

There were two.

chapters.title: The First Dinner as Mrs. Zhao
chapters.desc: Her first dinner as his wife. A broker puts his hand on her knee under the table, and her husband puts a knife through it.
chapters.epigraph: “He’s not a good man, Elowen. None of them are. Neither am I.”
chapters.content:
The contract said she didn’t have to go to his dinners unless she chose to. For two weeks she didn’t choose to.

Two or three nights a week he went out in a dark suit and came back long after midnight. She heard him on the stairs. In the morning there were two coffees in the kitchen like nothing had happened. She never asked where he went. Or who with. The contract didn’t say she couldn’t. But some part of her didn’t want to know. The same part that had learned at eight not to open the long boxes in the garage.

Then, at the end of the second week, she found herself standing at her wardrobe holding the dark green dress. Oh. So she’d chosen. Apparently.

“I’m coming tonight.”

Breakfast. His coffee stopped halfway to his mouth.

“You don’t have to.”

“I know.”

He put the cup down. He looked at her the way he’d looked at her in the registry, when the clerk asked the only question that counted.

“It’s a man called Maartens. A broker. Dutch. He buys for a general in the south whose country can’t buy from anyone legally.” A beat. “So he buys from me.”

She waited.

“He’s not a good man, Elowen. None of them are. Neither am I.”

“I know what you are.” She buttered her toast. Her hand was perfectly steady. “I want to see it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

When she got home from the shop to change, there was a flat dark box on her bed. It hadn’t been there that morning.

Inside, on grey velvet, two earrings. Square green stones. The same deep green as her ring. Each one on a short gold drop. No note. No receipt. No shop name on the box. If she asked what they cost, he’d look at her like she’d asked what the weather cost. She nearly put them back on his bed.

She’d paid for every piece of jewellery she owned with her own money. That was why she owned about four pieces. She stood there with the box open, telling herself that, very firmly. Then she held one up to the green dress in the mirror. Exactly right. Of course it was.

She pictured him at a jeweller’s counter for the second time in a month, saying something blunt like the same green, and the jeweller sweating. She put them on.

He was waiting in the hall in his dark suit. He looked at her ears. Then the rest of her. A muscle went in his jaw. He said nothing about the earrings. Not one word. He opened the door for her, and as she went past he spoke low, right by her ear.

“Stay where I can see you tonight.”

“Are you going to say anything about the earrings?”

“No.”

“Do they look stupid?”

“No.”

“Then what?”

He shut the front door behind them and didn’t answer. Bao, holding the car door, was smiling at the gravel.

It didn’t sound like a safety rule. It sounded like a warning about where he planned to look. All night. Her ears went hot under the green stones.

✦ ✦ ✦

The restaurant was on the top floor of a hotel by the harbour. No prices on the menu. A private room behind a carved wooden sliding door. A round table. A window full of black water. A lazy Susan already loaded with cold dishes. Jellyfish. Sliced beef shank. Cucumber smashed with garlic. Maartens was already there. Fifties. Red face. Thinning sandy hair. Big friendly laugh. He jumped up and shook Zhao’s hand with both of his. Then he turned to Elowen and looked at her the way the men at the market looked at fish.

“So this is the wife.” In English. “Zhao! You never told me she was so pretty!”

“Mr. Maartens.” Elowen answered in English too, and sat down.

“And she speaks English! Zhao, where did you find her?”

“A flower shop.”

“Ha! Ha. No, really.”

“A flower shop.”

Maartens looked at him. Laughed again, less sure. Reached for the jellyfish.

Two other men in the room. One stood behind Maartens’ chair with his hands folded. Big. Shaved head. A jacket that didn’t close over whatever was under it. The other was Bao, by the door, looking at nothing. Zhao sat beside her and put his arm along the back of her chair. Not touching her. Not once, all night. Just there. Along the back of the chair. Every time Maartens laughed she could feel it, a few centimetres from her shoulders.

Two hours. She hardly spoke. She ate a little of everything and listened. And bit by bit, from the edges of what the men said, she worked out what her husband did.

It wasn’t a film. Nobody said guns. They said units. Lots. The agricultural order. A cargo flight that would leave one country and land in another. And the papers. A certificate saying the units were going to the army of some third country that was allowed to buy them. Maartens made a joke about the official who stamped it. He’d apparently been paid more than the units were worth. Maartens thought that was hilarious.

“And after?” Zhao turned his glass on the tablecloth. “When they land?”

“After’s my problem!” Cheerful. “You’ll never see them again.”

But somebody would. Somewhere. On somebody. She looked at her husband’s hand on the white cloth. Scarred knuckles. A thin white line across the back of the thumb. Two weeks ago that hand had carried her mother’s lemon tree up the steps with both arms underneath it. How were both of those true? How did that work? She honestly didn’t know.

✦ ✦ ✦

It happened over the fruit. Maartens had drunk most of a bottle of baijiu by then. He’d stopped being careful. He leaned back in his chair with his face shining and looked at Elowen across the table.

“A florist. Zhao, you surprise me. All this time I thought you didn’t care about anything but money, and you go and buy yourself a florist.” He laughed. “Does she come with the shop? Or does the shop come with her?”

Elowen kept peeling her lychee. The arm along the back of her chair didn’t move.

“No, really, I’m jealous. My wife can’t keep a cactus alive.” He poured himself more. “Tell you what. If you ever get bored, Zhao, I’ll rent her for an evening. Name your price! You’ve always been reasonable about prices.”

He laughed again. The big man behind him smiled. Under the table, a hand landed on her knee. Hot. Damp. Heavy. It squeezed.

She stopped. Everything stopped. It wasn’t fear, exactly. It was like her body had walked off somewhere a long way away and left her sitting there with a half-peeled lychee in her fingers and a stranger’s hand on her leg, and she couldn’t make a single part of herself move. Not her hands. Not her mouth. Nothing.

She’d been in a lot of rooms with dangerous men. Baba’s visitors. The rose man. None of them had ever touched her. She didn’t make a sound. Her face didn’t change. She’d been keeping her face still for twenty years. She was very, very good at it. But Zhao was looking at her face. He’d been looking at it all night.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stood up. No hurry. He walked round the table. Past the lazy Susan. Past the window. He stopped behind Maartens’ chair. The big man stepped forward, hand going inside his jacket.

“I wouldn’t.” Bao, from the door. In English. Calm as anything.

A little metal click. The big man stopped. Maartens twisted round in his chair, still smiling.

“Zhao? What are you—”

Zhao reached under the table, took Maartens by the wrist, and pulled his hand off Elowen’s knee and up onto the tablecloth. Flat. One smooth movement. Like a man laying down a card. Then he picked up the fruit knife beside Maartens’ plate and drove it straight down through the back of the hand and into the table.

The first noise Maartens made wasn’t a scream. It was a high breathless huh. All the air punched out of him. Then he looked down. At the knife standing up out of his hand. At the dark circle spreading slowly on the white cloth. Then he screamed.

Zhao kept one hand on the handle. He leaned down, close to Maartens’ ear.

“Apologise to my wife.”

“Jesus—Jesus Christ, Zhao—”

“Not to him. To her.”

“I’m sorry! I’m SORRY, Mrs. Zhao, I’m sorry, I’m so sorry—”

Zhao turned the knife a quarter turn in the wood. Maartens howled. And Elowen heard her own voice. Very clear. A voice she didn’t recognise.

“Zhendong.”

He looked at her. His name. She’d never used it. Not once, till now, in a room that smelled of blood and lychees.

“Take it out. He needs that hand to sign.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, she couldn’t remember deciding to say it. She remembered the room going quiet except for Maartens crying. The blood on the cloth. The lychee, still half-peeled, in her fingers. She put it down on her plate. Gently. Like a flower.

She remembered Zhao pulling the knife out. Maartens folding over his hand. The big man with the shaved head staring at her like she was the scary one. And she remembered picking up the contract they’d been talking round for two hours. Reading the last page. Saying, in English, in her wedding-card voice:

“The price is twenty per cent higher. For the inconvenience.”

Maartens looked up at her through his tears. Grey in the face.

“And you’ll pay for the tablecloth.”

He signed with his left hand. It barely looked like a signature. It didn’t matter.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car, she started to shake. Hands first. Then arms. Then shoulders. She couldn’t stop it. She sat in the back seat next to her husband with her hands jammed together between her knees and shook so hard her teeth clacked.

He didn’t touch her. He sat at the far end of the seat, hands on his own knees, looking straight ahead. Blood on his right cuff. Bao drove like glass and never looked in the mirror once.

She could still taste the lychee. Sweet. A bit sour. And under it, from somewhere, the copper smell of that tablecloth. Her knee was damp where the hand had been. She could feel the exact shape of it through the dress. Five hot fingers. Every time the car turned, she felt it again and her stomach rolled over. She pressed her knees together harder. Her teeth kept going.

He moved. Slowly, so she’d see it coming. He put his hand on the seat between them. Palm up. Open. Then he took his eyes off it and looked out of the window.

“It’s there. You don’t have to… it’s just there.”

She looked at it. A big scarred hand, palm up on the leather. Not reaching. Just there. She didn’t take it. She looked at it the whole way along the harbour. It didn’t move. It didn’t give up. After a while her teeth stopped.

“You did that in front of me.”

“Yes.”

“You put a knife through a man’s hand. At a dinner table.”

“He put his hand on you.”

“I would have handled it!”

He turned his head and looked at her.

“How?”

Not mean. Like he actually wanted to know. She opened her mouth. Shut it. She thought about her body walking off. Her hands that wouldn’t move. Sitting there holding a lychee while a stranger squeezed her knee.

“I don’t know.”

It came out as a whisper. She hated that. He looked away again.

“I know. So I didn’t wait to find out.”

His hand stayed on the seat all the way home.

✦ ✦ ✦

She couldn’t sleep. She lay in the big bed staring at the ceiling. Every time she shut her eyes she saw the knife going down. Heard the sound it made going into the wood. Not loud. A dull wet thock. Like a spade into soil. And his face. That was worse than the knife. Calm. Almost gentle. The same face he wore carrying buckets at the market.

I know what you are. I want to see it. Well. She’d seen it.

Deep in the night she got up for water, opened her door, and nearly trod on him. He was sitting on the corridor floor with his back against the wall beside her door. Still in the shirt from dinner. He’d rolled the cuff so the blood didn’t show. Knees up, arms resting on them. He looked up at her in the dark without any surprise at all. Like he’d been waiting for the door.

“What are you doing out here?”

“Sitting.”

“Why?”

He looked at his hands.

“Because you were afraid. And I didn’t know if it was him or me.” A pause. “If it was him, I’m between you and the stairs.”

“And if it was you?”

“Then you know where I am. You don’t have to wonder.”

She stood in the doorway in her pyjamas and looked down at him.

“Did you do it because I’m yours? Like a car? Like the house? Because he touched something that belongs to you?”

He didn’t answer for so long she thought he wasn’t going to.

“I did it because he made you go still. Completely still. Like a rabbit.” He lifted his head. “I’ve seen people do that. I’ve made people do that.”

His voice dropped.

“I never wanted to see you do it. Not once.”

She had to look away. She went past him to the bathroom. Drank a glass of water. Came back. He was sitting exactly where she’d left him. She sat down next to him on the floor.

She hadn’t planned it. Back to the wall. Her shoulder a few centimetres from his. Knees up. The place on her left knee was still there under her pyjamas, five hot fingers, like it had been stamped on.

She picked his hand up off his own knee. He let her. She put it on hers. Flat. Right over the place. He went rigid. His hand lay there like something he’d been handed and was terrified of dropping.

“That’s where.” Her voice wobbled. Fine. Let it. “I can still feel it. I want to feel this instead.”

No squeeze. Not even his thumb moved. He just let the weight of his hand sit there, warm through the cotton. Slowly the other hand faded out from under it. Like a bruise under a cold cloth. She turned her head. He was already looking at her. A few centimetres away, in the dark.

“Can I?”

Barely any voice at all.

She kissed him instead of answering. Once. On the mouth. Then she just stayed there, her lips on his, and felt him breathe out against her, a long shaking breath he must have been holding since the restaurant. His hand on her knee didn’t move. That was the part of him she could feel trembling. She drew back. He closed his eyes.

She got up and went into her room. She didn’t shut the door all the way. She left it open a hand’s width. Like Ev at home, when she couldn’t sleep, so she could hear the stairs.

On the other side, in the dark, she heard him let out a breath. She heard him stay.

chapters.title: The Night the Delivery Van Burned
chapters.desc: Someone sets fire to her van with Xiao Pan standing next to it. Zhao goes to the Qiu brothers’ warehouse and comes home with a burn she holds under the cold tap.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t pop the blisters. If it gets hot or starts to smell, you go to a doctor. A real one.”
chapters.content:
“Miss Lin. Miss Lin. There’s a new one out. Red. Seventeen months of savings. Seventeen! If I skip lunch, fifteen.”

“You’re not skipping lunch.”

“Fourteen if I skip lunch and dinner—”

“Xiao Pan. Ribbon.”

He passed her the ribbon. He was nineteen and had worked for her two years. Scooter deliveries in the week, the van at weekends, and a motorbike in his head at all times. She’d once made him a bouquet shaped like one as a joke. He’d kept it till it went brown.

Friday night. A big wedding in the morning. Two hundred guests. Thirty table arrangements. An arch of white roses for the hotel garden. They worked till her eyes stung. Then he went out to start loading the van, so they could leave the second it got light.

“Take the arch roses first. Gently!”

“I’m always gentle, Miss Lin. I’m the gentlest man you know.”

She was sweeping stems off the floor when she heard it. Not loud. A soft whump. Like a big rug being shaken out of a window. Then light. Orange. Flooding through the shop window, throwing the shadow of every flower up the back wall. Then Xiao Pan screaming.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t remember running. She was in the shop. Then she was in the street, and the van was on fire.

The whole back of it. A roaring yellow column. Roof already black. Windows popping one after another. The heat hit her like a wall. Through the smoke she saw two figures running off down the street. Already at the corner. Gone. Xiao Pan was on his knees on the pavement. He was holding his hands out in front of him. Away from his body. Like they belonged to someone else.

“The roses… I tried to get the roses out, Miss Lin, I opened the door and it just, it just—”

His palms were red. Shiny. Wrong. Already starting to bubble. She grabbed his jacket collar and dragged him backwards. To the doorway. Through the shop. To the little sink at the back. She turned the cold tap on full and shoved his hands under it. He screamed again when the water hit.

“I know. I know. Keep them there.”

Mama had taught her this, the day she burned herself on the kettle at six. Cold running water. Twenty minutes. No ice. No butter. Nothing else.

“Twenty minutes. Count with me. Don’t take them out.”

“Miss Lin, it hurts, it HURTS—”

“One. Two. Count, Xiao Pan! Three…”

Outside, the fuel tank went with a bang that rattled every bucket in the shop. She held his wrists under the water with one hand and rang an ambulance with the other. Then her thumb was already moving, and she rang the only other number in her head. He picked up on the first ring.

“Elowen.”

“The van. They burned the van. Xiao Pan… his hands—”

“Are you hurt?”

“No. No, I’m—”

“Stay inside. Lock the door. I’m coming.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The burns unit at City Hospital was on the sixth floor. It smelled of antiseptic. And something sweet underneath that she didn’t want to think about. The doctor was young and grey with tiredness. Second-degree burns, she said. Both palms. The insides of the fingers. Partial thickness.

“The cold water helped a lot. Whoever did that probably saved him a great deal.”

“Will he… his hands. Will he be able to use them?”

“Yes. We’ll dress them, watch for infection. In a week or two we’ll know if the right one needs a graft.” She hesitated. “He’ll have scars.”

“He was trying to save the roses.”

The doctor looked at her kindly. Too kindly. Elowen wanted to scream at her.

“They usually are. People always try to save something.”

Xiao Pan was asleep now. Full of painkillers. Hands wrapped in thick white dressings like boxing gloves. His mother was on a night bus from the countryside. Elowen sat by the bed in her work apron. Soot on her face. Smoke in her hair. She didn’t move.

She kept hearing it. Whump. His voice gone high as a little boy’s. I tried to get the roses out. Every time the ward doors swung she smelled it again, burnt rubber and wet ash, and her stomach turned over. Her lips kept counting on their own. Fourteen. Fifteen. She had to press them together to stop.

Why had he been standing by the van? Because she’d sent him. Because there was a wedding first thing and she’d wanted to go home at a decent hour. So who had done this, really? She sat with that. She didn’t cry. His mother was on a bus. Somebody had to be sitting here when she arrived.

She heard him before she saw him. The corridor changed. The nurses’ voices dropped. Zhao stopped in the doorway. He looked at Xiao Pan. The white gloves. Her.

He came and crouched by her chair and looked at her face. He didn’t touch her. He took a clean handkerchief out of his pocket and held it out. She didn’t understand. Then she did. Soot. All over her cheek. She took the handkerchief. She didn’t use it. She just held it.

“Your hands.”

She looked down. She hadn’t thought about her hands at all. The right one was red across the back from the heat of the van. Along the side of her first finger there was a blister the size of a fingernail. White and full. From grabbing Xiao Pan’s collar. She hadn’t felt it. She felt it now. Zhao looked at it. Didn’t touch it. His jaw moved, once. He turned his head toward the nurses’ station.

“Her too.”

“It’s nothing. It’s a blister.”

“Her too.”

Not loud. A nurse was already on her way. He stayed crouched beside the chair the whole time she cleaned it and taped a white square of gauze over it. He watched every move the nurse’s hands made. Like he was learning it for an exam.

“The Qiu brothers.”

“Yes.” He stood. “The younger one. Qiu Lei. He’s got a camera on his own warehouse door. He’s very stupid.”

His voice was even.

“They want me to know they can reach you. That’s what this is. A message.”

“Where are you going?”

No answer. She stood up too.

“Don’t. Zhendong. Don’t.”

“It isn’t for you.” He was already turning to the door. “It’s business. They burned a vehicle registered to my wife’s company. If I let it go, every man at the Docks knows he can burn anything of mine.”

She looked at him. That was the voice he used on Maartens. On the rose man. Flat. Reasonable. And it was a lie. They both knew it. She’d seen his face in the doorway when he looked at Xiao Pan’s hands.

“You promised. In the contract. You said you’d tell me when you can’t tell me something. You said you would never make something up.”

He stopped. The ward was silent except for a machine beeping somewhere. He stood with his back to her. Then he turned his head. Just enough that she could see the side of his face.

“Then I can’t tell you.”

He went.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Qiu brothers’ warehouse was on the old road to the market. Long. Dark. Rusted roof. A yard full of stolen scooters. For a month Zhao had driven past it every morning with his wife asleep against the car window. Every morning he’d looked at it. Every morning he’d kept driving. Tonight he didn’t keep driving. He took six men. He didn’t need six. He took them so there’d be witnesses. By morning, every man at the Docks would know exactly what had happened and exactly why.

Bao glanced at him in the car.

“Boss. How far?”

“Nobody dies.”

“That’s… not far.”

“She’d know.”

Bao didn’t ask how. Bao never asked how. Qiu Lei was in the back office with three friends and a bottle. Still laughing about it. A phone on the table was playing a video somebody had shot of the van burning. They were watching it again. They stopped laughing when the door came in.

It didn’t take long. Two of the friends ran. The third went for something in his belt. Bao put him on the floor and knelt on him. Qiu Lei backed into the corner with his hands up, talking fast. His brother’s idea. Nobody was meant to get hurt. Just a van. Just a van! Just flowers—

“A boy was standing next to it.”

“I didn’t know! I swear, I didn’t see him, I didn’t—”

“You didn’t look.”

There was a steel oil drum in the yard behind the office. The kind they burned rubbish in to keep warm. Still smouldering. Zhao’s men dragged Qiu Lei out to it. Zhao picked up a can of petrol from beside the door. Qiu Lei’s own can. He poured a little into the drum. The flames came up with a soft roar. Yellow. Hungry. Exactly the colour of the van.

He took Qiu Lei by both wrists. He held them over the drum. Not in it. Over it. Close. Qiu Lei threw his whole weight back against him, screaming, kicking, begging. Zhao held his hands steady over the fire and counted. Out loud. Under his breath. The way his wife had counted for the boy under the cold tap. He got to twenty.

He let go. Qiu Lei dropped onto the concrete with his hands curled against his chest, sobbing. Palms red. Blistered. Shining. Zhao looked down at him.

“Cold running water. Twenty minutes. No ice. Nothing else.” He turned away. “That’s more than you gave him.”

They burned the warehouse after. All of it. The stolen scooters. The stock. The office. The phone, with the video still playing on the table. They stood in the road and watched it go. The fire brigade took a long time to come out to the old road. Everyone at the Docks knew they always did. Qiu Wen, the older brother, came in a car with no lights. He got out and stood at the edge of the road. Looked at the fire. At his brother on the ground. At Zhao. Zhao walked over.

“Your brother will be fine. He’ll have scars. The boy will have scars too.”

Qiu Wen was shaking with rage. “You’re a dead man, Zhao. You think you can—”

“Next time it won’t be your stock. It won’t be your brother. It’ll be you.” He looked at the roof starting to sag. “And my wife isn’t business. Tell everyone. That’s the message.”

He checked his phone on the way back to the car. Nothing from her. Of course not. He’d walked out on her in a hospital. He typed home? and deleted it. He typed it again. Deleted it again. Bao cleared his throat. Twice.

“Boss. Your arm.”

He looked. He hadn’t noticed.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came home as the sky went grey over the sea. She was in the kitchen. She’d come back from the hospital when Xiao Pan’s mother arrived. She hadn’t gone to bed. She’d sat on one of the tall wooden stools with a cup of tea that had gone stone cold, and waited. He stopped in the doorway. He smelled of smoke. Not the van smell, sharp with rubber and plastic. Older. Heavier. Wood and petrol and something else. They looked at each other.

“Is anyone dead?”

“No.”

“Is that true?”

“Yes.” He didn’t come in. “Qiu Lei has burns on his hands. Their warehouse is gone. Nobody is dead.”

She looked at him. Then down at his left arm, where the sleeve was shoved up. An angry red patch on the inside of his forearm. Shiny. Raised.

“You’re burned.”

He glanced at it like it was somebody else’s arm. “It’s nothing.”

She got up. She took him by the wrist, the same way she’d taken Xiao Pan, and pulled him to the sink. Cold tap. On. His arm. Under. He went rigid. Same as the photo booth, when she’d put her head on his shoulder. Like nobody had ever done this for him and he didn’t know yet if it would hurt.

“Twenty minutes.”

“It’s nothing—”

“Twenty minutes!” She held his wrist there. “Don’t take it out.”

So he didn’t.

They stood at the sink in the grey light. Her hand round his wrist. Water running over the burn. Outside, the dogs had come to the kitchen door and were sitting with their noses on the glass. At the end of the hall, the lemon tree was starting to catch the light.

“I told you not to.”

“You told me not to kill anyone.” He was watching the water. “I didn’t.”

That wasn’t what she’d said. It was what she’d meant. How did he do that? She looked at his arm under the tap. The old white scars on his knuckles. The thin line across his thumb. And this new one. Which he’d got holding a man’s hands over a fire. Which she was now nursing at her kitchen sink like it was Xiao Pan’s.

She thought about the boy in the bed with his hands wrapped in white. The roses. The two figures running off down the street. Laughing. They’d been laughing. And somewhere deep down, where she didn’t want to look, she was glad. Glad they were burned. Glad the warehouse was gone. Glad that somewhere in the city right now Qiu Lei was holding his hands under a cold tap, crying, and he’d be scared for the rest of his life to come near her shop. She hated herself for it.

“Thank you.”

It came out as a whisper. He turned his head. She didn’t look back. Eyes on the water. Hand on his wrist. Face still. If she looked at him, she had no idea what would happen.

She felt him lift his free hand off the counter. It came up toward her face. She felt its warmth by her cheek. It stopped an inch away. Like it always stopped. She heard his breath go out of him, rough. This time it didn’t wait. His thumb came the last inch and wiped the soot off her cheekbone. Once. Hard. Then his hand slid back into her hair and turned her face to him and he kissed her.

He hadn’t asked. Some far-off part of her noticed, the way she’d notice a short bunch of roses. The rest of her grabbed the front of his smoky shirt with her free hand and hauled him down to her.

He didn’t take his arm out from under the tap. That was what she’d remember afterwards. He kissed her with the cold water still running over the burn and her hand still locked round his wrist. She’d said twenty minutes. He wasn’t breaking that either.

His mouth tasted of smoke. So did hers. Short and rough and grateful. A kiss for the end of a terrible night when there’s nothing to say. She kissed him back the same way, the gladness and the hating it all knotted up together, until she heard herself make a noise and had to stop.

He let her go. His hand went down flat on the steel counter and pressed. Hard. Holding the whole house down with it. Neither of them said a word until the twenty minutes were up.

✦ ✦ ✦

She turned off the tap. Dried his arm with a clean towel. Patting, no rubbing. She found cling film in a drawer, still in its box, naturally, and wrapped it loosely round the burn. The way the nurses had wrapped Xiao Pan before the proper dressings.

“Keep it clean. Don’t pop the blisters. If it gets hot or starts to smell, you go to a doctor. A real one.”

“Yes.”

“A proper one. With a sign on the door.”

“Hm.”

“Don’t ‘hm’ me. A sign. On the door. Promise.”

“…Yes.”

Then he held out his hand. Palm up. Waiting. She frowned at it. Then she understood, and put her right hand in it. He turned it over. Looked at the gauze on her finger. One edge of the tape had come up in the water. He pressed it back down with his thumb. Slowly. All the way along. Till it stuck. He let her go.

She rinsed her cup. She walked past him to the stairs.

“Elowen.”

She stopped with her hand on the banister.

“The hospital. The boy’s bills. Grafts, if he needs them. His wages till he can work. And the van. I’ve already—”

“I know. The nurse told me. Bao came to the desk and paid for everything for a year. In cash. He booked his mother a room at the hotel across the road for as long as she wants it. And asked them not to tell anyone.”

He said nothing.

“She told me anyway.” Elowen looked back down the stairs at him. “I think she was scared of him.”

She went up. She didn’t sleep. But she lay in the big bed with the door open a hand’s width, and she listened. Him on the stairs at last. Stopping outside her room. The slide of his back down the wall as he sat on the floor.

Last time she’d lain awake listening to it. This time she fell asleep to it.

chapters.title: Zhendong, Stay
chapters.desc: A typhoon, a fever and a power cut. She asks him to stay, and in the morning she asks for more.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t touch me unless I ask.” — the contract, page two, line six
chapters.content:
The typhoon warning went up on Wednesday afternoon. By evening the sky over the Iron Docks had gone the colour of a bad bruise, the cranes had stopped, and the sea below the house was white all the way out. Elowen missed most of it. She was busy having a fever.

It had been coming for days. Afternoons at the hospital with Xiao Pan. The market in the dark every morning. The shop in between, trying to fill wedding orders with no van and no delivery boy. On Monday she’d stood at a bus stop in the rain holding a box of peonies. She hadn’t slept properly since the fire. Wednesday morning, her throat hurt. By lunch, everything hurt. In the afternoon, at the workbench, she put her knife down because she couldn’t feel her fingers right.

Next thing she knew, Bao was in the shop. Then she was in the back of the car, and the city was sliding past in grey streaks.

“He told me to bring you home. He saw your face this morning.”

“I was fine this morning.”

Bao looked at her in the mirror. Said nothing. Very loudly.

“I was fine, Bao.”

“Yes, Mrs. Zhao.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao met the car at the door. He took one look at her and picked her up. She meant to argue. The contract. But when she stood up the world tipped sideways and her legs quit, and then she was off the ground. One arm under her knees. One behind her back. Held against his chest as easily as he’d carried the lemon tree. His shirt smelled of rain and soap.

“I can walk,” she told his collar.

“I know.”

He didn’t put her down. Up the stairs. Past the little room. Down the corridor to the big room at the end. He laid her on the bed and stepped back fast, like he’d touched a hot pan.

“I’ll get Bao’s wife. She can—”

“No.” She shut her eyes. The ceiling was spinning. “I don’t want anyone.”

A pause.

“Medicine. What do you take?”

“Paracetamol. In my bag. And water. Lots.”

He went. He came back. He stood by the bed reading the side of the paracetamol box. Then he turned it over and read the other side. Then he read the first side again.

“It’s paracetamol. Not a bomb.”

“It says not more than four times in a day.”

“I know what it says.”

“Hm.” He shook two tablets onto his palm and held them out with a glass of water.

She took them. Half the water went down her chin. She was too tired to care. He took the glass off her before she dropped it. Then he stood there. Looking at her. His hand opened and closed at his side.

“Can I?”

“Can you what?”

He didn’t explain. He bent down and stopped. Waited.

“…Yes. Whatever it is. Yes.”

He put his forehead against hers. Just that. Cool skin on hot. Eyes shut. He held it there for three breaths like he was reading a thermometer with his face. Then he straightened up, and his mouth had gone hard and flat.

“You’re burning.”

“I’m fine.”

He pulled the duvet up to her shoulders. Without touching her once.

“I’ll be outside.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She drifted. Somewhere under her, through the floor, the kitchen. His voice on the phone. Low. Getting less patient.

“…How much water?”

A pause.

“What is a handful. Whose hand.”

Another pause.

“It’s sticking. It’s sticking to the bottom. Why is it—no. No, I’m stirring. I AM stirring.”

Elowen lay in bed with her eyes shut and laughed so hard it hurt her ribs. He came up later with a bowl. Congee. He put it on the bedside table next to the empty vase and stood back like he’d planted a bomb.

She sat up and tried it. It was the worst congee she’d ever eaten. Lumpy on top. Burnt underneath. He’d salted it like he was preserving a fish. She ate the whole bowl.

“Is it bad?”

“It’s awful.”

He looked at the empty bowl. At her.

“Then why—”

“Because you made it. Go away. I’m sleeping.”

He picked up the bowl and went. She heard him stop in the corridor. Then nothing. Then, ages later, the stairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

The power went after dark. She was half asleep. Hot ugly dreams. The van. Xiao Pan’s hands. The knife going into the table with that wet thock. Outside, the wind had been building for hours, a long climbing howl round the corners of the house. Then a crack, somewhere down the hill. Every light went out at once.

Total dark. No streetlights. No glow from the Docks. Just wind, and rain slamming the bulletproof glass in flat hard sheets, like handfuls of gravel. She lay very still. She’d never been scared of the dark. Never. But she was twenty-four and burning and wrung out, and the house was huge and strange round her, and for a second she felt about eight.

“Elowen.”

His voice. From the doorway. Low.

“The generator’ll come on in a minute. Bao’s gone down to it. Don’t be frightened.”

“I’m not frightened.”

“All right.”

She heard him sit down on the floor just inside the door. Same as every night outside it. The wind screamed. Something banged against the side of the house. A loose shutter. Again. Again. Again. The generator didn’t come on.

“Zhendong.”

“I’m here.”

She didn’t know she was going to say it. Afterwards she’d blame the fever. Or tell herself the fever had just burned off whatever part of her would normally have stopped it.

“Stay with me.”

For a second even the wind seemed to drop.

“I am staying. I’m right here.”

“No.” She turned her head on the pillow, toward his voice. “Here. Not by the door.”

Nothing. For so long she thought she’d imagined saying it. Then she heard him get up. Cross the room. Slow. Feeling his way in the dark. The mattress dipped as he put a hand on the edge to steady himself. He didn’t sit on the bed. He sat on the floor beside it, back against the frame, so his shoulder was right by her hand.

“Here.”

She walked her fingers across the sheet till they found his shoulder. His arm. His hand on his knee. She held it. All of him locked up. Same as always. His hand was big and rough and so much cooler than hers. After a while, like he thought she might take it back, his fingers closed round hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

The generator never came on. She found out later a tree had come down across the line to the guardhouse, and Bao had spent half the night out in the storm with a chainsaw and a torch. She didn’t care. In the dark, with the end of the world going on outside, she lay with her hot hand in his cool one and listened to him breathe.

“Tell me something.”

“What?”

“Anything. Something true.”

So long she thought he’d dropped off sitting up. Then he spoke. Low and even. Like reading off a page.

“When I was fifteen I was in a detention centre in the north. Young offenders. I stole a truck full of copper wire. I couldn’t really drive it. I hit a wall.”

She waited.

“Chen Si came in that November. Sixteen. His family had been important. Then somebody made them disappear. He did something clever and illegal to get money, and they caught him.” A pause. “He was small then. Thin. He talked like a rich boy. The others didn’t like it. They used to wait for him in the showers.”

The wind howled. Her fingers tightened on his.

“There was a riot in Block C. In January. Somebody set the mattresses on fire and the guards locked the doors and left us in there. Some of the older boys thought it was a good night to settle things.”

“And Chen Si…”

“Three of them went for him. One had a bit of bed frame. Sharpened.”

“What happened?”

“I was there. I got in the way.”

She lay in the dark and thought about how he always stood. A bit turned. Always between her and the door. She let go of his hand. She reached out blind and found his shirt. The side of his ribs. She laid her palm flat.

And there it was. Under the cotton. A long ridge of raised scar. From under his arm almost to his hip. He’d gone completely rigid.

“Here?”

“Yes.”

She left her hand there. She could feel his heart under her palm. Hard. Fast. Way too fast for a man sitting still on a floor.

“Chen Si got us out.” His voice wasn’t quite even now. “The drains. He’d studied the building plans for weeks. Every pipe. He dragged me most of the way. I don’t remember a lot of it. When we came out it was snowing.” A breath. “And he was covered in blood. And it was all mine.”

She didn’t say anything. What was there to say?

“He’s my brother. That’s all.” Quieter. “That’s the true thing.”

She slid her hand back down and found his again.

“Thank you.”

He didn’t answer. His thumb moved once over her knuckles.

“You can ask me something too. If you want. Anything. That’s fair.”

She felt him tense up. The storm hammered the glass. She waited. There was a question in him. She could feel it. Something heavy he’d been carrying around for years. She didn’t know what. He was holding it the way he held everything. Both arms underneath.

“What was your mother like?”

She smiled in the dark. That wasn’t it. She let him have it anyway.

“She was a florist. Before she married Baba.”

“Hm.”

“She sang when she cooked. Terribly. Like, really terribly. The neighbours used to bang on the wall.”

She could hear him listening.

“She kept the lemon tree on the balcony. Twenty years. She gave Baba the fish belly every night and he gave it back every night. She took me to the market when I was eight, in the dark, wrapped up in her coat. Bought me soy milk from the man at the door. Blew on it, because I always…”

“Burned your tongue.”

“Burned my tongue.” Her voice wobbled. “And then she went into hospital to have Eliana. And she didn’t come home.”

His hand turned over under hers so their palms were together. She kept talking until her voice gave out. Small stupid things. The song Mama sang wrong. The coat with the torn pocket. Not a word. He just didn’t let go. She didn’t remember falling asleep. Only that the last thing she felt was his thumb going once, light, across the back of her fingers.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she woke up, the storm was gone. Clear light through the window. Scrubbed bright. The kind of light you only get after a typhoon. The fever had broken in the night. Her pyjamas were damp. Her head felt light and empty. Her whole body felt like it had been beaten all over, gently, by someone who loved her. Her hand was still in his. He was asleep.

Same place on the floor against the side of the bed. Except at some point his head had tipped over and landed on the edge of the mattress, right next to their hands. Face turned toward her. Mouth a bit open. A crease in his cheek from the sheet.

She didn’t move. She just looked. She hadn’t seen him asleep before. His face without that stillness. Without the waiting. Asleep, he looked younger than twenty-five. Tired all the way down. There was a scar under his jaw she’d never noticed. His eyelashes were longer than they had any right to be.

She lifted her other hand and touched his hair. Softer than she’d expected. She pushed a bit of it off his forehead. At the back, the piece from the registry was sticking up again. Of course it was.

His eyes opened. He didn’t move. Didn’t lift his head. He lay there with his cheek on the mattress and looked at her, and she watched him wake up properly. Work out where he was. Notice her fingers were still in his hair. Neither of them looked away.

“Your fever broke.” Rough with sleep.

“Yes.”

“How do you feel?”

She thought about it.

“Better.” Then, before she could chicken out: “Do you remember the contract? Page two. Line six.”

He knew it by heart. She’d known he would.

“You don’t touch me unless I ask.”

“I’m asking.”

His whole body stopped.

“Asking what?”

She didn’t answer with words. She slid her fingers out of his hair and down to his jaw. Held it lightly. Leaned down toward him. He didn’t come up to meet her. But his eyes had gone to her mouth and stayed there, dark. His breathing had changed. The hand on the mattress had closed in the sheet so hard the cotton pulled tight across the bed. She could see the tendons standing out in his wrist.

Every bit of him was leaning toward her. Except the bit that had signed her contract. He’d kissed her in the basement. Against her door frame. At the sink with his arm under the tap, the one time he forgot to wait. He’d been the one to stop, every time. But he had never come near her in a bed. A bed was a different line. He’d drawn it himself. He wasn’t crossing it unless she was sure. Unless she came all the way. So she came all the way.

✦ ✦ ✦

It wasn’t like the other times. Her lips were dry and cracked from the fever. His were warm and didn’t move. For a second he didn’t kiss her back at all. He just stayed there, her mouth on his, in her bed. Like this was the one place he’d never let himself imagine, and if he moved it would all stop. She felt his breath catch. Felt the rough edge of his jaw under her fingers where he hadn’t shaved. Then, slowly, he kissed her back.

The same way he’d held her hand in the dark. Like every second was a question. His hand came up off the mattress and found her face, and it was shaking. This man had held another man’s hands over a fire without blinking, and his big scarred hand was trembling against her cheek. His thumb moved along her cheekbone. His mouth softened. Opened a little. She tasted salt. Yesterday’s coffee.

Then the care went out of it. He came up off the floor onto his knees beside the bed. His hand slid back into her hair. And he kissed her properly. Deep. Hungry. Like he’d been starving in the same house as her for weeks and somebody had finally said he could eat.

She felt it all the way down her spine. Her fingers knotted in his shirt and pulled. A sound came out of her. Low. From somewhere in her throat. Was that her? He stopped. It cost him. She could see it cost him. He didn’t pull away. He just stopped, and put his forehead on hers, and stayed there breathing hard, his hand still buried in her hair and shaking. Eyes shut. All of him holding back. A dog on a short lead.

“You have a fever.”

“It broke.”

“Last night you had a fever.” Very low. “You might not… you might not mean it.”

She opened her eyes and looked at him from two centimetres away. The closed lids. The stupid long lashes. The sheet crease in his cheek. A man who’d rather stop kissing her than take one thing she didn’t mean to give.

“Then I’ll ask again. When I don’t have a fever.”

His eyes opened.

“Soon.”

Rough. Almost an order. Then, lower, like it hurt him to say it:

“And you’ll mean it?”

For a second she heard it under his voice. The question he’d held all night in the dark and hadn’t asked. It was under will you mean it. Older than that. More frightened. She didn’t know yet what it was.

“Yes.”

He looked at her. Then he shut his eyes again, turned his face, and pressed his mouth to the inside of her wrist. Right on her pulse.

“Okay.”

Against her skin. Barely a word. Outside, the storm had left the whole hill wet and shining. Down in the garden, Dumpling and Noodle were barking their heads off at a fallen branch. Somewhere below, Bao’s chainsaw started up again. Elowen lay in the big bed with her hand on her husband’s face and her wrist against his mouth, and thought, very clearly:

Oh.

Oh, no.

chapters.title: Page Two, Line Six
chapters.desc: A week of him not touching her. Then she leaves a thermometer by his soup, says “page two, line six,” and this time nobody has a fever.
chapters.epigraph: “Then I’ll ask again. When I don’t have a fever.”
chapters.content:
For a week, nobody mentioned the bed.

He drove her to the market at four. He carried the buckets. He ate fried eggs on rice on his stool behind the counter. At midnight Xiao Pan sent a photo of himself in soft white gloves, trying to hold a spoon. Underneath, in capitals: MOTORBIKE IN 6 MONTHS.

“He’s going to break his other hands,” Elowen said.

“He only has two.”

“That’s my point!”

Everything was normal. So normal it was suspicious. He didn’t touch her. Not her fingers when he passed her a cup. Not her shoulder when she fell asleep against the car window. On Thursday a trolley came round the end of the flower aisle too fast, and his hand shot out to pull her back, and stopped. A centimetre from her arm. It hung there in the air.

“Watch out.”

The trolley missed. His hand went back in his pocket. Granny Su took the cigarette out of her mouth.

“What was that?”

“Nothing.”

“That was a man who wants to grab his wife and won’t.” She squinted at Zhao. “Are you sick?”

“No, Grandmother.”

“Then what’s wrong with you?”

Zhao picked up the ranunculus and walked off with them. Granny Su looked at Elowen. Elowen counted change very, very hard.

What was wrong with him was the fever. He’d kissed a woman at thirty-nine degrees and decided it didn’t count. You might not mean it. So now he’d wait. He’d sit outside her door till they were both ninety, because the contract said unless I ask. Did he think she’d forgotten? She hadn’t forgotten a thing. That was the problem.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the sixth night she heard him through the hand’s width of open door. Back to the wall, where he always sat.

“Ask me again.”

Barely a voice. She lay in the dark with her heart going like a bird against glass. She didn’t answer. Not yet. Not with one degree of fever left anywhere in her. When she asked, he’d have nothing to argue with.

She heard him wait. Then she heard him stop waiting and just stay.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the eighth night he came home late. She’d been on the tall stool at the kitchen counter for an hour. She’d rehearsed it in the shower. In the garden, with Dumpling. Near the soup. He stopped in the doorway. Dark suit, tie pulled loose, somebody else’s cigarettes on him. A broker in the north had wanted to talk prices till midnight, and it was all over his face.

There was soup at his place. Chopsticks. A spoon. And beside the spoon, a thermometer.

The tiredness went out of him all at once.

“Are you sick?”

He was already coming toward her.

“No.” She held it up so he could read the screen. “Thirty-six point six. I took it an hour ago. And when I heard the car. And just now.”

He stopped. He read it twice. His face didn’t move. His hand did. It closed at his side, slowly, and opened.

“Elowen.”

“You said I might not mean it. Because of the fever.” Steadier than she felt. Good. “So I waited till I didn’t have one.”

She put the thermometer down. Click.

“Page two. Line six.”

He didn’t move. One horrible second. What if she’d got it wrong? What if he sat outside her door for some other reason? Guard duty. Habit. And she was sitting in a kitchen at midnight with a thermometer, making a complete idiot of herself—

“There was a word crossed out,” he said. “On that line.”

Oh, for god’s sake.

“You read it. That night. Through the scribble.”

“Yes.”

“You never said!”

“You said it was none of my business.” One step into the kitchen. “You don’t touch me ever. Then you crossed out ever.”

“I changed my mind about it.”

“At four in the morning.”

“How do you know it was four in the—”

“You’d changed pens.”

He’d looked at the ink. He’d held her contract up to the lamp, noticed the pen, carried it in his jacket for seven weeks, and never said a word.

“Yes. Four in the morning. I didn’t know why.”

“And now?”

“Now I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Four strides. His jacket came off on the way and landed somewhere near the dogs’ bowls. He stopped right in front of her stool with a hand flat on the counter on each side of her. The stool was high. For once their eyes were level.

He lifted one hand. It stopped by her cheek, a centimetre off, same as at the market. Except this time it was shaking.

“Say it.”

“I said it. Page two—”

“Not the contract.” All the way down, his voice. “You. Say what you’re asking.”

Scarred knuckles. The white line on the thumb. That hand had put a knife through a man’s hand at a dinner table. It had carried her mother’s lemon tree up the steps like a baby.

“I’m asking you to touch me.”

The hand came the last centimetre.

He took her face in both hands and kissed her, and it was nothing like the others. The others had been questions. This was the answer. Slow and deep and sure, like he’d planned it a long time ago and wasn’t letting anybody rush it. Not even himself.

She made a noise into his mouth. Oh no. What was that? He heard it. His hands tightened on her jaw and he kissed her harder. She grabbed his shirt in both fists. The stool rocked. He caught her and lifted her off it altogether, one arm round her waist, like a bucket of roses, and then she was sitting on the counter with the soup somewhere behind her. Who cared about soup?

He stood between her knees and didn’t stop. Her jaw. The corner of her mouth. A place under her ear she hadn’t known existed until he found it and she shivered from scalp to heels.

“Zhendong—”

“I know.” Rough, against her throat. “This spot. A week. Outside your door. Every night.”

Her stomach flipped like a coin. His hands were on her waist, over her jumper. Shaking a bit. Not moving. Like he’d made them promise.

She put her hands on top of his.

“You can.”
