His eyes had gone black. She moved his hands herself, up under the hem, flat on bare skin. He shut his eyes. His thumbs went once along her lowest ribs and she gasped out loud.

“Not here.” Pure gravel.

“What’s wrong with the counter?”

“Nothing.” His forehead came down on hers. “That’s the problem.”

She laughed into his mouth, shaky and stunned.

He picked her up the way he’d carried her in out of the typhoon. Except she wasn’t burning now. Now she put her arms round his neck and her mouth on his throat, right on the jump of his pulse. Then, because she’d apparently lost her mind, she bit it.

He stopped dead on the third stair.

“Elowen.”

“Keep walking.”

He kept walking. Faster. At the top he went straight past the little room and didn’t even look at it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The big room was dark except for the Docks. Orange and white light slid over the ceiling as the cranes turned. He set her on her feet by the bed, kissed her once more so hard she swayed, and made himself step back. Fists at his sides. Chest going like he’d run up the hill.

He’d had his yes. He was giving her the first part. Her way.

So she pulled his tie off and dropped it. Then the buttons. Florist’s fingers. Good with wire, good with ribbon, completely useless with buttons. He stood there and let her fight every one.

“There are too many.”

“Hm.”

“Who needs this many buttons?”

“I’ll buy shirts with fewer.”

“Don’t you DARE buy anything.”

She got the last one and pushed the shirt off his shoulders, and heard the breath go out of him.

In the orange light she could see his scars. She’d felt the long one in the dark. She hadn’t known about the rest. A round puckered mark on his left shoulder. A white line along the collarbone. Three short ones on his forearm, neat as stitches. And low on his side, a rough shiny patch, older than any of them.

She touched the round one.

“This?”

“A bullet. In the south.” He swallowed. “Went straight through.”

She bent her head and kissed it. He made a noise like she’d hit him.

“This?”

“A bottle. I was nineteen.”

She kissed that one. Then the three on his forearm. One, two, three.

“Steel sheet. At the yard.” His voice was going. “Eleven.”

His hand came up into her hair at last. Not pulling. Holding on. She skipped the shiny patch. He’d gone rigid when her fingers passed it. Later.

She knelt on the bed for the long one, the Block C one, and put her mouth to the top of it under his arm. Then lower. All the way down to where it ended above his hip, like a river on a map.

When she looked up, his eyes were wet.

“People see them and look away. Or they ask if I killed the man.”

“Did you?”

“Some of them.” His thumb on her cheek. “Nobody asks where it hurt.”

She sat back on her heels. Big, dangerous, scarred, shirt on the floor, whole heart on his face. And she knew. This wasn’t for Baba. Or the contract. Or Xiao Pan’s hands. She wanted him. She had for longer than she’d let herself notice.

That scared her so badly she grabbed the hem of her own jumper just to stop thinking.

He caught her wrists.

“Let me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He lifted the jumper over her head. Then he folded it. Sleeves in. In half. On the chair. She laughed out loud. He looked at her laughing like he wanted to keep it in a drawer.

He took her right hand and eased the heavy ring over her knuckle, slowly, like it might hurt her. He dropped it in the empty vase by the bed. One clear note on the glass.

Then he just looked. So long she lifted her arms to cover herself. He caught her wrists and put them back at her sides.

“Don’t. Please.” Hoarse. “I’ve waited a month. Let me look.”

She let him. It was harder than walking into the Iron Docks. Her skin went hot everywhere his eyes went. And his jaw was tight, and his fists were tight, and who was scared here? Not her. Him.

“Zhendong. Touch me.”

He went down on his knees. Her stomach first, just above her waistband, so light her knees nearly quit. Her hip. Her ribs, one at a time, climbing. And before each one he stopped and looked up and waited, until she nodded, until she said yes, until she was pulling him closer by the hair before he’d even stopped.

His hands were rough. Rope, steel, the grip of a gun. They felt like a man who knew exactly how much force broke things, using none of it.

When he stood and kissed her again it was deeper. Bare skin to bare skin, his heart slamming into hers. She made the noise again. He made one back. Nearly a growl.

“The first night. In the rain.” Against her mouth. “You threw a towel at me.”

“You were dripping on my floor.”

“I thought, if any man ever touches her, I’ll kill him.”

The sensible part of her, the part that wrote three-page contracts, tried very hard to be offended.

“You can’t say things like that.”

“I know.” His teeth on the curve of her shoulder. Gently. She gasped. “Tell me to stop.”

“Don’t you dare.”

She heard herself. She nearly died.

✦ ✦ ✦

He laid her back on the white sheets and held himself over her. And stopped. One more time.

“Tell me to stop and I’ll stop. Any time. Even now. Even…”

She put her hand over his mouth.

“Zhendong. I’m a very organised person. I wrote you three pages. If I wanted you to stop, I’d have put it in writing.”

He laughed into her palm. A real one. She felt it everywhere.

He laced his fingers through hers and pressed her hand into the pillow. And then he was slow. Horribly slow. He touched her like he’d watched her hands on the roses that first night. Finding every place that made her breath catch. Going back to it. Watching her face, until she was arching off the sheets with her nails in his shoulders, saying his name in a voice she’d never heard come out of herself.

He stopped. Right there. The monster.

“Again.”

“Please—”

“No. My name.”

“Zhendong.”

He shut his eyes like she’d struck him. After that there was no more asking. He was so careful at first that she had to pull him down to her, and when she did, something in him broke wide open. He held her like the world was ending and she was the one thing he got to carry out. Elowen. Elowen. Into her throat, over and over, like a word he’d only just learned and didn’t trust to stay. She held on to his shoulders, to the scars she’d kissed, and when everything in her went bright and far away his arms locked so tight she couldn’t breathe.

Who needed to breathe?

He made a sound against her neck she’d hear in her sleep for a week.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay on his chest and listened to his heart come down. Out on the water a ship sounded its horn. His thumb went up and down her spine, bone by bone. Was he counting them? He was totally counting them.

“Is this all right?” To the ceiling. “Did I… are you…”

The man who’d walked into the Qiu brothers’ warehouse at two in the morning without blinking. Lying in her bed, rigid, terrified he’d broken something.

She put her chin on his chest so he had to look at her.

“You folded my jumper.”

He blinked.

“In the middle of all that. You folded my jumper. You took my ring off like it was going to snap. And you asked if I was sure four times.” Her eyes stung. Fine. “Five.”

“Six. I counted.”

She laughed and hid her face in his chest. All the stiffness ran out of him at once, like water out of a bucket. He went heavy and warm underneath her.

“Can I stay here tonight?” Into her hair.

“It’s my room. I was about to ask you.”

He stayed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her alarm went off in the pitch dark. She killed it before it rang twice. He didn’t wake. Zhao Zhendong, who woke when a dog turned over in the garden, slept through it like a stone.

She thought about Granny Su. The ranunculus. The soy milk man asking where her husband was. She typed one-handed, so she wouldn’t move his arm.

Elowen: granny su not coming today. please keep my ranunculus for tomorrow

Five years. She’d never missed a working morning. Not with flu. Not on her wedding day.

She put the phone face down next to the vase with her ring in it, and shut her eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke to daylight and panic. Light. There should not be light. He sat up so fast the duvet slid off the bed. Watch. Car. If they left now they’d catch the end of Granny Su’s—

A hand closed on his wrist.

“I didn’t go.”

Hair everywhere. A crease on her cheek from his shoulder. She was wearing his shirt from last night. It came down to her knees. He couldn’t look at anything else.

“I texted Granny Su.” She tugged until he lay back down. “She answered.”

She held up the phone.

Granny Su: ABOUT TIME

She’d gone to the market on their wedding morning. On the morning of the typhoon, with her throat already burning, while he sat in the car with his hands locked on the wheel. She had never missed it. Today she had. For this.

She curled into his side. He put his chin on top of her head and held on.

✦ ✦ ✦

She fell asleep again. He didn’t. The voice in the back of his head didn’t stop. It only went lower.

She wanted you. That’s true. It isn’t the same. She chose a contract. She chose her father. You were the price.

Her hand lay open on his chest, over his heart. A pale band on her middle finger where the ring had been.

He could wake her. One question. Did you marry me for love, or to keep him safe from me?

He opened his mouth. She sighed and pushed her face harder into his shoulder. Her fingers closed a little on his chest.

He shut his mouth. He’d burn the Docks down before he risked this morning.

He’d ask another day.

chapters.title: The Florist’s Husband Is Not Allowed Behind the Counter
chapters.desc: Her husband starts coming to work and her takings drop by a third. She puts up house rules. He breaks rule two in four days and gets punished in the cooler.
chapters.epigraph: “Rule one: no frightening the customers. Rule two: see rule one.” — handwritten sign, back wall of Elowen’s
chapters.content:
The trouble with sleeping with your husband, it turned out, was that he started coming to work.

Not every day. He had his own work, the kind that happened in the north of the city after dark and came home smelling of cigarettes he didn’t smoke. But on the days when his meetings were late, or cancelled, or he simply decided there weren’t any, he drove her to the market at four. He carried the buckets in at six. He ate his eggs on the stool.

And then he didn’t leave.

He stood in the corner by the eucalyptus with a newspaper and watched the door.

By Friday her takings were down by a third.

“You’re frightening people.”

“I’m reading.”

“You’ve been on the same page for an hour.”

He looked down. Property section. He lowered it.

“The man at ten. Grey jacket. He looked at the till twice before he looked at the flowers.”

“He was choosing between roses and carnations for his mother.” Snip. A stem end hit the floor. “He was working out if he could afford the roses. He bought carnations. Because you stared at him.”

Zhao thought about it.

“He could have afforded the roses. His shoes were new.”

“Zhendong!”

“Hm.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The wholesale driver was a different matter.

He parked his lorry across her loading space on Friday and left it there for an hour. When Elowen went out and asked him to move it, he called her a word she didn’t repeat later and told her to wait like everybody else. Then he laughed, because his mate in the cab laughed.

Inside the shop, the newspaper went down.

Zhao didn’t hurry. He never hurried. He walked out onto the pavement, put one hand on the back of the man’s neck, not hard, and steered him round to the far side of his own cab. Out of sight of the window. The mate in the cab found something interesting in the glovebox.

It took about a minute.

Zhao told him three things. Low and even, like reading out a delivery note. The name of his depot manager. The name of the school his daughter went to. And the name of the woman in the shop, which was Mrs. Zhao, in case he’d been unclear.

No more touching. No need. The man’s knees were doing something on their own.

“Move the lorry.”

“Yes. Yes, sir, I’m moving it, I’m—”

“Not to me. To her.”

The driver came back round the cab grey and sweating. He moved the lorry two streets away. After that he carried every box in by hand, and called her Mrs. Zhao, and looked at the floor while he did it.

Zhao came back in and picked up his paper.

“Is the door too much draught for the delphiniums?”

She stared at him.

“What did you say to him?”

“I asked him to park somewhere else.”

“Zhendong.”

“Politely.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She got it out of him that night. In bed, with the light off, which was cheating, because she couldn’t see his face.

“His daughter’s school.”

“Yes.”

“You told a lorry driver the name of his little girl’s school.”

“Yes.”

“That’s horrible.”

“Yes.”

She lay on her back and stared at the ceiling. The awful part? He wasn’t sorry. He wasn’t pretending to be. The worse part was the hot, mean little spark under her ribs when she pictured the man’s knees going.

“Did it work?”

“He calls you Mrs. Zhao.”

It had worked. Obviously. She rolled over and poked him in the chest.

“Not the kids. Next time. Leave the kids out of it. That’s mine. That’s my line.”

He was quiet so long she thought he’d fallen asleep.

“…Hm.”

“That’s not a yes.”

“It’s a yes.” He caught the poking finger and held it against his chest. “Anything else?”

“You don’t say my name to people like that.”

“I said your name so he’d remember it.”

“Zhendong!”

“He’ll remember it.” He kissed the finger. Then the next one. “Go to sleep, Mrs. Zhao.”

She did not go to sleep for quite a while. That was entirely his fault.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday she wrote a sign and taped it to the back wall, right where he’d see it every time he looked up.

HOUSE RULES

1. No frightening the customers.

2. The husband is not allowed behind the counter.

3. The husband does not count other people’s change.

4. The husband does not ask delivery drivers where they parked.

5. If the husband needs something to do, he can sweep.

He read it. All five. Twice. She waited for an argument.

He took the broom from the corner and swept.

He swept the shop floor like it owed him money. Xiao Pan came in from the back with his hands in soft compression gloves, banned from lifting anything heavier than a vase, and stopped dead.

“Miss Lin.” A whisper. “Is the floor meant to shine like that?”

“No.”

“He’s doing the corners. With his fingers.”

Zhao was crouched by the cooler, picking a single rose petal out of the gap under the door with two fingertips. Like it was wired to something.

Xiao Pan watched for a long moment.

“I think he might be in love with you.”

Elowen dropped her scissors.

From the floor by the cooler, without looking up, Zhao said, “Hm.”

Xiao Pan went red to the ears and remembered something urgent in the back.

She picked up the scissors. Her hands weren’t quite steady. Her husband was still by the cooler with a petal between two fingers, not looking at her so carefully that she knew he’d heard every word.

What did hm mean? Yes? No? Mind your own business, Xiao Pan?

She cut a stem too short and had to throw it away.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rules lasted four days.

On Wednesday a woman came in to order flowers for her own funeral. Eighty-one. Tiny. Sharp as a pin. She knew exactly what she wanted.

“White lilies. Not the kind that stink.”

“No stink.” Elowen wrote it down.

“Chrysanthemums. Yellow. White is boring. I’ve been to enough boring funerals.”

“Yellow.”

“And something blue. My husband always said blue suited me.” She tapped the counter. “He’ll be waiting. I want to look nice.”

Elowen was good with people planning to die. Five years of practice. She was halfway down the order form when the old woman stopped and looked past her, at the corner.

“Who’s that?”

Elowen didn’t turn round. “My husband.”

The old woman peered at Zhao over her glasses. Zhao lowered his newspaper. They looked each other over across the shop. Neither one looked impressed.

“Young man. Come here.”

He came. He stood in front of her with his hands at his sides like a soldier at inspection.

“You look like you’ve been to a lot of funerals.”

“Yes, Grandmother.”

“What flowers did they have?”

It took him a while.

“Mostly none.”

The old woman looked at him. Then she nodded, like he’d passed something.

“Delphiniums, then. For the blue. My husband grew them.”

Zhao glanced at Elowen.

“They don’t like draughts. Tell your family to keep them away from the door.”

The old woman laughed. A dry, cracked, delighted laugh. She patted his arm twice and paid in cash, and at the door she pointed one finger back at him.

“You. Feed her. She’s too thin.”

“Yes, Grandmother.”

The bell went. Elowen stood at the counter with the form in her hand and looked at her husband.

“You’re behind the counter.”

He looked down. He was. He’d walked round it without noticing.

“Rule two.”

He looked at the sign. Then at her. And the corner of his mouth went up and stayed up. Crooked. Rusty. A real smile. She’d never once seen it in daylight.

“Then punish me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The walk-in cooler was at the back, behind a heavy insulated door. Inside it was one degree. Dim. Wet leaves and roses and the sweet chemical smell of flower food. Her breath came out white.

She’d gone in for the lilies.

He’d followed her in, and he let go of the door on purpose.

It swung shut with a thud. The seal caught. Click. The street was gone. Just the fan humming and the two of them in a space built for buckets.

“You can’t be in here.”

She turned round with the lilies in her arms and he was right there. She had nowhere to go except back into the white roses.

He took the bucket off her and set it on the floor.

“Zhendong. It’s one degree.”

“I know.” A hand on the shelf each side of her. Not touching. Caging her in the roses. “You’re shivering.”

She was. Her bare arms had gone to goosebumps. Her breath was clouding into his.

He bent his head and stopped. A breath away. And waited.

“Say yes.”

She didn’t. She grabbed his collar and closed the gap herself. That was her yes.

His mouth was the only warm thing in the room. She made a noise and fisted his shirt, and he pressed closer, and the shelf rattled behind her. A dozen white roses shivered on their stems. Freezing water went straight down the back of her neck.

“AH— cold, cold, cold—”

He laughed into her mouth. He caught the drop with his thumb at the nape of her neck, and then his whole warm hand was there under her hair, and his other arm was round her waist, pulling her off the icy shelf and into him.

Cold air on her arms. Heat all down her front. Roses so thick she could taste them. Xiao Pan might open that door any second. He wouldn’t. The boy had taken one look at Zhao following her into the cooler and fled to the front with a look of deep personal suffering.

When they came apart her lips were tingling and her nose was cold. What had she come in for?

“That was not a punishment.”

“No.” He picked up the lilies and handed them to her. “But now you’re warm.”

✦ ✦ ✦

When they came out, Xiao Pan was wrapping a bouquet with enormous concentration. The tips of his ears were scarlet.

Elowen put the lilies down and went back to the funeral order like nothing had happened. Zhao went back to his corner and opened the paper at the property section.

After a while, Xiao Pan cleared his throat.

“Mr. Zhao.” He didn’t look up from the ribbon. “I wanted to say thank you. For the hospital. Miss Lin told me.”

The paper didn’t move.

“How are your hands?”

“Better. The doctor says no grafts. I have to squeeze a ball a hundred times a day.” A pause. “I can’t ride a scooter yet. Or a motorbike. Not for six months.”

“I know. I asked.”

Xiao Pan looked up.

Behind the newspaper, like it was nothing, Zhao said, “There’s a garage near the Docks. A woman called Jinx builds bikes. She owes me a favour. In six months, when your doctor says yes, you go and see her, and you tell her my name.”

The boy stared at the newspaper. His mouth opened. Nothing came out.

“It’ll be a small one. You’ll wear a helmet. If I see you without the helmet, I take it back.”

Xiao Pan made a sound that wasn’t a word, put down the bouquet, and ran into the back.

They heard him blow his nose. Twice.

Elowen pointed her pen at rule one on the wall.

Zhao turned a page. “He’s not a customer.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The vans came on Friday.

Two of them, white and new, nose to tail outside the shop when she came to unlock at six. Elowen’s on both sides, the letters copied off the sign over her own door. One was refrigerated. The other had racks built into the back so the buckets couldn’t tip on corners, and a low step that folded down, so nobody with healing hands would ever have to lift a box higher than his waist.

Two sets of keys lay on the counter by the till.

She’d bought the old van herself, second-hand, at twenty. Eleven months of savings. She’d loved it like the first thing that was completely hers.

“I’ll pay for them.”

He set the buckets down exactly where she liked them.

“They burned your van because of me.”

What could she say to that? Nothing. So she did the sum anyway, that night at the kitchen counter, and moved the first payment from the shop account into his.

The next morning it was back in hers. No note.

She moved it again.

It came back again.

“Stop sending it back.”

“Stop sending it.”

“I’m not a charity, Zhendong!”

“No.” He put her coffee in front of her. Half sugar. He’d never once asked how she took it. “You’re my wife.”

That was not an argument. That was cheating. She opened her mouth and couldn’t find the end of the sentence.

On the third morning Xiao Pan sat in the driver’s seat of the refrigerated van with his gloved hands on the wheel, not allowed to drive it for another six months, and cried. After that she stopped moving the money. It hurt her pride less than she’d expected. That annoyed her more than the vans.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she climbed onto a bucket to take the sign down.

He was holding the bucket. She hadn’t asked him to. He’d just appeared under her and put his hands on it.

“You’re keeping it?”

“I’m putting it in the drawer.” She peeled off the tape. “For evidence.”

“Of what?”

“That I tried.”

She climbed down. He took the sign out of her hands and read it again under the shop light. Then he took the pen off the counter. The good pen. The one for wedding cards.

“That’s my—”

He drew one neat line through rule two. Next to it, in square blunt capitals, he wrote four words. Then he gave her the sign and the pen back and went to start the van.

She looked down.

Except when she says so.

She stood in her own shop with her cheeks on fire. Was that a rule or a threat?

“Elowen.” From the door. Keys in his hand. “Are you coming?”

“Yes.”

“Hm.” He held the door. “Say it like that more.”

chapters.title: Thorns at Six in the Morning
chapters.desc: He learns to strip roses and bleeds on two hundred of them. Chen Si comes in for anniversary flowers and finds his brother in her apron.
chapters.epigraph: “Loose. Like this. Let it move in your hand. You’re not fighting it.” — Elowen, at the workbench, six a.m.
chapters.content:
“Give me the knife.”

Monday, barely light. The market haul covered the whole workbench. Four hundred roses up from the south, still in their cardboard sleeves, heads packed tight as fists. Every one had to come out of its sleeve, lose its lower leaves and the worst of its thorns, get a fresh cut on the angle, and go into a bucket before nine.

On a normal Monday, she and Xiao Pan did it in two hours. Xiao Pan’s hands were still in gloves. So: three hours. Her. Alone.

“You don’t know how.”

“Show me.”

She looked at him. Jacket off. Sleeves rolled. The burn on his forearm had healed to a shiny pink patch. He was looking at the roses like they were a rifle laid out on a cloth.

At the market that morning he’d bought her soy milk from the man at the door and blown on it before he handed it over. Hadn’t said a word. Just blown on it, twice, and held it out. She’d stood there holding the cup with her throat gone tight, because nobody had done that since Mama.

So, fine. He could have the roses.

She handed him a stem and the stripper. A little metal clamp with a hole in the end.

“Close it round the stem. Pull down, toward you. Not too hard or you’ll take the bark off and it rots. Leave the top two sets of leaves. They help it drink.”

He closed it. He pulled.

It went down the stem in one clean stroke. Every leaf. Every thorn. And somehow, a strip of skin off the side of his thumb.

He looked at his thumb. A bead of blood came up, bright red.

“The thorns go in the tool,” Elowen said. “Not in you.”

“I see that now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

An hour later he’d done sixty roses and bled on about twenty.

He was slow. So careful it made him slower. He held each stem like it might go off. He checked every one in the light afterwards, ran a finger down the bark for the thorns he’d missed, found them, said nothing, and bled again.

He didn’t complain. Not once.

Everyone complained about roses. Students, part-timers, Xiao Pan’s cousin for one disastrous Valentine’s Day. Roses were the worst job in the shop. They shredded your hands and there were always more.

He pulled a thorn out of his fingertip with his teeth and reached for number sixty-one.

“Stop. Let me see.”

He put it down. She turned his hand over.

It was a mess. Nicks all over the fingers. A thorn still stuck in the web between thumb and first finger, tiny and black. New scratches on top of old calluses on top of old scars.

“You’re holding it like it’s going to bite you.”

“It does bite me.”

“Because you’re holding it like that.”

She stepped behind him and reached round, her chest against his back, and put her hands over his on the stem.

“Loose. Like this. Let it move in your hand. You’re not fighting it.”

The stripper closed. They pulled down together. Smooth. Not too hard.

Leaves gone. Thorns gone. Skin still attached.

“Oh,” he said.

She didn’t let go. Her cheek was against his shoulder blade. She could feel him breathing. She could feel how still he’d gone. He always went like that when she touched him without warning. Like he was waiting to find out if he was allowed.

“Again.”

They did the next one together. And the next.

“Where did you learn to be this careful?” she asked, around the tenth.

His hands paused under hers.

“The yard.”

“Where you carried steel.”

“Old Zhao said if you dropped something, it cost him money.” He reached for another stem. Even voice. “And if it cost him money, it cost you.”

“What did it cost you? When you did?”

The cooler fan hummed. A delivery van went past.

“There’s a scar on my side. Low. You didn’t ask about it.”

She remembered. The shiny patch. The way he’d locked up when her fingers went past it, that first night.

“I didn’t ask.”

“I know.” He stripped the rose clean. “He kept a stove in the office. For the winter. I dropped a box of bolts. I was nine.”

Nine.

She took her hands off his. She put her arms round his waist from behind instead and held on, face pressed between his shoulder blades. She couldn’t think of a single thing to say. What was there? Sorry? Sorry was for spilled tea.

After a moment he put down the stripper and covered both her hands with one of his, where they were locked over his stomach. His thumb was still bleeding a bit. She didn’t care.

“It was a long time ago. He’s dead. I don’t think about it.”

“You think about it every time you pick up something that might break.” Into his shirt. “You carried my mother’s tree up the steps like it was glass. You carry the buckets like they’re glass.” She squeezed. “You hold me like that.”

He didn’t answer for a long time.

“Is that bad?”

She thought about the knife going into a dinner table. A man’s hands over an oil drum. All the things those hands did when she wasn’t looking.

“No. It’s the opposite.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The bell went. Chen Si walked in.

Camel coat. Takeaway coffee. He stopped just inside the door and looked like a man who’d walked into a room and found his brother in an apron.

Because Zhao was in an apron. Elowen had tied it on him after the third time he bled on his own shirt. Green. ELOWEN’S across the chest in white. About a head too short for him. She’d had to stand on her toes to get it over his hair, and he’d ducked for her without being asked.

“Good morning.”

“Si.” Zhao didn’t look up from his rose.

Chen Si walked over. He looked at the buckets of finished roses, two hundred of them standing in rows. At the floor, ankle-deep in leaves and thorns. At his brother’s hands.

“You’re bleeding.”

“Roses.”

“Yes. I can see.” He put his coffee down on the counter, very precisely. “I’ve watched you take a bullet and finish your noodles before you let anyone look at it. I’ve never seen you bleed for a flower.”

Zhao reached for the next stem.

Chen Si watched a moment longer. Then he turned to Elowen with a small, polite bow.

“Mrs. Zhao. I’d like to buy flowers for my wife. Our anniversary’s on Saturday. I’d like to be the first to order.”

“What does she like?”

“Everything expensive.” He thought. “And whatever you’d never put in an arrangement for her. She’ll want to know why.”

Elowen almost smiled.

“Peonies. Out of season. Gold ribbon. And one carnation in the middle.”

“Why the carnation?”

“So she has something to complain about. She’ll enjoy it more.”

“A carnation. For Aurelia.” He seemed to be picturing it. “She’ll throw it at me.”

“Probably. Then she’ll keep it in a glass on her dressing table for a week and tell everyone how cheap you are.”

Chen Si looked at her like she’d made a chess move he hadn’t seen coming.

“Yes.” Slowly. “She will.” To Zhao: “Your wife understands my wife better than I do.”

“They went to school together.”

“So I keep hearing.” Chen Si picked his coffee back up. Then he looked at Zhao’s hands again and the smile went away. “Zhendong. A word.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They went out onto the pavement. Zhao still had the apron on. He’d forgotten. Two women with shopping bags slowed right down to look.

Chen Si waited until they’d gone past.

“Qiu Wen’s been asking questions. About the shop. What time she opens. Who drives the van now.”

“Let him ask.”

“He’s angry. His brother’s hands are still bad.”

“Good.”

“He’s quiet, Zhendong. Angry and quiet. I don’t like it.”

Zhao looked back through the window. She was at the bench with her head down, re-cutting a stem he’d cut badly. Fixing it without saying anything.

“If he comes near her, I’ll put him somewhere nobody finds him.”

“I know you will.” Chen Si turned his cup round in his hand. “That’s not why I came out here.”

Zhao waited.

“You’re in an apron. You’ve bled on two hundred roses. You look happier than I’ve seen you since we were fifteen.” A pause. “I’d like to know who this woman is. And how she did it.”

Zhao thought about it. About hands over his on a stem. Loose. You’re not fighting it.

“She showed me how to hold them.”

Chen Si looked at him for a long moment.

“Then teach me,” he said. “Aurelia keeps handing my roses back and telling me they’re not good enough.”

Zhao laughed.

Out loud. In the street. Head back. The two women with the shopping bags turned round and stared. Chen Si put his hand on his brother’s shoulder, briefly, and took it away again, and didn’t say anything about it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Inside, Elowen had watched the whole thing through the glass. She couldn’t hear a word. She’d seen Chen Si say something short and Zhao shake his head. Something longer, and Zhao look away down the street. And then the laugh.

She’d never heard him laugh like that. Not in daylight. Not with his whole chest.

He came back in still half smiling.

“What did he say?”

He picked up the stripper and a rose.

“He asked if I was all right.”

“And?”

“I said yes.” Strip. Into the bucket. “He wants lessons. Aurelia keeps giving his roses back.”

Elowen laughed so hard she had to sit down on the stool. His stool. The egg stool.

“You laughed at THAT?”

“You’re laughing at that.”

“I’m laughing at you. You’re in an apron.”

He looked down at himself. At ELOWEN’S across his chest. He’d forgotten again.

“Hm.”

He didn’t take it off.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her phone went eleven minutes after Chen Si’s car pulled away.

“Is it true?”

“Good morning, Aurelia.”

“Is it TRUE? My husband just rang me from the car. He never rings me from the car. He said, and I quote, Zhendong is wearing an apron with your enemy’s name on it.”

Elowen looked across the shop. Zhendong was wearing an apron with her name on it. He was frowning at a thorn.

“It’s my apron! I’m allowed to put my name on my own apron.”

“Send me a photo.”

“No.”

“Elowen. Lin Elowen. I’ve known you since we were fifteen and I have never once asked you for anything—”

“You asked me for flowers last month.”

“That was business. This is my soul.” A pause. Then, much too casually: “Also, what did he order? For Saturday?”

“Who?”

“Don’t do that. My husband. What did he order?”

“That’s between me and my customer.”

“I’ll pay you to tell me.”

“No.”

“I’ll pay you triple…”

“Goodbye, Aurelia.”

She hung up. The phone buzzed again instantly. She turned it face down on the counter.

Zhao was watching her from the bench.

“She wants a photo,” Elowen said.

He looked down at the apron. He looked at the phone. Then he went back to his rose.

“No.”

“Thank you.”

“She’d frame it,” he said. “At New Year. Over the table.”

He wasn’t wrong. That was the terrible thing. Aurelia absolutely would.

The phone buzzed a third time. Elowen picked it up and read it.

Aurelia: I KNOW IT’S PEONIES. HE ALWAYS SAYS PEONIES.

Elowen: wrong

Aurelia: WHAT. WHAT ELSE IS THERE

She put the phone in the drawer under the till and shut it, and felt better than she had all week.

✦ ✦ ✦

They finished the four hundred with nine minutes to spare.

She sat him down on the stool and went over his hands with tweezers and antiseptic and a little torch. One hand, then the other. The way Mama had gone over hers when she was small and had played in the rose buckets. She found six more thorns. She took them out one at a time. He watched her do it and didn’t move a muscle.

“Hold still!”

“I am still.”

“You’re breathing.”

“I’ll stop.”

“Don’t you dare stop!”

When she’d finished she put a plaster on the worst one, on his thumb. The shop was empty. The sign on the door said CLOSED for nine more minutes. So she lifted his hand and kissed the plaster.

He looked at her.

“Tomorrow I’ll be faster.”

“Tomorrow you’re wearing gloves. And you don’t have to hold everything like Old Zhao’s watching.”

He sat there with his hand still in hers.

“No,” he said. “I’m learning from you now.”

Then he used the hand she was holding to pull her in, off her feet and onto his knee on the stool, and kissed her. Not careful. Not even slightly. One hand spread wide on her back, the other in her hair, until her pen rolled off the counter and hit the floor and she forgot what day it was. When he let her go there were four minutes left on the sign. He was looking at her mouth like he was working out whether four minutes was enough.

“Open the shop.” Low. “Before I don’t let you.”

She got off his knee with her face on fire and turned the sign round. OPEN.

The first customer of the day walked in and found a pink-cheeked florist behind the counter. And a very large man in a very short green apron, sweeping thorns into a dustpan. One corner at a time.

“Is he… staff?” the customer whispered.

Elowen wrapped her tulips.

“He’s my husband.”

From the corner, without turning round, Zhao said, “Staff.”

chapters.title: The Rare Flower He Should Not Have Bought
chapters.desc: She reads him a paragraph about the rarest camellia in the world. Three weeks later the hill it grows on is in her name.
chapters.epigraph: “There are two in the world. One in London. One in New Zealand. Everyone says there might be a third.”
chapters.content:
It started with a magazine.

She took three. A trade one for florists, all wholesale prices and new chrysanthemums. A Japanese one about ikebana she couldn’t read but liked looking at. And a British gardening quarterly that cost a fortune to import, which she read in the bath, one article a night, like a novel. On a Sunday at the end of summer she brought it to the dinner table. Which she did not allow. But he was reading a shipping report over his soup, which she also did not allow, so tonight the rule was off. Nobody had said so. They’d both just looked at each other’s reading and said nothing.

“Listen to this.”

He looked up.

“There’s a camellia called Middlemist’s Red.”

She turned the page round. A flower so full and so deep a pink it was nearly a rose. Petal laid over petal in perfect circles.

“A man called John Middlemist took it to England in 1804. And then where it came from, it just… vanished. Every plant. Now there are two known in the whole world. One in a glasshouse in London. One in a garden in New Zealand.”

“Two.”

“Two. But there’s always been a rumour one survived over here. In an old garden. Or a temple. Or on a tea estate in the Greenstone hills.”

She read on.

“A botanist went looking in the nineties and found one on an estate that might be it. Might. The owner wouldn’t let anyone take a cutting to test it. He said the plant was older than his family and it wasn’t for sale.”

She put the magazine down.

“My mother had a picture of it on the kitchen wall. Cut out of a calendar.” She smiled at her soup. “She said it was the rarest flower in the world. She said rare things should be left where they are, because the minute somebody tries to own them, they die.”

She went back to her soup. He finished his soup, and his shipping report, and washed his bowl.

She forgot about it.

He didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went up to bed. He went into the bathroom and took the magazine off the edge of the bath. There was a coffee ring on the cover. Hers. She put her cup on everything.

He read the article standing up. Then sitting on the closed toilet lid, because his legs wanted to. Page forty. The last paragraph. The one she hadn’t read out.

Mr. Wen, now in his eighties and in poor health, has said his children intend to sell the estate after his death. Two developers have already made offers for the land. It is not known what would become of the plant.

He read it four times. The minute somebody tries to own them, they die.

He went down to the kitchen and rang a lawyer at midnight. The lawyer said a great many things about land-use rights and families and time. Zhao listened to about a third of them.

“Find out who the developers are.”

“Mr. Zhao, it’s—”

“Then find out tomorrow.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first developer wanted a golf course. Bao went to see him. Bao took a box of mooncakes. He stayed an hour and talked about his wife’s knees. By the end of the hour the developer had decided golf was a dying sport.

The second developer wanted holiday villas. He was harder. He had friends. He told Zhao on the phone that he’d heard of him, and wasn’t impressed, and there were laws.

Zhao went to see him himself. He didn’t bring a box of anything. He sat in the man’s nice office in a chair that was too small and looked at him. He looked at the photographs on the desk. The man’s son at a university abroad. The man’s boat. He picked up the photograph of the boat and looked at it for a while.

“Nice boat.”

“What do you want?”

“The hill.”

“I’ve made an offer. It’s a fair—”

“Withdraw it.”

“Or what?”

Zhao put the photograph back. Exactly where it had been. Then he moved it two centimetres to the left, so the man would see it every day and know it had been moved.

“I’ll buy you a new boat,” he said. “If this one sinks.”

The man withdrew his offer by lunch.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Wen was harder than both developers put together. The lawyer rang. Mr. Wen said no. The lawyer rang again. No. The lawyer rang a third time and Mr. Wen hung up before he’d finished saying hello.

So Zhao rang him.

“Who’s this?”

A thin, crackly, furious old voice. Somewhere behind it, chickens.

“My name is Zhao Zhendong.”

“I know who you are. You’re the one with the lawyer. The answer’s still no.”

“I don’t want the flower.”

A pause. The chickens went on.

“Everybody wants the flower.”

“My wife looks at a picture of your flower the way I look at her.” He hadn’t planned to say it. It came out anyway. “I don’t want anyone to dig it up.”

The pause went on so long he thought the line had gone.

“That’s all?”

“That’s all.”

Another pause. Then a noise down the phone. Was the old man laughing? Coughing? Both.

“Send your lawyer back. But I want to meet her.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The envelope came to the shop three weeks after the soup. Wednesday. By courier.

Thick, cream, the same law firm Chen Si used for everything. Forty pages stapled together in tiny type. She read the first page at the counter with a bunch of eucalyptus in her other hand.

Then she put the eucalyptus down. Then she read it again.

A deed. Land-use rights. Twenty hectares of terraced hillside in the Greenstone hills. A hundred and sixty years of tea. A main house, two drying sheds, a walled garden. The Wen Family Tea Estate. Previous holder: Wen Guoliang, eighty-four. New holder:

Lin Elowen.

Not his name. Hers. Alone. Like on the sign over the door.

At the back, in an envelope inside the envelope, there was one photograph. A mossy garden wall. A dark glossy shrub against it, taller than a man. And half hidden in the leaves, three flowers. So full. So deep a pink. Nearly roses.

Xiao Pan looked up from his bouquet at the noise she made.

“Miss Lin? Are you okay? Are you sick? Should I get—”

She was already reaching for her phone.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was at the Docks. She went there. She didn’t take the bus. She took a taxi, which she never did. She walked past Bao at the door without a word and up the stairs into the long bare office. Zhao was at the whiteboard with three men she didn’t know and a map of somewhere with a great many arrows.

All four turned round.

She held up the envelope.

“Out.”

To the men. His eyes stayed on her. They went fast. One of them left his coffee.

The door shut. She walked to the desk and put the envelope down on it, very precisely. The way she’d once put down three pages of terms.

“You bought a mountain.”

“A hill.” He didn’t move. “The house needs a roof. The tea’s good. Mr. Wen says the oolong off the top terraces won a prize in 1987—”

“Zhendong.”

He stopped.

Her hands were shaking. Was it anger? Something else? She pressed them flat on the desk.

“You can’t do this. You can’t buy me things like this. I told you about a flower. A flower. In a magazine. And three weeks later there’s a deed on my counter with my name on it, and an old man’s sold his family’s land for… how much? How much did you pay him?”

He told her. She sat down in the chair in front of the desk. Her legs had stopped working.

“That’s more than Baba’s whole business!”

“It’s less than two containers.”

“That’s NOT the point.”

“Then what’s the point?”

He came round the desk. He didn’t touch her. He crouched beside the chair so his eyes were level with hers.

“Tell me what I did wrong. I want to understand.”

He meant it. He wasn’t defending himself. He looked at her like he’d looked at the roses that first morning. A man who’d picked something up the wrong way and wanted to be shown.

“My mother said rare things should be left where they are. The minute somebody tries to own them, they die.” Her voice wobbled. “And you went and bought it. Like a car. Like the house. Like…”

“Like you?”

She stopped. Down in the warehouse a forklift beeped.

He reached past her and picked something up off the desk. Her magazine. Coffee ring and all.

“You took that from the bathroom?”

“Page forty.” He opened it and gave it to her. “Last paragraph. You didn’t read that bit out.”

She read it. Two developers have already made offers. She looked up.

“A golf course. Holiday villas. They’d have flattened the garden in a week. Or somebody would’ve dug the plant up and sold it to a collector.” He took the magazine back. “The two in London and New Zealand have guards. Did you know? People have tried to steal cuttings.”

“I didn’t know.”

“So I bought the hill. Not the flower. The hill round it. So nobody else can.” He ticked it off on his scarred fingers. “Mr. Wen stays in the house as long as he lives. His grandson runs the tea. The garden doesn’t change. Nobody touches the plant without your permission. It’s in there. Page twelve.”

“Why’s it in my name?”

“I don’t know anything about flowers.” A shrug. “You do.”

She sat in the chair and looked at him. He’d read her magazine at midnight. He’d found the paragraph she hadn’t bothered to finish. And then he’d spent more than her father’s whole business so one old flower on a hill a thousand kilometres away could stay exactly where it was.

What did the developers say? She didn’t ask. She found she didn’t want to know. That probably said something about her. She’d think about it later.

“You could have asked me.” It came out tiny.

“You’d have said no.”

“Yes.”

“That’s why I didn’t ask.” The corner of his mouth moved. “Once. I promise. Next time I want to buy you a mountain, I’ll ask first.”

She laughed. Wet. She put her hand over her mouth.

“You’re impossible.”

He took her hand away from her mouth and held it, thumb on the heavy ring.

“Is it real? The plant? Is it really Middlemist’s Red?”

“Don’t know. Mr. Wen won’t let anyone test it. He says it was his grandfather’s grandfather’s, and that’s good enough.” He looked at her. “He says the new owner can test it if she likes. But he wants to meet her first.”

“Meet me?”

“He wants to see the face of a woman a man would buy a mountain for.” Straight face. Not a flicker.

She stood up out of the chair. He was still crouched beside it. It put his face exactly at the height of her hands. So she took it in both of them, stubble rough on her palms, and kissed him.

He made a surprised noise into her mouth. Then he came up off his heels to meet her, one hand on the chair, one at her waist. He kissed her back until she was leaning on the desk and the deed was sliding off it onto the concrete. Who cared about the deed? His mouth went soft and then not soft at all, and his hand closed in the back of her shirt like somebody might try to take her out of the room.

The door opened. One of the three men stood there. He’d come back for his coffee. Zhao didn’t lift his head. He lifted one hand off her waist and pointed at the door.

The man went out again without his coffee and shut it very carefully behind him.

“You’re still impossible,” she said, against his mouth.

“Hm.”

He kissed one corner of her mouth, and the other. Then he bent and picked the deed up off the floor and put it back in her hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stayed for the rest of the meeting. She hadn’t meant to. He’d simply pulled out a second chair beside his own. The three men came back in. They looked at her. At him. At the chair.

“My wife.”

They nodded at her. Very politely. One of them was sweating. She sat. She understood about one word in four. Routes. Weights. A port she’d never heard of. Halfway through, without looking away from the map, he took her hand off the arm of the chair and kissed her knuckles. Once. Then he put it back where it had been and went on talking about a ship.

The man who’d forgotten his coffee looked at the ceiling for the rest of the meeting.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she couldn’t sleep.

She lay in the big bed with the photograph on the pillow and looked at it in the light from the Docks. She thought about the calendar picture on Mama’s kitchen wall. Gone yellow. Curling at the corners. She’d eaten breakfast under it every morning of her childhood.

He slept in her bed now. Most nights. Some nights he still came in late, sat down outside the door out of habit, and she had to go out and fetch him in. He was asleep on his back with one arm flung over his head. Asleep, he looked about nineteen.

I didn’t buy it to own it.

Like you?

She put her hand on his chest, over his heart.

“I’ll go,” she whispered. “To the hill. I want to see it.”

He was asleep. Obviously.

“Booked the tickets.” Eyes shut. “Friday. Two seats. The hills are very wet in September. Bring boots.”

She hit him in the chest with the photograph. He laughed, low and sleepy. He pulled her down on top of him, photograph and all.

“You were AWAKE.”

“Hm.”

“How long have you been awake?”

“Since I’ll go.”

She laughed into his neck until her eyes were wet. The photograph got crushed. She’d have to flatten it under the dictionary in the morning.

She didn’t care.

chapters.title: The Estate in the Rain
chapters.desc: An old tea estate, a man who won't sell his flower, a shooting lesson on a wet terrace, and two days of rain with the road washed out.
chapters.epigraph: “Rare things should be left where they are.”
chapters.content:
The Greenstone hills were green in a way the city never managed. Three hours on a plane. Four more in the car, up a road that got narrower and steeper and wetter every kilometre, until they were crawling along a ledge cut into the mountain with tea falling away below in dark neat terraces. Like stairs for a giant. Mist in the valleys. Rain since the airport.

Elowen didn’t say a word for the last hour. Her face was nearly on the glass. At the bottom of the estate road, a car was parked under a tree. Bao stood beside it with two other men. He lifted one hand as they went past.

“You brought guards.”

“Bao likes tea.” Zhao kept his eyes on the road. “He asked to come.”

“Bao asked to come.”

“Hm.”

“To a mountain. In the rain. For tea.”

“He likes it very much.”

She looked at him sideways. He drove. The air coming through the vents smelled of wet leaves and woodsmoke, and she was too happy to argue about anything. Even Bao.

✦ ✦ ✦

The house at the top was old and low and grey, round a courtyard. The tiled roof sagged in the middle like a tired horse. One end of it was falling down. The other end had smoke coming out of the chimney. Mr. Wen was waiting under the eaves.

Tiny. Bent. A face like a walnut. A long white wisp of beard. A walking stick made from a twisted tea branch. Beside him stood a young man of about twenty in a rain jacket, already wincing. Grandsons always know. Elowen got out into the rain.

The old man looked her over. Her face. Her hair coming loose in the wet. Her muddy boots. The heavy gold ring on her middle finger. Then Zhao came round the car, and the old man’s eyebrows went all the way up into his hat.

“Hm.”

His grandson shut his eyes.

“So.” A thick southern accent. She had to concentrate. “You’re the one.”

“Sorry?”

“The one he bought the mountain for.” The stick pointed at Zhao, who’d come to stand behind her shoulder with rain running off his hair. “His lawyer rang. I said no. Three times! Then he rang. And you know what he said?”

“Grandpa—”

“He said, My wife looks at a picture of your flower the way I look at her. I don’t want anyone to dig it up.” The stick waggled. “That’s all. Not one word about money. So I said yes.”

Elowen turned round and looked at her husband. Zhao was studying the roof. Hard. Like he was going to be tested on it later.

“Grandpa,” the grandson said faintly. “Please.”

“What? It’s true.” Mr. Wen set off across the courtyard, stick first. “Come. See it before the light goes. Then we eat. Then you tell me you want to test it with your machines, and I tell you no.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The walled garden was up a flight of mossy steps behind the house. The wall was taller than Zhao. The gate had gone silver with age. Mr. Wen pushed it open with the stick.

Inside it was quiet. The trees broke the rain up. Herbs gone wild. A stone basin full of water and floating leaves. A pomelo tree. A bench. And against the far wall, dark and glossy and dripping, taller than a man, the camellia.

It was in flower. That was impossible. Camellias flowered in late winter. She’d sold them every February for five years.

“It does that sometimes.” The old voice, behind her. “When it likes someone.”

Five flowers. Maybe six. Half hidden in the leaves. Each one exactly like the photo. Exactly like the yellow calendar picture on Mama’s kitchen wall. So many petals laid over each other, so deep a pink that in the grey light it almost glowed. A rose that wasn’t a rose. A flower that had vanished from half the world and survived, maybe, here. On one hill. Behind one wall. Because one family wouldn’t sell it.

She walked across the wet grass and stopped in front of it. She didn’t touch it. She just stood there with rain running down her face, for so long that Mr. Wen sat down on the bench and his grandson went for an umbrella. Zhao stayed by the gate.

When she finally turned round she was crying.

“My mother…”

She couldn’t finish. He crossed the garden. He stood beside her and didn’t say anything. He tilted his umbrella over her until the whole of it was over her head and his left shoulder was soaking. She leaned against his arm. He put it round her.

On the bench, under his grandson’s umbrella, Mr. Wen watched them.

“Hm,” he said again. It sounded different this time.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was bamboo shoot soup, cured pork, greens from the garden, and a pot of the prize-winning oolong. Bao drank it with his eyes shut like a man in church.

“Well?” Mr. Wen narrowed his eyes at her. “Do you want to test it?”

“No.”

“No? Don’t you want to know?”

She turned her cup in her hands.

“If it’s real, it’s the rarest flower in the world. Everyone will want it. Someone will try to steal it. We’ll need walls and cameras and guards.” She looked at Bao. Bao looked at his tea. “And if it isn’t, it’s a beautiful old camellia your grandfather’s grandfather planted, and everyone leaves it alone. Either way it stays in the garden. Either way it’s the same flower. The test doesn’t change anything that matters.”

Mr. Wen looked at her for a long time. Then he turned to Zhao.

“You chose well.”

Zhao put his spoon down.

“She chose.”

Something in how he said it made Elowen look up. But he’d gone back to his soup. His face told her nothing at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when she’d gone to wash, the old man poured Zhao more tea and didn’t let go of the pot.

“She chose, you said.”

“Yes.”

“You said it like a man reading his own sentence.” Mr. Wen sniffed. “Sixty-one years I was married. I know what that sounds like.”

Zhao drank his tea.

“She married me for her father. It’s not a secret.”

“Hm.” The old man put the pot down. “She cried in my garden. In front of you. Do you know how many women cry in front of a man they bought?”

“She didn’t buy me.”

“Not many. That’s how many.”

Zhao didn’t answer. The old man poked him in the knee with the stick, quite hard.

“You’re an idiot. A good one.” Another poke. “Go to bed.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning the rain stopped for two hours, and he taught her to shoot. She hadn’t asked. After breakfast he took a canvas bag out of the car and walked her down to the bottom terrace. An old drying shed stood against the hillside there with nothing behind it but rock. He set six empty tins along a fence rail.

“No,” Elowen said. “I’m a florist.”

“You live in a house with fourteen locks and a steel room in the basement.” He unzipped the bag. A small black pistol. Ear defenders. “The code gets you into the room. This is for if you can’t get to the room.”

She looked at it. She thought about Maartens’ hand on her knee. How her body had walked off and left her sitting there with a lychee. She held out her hand.

He was a good teacher. That surprised her. Patient. He never raised his voice. He showed her how to stand. How to hold it. How to check it was safe. All from one step behind her shoulder. He didn’t touch her once. The first shot went into the hillside a metre left of the tins. The noise was enormous. She dropped the gun on the grass.

He picked it up. Checked it. Put it back in her hands.

“Again.”

Ten shots. Nothing. And he was still a step behind her, keeping that exact distance, and she could hear in his voice what the distance was costing him.

She lowered the gun and looked round.

“I showed you how to hold the roses. Show me.”

He went still. Then he stepped in behind her, his chest against her back, and closed his hands over hers. The way she’d closed hers over his at the workbench.

“Loose.” Low, by her ear. “Let it move. You’re not fighting it.”

“That’s my line!”

“Hm.” She felt it through her back. “I listened.”

Her next shot went a metre wide. Her entire body had forgotten what it was doing. Not a word. He didn’t move away either. Twenty shots, two tins. Forty, five. Her arms ached and her ears rang under the defenders and her hands smelled of metal.

On the forty-first she hit the last tin dead centre. It spun off the rail and bounced down into the tea bushes.

“YES! Did you see that? Did you SEE—”

Behind her, he laughed. She turned round with the gun pointed at the ground, the way he’d taught her. He was standing back with his hands in his pockets, looking at her. Proud. And something hungrier underneath.

“What?”

“Nothing.” He took the gun, checked it, put it away. “You didn’t shut your eyes. Not once.” He zipped the bag. Then he straightened up and looked at her properly. Wet terrace. Hair coming down. Red cheeks. Hands still shaking from the noise. “Look at you.”

He didn’t seem to have anything to add to that. He dropped the bag on the grass and took her face in both hands and kissed her. Right there on the open terrace. Hard and deep, like he’d been holding it in for forty-one shots. Her ears were still ringing. She grabbed his wrists and kissed him back, and felt him smile against her mouth.

Up on the steps, Bao, who’d come to see what the noise was, turned round and went straight back up. The rain started again while he was still kissing her. He didn’t stop for that either.

✦ ✦ ✦

It didn’t stop for two days. The road washed out at the second bend. Mr. Wen’s grandson came back from looking at it soaked to the waist.

“Nobody’s going anywhere. The county will send a digger. Tuesday. If we’re lucky.”

“And if we’re not?”

“Thursday.”

They had the room at the end of the east wing. The only one where the roof didn’t leak. White walls. A wide old carved bed with a quilt that smelled of camphor. A charcoal brazier in the corner. A window full of grey cloud and the sound of water running everywhere, off the eaves, down the steps, down the hill. No electricity in the east wing. The grandson brought candles.

She came in from the courtyard with her hair dripping. He sat her on the edge of the bed and dried it with a towel, slow, section by section, like it was a job that mattered. Then he knelt to light the brazier. The charcoal caught. Red light came up over his face from below.

She’d never been anywhere with him where nobody could reach them. No signal. She’d checked. No road. No Docks. No brokers at midnight. No Qiu brothers, no Baba, no market at four. Nothing either of them had to ask, or prove, or wait for.

Just a room. A fire. Rain.

“Zhendong.”

He looked up. Nothing else. She didn’t need to. He got up and crossed the room. She reached up, took his hand, and pulled him down.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first time had been a question, asked six times. He’d counted. This time it was slow because they had nowhere to be. She undressed him by the brazier with the red light on his skin, and this time she didn’t ask about the scars. She knew them now. She kissed them in order, like a path she’d walked before. He stood with his head bowed and his hands in her hair and let her. When she got to the long one on his ribs he said her name and his voice cracked straight down the middle.

Then he turned her round. Hands on her shoulders. Gentle. Until her back was to him and she was facing the fire. He took her hair down first. Every pin, one at a time, into his palm. When it fell he gathered it in one hand and moved it over her shoulder.

Then he put his mouth on the back of her neck. She gasped. Who knew? Who knew about the back of her neck?

He found out about it for her. Slowly. Every centimetre. Warm and open, his stubble scraping, until she reached back blind and grabbed his thigh to stay upright. His hands came round her from in front and undid her shirt, button by button, his chin on her shoulder, watching his own hands do it in the red light. When it was open he spread both palms flat on her stomach and held her back against him. He breathed into her hair.

“I can feel your heart. From here.”

“It’s going very fast.”

“I know.” His hands moved up. “I’m going to make it go faster.”

She laughed. It turned into something else halfway through.

✦ ✦ ✦

He laid her down on the camphor quilt and took his time. More time than she’d known a person could take. He learned her the way he’d learned roses. Slowly. All of it. The inside of her elbow. The back of her knee. The soft skin inside her hip, where just his breath made her whole body go tight. Every place that made her breath catch, he went back to. When she reached for him he caught both her wrists in one hand and held them over her head, gently.

“Not yet.” Against her stomach.

She could have killed him.

“Zhendong.”

“Not yet.”

“I’m asking!”

He lifted his head. In the candlelight his eyes were black and his mouth was soft and he was smiling. The smile almost nobody got.

“I know. Page two, line six.” His thumb moved on her wrist. “I want to hear you ask properly.”

So she asked properly. She told him exactly what she wanted. Voice shaking. Words she’d never said out loud to anyone in her life. She watched them land on him one by one. His breathing changed. His hand tightened on her wrists. Then let go.

“Again,” he said. Hoarse.

She said it again. He stopped making her wait.

At some point she opened her eyes. He was watching her face in the candlelight with a look so naked it scared her more than anything she’d ever seen him do with a knife.

“What?” A whisper.

He shook his head. He put his mouth on her throat, on her pulse, and stayed there. She felt him tremble all the way through. She wrapped herself round him and held on. Rain on the roof. Charcoal ticking. The whole slow world went narrow and bright, and broke. Her first. Then him. His name in her mouth. Hers in his.

✦ ✦ ✦

Much later, she lay across his chest under the quilt with her chin on her hands and looked at him. One of his arms was behind his head. The other was moving slowly up and down her bare back.

“At dinner. Yesterday.” She watched his face. “Mr. Wen said you chose well. And you said she chose.”

His hand stopped.

“What did you mean?”

The rain filled the gap. She could feel his heart under her chin. Slow. Heavy.

“That you walked into my office,” he said finally. “Not me into yours.”

True. But there was something under it. Something bigger he wasn’t saying, like a stone under a quilt. She almost asked. She opened her mouth.

But his hand had started moving again. Slow. Warm. And she was so tired and so happy, happier than she’d been since she was a little girl eating breakfast under a yellow calendar picture. She didn’t want anything else in this room. Not one thing.

“I’m happy,” she said instead.

His hand stopped again.

“Here. Right now.” She put her cheek down on his chest. “I don’t think I’ve been happy since my mother died. Not like this. I didn’t even know I wasn’t. Until now.”

He pulled her up the length of him until her face was beside his on the pillow, wrapped both arms round her, and held on so hard she could barely breathe. She fell asleep like that.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stayed awake until the candles went out. I’m happy, she’d said. Here. Right now.

Happy. She hadn’t said the other word.

He lay in the dark with her breath on his neck and told himself it didn’t matter. Rain on the roof. The old man’s stick in his knee. Do you know how many women cry in front of a man they bought?

He wanted to believe it so badly his teeth hurt.

He held her tighter. He didn’t sleep.

chapters.title: Lin Jian Comes to Dinner
chapters.desc: Her father comes to dinner at last. Zhao cooks her mother's fish for him, and Lin Jian tells him he was only ever the price.
chapters.epigraph: “He’s frightened of you. It looks the same in my family.” — Elowen, buttering toast
chapters.content:
“He’s coming on Saturday.”

Zhao put his coffee down.

“Who?”

“My father. For dinner.” Elowen buttered her toast. “I asked him and he said no. I asked again and he said no. Then I said I’d stop coming to Sunday lunch, and he said yes.”

“You blackmailed your father.”

“I negotiated with my father. It’s a family skill.”

Seven months. Seven months married, and Baba hadn’t once set foot in the house on the hill. Every Sunday she went home to the Walled City for lunch, alone, and every Sunday he asked how the shop was. Never once how her husband was. He worked for Zhao the way he always had. Containers, officers, reports. And somehow he was never in a room with him longer than it took to hand over a folder.

The house had changed in seven months. She couldn’t have said when. Rugs in the hall. Books on the shelves. The dining chairs out of their plastic. In June, men had knocked through the wall behind the kitchen and built a glass room onto the south side. Slatted benches. A deep stone sink. A tap that ran warm.

“What’s it for?” she’d asked.

“Your plants.”

That was the whole explanation. The orchids and the herbs and the sad fern had moved in that afternoon. She’d stood in there among them for half an hour with the door shut, doing nothing, because nobody had ever built her a room before.

Zhao was looking at his coffee.

“He hates me.”

“He’s frightened of you. In my family it looks the same.” She put the toast on his plate. “Seven o’clock. Wear the blue shirt. Don’t bring a gun to the table.”

“I never bring a gun to the table.”

“You brought one to our wedding.”

“That was a registry office. Chen Si was there. Somebody had to. Chen Si never carries, and the man on the registry door had a—”

She leaned across the table and kissed him. Mostly to make him stop. He stopped. He tasted of coffee and he didn’t pull back. When she sat down again he was holding his cup halfway to his mouth like he’d forgotten what it was for.

“The blue shirt.”

He put the cup down at last. “The blue shirt.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday night she came home and the kitchen smelled of ginger.

Burnt ginger.

He was at the stove with his sleeves rolled up and her mother’s recipe card propped against the salt. The card. The one in Mama’s writing, gone soft at the corners, that lived in the drawer by the rice. There were three fish on the counter. Two of them had clearly been through something.

“What are you doing?”

“Practising.”

“That’s my mother’s card.”

“I asked Xiao Pan where you kept it.” He turned the fish. Some of it stayed in the pan. “He said the drawer by the rice. He said not to tell you he told me.”

“He’s dead!”

“Hm.”

She came and stood beside him. The third fish looked… almost right. Almost.

“You’re cooking Mama’s fish. For Baba.”

“He’ll know it’s hers.” He didn’t look at her. “I want him to know I can make it.”

She stood there with her bag still on her shoulder and couldn’t say anything at all. So she took the spatula out of his hand.

“Lower heat. You’re frying it, not punishing it.”

“It started it!”

She laughed so hard she had to put the bag down.

“Again,” she said. “From the start. And this time, when it sizzles, you don’t stab it.”

“It was looking at me.”

“It’s a fish, Zhendong. It’s dead. It’s not looking at anyone.”

He started again. From the start. He didn’t stab it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday, Lin Jian arrived at six fifty-eight. Two minutes early. In a car he drove himself.

He did that only when nobody else could be trusted to know where he was going. Nobody needed to know he’d driven to Zhao Zhendong’s house in his funeral suit to eat dinner.

He stopped at the bottom of the front steps and looked up. Concrete. Long windows. Cameras. The dogs came hurtling down the drive, skidded to a stop at his feet and sat, tails sweeping the gravel. Elowen had spent four months teaching them that people at the front door usually had food.

“They’ve got names now.” From the top step. “Dumpling and Noodle.”

Her father looked at the dogs. Then at her.

“Your mother named our first dog Mantou.”

He came up the steps.

She took his coat. She walked him down the hall. And halfway down the hall he stopped.

The lemon tree stood at the end of the corridor, in front of the long window, where Zhao had put it the first day. It had grown. New shoots in the summer. Five lemons on it now, small and green, the leaves shining in the light off the Docks.

Lin Jian stood in the arms dealer’s hallway and looked at his dead wife’s lemon tree.

He walked up to it and touched one leaf with a fingertip.

“Twenty years she kept this.” He didn’t turn round. “On the balcony. It never had more than three lemons. Never.”

“It likes the window.”

Zhao was in the kitchen doorway. Blue shirt. Hands at his sides. Her father turned and looked at him. He looked back.

“He waters it on Thursdays,” Elowen said. “I forgot once and it nearly died. Now he has an alarm on his phone.”

Lin Jian’s eyebrows went up and stayed up.

“Once a week. It doesn’t like the cold.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was bad.

Nobody shouted. Nobody threw anything. It was bad like a long drive with the radio off. Every minute took ten.

Fish with ginger. Red-braised pork, because it was Baba’s favourite. Green beans. Lotus root soup. Elowen talked the whole time. The shop. Xiao Pan’s hands getting stronger. Raiden’s new job drawing buildings in the south. Her father answered in single words. Zhao didn’t answer at all.

Zhao’s arm lay along the back of her chair. Not touching her. Just there. Her father looked at it twice.

She gave her father the fish belly. He gave it back.

She gave it to Zhao. Zhao looked at it for a moment and put it in her father’s bowl.

Lin Jian looked at the fish belly, back in his bowl for the second time. His mouth pulled tight.

“Her mother did that.” To Zhao. Abruptly. His first full sentence of the night. “Every night. Gave me the belly. Twenty years.”

“She told me.”

“Did she tell you I gave it back? Every night?”

“Yes.”

Lin Jian picked it up with his chopsticks. He held it there. Then he put it in his daughter’s bowl.

“Eat. You’re too thin.” Rough. “Doesn’t he feed you?”

“He feeds me. He makes breakfast at four in the morning.”

“Four?”

“The market.” Zhao, not looking up.

Lin Jian ate a piece of the fish. He chewed. He stopped chewing.

He looked at his plate for a long time.

“Who made this?”

Elowen opened her mouth. Zhao got there first.

“I did.”

Her father didn’t say anything. He ate the rest of it. Every piece. When he’d finished he put his chopsticks down very straight beside the bowl.

“Too much ginger.”

“Yes.”

“She used too much ginger too.”

Elowen had to get up and fetch the tea.

✦ ✦ ✦

She left them alone. On purpose.

It was a risk. But she knew her father. Whatever he’d come to say, he’d never say it with her in the room, and it had been sitting in him for seven months like a stone.

She filled the kettle slowly. She stood by the stove and listened.

Nothing. Then Baba. Low.

“She did it for me.”

The kettle began to tick.

“You know that.” His officer voice. The one for men who’d changed the price. “Whatever she tells you. The dogs. The tree. Four in the morning. She married you because she was afraid of what you’d do to me. She put herself between us. That’s my daughter. She’s been doing it since she was seven.”

Nothing from Zhao. Was he even breathing in there? Was he looking at Baba, or at the table?

“So remember it. Every day. When you look at her. She didn’t choose you. She chose me. You were only the price she paid.”

The kettle boiled. It screamed. She didn’t move.

In the dining room, nothing. For so long.

Then Zhao. Even.

“I know.”

That was all. Two words. Why wasn’t he angry? Why wasn’t he anything? No anger at all. The way he’d said yes at the registry when the clerk asked if he married of his own free will.

She took the kettle off the heat with a hand that didn’t feel like hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

She poured three cups. She talked about the weather. Her father drank his in four swallows and said he had to go.

On the front steps, in the dark, with the dogs sniffing his shoes, he turned.

“Elowen. Are you all right? Truly?”

Funeral suit. Grey hair. His hands weren’t shaking tonight. First time in years.

“You shouldn’t have said that to him.”

He went still.

“I heard you. From the kitchen. Every word.”

“It’s the truth.”

“It was the truth!” Her voice cracked. She made it stop. “Seven months ago it was the truth. You don’t know what it is now. You never asked. You come to my house for the first time and you see my mother’s tree with five lemons on it, you see he’s got an alarm for it, he made you her fish, Baba, and you still go in there and tell him…”

She stopped. She was going to cry. Not on the front steps. Not in front of her father.

Lin Jian looked at her in the light from the door.

“And what is it now?”

She opened her mouth.

Nothing came. Not here. Not to Baba. Not before she’d said it to the man inside.

Her father saw her face. His own fell. All at once he looked old. And sorry.

“Ah.” Barely a sound. “Ah, Elowen.”

He touched her cheek, the way he had when she was small. Then he went down the steps to his car, and the dogs walked him to the gate, and he drove himself away.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao was in the basement.

He was at the bench under the hanging lamp with a rifle in pieces on the cloth. He wasn’t cleaning it. His hands were flat on the wood on either side of the pieces, and he was looking at them.

She came down the stairs. He didn’t turn round.

“He was wrong.”

“He was right.” Eyes on the rifle. “You did choose him. You told me so. In my office.”

“That was seven months ago. Things change.”

He picked up one piece. Put it down.

“I know.”

The same I know. Flat. Finished. A man agreeing to a price he’d already decided to pay.

She came and stood beside him. It was right there in her throat. The word she couldn’t say on the steps. Huge and terrifying. It’s not true any more. I didn’t choose you then. I choose you now. I—

He looked up.

He wasn’t angry. Not even hurt, exactly. He looked like a man who’d heard something he’d always known, said out loud by someone else, and was putting it away somewhere safe. The way he put guns away. So it would never go off by accident.

If she said it now, he wouldn’t believe her. She could see that. He’d think it was because of Baba. Because she felt sorry for him. Because she was a woman who stood between people and the things that hurt them, and had been since she was seven.

He’d think it was another contract.

So she didn’t say it. She put her arms round him from behind and pressed her face between his shoulder blades.

“Come to bed.”

After a while, his hand came up and covered both of hers.

“The blue shirt.” He was still looking at the rifle. “Was it right?”

It was so small. So careful. From a man who’d just been told he was the price of her. She laughed into his back before she could stop it, and the laugh came out wet.

“It was right. You looked very handsome. He noticed. He hated it.”

“Hm.” She felt his back loosen. One centimetre. “Good.”

“And the fish.”

“Too much ginger.”

“He ate every piece, Zhendong.”

He didn’t say anything to that. His thumb went over her knuckles. Once. Twice.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t wait for her to reach for him.

He kissed her at the bedroom door before she’d found the light switch. Hard. Both hands on her face. Then he walked her backwards to the bed and laid her down and didn’t let her look anywhere but at him. Slow and fierce at the same time. His hands holding her jaw. Her name, over and over, rough, like he was arguing with somebody who wasn’t in the room.

“Look at me.”

“I am looking at you.”

“Keep looking.”

She kept looking. Right to the end, when her eyes wanted to close and he wouldn’t let them, and she was saying his name and he was saying hers, and she couldn’t tell any more which of them was shaking.

Afterwards he held her so tight she could feel his heart through her back.

“Price or not,” he said into her hair. Low. Mostly to himself. “You’re mine now. I’m not giving you back.”

She lay in the dark with her eyes open.

Then ask me, she thought. Ask me why I stayed.

He didn’t ask.

She didn’t say it.

Neither of them slept.

chapters.title: The Shop Gets a New Floor
chapters.desc: Raiden puts a steel room under the tulips. Over the hole in her floor, Zhao tells her brother he loves her. She hears it from the doorway.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ve always wanted to put a bunker under a bucket of tulips. Is that strange? Don’t answer that.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
“Jie!”

Raiden kissed her on the cheek and dumped a roll of drawings on her workbench, right on top of a half-built wedding bouquet.

Monday. October. Behind him on the pavement: three builders, a van full of tools, and her little brother’s face doing the sunny, total innocence she’d learned to be scared of when he was ten.

“You look wonderful. Have you lost weight? Don’t answer that, it’s rude. I’m here to fix your floor.”

“There’s nothing wrong with my floor.”

“There is everything wrong with your floor.” He unrolled a drawing. “Concrete straight onto fill from 1964. No damp course. It’s cold, it’s cracked, you’ll have arthritis by forty.” Tap. “Also it doesn’t have a steel room under it with its own air supply and a hatch hidden under the second row of buckets.”

Elowen looked at the drawing. Then at her brother.

“Who asked you to do this?”

His eyes went huge. “Nobody! It was my idea. A gift. From a loving brother to his beloved sister.” A pause. “Who happens to be married to a man people shoot at.”

“Raiden.”

“Who rang me on Thursday at two in the morning and said, I quote, How long to build a room nobody can get into under a flower shop. Me: Who is this? Him: Your brother-in-law. Me: It’s two in the morning. Him: Yes. Click.”

Elowen shut her eyes.

“He didn’t tell me.”

“Course he didn’t tell you. You’d have said no.” Raiden rolled the drawing up. “He’s paying triple. I’ve already spent it. Move your roses.”

“And the landlord? You can’t put a steel room under somebody else’s building!”

Raiden gave her a look of deep, deep pity.

“Jie. Read your post.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The letter was at the bottom of the pile under the till. Same law firm as the deed to the hill. The building had changed hands in September. The shop, and the two flats upstairs where an old couple and a young schoolteacher lived. Her landlord had been about to sell to a man who built hotels. He’d sold to Lin Elowen instead.

She took it home and put it on the bench in the basement, in front of her husband.

“You said you’d ask first.”

“That was mountains.”

“Zhendong!”

“The hotel man wanted it empty by spring.” He didn’t pick the letter up. “Now nobody can put your rent up. Nobody can tell you to go.”

She’d paid that rent on the first of every month for five years. Never once late. She’d been prouder of it than of anything she owned.

So she didn’t argue. She worked out what the rent would have been, opened an account in the building’s name at her own bank, and paid it in on the first of every month. For the roof. For the pipes. For the old couple’s stairs.

He never asked about it. She never told him. Was that the most married thing either of them had ever done? Probably.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hotel man had come to the Docks in person. He’d already shaken hands with the landlord on a price. When the landlord changed his mind overnight, the hotel man came out to the long bare office with a lawyer and a lot of words about contracts.
