“Detective Song.” He took a small leather wallet out of his coat and showed her the badge like it was a bus ticket. “I’m not here officially.”

“You just showed me your badge.”

“So you’d know I was telling the truth about the not-officially part.” He put it away. He took a mint out of his pocket instead and unwrapped it. “Can we talk?”

Xiao Pan, at the counter, had gone the colour of printer paper.

“It’s fine. He grew up next door. He used to steal our persimmons.”

“Your sister threw them at me. The little one. From the top window.” He put the mint in his mouth. “Very good aim for a four-year-old.” He glanced at Xiao Pan. “He can stay. I won’t say anything he can’t hear.”

Xiao Pan did not look like a person who wanted to hear anything ever again.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t sit down. He stood by the roses with his hands in his coat pockets and told her things in a flat voice. Facts first. No adjectives.

“The notice isn’t the problem. Not here. Your husband’s got friends in the right offices. Chen Si made sure of that years ago. Nobody in this city’s going to arrest him because Lyon asked nicely.” He touched a petal. “The problem’s the report.”

“The UN panel.”

“You read it?”

“All two hundred pages.” Every night that week. In bed. While his phone rang. “It names eleven companies. Seven are his. It describes four shipments. It’s got photographs of crates in places I’ve never heard of.” She stopped. “It’s very detailed.”

“Too detailed.”

He looked at her properly.

“Panels like that work from seizures. Flight records. Paperwork. They don’t usually get the names of shell companies registered in back offices in this city. They don’t usually get the dates right.”

“So someone told them.”

“Someone told them a lot.” He crunched the mint. “And now every man your husband ever cheated or embarrassed knows two things. He can’t leave the country. And his buyers are nervous.”

“A wolf with a bad leg.”

“Yes.” He didn’t seem surprised she’d got there first. “Somebody wants him gone. And people like that don’t check who’s standing next to him when they try.”

A bus went past outside. The buckets shivered.

“Why are you telling me this?”

He was quiet for a bit. He looked at the roses, not at her.

“When I was eleven, my dad arrested a man who owed your dad money. Next morning there was a dead cat on our step. My mum cried all day.” He rolled the mint wrapper into a ball. “And that afternoon you came over the wall with a shoebox and a trowel. You buried it under our persimmon tree. You made a cross out of lolly sticks. You didn’t say anything. You were ten. You just did it and went home.”

She’d forgotten. She remembered now. The weight of the box. The cold earth under her nails.

“I owe you a cat. This is the cat.”

He turned to go. At the door he stopped with his hand on it.

“Page sixty-one. Footnote nine.” He didn’t turn round. “Look who registered the third company. Then tell your husband.”

The bell went.

Xiao Pan came slowly out from behind the counter.

“Miss Lin. You buried a cat?”

“It was a long time ago.”

“That’s so metal!”

“Buckets, Xiao Pan.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She found it that night, in bed, with the report on her knees.

Her phone was on four per cent. She went to plug it in at the wall and stopped. There was a charger on her side of the bed. Coiled up neatly. There hadn’t been one yesterday. There was one in the kitchen now, too. And the car.

He hadn’t said a word.

She plugged in. She turned to page sixty-one. Footnote nine. Tiny print.

Northgate Agricultural Holdings Ltd. was incorporated in this city in 2015. The original registering agent, a Mr. Kang Ji, is understood by the Panel to have provided substantial documentary assistance to its inquiries.

Kang.

She sat there and looked at the name.

The office at the Docks. Kang on the desk with his sunflower seeds. Her on the third step down, with Bao’s hand on her elbow, hearing it. A crack like a branch over a knee. Then again.

He won’t hold a pen again.

So Kang had found somebody to hold it for him.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took it down to the basement.

He was at the bench under the lamp, phone face down in front of him. He looked up when she came down, and he looked so tired. Shadows under his eyes like thumbprints. Like the day she first walked into his office.

She put the report on the bench, open at sixty-one, and put her finger on the footnote.

He read it.

He read it again. Nothing in his face moved. His hand on the bench closed into a fist and then lay flat.

“Song Wei Long.”

“He came to the shop. Not officially.”

“Bao told me.” He didn’t look up. “What did he want?”

“To give me back a cat.”

That made him look up.

“Long story. He’s a friend. He was warning me.” She sat on the stool next to him. “He says somebody wants you gone. And they won’t care who’s standing next to you.”

“He’s right.”

“I know he’s right.”

“Then you should—”

“Don’t.” She was already shaking her head. “Don’t tell me to shut the shop. Don’t tell me to go to Baba’s. Don’t tell me to go and sit on the mountain until it’s over.”

He was quiet.

“I was going to say take the gun. The small one. From the drawer. Keep it at the shop.”

Oh.

“Oh.”

“I know you won’t shut the shop.” The corner of his mouth moved. Too tired to finish being a smile. “You went to the market the morning we got married. You’re not going to hide because of a footnote.”

She looked at him. This hunted, wrecked man under a lamp in a room full of guns. Who knew her well enough not to ask her to run.

He looked back down at the page and turned it over. Was he even reading it? He was not.

“The detective. He sat on your wall. Eating ice lollies. Eliana told me.” He turned another page. “She says you were going to marry him. When you were nine.”

She stared at him.

Then, despite the footnote, despite everything, her mouth started to go.

“He cried when a bee stung him.”

“Good.”

It wasn’t quite a joke. That was what made her laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got up and stood behind him and put her hand on the back of his neck. He turned on the stool and pulled her in between his knees with both arms round her waist. Hard. He pressed his face into her ribs.

He held on like the report on the bench was a tide coming in.

“Kang. What will you do?”

“Nothing.”

She waited.

“He’s in a hospital in Singapore with a new name and a lawyer somebody else is paying for.” Muffled, against her. “I can’t reach him. Not with everyone watching.” A pause. “I should have killed him at the Docks. I didn’t. Because you were on the stairs.”

Her hand stopped in his hair.

“I’m not blaming you. I’m telling you so you know.” He breathed out against her pyjama top. “That was the choice. I made it. I’d make it again. But somebody’s going to pay for it. And I don’t know yet who.”

She stood in the basement with her hand on the back of her husband’s neck and the UN report open behind him. She’d been glad, that day at the Docks. Glad it was only his hands.

What was she glad of now? She didn’t know.

She took his face out of her ribs and tipped it up. He let her. She kissed him. Slowly. The way he’d kissed her down here the first night, with six numbers crushed in her fist.

He was so tired he didn’t kiss her back at first. Then he did. His arms went tight round her waist. He stood up off the stool without letting go and walked her backwards into the edge of the bench, and the report slid shut behind her.

“Not here.”

He said it against her mouth. With both hands already under her pyjama top. She laughed so hard she had to hold on to his shoulders.

“Not here? Zhendong… look where your hands are!”

He looked. He actually looked, like he was surprised to find them there.

Then he picked her up, the way he had the night of the typhoon, and carried her up the concrete stairs. He turned the light off behind them with his elbow. Kang’s footnote stayed down there in the dark.

✦ ✦ ✦

She fell asleep with her face in his neck.

He didn’t. He lay there and listened to her breathe until it went slow and even. Then he reached over her for his phone.

He’d had a file on Song Wei Long since the week of the registry. Two pages. Policeman’s son. Grew up next door to his wife. Honest, mostly. Clean enough to be a nuisance. Sat on her wall.

He opened it. At the bottom he added one line.

Cried at a bee.

Then he put the phone down, and put his arm back over her, and slept.

chapters.title: The Order She Wouldn’t Fill
chapters.desc: A man with a forgettable face orders two funeral wreaths with her husband’s name on the ribbon, and she rings the detective first. Zhao walks out on her for the first time, and comes back from Chen Si’s very late with an apology.
chapters.epigraph: “I should’ve rung you anyway. And trusted you to hear me say don’t.” — Elowen
chapters.content:
Afterwards, all she could give Wei Long was this. Grey jacket. Cigarettes. Cash.

“That’s it?”

“He had a face like a car park.”

“That’s the point of him.”

The man had come in on a Wednesday at eleven. The dead hour, between the office people and lunch. Middle-aged. Middle height. The kind of face you forgot while you were still looking at it.

“Two funeral wreaths. The big ones. White chrysanthemums, white lilies.”

She opened the order book. “Name for the ribbon?”

He told her.

Her pen had written the first character before her ears caught up with her hand.

She stopped.

He was smiling. Pleasant. The way men smile at waitresses.

“And the dedication. In deepest sympathy. Taken too soon.” He watched her not write it. “Deliver to Northgate Industrial Pumps. The Iron Docks. On the ninth.”

The ninth. Two weeks.

He put a stack of notes on the counter. Far too many.

“Keep the change. You’re the best in the city, everyone says. It should be done properly.” He turned to go, then turned back, like he’d nearly forgotten his umbrella. “Oh. And a small one. White peonies. For the widow.”

The bell rang behind him.

At the back, Xiao Pan put his broom down very slowly.

“Miss Lin. Was that…?”

She was looking at the order book. One character, in her own handwriting. Zhao.

She tore the page out. Her hands were steady. Why were they steady? She folded it in half, and in half again. She picked up the money and walked out onto the pavement and looked up the street. Then down.

Gone.

She went back in and picked up the phone and rang Wei Long.

Not her husband.

✦ ✦ ✦

Bao had been across the road. Bao was always across the road.

At twelve the door opened and Zhao came in. He turned the sign to CLOSED without looking at it. He shut the door behind him.

“Xiao Pan. Lunch.”

“I already had—”

Zhao put a note on the counter. “Have it again.”

Xiao Pan looked at the note. At Elowen. At the note.

“Take it,” she said. “Go.”

He went. He took the note. He looked back through the window twice.

Zhao stood in the middle of the shop.

“You rang the detective.”

“He’s the police.”

“You rang the police. Before you rang me.”

There was something in his voice she’d never heard in it. Not anger. Something with the skin off.

“Because if I’d rung you, you’d have gone after him. And then you’d have done something to him. And he was a messenger, Zhendong. Somebody paid him to walk in here and smile at me. That’s all.”

“That isn’t all.”

He didn’t raise his voice. That was worse.

“He came into your shop. He stood at your counter. He ordered my funeral from my wife.” His jaw moved. “And he asked for peonies for the widow.”

“So he wants to frighten you.”

“He wants me to know they can reach you whenever they want.” A step closer. “The van was a message. This is a message. The next one won’t be.”

“Then what do you want me to do?”

Nothing.

“Say it. Go on. Say what you want.”

“I want you to close the shop.”

It dropped into the room like a bucket.

Her face went cold. All of it, at once. He saw. He shut his eyes, quick, like he’d walked into a door. When he opened them he’d already taken it back.

“No. I know you won’t. I’m not asking.”

“Then what are you asking?”

“Ring me.” Rough. “Before the police. Before anybody. A man walks in here and says my name, you pick up the phone and it’s me.”

“So you can break his hands for smiling at me.”

“Yes.”

He didn’t soften it. He never did.

“That’s why I didn’t.”

“He ordered my funeral from my—”

“And next week it’ll be something else! And the week after. There’s always going to be something else, as long as you’re you.” She came round the counter. “I knew what you were when I married you. I walked into your office. I said I wanted to see it. I saw it. I stayed.”

He didn’t argue.

“You said it anyway. Close the shop.” Her voice cracked. She made it stop. “I’m not living in your house behind fourteen locks waiting for you to come home. I’m not. I’ve been careful my whole life so everyone else could be safe. Baba. Raiden. The girls. You.”

“Elowen—”

“This shop is the one thing I ever made just for me. And I’m not shutting it because a man in a grey jacket smiled at me.”

The cooler fan hummed. That was the only sound.

He looked at her for a long time.

“It’s not the only thing.”

Low.

“You said it’s the only thing you made for you.” He didn’t look away. “There’s a mountain with your name on it. There’s a dog called Dumpling. There’s a man who sweeps your floor.” His jaw was tight. “I thought maybe some of those were yours too.”

She opened her mouth. Nothing.

He turned round and walked out. The bell rang.

She stood in the middle of her warm new floor with a folded order form in one hand and a stranger’s money in the other.

He’d walked away from her. He’d never done that. Not once.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two the bell went and it was Bao.

Not across the road. In the shop. He took the folding chair from behind the cooler, carried it to the corner by the window, sat down on it and opened a newspaper.

She stared at him.

“Bao.”

“Mrs. Zhao.”

“What are you doing?”

“Boss says I sit inside now.” He turned a page. “Corner. With the paper.”

“Did he.”

“He didn’t say it nicely.”

“I didn’t agree to that.”

Bao looked at her over the sports pages with enormous sympathy. He didn’t move. Not one centimetre.

Xiao Pan came back from his second lunch with a bag of pork buns and stopped dead in the doorway.

“Why is Uncle Bao inside?”

“Because my husband walked out of here and then sent a man to sit in my corner.”

Xiao Pan looked at Bao. Bao looked at the racing results.

“Is that… good?”

“No!”

“Okay.” He put a pork bun on the counter in front of her anyway, very gently, like you’d feed a tiger. “You didn’t eat. Uncle Bao says you didn’t eat.”

“Uncle Bao has been inside for ten minutes.”

The newspaper rustled. “I see a lot from the corner.”

She ate the bun. She was furious the whole time. It was a good bun.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t come home for dinner.

She sat at the clean table in front of the fish. Then she didn’t eat it. She sat there looking at his chair.

At ten she took the fourteenth key down to the basement. First time she’d used it. The lamp was off. Cold. Dark. It smelled of oil, and he wasn’t in it. She stood at the bottom of the stairs feeling like she’d walked into a church after the funeral had already gone home.

At eleven she sat on the bottom stair in the hall. By the lemon tree. Dumpling came and put his chin on her knee. Noodle lay across her feet like a draught excluder.

She texted.

Elowen: come home

Nothing.

Elowen: i’m not angry

Nothing.

Elowen: i’m a bit angry

Elowen: where are you

Read. No dots. Nothing.

Half eleven, she rang. It rang until it stopped. Midnight, she rang again and sat with the phone against her ear, listening to it ring in a car or a room or a gutter somewhere she couldn’t see.

Taken too soon.

The next one won’t be, he’d said. He’d meant it about her. It worked the other way round too. It had always worked both ways round. Why hadn’t she thought of that at the counter?

She didn’t ring a third time. She put the phone face down on the step and jammed her hands between her knees.

Every time a car came up the road from the Docks, her whole body went tight. Until it went past the gate.

Five cars. She counted.

Not one of them was his.

✦ ✦ ✦

At one she heard the car.

He came in without a sound. He always did. He saw her on the bottom stair in her pyjamas with a dog on her feet and stopped in the doorway.

He’d been drinking. Not much. She could tell from how carefully he shut the door.

“Where were you?”

“Si’s.”

“Did you talk?”

“He talked.” He took his coat off and hung it up. He didn’t come any closer. “Aurelia talked more. She called me a coward. And an idiot. And a… caveman. In Italian. Then in English, in case I’d missed anything.”

A laugh tried to get out of her. She sat on it.

“What did Chen Si say?”

He looked at the lemon tree.

“He said the day he married her, she told him if he ever tried to keep her somewhere safe, she’d leave and take half his men with her.” A pause. “He said she meant it. He said that’s why he married her.”

She didn’t say anything.

“He said I didn’t marry a woman who’d let me lock her in a basement. I married the one who walked into the Iron Docks with three pages of terms and read my routes better than my own men.” He finally looked at her. “He said if I wanted something to keep safe in a room, I should’ve bought a bird.”

She laughed. It came out wet. She put her face down on her knees.

He crossed the hall and sat on the stair next to her. Not touching. An inch between their shoulders. Dumpling moved over to lean on him instead. Traitor.

“I’m sorry.”

She lifted her head.

A year and two months. She’d never heard him say it. To her or anybody.

“When Bao rang.” He was looking at the floor. “I was in a meeting. I stood up in the middle of it and walked out. I drove to the shop. And the whole way…” He stopped. Started again. “The whole way I could see you at the counter. On your own. And him in front of you. Smiling.”

His hands were clasped between his knees. They weren’t steady.

“I’ve been shot. I was in Block C. I’ve never…” His thumb dug into his own knuckle. “I didn’t know what to do with it. So I said the stupid thing. I wanted to put you somewhere it couldn’t get to.”

“I know.”

“I took it back.”

“You did.” She leaned over and closed the inch. Shoulder to shoulder. “And I should’ve rung you. Not Wei Long. You. First.”

“You were right. I’d have gone after him.”

“I know. I should’ve rung you anyway. And trusted you to hear me say don’t.” She pulled his hands apart and took one of them. “You listen to me. You always listen. I should’ve let you.”

He looked down at their hands.

“And the other thing.” Quieter. “The mountain. Dumpling. You.” She swallowed. “It isn’t the only thing. Not any more. I don’t even know when that happened.”

He didn’t say anything. His hand turned over in hers and held on.

✦ ✦ ✦

“The shop stays open.”

He nodded.

“Bao stays inside. In the corner. With your newspaper.”

“He’s already there.”

“I know he’s already there. Now it’s my term. Not yours.”

“Yes.”

“And the gun goes in the drawer under the till. You win that one.”

“Yes.”

“And if anyone walks in and orders anything with your name on it ever again, I ring you first.” She squeezed his hand. “And you don’t kill them.”

He thought about it. Actually thought.

“I don’t kill them first.”

She laughed. She couldn’t help it. He turned his head, and his face was right there, a breath away, and he stopped.

Of course he stopped. He always stopped. Even now. Even drunk on Chen Si’s whisky at one in the morning, after the worst day they’d had, he stopped a breath from her mouth and waited.

“Oh, for god’s sake. Yes.”

She grabbed his collar and pulled him the last inch.

He kissed her on the bottom stair with one hand along her jaw. Slow. Then hard. Then a bit desperate. Like water after a long day with none. Noodle got up and left in disgust. When he stopped, he kept his forehead on hers.

“Don’t let me walk out on you again.” Barely a voice. “Come after me. Or I’ll come back. One or the other.”

“You did come back.”

“At one in the morning.”

“Next time come back by ten.”

He breathed out against her mouth. Nearly a laugh.

She was shivering. She hadn’t noticed. He had. He got up, took his coat back off the hook, and put it round her shoulders. Then he crouched down and did up one button at her throat. Just one. Very carefully, like it was the most important button in the city.

“I’m not cold.”

“Your teeth are going.”

“That’s… emotion.”

“Hm.”

He picked her up off the stair, coat and all.

“I can walk.”

“You can walk tomorrow.”

He carried her up past the little room, all the way to the end of the corridor. He didn’t put her down until he had to.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was asleep in his coat before he’d got the light off.

He sat on the edge of the bed. Her apron was on the chair where she’d thrown it. Something was sticking out of the front pocket. A folded square of paper.

He unfolded it.

One character, in her handwriting. Neat. Small. His name. Then nothing, where her pen had stopped.

He looked at it for a long time.

Then he folded it again along the same creases and put it in his wallet. Behind the registry photograph. Red background. Her head on his shoulder, smiling at the camera because the photographer told her to.

The ninth. Two weeks.

He set an alarm for four. He didn’t sleep.

chapters.title: Glass
chapters.desc: Nobody says the date out loud. He buys her soy milk at the market, a little girl wants sunflowers with a yellow ribbon for her grandmother, and then a car comes down the street too slowly.
chapters.epigraph: “This light stays on. I’ll come.” — note taped to a wall, under the second row of buckets
chapters.content:
Nobody said the ninth all morning. Not him. Not her. It was very impressive. They should have got a prize.

The market at four, in the dark. Wet concrete. Diesel. The flower sellers’ lamps strung along the wall like somebody’s washing. He carried the buckets. She argued with the eucalyptus man about money. Normal. Totally normal.

At the gate, the soy milk man had his big steel pot going. Zhao stopped. He’d never stopped there before.

“One. Hot.”

He paid. He took the lid off the paper cup and blew on it. Twice. Then he held it out to her. She looked at the cup. Then at him.

She blew on it, because I always… Burned your tongue.

She’d told him that in the dark, in a typhoon, with a fever. Months ago. He’d been sitting on the floor holding her hand. She hadn’t thought he was even listening.

“You remembered that.”

“Drink it before it’s cold.”

She drank it. It was too sweet. The man always put too much sugar in. Mama used to say so every single time, and then buy it anyway. Her eyes went hot and she blamed the steam.

He walked on the road side of her all the way back to the car. He always did that. This morning he did it with his hand on the back of her neck.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car she held the empty cup in her lap.

“Did you talk to Raiden?”

“Hm.”

“That’s a yes. What did he say?”

“The plaster itches. The nurses are cruel.”

She snorted. Her little brother. Hit by a van on Friday night, lying in that hospital bed with his face all swollen, one arm strapped up, three ribs cracked. Pretending to be asleep. Badly.

“He’s hiding something.”

Zhao watched the road.

“He’s got that face. The innocent one. Like when he was twelve and broke the neighbour’s birdcage.” She turned in her seat. “You know something.”

“I know lots of things.”

“About Raiden.”

“Hm.”

“Zhendong.”

“He’ll tell you. When he wants.”

She stared at him. He kept driving. Completely calm. Oh, he knew something. He absolutely did. And he was keeping it for her brother. Against her. Unbelievable.

She was still annoyed about it when they got to the shop. He carried the last bucket in. He kissed the top of her head. Then he stopped in the doorway.

“I’ll be back at six. For closing.”

“You don’t have to.”

“I know.”

He looked at Bao, in the corner with the paper. Bao looked back. Something went between them that she wasn’t invited to.

She grabbed his collar before he could turn round and pulled him down and kissed him. Hard. Right there in the doorway, with the shutters half up and Xiao Pan pretending to be very interested in a bucket. When she let go he didn’t move. He stood with his head still bent.

“What was that for?”

“Nothing.”

“Elowen.”

“Luck. Go to work.”

He looked at her mouth for a second longer. Like he wanted to argue about it.

“Six.”

“Six.”

Then he went.

✦ ✦ ✦

Unknown: Eaten?

Elowen: yes

Unknown: What.

Elowen: food

Unknown: Name one food.

Elowen: a bun

Unknown: Bao says half a bun.

She looked at the corner. Bao was reading the racing results with tremendous concentration.

Elowen: bao is a liar

Unknown: Bao is never a liar. Eat the other half.

She ate the other half. Bao turned a page. He might have been smiling. It was hard to tell under the paper.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four a woman came in with a little girl. The girl was six and called Mimi. She wanted sunflowers. For her grandmother, who was in hospital. She’d chosen them herself from the bucket and she stood on tiptoe at the counter with her chin on the edge, watching Elowen’s hands like a cat watching a fish tank.

“Can I have the ribbon yellow?”

“You can have any colour you want.”

“Yellow.”

“Obviously.”

“Grandma’s in the hospital because her heart’s tired.” Very serious. “The doctor said.”

“Then she needs really loud flowers.”

Mimi frowned. “Sunflowers are loud?”

“The loudest ones I’ve got.”

“LOUDER than roses?”

“Roses are basically whispering.”

Mimi looked at the roses in their bucket with deep suspicion. Her mother laughed for the first time since they’d come in.

Xiao Pan was at the back by the cooler, squeezing his rubber ball. The physio had told him a hundred a day for his hands. He did them out loud. Every single one.

“Ninety-one. Ninety-two.”

“Why’s he counting?” Mimi whispered.

“He’s exercising.”

“With a ball?”

“Ninety-three. It’s very hard,” Xiao Pan told her. “Ninety-four.”

Mimi giggled.

It was a grey afternoon. Not raining. The street was quiet. Elowen had been thinking about the date since four in the morning. At the market. In the car. Over the bun. And then a little girl had walked in wanting sunflowers, and for ten whole minutes she’d forgotten. She tied the bow. Fat. Yellow.

“Is it pretty?”

“It’s very pretty. Your grandma’s going to—”

A car came down the street too slowly. Bao’s newspaper came down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, it came back in pieces. Never all at once.

Bao moving. Not getting up. Moving. Already across the shop before the paper hit the floor. Shouting a word she didn’t catch. A dark car outside. A back window sliding down.

The sound.

Not a bang. Not like films. A flat, hard cracking, over and over, so loud it was inside her head. The big front window went white all at once. The whole pane. Then it came in.

Glass everywhere. Flying. Glittering. Coming down on the buckets and the counter and the floor like hard rain. The sunflowers burst off the counter in a spray of yellow. The bucket of white peonies by the window jumped and fell over. Something hit the wall behind her head like a hammer, and the ribbon shelf came down.

She was on the floor. How? She didn’t remember going there. Bao had come over the counter. Actually over it, like a fence. He was on top of her. Somewhere a little girl was screaming. The cracking went on and on and on—

Then it stopped. An engine. Roaring. Going away.

Ringing. One high thin note in both ears.

“Mrs. Zhao.” Bao’s voice. Close. Very far off. “Mrs. Zhao. Are you hit? Talk to me.”

“The girl.” Her mouth didn’t feel like hers. “The girl. Mimi—”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mimi’s mother was flat on the floor by the door with her daughter under her. Both arms locked round her. Xiao Pan was lying across both of them.

He’d come from the back of the shop the second the window went white. He was lying across a stranger and her kid with his healing hands over his own head. His back glittered. It was covered in glass.

“Is anyone hurt?” Her voice came out steady. How? “Xiao Pan. Are you hurt?”

“I don’t… I don’t know…”

“Bao?”

Bao was already up. At the empty window frame with a gun in his hand she hadn’t known he had, looking up and down the street. Every bit of him pulled tight.

“Gone. For now. They might come back. We need to get you out the—”

“The floor.”

He turned.

“Raiden’s floor. Under the tulips.”

She was crawling before she’d finished saying it. Across her own floor. Through the glass. On her hands and knees. To the second row of buckets. The tulips were still standing.

Pink and white. In their bucket. Not a scratch on them. Everything else smashed to bits around them, and the stupid tulips just standing there.

She shoved the bucket aside. Water slopped over her hands. She found the edge of the drain cover, the one Raiden had shown her, and pulled. It came up.

A ladder, going down into the dark. Then the light from the shop fell on the first rung, and another light came on underneath. Warm. Steady. Gold. Like late afternoon.

“In. All of you. Now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mimi first. Her mother passed her down. Elowen was two rungs down the ladder. She took her, held her tight, carried her the rest of the way. Put her on the blankets at the bottom.

Mimi had stopped screaming. She was staring at the light in the ceiling with huge eyes.

“Is this a secret room?”

“Yes.”

“For spies?”

“For florists.”

Then the mother. Then Xiao Pan, shaking, glass coming off his back in little tinkling showers.

“Bao!”

His face appeared in the square of the hatch. Dark against the grey light of the wrecked shop.

“I stay up here. Close it from inside. There’s a bolt.” He looked down at her. “Don’t open it for anybody who isn’t me or him.”

“Bao, no—”

“Mrs. Zhao.” Calm. Completely calm. “That’s my job. Close it.”

The hatch came down. The light stayed on. She found the bolt where Raiden had said it would be. She slid it home. Heavy. Final.

Then she couldn’t let go of it.

Her hand had locked round the cold steel. Her knees were going on the rung. Her palms stung, scraped pink from the crawl. Through the steel, faintly, she could hear Bao up there. Glass crunching under his shoes. A bucket kicked out of the way. One man on his own with a gun and no window. Because it was his job.

She made her fingers open. One. Two. Three. Four. She climbed down the last rungs and her legs nearly went at the bottom, and she put her hand flat on the new concrete wall until they remembered how to hold her up.

✦ ✦ ✦

The room under the shop was warm. It smelled of new concrete and clean blankets. Mimi sat in her mother’s arms staring at the light. Xiao Pan sat against the wall breathing in short fast gulps, looking at his hands.

Elowen picked up the phone on the wall.

There was nothing to dial. It went through the building next door, Raiden had said. It only rang one number. Eliana had rigged it so the second the receiver came off the hook, that number was already ringing. It rang once.

“Elowen.”

His voice. Much too calm.

“They shot the window.” It came out in a rush. “A car. Bao’s up top. We’re under the tulips. Me, Xiao Pan, a mum, a little girl. Nobody’s…” She looked at Xiao Pan’s back. Glittering. “I don’t think anyone’s badly hurt.”

“Are you hurt?”

“No. I don’t think so. I don’t…”

She put her free hand up to her neck. Something there was warm. Wet. Her fingers came away red.

She looked at them in the gold light. Red. Real, bright red, running down between her fingers into her palm. Oh.

“Elowen. Talk to me.”

She found it with her fingertips. Low on the side of her neck. Just above the collarbone. A cut. Not deep, she thought. She could feel both edges. A sliver of the window had come through the air and opened her like a knife opens a stem. A clean cut.

“A bit.” Now her voice was shaking. Finally. “Glass. On my neck. I think it’s small. It’s… bleeding.”

There was a sound on the line. Not a word. Something big, breaking, a long way down.

“Press on it.” His voice had gone strange. Every word put down carefully, like a foot on ice. “Something clean. The blankets. Press hard. Don’t look at it. Keep pressing.” A breath. “I’m in the car. Eight minutes. Keep the hatch shut. Stay on the phone. Don’t hang up. Talk to me.”

“I’m talking.”

“Keep talking.”

Mimi’s mother was staring at her over her daughter’s head. White. Shaking.

“Who are you?” A whisper. “Is this… was this because of you?”

Elowen held the blanket to her neck and made herself look back.

“Yes. I’m sorry. I’m so sorry.”

The woman didn’t say anything. She pulled Mimi tighter and put her cheek down on her hair, and didn’t look at Elowen again.

Fair enough.

She pressed a corner of blanket hard into her neck. Mimi was watching her. Elowen smiled at her. Unbelievably, Mimi smiled back.

“The sunflowers. I’d just done the ribbon. Yellow. She picked it. They went everywhere.”

“I’ll buy her more.”

“And the window. Raiden’s going to be furious. He’s got one arm and he’ll still try to fix it.”

“I’ll buy a new window.”

“And Xiao Pan.” She looked at the boy against the wall with glass in his hair. “Xiao Pan lay on top of a stranger and her little girl. With his hands still healing. He didn’t think. He just did it.”

Nothing on the line for a while. Just an engine, going much too fast.

“Tell him his motorbike’s going to be a very good one.”

She laughed. It came out a sob.

Across the room, Xiao Pan’s head came up.

“What? What did he say?”

“He says your motorbike’s going to be a very good one.”

Xiao Pan put his face in his hands and burst into tears.

“Elowen.” So low she had to jam the receiver against her ear to hear it over the engine. “When I get there I’m going to hold on to you. I’m not letting go. Not for the doctor. Not for anybody. Tell me that’s all right.”

Even now. With her window all over her floor and her blood on a blanket. He was asking.

“Yes. Hurry.”

On the wall by the phone was a square of paper. Blunt capitals she’d have known anywhere.

This light stays on.

I’ll come.

She pressed the blanket harder and shut her eyes. Knocks on the hatch above her head. Three. Then two.

“It’s me.”

She slid back the bolt.

chapters.title: Nobody Else Touches Her
chapters.desc: He sends her sister out of the bathroom and puts the strips on her neck himself, shaking the whole time. Before dawn he tells her how long he’ll be gone, and she doesn’t say don’t.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m the best in my year at suturing. I practise on bananas.” — Elara Lin “No.” — Zhao Zhendong
chapters.content:
He missed the last three rungs.

He didn’t climb down so much as drop. He landed in a crouch on the concrete and the whole little room shook. Mimi squeaked.

Then he looked at her.

Elowen wished she’d hidden the blanket. Too late. His eyes went to her neck and stayed there. The red coming through the wool. Her fingers, red to the knuckle.

His face went white. Not pale. White, like somebody had pulled a plug out of him.

He crossed the room in two steps and went down on his knees on the blankets. He didn’t stop a breath away. He’d asked on the phone, and she’d said yes, and that was that. He put his hand over hers on the blanket and pressed. His other arm went round her back and pulled her into him so hard her teeth knocked.

He was shaking. She could feel it through her own hand.

“Let me see.”

“It’s small.”

“Let me see.”

She let go. He lifted one corner of the blanket and looked. He didn’t blink. Was he even breathing?

“Three centimetres.” Flat. Much too flat. “Clean. Not deep. It missed… It missed everything.”

“I told you. Small.”

He put the blanket back and kept his hand on it. Then he started on the rest of her. Her face. Her hair. Shoulder, elbow, wrist, every finger. Fast and rough, like a man patting his pockets for his keys.

“Zhendong. I’m here. All of me.”

“Hm.”

He didn’t stop until he’d done both hands.

Behind him, Mimi’s mother had dragged her daughter into the corner. She was looking at him like he’d come down the ladder with a knife in his teeth. Xiao Pan had flattened himself against the wall.

“Bao.”

Bao’s head came through the square of the hatch. His left sleeve was black and wet from the wrist up.

“Boss.”

“Your arm.”

“The window. It’s nothing.”

“Hospital.”

“After.”

Zhao let it go. Zhao never let anything go. Elowen stared at the side of his face.

“The woman and the child go to City Hospital. The grandmother’s there.” He still hadn’t turned round. “Pay for all of it. Hers too. Whatever ward she’s on, move her to a better one. The boy has glass in his back. He goes with them.”

“Yes, boss.”

“And sunflowers.”

Bao actually blinked. “Boss?”

“She was buying sunflowers. Get her sunflowers.”

Mimi’s mother made a sound in her throat. Zhao turned his head and looked at her, just once, and she shut her mouth so fast her teeth clicked.

“Nobody will say your name. Nobody will come to your door.” His voice didn’t change at all. “If anyone does, Bao gives you a number. You won’t need it.”

Mimi wriggled out from under her mother’s arm.

“Are you the husband?”

The whole room froze. Even Bao, upside down in the hatch.

“Yes.”

“She said you’d come.” Mimi pointed at the square of paper on the wall by the phone. “It says.”

He looked at the note. Blunt capitals. His own.

“Miss Lin…” Xiao Pan, from the wall, in a tiny voice. “Your neck. Is it going to…”

“It’s a scratch, Xiao Pan.”

“That’s a lot of blood for a scratch!”

Zhao’s head turned. Xiao Pan shut up so fast he bit his tongue.

Then Zhao picked Elowen up off the blankets like she weighed nothing, blanket and blood and all, and went up the ladder with her. She never did work out how. One arm, a ladder, a grown woman. Bao held the hatch.

“Mind your head, Mrs. Zhao.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The shop was gone.

He’d known it would be. He hadn’t known what it would sound like. Glass under his shoes with every step, a dry crunch like walking on sugar. Water everywhere. Sunflowers all over the floor, yellow faces down in the wet. The ribbon shelf on its side with every roll unwinding at once.

She’d turned her face into his shirt so she wouldn’t have to look. Good.

By the window a bucket lay on its side. White peonies, spilled out across the tiles. One of them had its head half snapped off.

Peonies. For the widow.

He stopped. He bent, with his wife still in his arms, and picked it up by the stem and put it in his coat pocket.

She lifted her head. “What are you doing?”

“Nothing.”

She looked at him. She didn’t ask again.

One of the men from the Docks drove. Bao went with the others. In the back seat Zhao didn’t put her down. He held her across his lap with the blanket pressed to her neck under his palm and his chin on top of her head. Her phone buzzed in her apron. Again. Again. Baba. Baba. Aurelia. Baba. Raiden. His buzzed in his coat. He didn’t answer anything.

“Your shirt.”

“Hm.”

“It’s ruined. There’s blood all down the—”

“Elowen.”

“What?”

“Stop talking about the shirt.”

She laughed. It came out with her teeth chattering. When had they started doing that? She couldn’t make them stop.

He held her tighter. In his head, quite calm, he was already making a list. Car. Driver. Gun. Whoever had paid for the gun. He didn’t need to write it down.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was glass in her hair.

She found out on the edge of the bath in the big bathroom upstairs, when she turned her head and something bright fell out of it and ticked on the tiles. Then another. A whole glittering handful had got caught in the knot at the back.

He saw the first one fall. He didn’t say a word. He just started taking it out. One sliver at a time. Fingertips only. He laid every piece on the edge of the basin in a line, and his lips moved. Counting. Was he counting so he wouldn’t do anything else? Probably.

Thirty-one.

Elara arrived at five, straight from City Hospital, where she’d been sitting with Raiden. She was twenty-one, the fourth of the five Lin children, in her fourth year of medicine, and she came up the stairs two at a time with her hair falling out of its clip and a bag that clinked. She looked at the towel on her sister’s neck. She looked at the line of glass on the basin. Then she turned into somebody Elowen had never met.

“Okay! Hi. Jie, tilt your head. Brother-in-law, move please. Thank you. Lights. More lights. There.” She bent close. “Oh, that’s nothing. That’s a paper cut with ambitions. Clean edges. Nowhere near anything you need. Strips, maybe one stitch at the deep end if you want it pretty.” She snapped on gloves. “Brother-in-law, you can wait outside.”

He didn’t move.

“It’s fine. Honestly. I’m the best in my year at suturing. I practise on bananas.”

“No.”

Elara blinked at him.

“I’ll do it.”

The bathroom went very quiet. Somewhere downstairs, Dumpling whined at the door.

“With respect… you’re not a doctor.”

“No. Tell me what to do. I’ll do it.”

“You’re shaking.”

“I know.”

Elara’s phone went off in her pocket. She looked at the screen and groaned.

“It’s Raiden. If I don’t answer he’ll walk here.” She put it on speaker.

“Is she okay? Elara. Is she okay?”

“She’s fine. Lie down.”

“I’m coming. I’m signing myself out. The window, I can fix the window, I’ll get the—”

“You have one arm in plaster and three cracked ribs.”

“I have one GOOD arm!”

“Raiden, there’s a nurse standing behind you. I can hear her.”

A muffled argument. A woman’s voice saying Mr. Lin, bed. Now. The line went dead. Elara put the phone away. She looked at her brother-in-law. At his fists, clenched at his sides to stop them going. At the blood all down his shirt. Then she looked at Elowen.

Elowen was looking at her husband.

“Elara. Show him. Then wait outside.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elara showed him. Twice. She laid it all out on a clean towel on the counter. Saline. Gauze. A strip of tiny white tapes. Scissors. Clean it, dry it, pull the edges together, strips across, not too tight. Leave it alone. Keep it dry.

At the door she stopped.

“You’ve done this before.”

“On myself.”

Her eyes went to his forearms. The old scars. The shiny patch from the burn.

“Yeah. I bet you have.” She pointed at him with a glove. “If it bleeds through, you call me. I’m downstairs eating your fridge.”

She shut the door.

He scrubbed his hands at the basin. Between the fingers. Under the nails. The same way he cleaned a gun on the bench, every piece in order. When he turned round his hands were red from the hot water, and still shaking. He knelt on the tiles in front of her, so her neck was level with his face.

“Tilt your head.”

She tilted it. He took the towel away. Cold air touched the cut. She felt him look at it. He wet the gauze and started.

It stung. She hissed. His hand jerked back like she’d bitten it.

“Sorry.”

“It’s fine.”

“Sorry.”

“Zhendong. It’s fine.” She closed her fingers round his wrist. “Keep going.”

He kept going. Little dabs. The dried blood round the edges. The trail of it down to her collarbone, into the hollow of her throat. Every time she flinched, he stopped. Every time he stopped, she said keep going, and he did. His hands never stopped shaking. They never slipped either. How did he do that?

She’d watched this man put a fruit knife through another man’s hand at a dinner table. She’d watched him come home smelling of a burned warehouse. She’d sat on the basement stairs while he stripped a rifle at two in the morning, calm as a pond.

Scared, though? Never. Not once. Not of anything.

He was scared now. It was all over his face. In his breathing, short and careful through his nose. In his eyes, which hadn’t left the cut since he knelt down.

He dried it. He tried to open the packet of strips and his fingers couldn’t manage it. He tore it open with his teeth. First strip. Across. Edges together. She didn’t feel a thing.

Second. Third. Fourth.

On the fifth his hand finally slipped. Just a little. His knuckle brushed the side of her throat. He made a noise like he’d been punched.

“Zhendong…”

He laid the sixth. He smoothed the ends down with one fingertip. Then he sat back on his heels on the bathroom floor and looked at it. Six white strips on his wife’s neck.

He put his face in his hands.

No sound at all. Just his shoulders, going. It took her a second to understand what she was looking at. He was crying. He didn’t know how to do it out loud. Had anyone ever taught him? Who would have?

She slid off the edge of the bath onto the tiles. She took his wrists and pulled his hands down.

His face was wet. His eyes were red. He looked at her like the camellia on the mountain. Like the last one left.

“I should have been there.” He barely had a voice. “I was at the Docks. I knew it was the ninth. I knew. I should have shut the shop. I should have made you…”

“You couldn’t have made me.”

“I should have tried.”

“You did. At the counter. Then you took it back, because you know me.” She held on to his wrists. “And Bao was there. Raiden’s floor was there. The light came on. Who put all that there? You. You rang my brother at two in the morning. You wrote the note.” Her voice broke right in the middle. “I’ll come. You came. Eleven minutes. I counted.”

He stared at her.

“Eight. I said eight.” He swallowed. “There was a bus.”

She laughed. She cried. Both at once, a horrible wet noise. He reached for her, and his hands stopped an inch from her. Hovered. Wouldn’t land. Like she’d break if he touched her wrong.

“Page two. Line six.”

His eyes came up.

“I’m asking. Hold on to me.”

He fell forward into her. Arms round her, his face in the other side of her neck, his whole big body going. She held his head and let him shake.

Then she got fed up with him being careful. She took his collar in both fists and pulled his mouth down to hers.

He went rigid. Then he made a sound against her lips, low and cracked, right out of his chest, and kissed her back. He tasted of salt. His hand came up to cradle her jaw on the good side, thumb nowhere near the strips, and he kissed her like he was checking she was warm.

“Your neck,” he said into her mouth.

“Is fine. Shut up.”

He shut up.

✦ ✦ ✦

She still had glass in her hair. She could feel it, fine as sand, every time she moved.

“I need to wash it.”

“Keep them dry. Elara said.”

“Then hold a towel on them.”

So he did. She knelt at the side of the bath with her head over it, and he folded a hand towel into a thick pad and held it against the strips with one hand. With the other he ran the shower head over her hair. Warm. Then shampoo. Then his fingers, working it through, slow. Rinse. Again. He checked every bit of her scalp with his fingertips like he was looking for more glass. He probably was. He pulled the elastic out of her hair to get at the knot. He didn’t put it down anywhere. He put it on his own wrist.

She saw. She didn’t say anything. Her face went hot under the water.

When she was wrapped in a towel on the bath mat, Elara knocked and put her head round the door with a box.

“Painkillers. Two now, two before bed. It’s on the box.”

He took it. He read the box. Then he turned it over and read the back. Then he opened it and unfolded the leaflet.

Elara watched him read the whole leaflet. Both sides.

“It’s paracetamol. Not a contract.”

“Hm.”

“Jie. He’s reading the side effects.” Elara looked delighted and horrified at once. “Who reads the side effects? Nobody reads the side effects!”

“He reads everything twice.”

“Baba’s ringing me every five minutes, by the way. He wants to know if he should come.”

Elowen looked at her husband. Her husband was on the bit about overdoses.

“Tell him tomorrow.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t sleep.

She knew because she didn’t either. She lay on her side in their big bed with her back to him and his arm round her waist. Every so often his hand came up to her neck. To the edge of the strips. Stayed there, barely touching, then went back to her waist. Checking. All night. The elastic was still on his wrist. She could feel it against her stomach.

When the window went grey, he got up. She heard him dress in the dark. She heard him open his drawer, the one in his bedside table she’d never asked about. Something heavy went into his coat.

She didn’t turn over.

“How long?”

He stopped.

He came round to her side of the bed and crouched by it so their faces were level. Grey light. She could see him now. The fear had gone out of his face. What was left was cold and flat and a very long way off.

“Forty-eight hours.”

She looked at him.

Mimi’s yellow ribbon. Xiao Pan’s back, glittering. A man in a grey jacket asking for peonies for the widow. I don’t kill them first.

She should say don’t. She knew she should. He’d listen. If she said it, he’d take off his coat and get back into bed and hold her till the market.

Did she want him to?

She put her hand on his face.

“Come back.”

He turned his head and kissed her palm.

“Keep them dry.” Against her skin. “The strips.”

Then he kissed her mouth, once, hard, with his hand spread on the back of her head, and he was gone. Stairs. Front door. The car on the gravel.

She lay there with her hand still warm. Then she reached for her phone.

Elowen: 48. i’m counting

Three dots. Gone. Three dots.

Unknown: Hm.

She laughed into his pillow. Who texts hm?

chapters.title: Forty-Eight Hours
chapters.desc: Forty-eight hours, from his side. A boy who stole a car, a driver in the harbour, a shooter on a landing, and a koi pond on the coast.
chapters.epigraph: “Every time you see a flower shop, for the rest of your life, you cross the street.” — Zhao Zhendong
chapters.content:
Hour 1.

Bao was at the wheel with the engine running. His left arm was bandaged from wrist to elbow. Fresh. White. Somebody at City Hospital had done a neat job.

“How many?”

“Fourteen, boss.”

“Hm.”

“The nurse said I was very brave.” Bao looked straight ahead through the windscreen. “I wasn’t.”

Zhao got in the back. On his left wrist, under the cuff, was her black hair elastic. He’d noticed it on the stairs. He’d thought about taking it off. He hadn’t.

“Where?”

“The Docks. Then wherever it goes.”

Bao put the car in gear with one hand.

“The little girl got her sunflowers.”

“Good.”

“Biggest ones at the market. Granny Su opened up for me.” A pause. “She cried. Granny Su, I mean. Then she hit me with a bunch of lilies for not looking after Mrs. Zhao.”

“Hm.”

“I deserved it.”

Forty-eight. He’d said it to her face. So now it was true.

Hour 2.

The office above Northgate Industrial Pumps had every light on. Eliana was on the laptop on his desk, in a hoodie three sizes too big, with three screens glowing behind her. Eighteen. Her father had told her not to get involved. Obviously.

“You didn’t open it.”

“Open what.”

“The footage. I sent it at midnight. Brother-in-law, I sent it at midnight.”

“I was busy.”

“Doing what?”

“Strips.”

Her face on the screen did something complicated. Then she clicked.

“Okay. Black saloon. The plates were off a car in the long-stay at the airport. Stolen two nights ago. After the shop it went west, then north on the ring road, then I lose it.” Click. “Then this. Behind the cement works. Half an hour later.”

A grey picture. A shape on fire.

“They burned it.”

“Faces?”

“Masks, in the car.” She pulled her sleeves down over her hands. “But the one who took it from the airport didn’t wear one. He’s a kid. Sixteen? He steals for anyone who pays. I’ve got his name. And his grandmother’s flat.”

“How?”

“You don’t want to know how.”

He didn’t. Bao, at the door, very obviously did.

“Brother-in-law…” Smaller now. “Is she actually okay? Elara says yes. Elara says yes about everything.”

“Six strips. Your sister told me what to do. I did them.”

“You did them?”

“Hm.”

She looked at him through the screen for a while. Then the address came through on his phone.

“Bring me their phones. Anybody’s. I’ll do the rest.”

“Go to bed, Eliana.”

“You first.”

The screen went black. Lin girls. Every one of them.

Hour 3.

Chen Si rang while Bao was bringing the car round.

“Who do you need?”

“Nobody.”

“Zhendong.”

“Keep the police off the roads I’m on. Keep Song Wei Long busy.” He watched the cranes swing over the water. “That’s all.”

“That isn’t all.”

He didn’t answer straight away.

“The window. I want glass in it by tonight. The kind that doesn’t break.”

“I sent a glazier this morning. He’s measuring now.” A pause. “Aurelia’s packing a bag. She wants to go to the house.”

“Let her. Elowen shouldn’t be on her own.”

“She’s packing a tracksuit. And ice cream.”

A scuffle on the line. Then a different voice, much closer to the phone.

“Zhendong. If you get yourself killed, I’ll tell her you cried at our wedding.”

“I didn’t.”

“I’ll tell her anyway! In detail!”

The scuffle again. Then Si, very dry. “She’s taken the car keys.”

Zhao didn’t say anything.

“Come back.”

Two words. The same two. He hung up before Si could hear what that did to him.

Hour 9.

The kid lived on the eleventh floor of a block by the railway, with his grandmother. The lift was broken. The kid opened the door in a vest, saw who was on the landing, and wet himself. Zhao didn’t touch him. He sat on the grandmother’s sofa under a calendar with a picture of a mountain on it. Bao filled the doorway.

“Who paid you?”

“I don’t… I just do cars, I didn’t know, I swear on my…”

“Who.”

“Little Fu!” The kid’s voice cracked in half. “He drives. He drives for anybody. He gave me two thousand for a car with dark windows, that’s all, that’s all…”

“Where is he?”

“Mahjong. Every night. Over the pharmacy in the old town. The one with the broken green cross.”

Zhao stood up. The kid flinched so hard he hit the wall.

“There was a little girl in the shop. Six. Buying sunflowers for her grandmother.” He looked round the room. The calendar. Two teacups on the draining board. “Next time somebody pays you for a car, you think about her.”

The kid didn’t understand. Zhao didn’t explain. On the way out he put two thousand under the grandmother’s teapot. Let him explain that to her.

On the stairs, Bao cleared his throat.

“Mrs. Zhao would’ve made him a cup of tea.”

“Hm.”

His phone buzzed on the sixth floor.

Elowen: all six strips still on. aurelia is here. she brought a tracksuit and no make-up. i didn’t know she owned either. dumpling won’t leave the bedroom door

He read it on the stairs. Again at the bottom. Again in the car. On her screen he was still Unknown. A year and three months, and she’d never changed it. He’d never asked. Why did he like that so much? He had no idea.

Zhao: Eat.

Elowen: you first

There was a bun stall at the lights.

“Stop.”

Bao stopped. Zhao bought a pork bun, ate it in four bites in the back seat, and sent her a picture of the empty paper bag.

Elowen: that’s a bag

Zhao: It had a bun in it.

Elowen: prove it

In the mirror, Bao’s eyes. “Boss. You’ve got crumbs on your—”

“Drive.”

Hour 17.

Little Fu was harder.

Thirty, thin, fast, and driving for bad men since he was twelve. He saw Zhao in the doorway of the mahjong room and went out of the back window without stopping to think. He made it across two roofs. On the third, Bao was sitting on a water tank with his bandaged arm in his lap, like a man waiting for a bus.

“Evening.”

They took him to the old north pier, where nobody went at night. Black water slapping the posts. Diesel and rot. Bao held him. Zhao asked him once who’d held the gun.

Little Fu laughed and spat on Zhao’s shoe. “No idea what you’re on about, big man.”

So Zhao put him in the water.

Head and shoulders. Bao had the ankles. Zhao had the collar, and he counted out loud, low and even. The way she’d counted for Xiao Pan under the cold tap. The way he’d counted over the oil drum.

At twenty he pulled him out. Little Fu came up choking. Zhao asked again. Little Fu said something about his mother.

Back in.

At thirty, out. Little Fu was crying now, sicking up harbour water, his whole body jerking. Zhao asked again in exactly the same voice.

“Tian! Tian Haoyu, it was Tian, he did the shooting, I only drove, I only drove, I didn’t know there was a kid in there, I swear—”

“Who paid Tian?”

“Lu. Grey jacket. Lu works for Qiu Wen, everybody knows…” He coughed up more of the harbour. “The money’s not Qiu’s. Qiu’s got a new partner. Foreign. The Dutchman.” A gasp. “The one with the hand.”

Zhao stopped moving.

A fruit knife. A white tablecloth. He’d let the man sign with his other hand and fly home to the south. Kang, whose fingers he’d broken and left alive, had given the UN his companies. Maartens, whose hand he’d pinned and left alive, had bought the bullets.

Si had said it to him at fifteen. In the dark, in the snow, with both hands on his face. Everything you leave behind you comes back. He’d thought Si meant Gao. Had Si meant every man he ever let walk away?

They left Little Fu on the pier with a broken arm and a phone number in his pocket.

“That’s Song Wei Long. You ring it. You tell him you steal cars.”

“I don’t steal cars, I drive—”

“You steal cars now.”

Little Fu looked at the water. Then he nodded so hard his teeth rattled.

Hour 30.

Tian Haoyu had a rented room over a karaoke bar on the east side, a rifle case under the bed, and a bag by the door for the first bus south. He was a professional. He heard them on the stairs.

He came out onto the landing with a pistol, and Zhao shot him twice before it was up.

Loud. Louder than the shop window, in that stairwell. Then quiet. Downstairs, through the floor, somebody kept singing an old love song. Badly. They didn’t even miss a line. Tian lay on his back. He was younger than Zhao had expected. Twenty-five, maybe. Eyes open. A fish tattooed on the inside of his wrist.

Zhao looked down at him and waited to feel something.

Nothing came. Not anger. Not the old cold from Block C. He checked, the way you’d check a pocket. Empty.

“Boss.” Bao, from the stairs. “Two minutes. Maybe three.” He looked at Zhao’s face. “You all right?”

“Yes.”

“…Okay.”

In the room: the rifle case. The bag. In the bag, an envelope of cash and a photograph. Her. Through the shop window, in her green coat. Last week, then. Laughing at something. Xiao Pan, probably. Somebody had drawn a circle round her face in red pen.

He looked at it until Bao said boss again.

He put it in his inside pocket. Next to the peony.

Hour 38.

They found Lu at his sister’s house in the suburbs, under the spare bed. Still in the grey jacket. Who hides under a bed in the jacket they’ve been described in? He talked before anybody asked him anything. So fast Bao had to tell him to slow down. Twice.

“It was Qiu. Qiu planned it. The wreaths were his idea, he thought it was funny, I said it wasn’t funny, I did say that!” He was sobbing. “The peonies were the Dutchman. On the phone. From Rotterdam. He said, tell him it’s for the hand. That’s what he said. For the hand.”

“Where’s Qiu Wen?”

Lu told them. Then he just cried.

“You smiled at her.”

“I’m sorry, I’m sorry, they paid me, please, I didn’t—”

“At her counter. You put money down and smiled at her and ordered my funeral.” Zhao’s voice didn’t move at all. “You looked at her face.”

He crouched. He took Lu’s face in one hand, thumb under one cheekbone, fingers under the other. Not hard. Just enough to make him look up.

“Every time you see a flower shop, for the rest of your life, you cross the street.”

He let go.

They left Lu on the floor of his sister’s spare room, alive, untouched except for that one hand. Some men came back if you left them. Not Lu. Lu would cross the road from a shop selling plastic roses until the day he died.

Hour 41.

On the coast road, his phone buzzed.

Elowen: i’m sleeping in your grey shirt. dumpling disapproves. come home and take it off me

He read it twice. In the dark of the car he smiled, and Bao, extremely busy with the road, didn’t see a thing.

Then he opened the house cameras.

He didn’t ask himself if he should. He never had. Hall. Kitchen, where Aurelia was eating ice cream out of the tub with a serving spoon. The landing. Dumpling, lying across the door of their room like a sandbag. The door open a hand’s width. Through the gap, the end of the bed, and one bare foot sticking out from under his shirt. He watched the foot until it moved. Then he turned the phone face down on his knee.

He didn’t answer her. Not yet. He put the shirt and the foot away, somewhere inside him where nothing else got in. Then he took the gun out of his coat.

Hour 46.

Qiu Wen had bought a villa on the coast with the Dutchman’s money. White walls. A gate. A koi pond lit from underneath, so the fish glowed orange in the dark like coins. Four guards. Two looked at who was coming through the gate, put their guns down on the gravel, and walked off down the road without a word. Sensible. The third lifted his at Bao. Bao put him down, and he didn’t get up. The fourth was Qiu Lei, the younger brother, with a cigarette in his scarred hand. He saw Zhao, dropped the cigarette, and ran.

Zhao let him run. Qiu Lei’s hands were already done.

Qiu Wen was by the pond in a silk dressing gown, shouting into a phone. He turned round. He didn’t run. Zhao would give him that.

“I can pay.” His chin came up. “Whatever the Dutchman gave me. Double! His accounts. His routes. The man who gave Kang to the UN, I’ve got the name, I can…”

“You ordered flowers for my widow.”

Qiu Wen swallowed.

“It was a message. It was business! You burned my warehouse. You burned my brother’s hands. We send each other messages, Zhao, that’s how it works, you know how it…”

Zhao took the photograph out of his pocket and held it up in the orange light off the water.

“You put a circle round her face.”

Qiu Wen looked at it. Zhao watched him get there. No price. No table. Nothing to sell.

He opened his mouth to shout for his guards.

Zhao hit him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The jaw first, so there’d be no more offers. Then the collar of the silk dressing gown, and into the pond. Under, among the glowing fish. He counted. At twenty he brought him up. Qiu Wen tried to talk through the broken jaw and couldn’t. Back down. Zhao didn’t ask him anything. There was nothing left he wanted to know.

At forty, Qiu Wen stopped fighting.

Zhao kept counting. Out loud, low, the same voice as the pier. All the way to a hundred. Then he let go.

The fish had all gone to the edges. The water went flat. His sleeves were wet to the elbow. He took the peony out of his coat. Two days in a pocket. Crushed, brown at the edges. He dropped it in. It floated next to Qiu Wen’s head.

He took a photograph with his phone. The pond, the man, the flower. He sent it to a number in Rotterdam, with one word.

Zhao: Next.

“Boss.” Bao, from the gate. “Lights. Down the road.”

“Hm.”

In the car, Bao didn’t start the engine straight away.

“Rotterdam?”

“Not yet.”

Bao nodded like that was a perfectly normal answer. He started the car.

Hour 48.

He washed at the Docks.

There was a shower behind the office that the forklift drivers used. He turned it as hot as it would go. Hands. Arms. Face. Hair. Hands again. Again. The skin went red, then raw. The water going down the drain had been clear for ages. He kept going. Then he remembered the elastic. It was soaked through on his wrist. He took it off and held it in his palm under the water, and something in his chest missed a step.

He put it back on.

Clean clothes from the cupboard. An old grey sweatshirt, trousers too short in the leg. He took the photograph out of the wet coat and put it in the sweatshirt pocket. Then he put the old clothes in the furnace in the yard and stood there until they were gone.

Bao drove him home.

“She’ll ask, boss.”

“I know.”

“You going to tell her?”

“She’ll ask. I’ll tell her.” He looked at his hands. “Bottom of page three.”

Bao had no idea what that meant. He nodded anyway.

The sun came up grey over the sea as they turned onto the hill. The kitchen light was on. Bao switched off the engine. Zhao sat there with his raw hands on his knees and didn’t open the door.

Bao got out first. He stood by the car, waiting.

“Boss.”

“Hm.”

“Forty-seven and a half.”

Zhao looked at the kitchen window. He’d tell her about the half. She counted things.

He got out.

chapters.title: He Came Home Washed
chapters.desc: He comes home scrubbed raw and she asks if anyone’s dead. He tells her the truth, comes apart on the kitchen floor, and agrees that her father is hers to deal with.
chapters.epigraph: “Your hair’s wet. I can smell the soap from here. The cheap kind. From the Docks.”
chapters.content:
Aurelia’s phone went at five in the morning, and she answered it on the first ring, like she’d been sitting on it.

“Yes. Yes. Now?” She was already standing. “Okay. I’m going. Si… thank you.”

She hung up. She looked at Elowen, who was sitting up in the big bed in a grey shirt that wasn’t hers, with a dog across her feet.

“He’s coming home.”

Elowen didn’t say anything. She couldn’t. Her mouth had stopped working.

Aurelia didn’t wait for her to manage it. She found her shoes. She found her bag. She found her sunglasses, at five in the morning, and put them on top of her head. Two days in a tracksuit and no make-up, and she still looked like she’d walked off a magazine. It was honestly offensive.

At the front door she stopped and held out her hand.

“Phone.”

“Why?”

“Because I want to put my number at the top of your favourites, and you’re going to ring me later. Ring. Not text.”

Elowen gave her the phone. Aurelia scrolled. Then she stopped scrolling.

“Elowen.”

“What?”

“Who is Unknown?”

“…”

“You saved your husband as Unknown?” Aurelia’s voice went up into a register that made Dumpling’s ears flatten. “It’s been a year!”

“Fifteen months.”

“That’s WORSE!”

“I never got round to it.”

Aurelia stared at her over the phone. Then she handed it back, very slowly, like it was evidence.

“I’m counting this. I sat up with you for two nights. That’s a point. I’m ahead.”

“You ate all the ice cream. That’s minus one.”

“Darling.”

She stopped with her hand on the door.

“Did he ever tell you? When Si was poisoned. When he was in intensive care.” She sniffed. “Your husband sat outside his door on a plastic chair. Midnight till six. Fourteen nights. He hardly said a word to anyone the whole fortnight.”

“No.” Elowen’s throat had gone tight. “He never told me.”

“Of course he didn’t.”

“He sat outside my door for a month. When I moved in.”

“Of course he did.” Aurelia pushed her sunglasses down. Then up again. “Idiots. Both of them.”

She grabbed Elowen’s face and kissed her on the forehead, hard. Her eyes were wet. She’d deny that forever.

“Make him eat something.”

Then she was gone down the steps in her ridiculous tracksuit, and the car took her away.

✦ ✦ ✦

So Elowen made congee.

It was what Mama made when somebody came home from hospital. It was what she’d made for Baba the night the containers were seized. It was the only thing she could think of to do with her hands.

She heard the car. The dogs. Bao’s door. Then a long gap. Then his.

The front door.

She didn’t turn round from the stove.

He stopped in the kitchen doorway. She could feel him there behind her. Like weather.

She stirred.

“You showered.”

He didn’t answer.

“Your hair’s wet. I can smell the soap from here. The cheap kind. From the Docks.” She stirred again. “You stood in that shower for a long time.”

“Yes.”

She turned off the heat and put the spoon down on the counter. Carefully. The way he put things down. Then she turned round.

Grey sweatshirt. Old trousers, too short in the leg. His hair wet. His face scrubbed red. His hands were the worst. She could see them from across the kitchen, the knuckles pink and shining, like he’d tried to take the skin off.

And under the soap, so faint she might have made it up, something else. Harbour water. Smoke. Something sweet and metal she didn’t have a name for. She didn’t want one.

Bottom of page three, in his square hand: You don’t lie to me. And out loud, that same night: I won’t make something up.

“Is anyone dead?”

He didn’t look away.

“Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t move.

“Who?”

“The one with the rifle. Tian. Twenty-five.” Flat. Level. “He had a fish on his wrist.”

“Who else?”

“Qiu Wen. In his garden.” A pause. “One of Qiu Wen’s men. He drew on Bao.”

Three.

She stood at the stove and let the number go all the way through her. Down to her feet. Three.

“The driver?”

“Alive. He’s going to ring Song Wei Long and say he steals cars.”

“Does he steal cars?”

“No.”

A noise came out of her that wasn’t a laugh. She pressed her hand over her mouth.

“The boy who took the car is alive. Sixteen. The man in the grey jacket is alive.” His jaw moved. “He won’t come near a flower shop again.”

“Who paid for it?”

He looked at her.

“Maartens.”

She went cold all over. Hands first.

“The dinner. The hand.”

“He said the peonies were for the hand.” His voice didn’t change at all. “He’s in Rotterdam. I can’t reach him. Not with the notice.” A beat. “I sent him a photograph.”

She didn’t ask what of.

“Kang. And Maartens.” She could barely get it out. “Both of them. Because you left them alive. Because I was on the stairs. Because I sat at that table and said take it out—”

“No.”

He came one step into the kitchen.

“Because I left them alive. Me. I chose it.” He took another step. “I won’t do it again. Not with men like that. I need you to know what I am, Elowen. All of it. I won’t lie to you about it, and I won’t ever…”

He stopped.

Just stopped, in the middle. His mouth stayed open on the next word. His eyes had gone bright.

His hands had started to shake.

✦ ✦ ✦

It started in his fingers. Same as hers, in the car after Maartens. Then his arms. Then all of him. He stood in the middle of her kitchen in borrowed clothes and shook from head to foot, like he’d been out in snow, and he didn’t seem to know it was happening. He looked down at his own hands like they were somebody else’s.

“Sorry.” His teeth were going. “I don’t… This doesn’t happen. I don’t know why it’s—”

She crossed the kitchen.

She took him by both wrists, the way she had at the sink after the warehouse, and pulled him down. He came. He folded up onto the kitchen floor like someone had cut his strings. She went down with him. Both arms round him. Held on.

He shook so hard she felt it in her own teeth.

His face was in her shoulder, the side without the cut. His breath came in short hard pulls that weren’t quite sobs. His hands had grabbed fistfuls of the back of her dressing gown and wouldn’t let go.

She put her forehead against his. He was freezing. Clammy. How was he this cold? He’d just come out of a hot shower.

“I’ve got you.”

No answer. She didn’t need one.

Outside, the dogs had come to the glass door and sat with their noses on it. The congee went cold in the pot above their heads. She watched the oven clock over his shoulder and stroked his wet hair and didn’t say anything else.

It took twenty minutes.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards he lay with his head in her lap and his eyes shut. She sat with her back against the cupboard. Grey light. The dogs had given up and lain down.

He put his hand into the sweatshirt pocket and took out a photograph. He held it up without opening his eyes.

She took it.

Her. Through her own shop window, in her green coat. Laughing at something. Somebody had drawn a red circle round her face.

“It was in his bag.”

She looked at herself laughing. What had she been laughing at? Xiao Pan. The pigeon joke. Something about a pigeon and a bus.

“When I saw that, I stopped being scared.” His eyes were still shut. “I was scared from the phone call. The blanket. All of the first day. Then I opened the bag, and it just… stopped.”

“Okay.”

“After that, nothing. A whole day of nothing. The landing. The pond.” He opened his eyes and looked up at her. “That’s what frightens me now. Not what I did. That I didn’t feel it.”

She looked down at him. Scarred and scrubbed raw, with his head in her lap. He’d just told her he’d killed three people. He was more scared of not being scared than of any of it.

And there it was. Deep down, same as at the sink after the warehouse. The terrible thing. The gladness.

She was glad the man with the fish was dead. She was glad Qiu Wen was in his pond. Two nights in the big bed. Six strips on her neck. Aurelia talking at the ceiling. And the whole time she’d thought about Mimi’s yellow ribbon and Xiao Pan’s glittering back, and wanted them dead. Wanted it like water.

Was she ashamed? She checked. She waited for it.

No.

“You felt it.”

His eyes came up to hers.

“Just now. On this floor. You shook for twenty minutes.” She put her hand flat on his chest, over his heart. “That was you feeling it. It took a day to catch up.”

He looked at her. Then he turned his face into her stomach and got both arms round her waist and held on.

She held up the photograph. “Burn this.”

“No.”

“It’s got a target on it.”

“It’s got you on it.” Muffled, against her. “I’ll cut the circle off.”

She should have argued. She looked at the top of his wet head and didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

She reached up behind her without letting go of him and felt along the counter until she found the tin of hand cream she kept by the sink for after the market. She took his right hand. The worst one. She worked the cream into his knuckles one at a time, slow, the way she’d wrap a stem that got bruised in the van.

He opened his eyes and watched her.

“You scrubbed the skin off.”

“Hm.”

“You’re not allowed to do that.” She started on the left. “These are mine. You don’t take the skin off things that are mine.”

The corner of his mouth moved. Not a smile. That would come later, after he’d slept.

“Yours.”

“Page three. Somewhere. I’ll write it in.”

Then she saw her hair elastic on his left wrist. Soaked. Stretched. Two days on him.

“You stole my hair tie.”

He looked at it like he’d forgotten it was there.

“I want it back.”

“No.”

“Zhendong.”

He put his other hand over it. Like she might grab.

She held out her palm and waited. She could wait as long as he could. Longer. She’d married him, hadn’t she?

He looked at her palm. At her. At the palm. Then he peeled the elastic off his wrist, very slowly, and put it in her hand like he was handing over a kidney.

“Thank you.”

“Hm.”

She put it on her own wrist. He watched it the whole way.

✦ ✦ ✦

He ate two bowls of congee at the counter on one of the tall stools without being asked. Fast, at first. Then slower, when he remembered he could.

There was a grain of rice at the corner of his mouth. She reached over and wiped it off with her thumb. He stopped chewing. He looked at her thumb like she’d done something enormous.

“Eat.”

He ate. She sat across from him and turned her teacup round and round. Her ring kept sliding down her middle finger. It was always too big when her hands were cold.

“They knew the schedule.”

He looked up from the bowl.

“That photo was a week old. He knew what time I’d be at the counter. He knew Bao reads the paper in the corner and only looks up when the door goes. He knew the ninth was a Wednesday and Wednesdays are slow at four.” She put the cup down. “Somebody told them.”

“Yes.”

“Did Lu say who?”

He was quiet for a bit.

“He said the schedule came from the fixer’s people. That’s all he knew. The fixer’s people. Qiu Wen had someone inside.”

The fixer.

Baba.

She sat very still.

“I was going to go myself. Tonight. After I’d slept. To the Walled City.”

“No.”

He looked at her.

“No.” Her voice came out clear. It surprised her. “My family. You answer to me. In everything about my family. You signed it.” She held his eyes. “You don’t go to my father’s house. I go.”

“Elowen…”

“You’ve done your forty-eight hours. This one’s mine.”

“Forty-seven and a half.”

She stared at him.

“Why would you even know the half?”

“You’d have asked.”

She opened her mouth. She shut it. He was right. She absolutely would have.

“Take Bao.”

“Bao has fourteen stitches and hasn’t slept for two days.”

“Take Bao anyway.”

She nearly smiled.

“I’ll take Bao.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She came round the counter and kissed the top of his wet head. He shut his eyes and leaned into it. She stepped back.

He caught her wrist.

He got up off the stool and kissed her. No stopping a breath away. No waiting. One hand at her jaw, one hand flat on her back, her spine against the edge of the counter, and he kissed her like he’d been holding his breath for two days.

She grabbed the front of the sweatshirt and kissed him back.

Then he stopped dead. She felt him realise.

“I didn’t ask.”

“I noticed.”

“Elowen, I—”

“If you say sorry, I’m putting you back in the shower.”

He didn’t say sorry. He put his forehead down on hers and breathed.

“Go to bed. You’re falling asleep standing up.”

He didn’t let go of her wrist.

“With you. One hour. Then you go.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was asleep before she’d got the blanket over them. Flat out. Arm locked round her waist like somebody might come in the night and take her.

Her phone buzzed on the bedside table. She reached for it with her free hand, a centimetre at a time.

Bao: Car is ready when you are Mrs. Zhao.

Elowen: one hour. he said one hour

Bao: I know. I set a timer.

She bit the inside of her cheek so she wouldn’t laugh and wake him.

chapters.title: Elowen Goes to Her Father’s House
chapters.desc: She leaves her husband asleep with a second hair tie on his wrist and goes to the Walled City. Eliana has already found the man who sold her Wednesdays, and a message that says their father knew.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not supposed to be able to see Baba’s staff accounts. I can.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
Bao’s timer went off at exactly one hour. She knew because her phone lit up on the bedside table.

Bao: Now, Mrs. Zhao.

Then ten minutes to get out from under his arm. She counted.

He didn’t wake. When her weight went, he frowned, and his hand closed on the sheet where her waist had been. Grabbing at nothing. Then he was gone again.

She stood by the bed in her socks and looked at him.

Wet hair all over her pillow. Knuckles pink and shiny from the hand cream. One foot hanging off the mattress. He’d killed three people since Thursday. He slept with his mouth open.

Her old hair tie was still on his left wrist. Grey now. Stretched out of shape. Two days of harbour and blood and soap, and he still wouldn’t give it back.

Fine. If he was going to steal them, he could at least have a dry one.

She pulled a fresh one off her own wrist. Black, cheap, she had about a hundred. She worked it over his fingers, one knuckle at a time, and let it go next to the old one. Two. It sat there on the bone, by one of the old white scars on his forearm.

So he’d know. When he woke up and the bed was empty.

She bent and kissed the inside of his wrist, just above it. He made a noise in his throat. Didn’t open his eyes.

“Back by dinner.”

He didn’t hear her. Fine. The hair ties would tell him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Bao was at the bottom of the steps with the engine running.

Fresh bandage, wrist to elbow. He’d shaved. He looked like a man who’d been told to look like he’d slept.

“Mrs. Zhao.”

“You should be in bed.”

“So should you.”

He opened the back door for her. There was a paper bag on the seat. Warm. She looked in. Two egg tarts with the burnt edges. From the bakery by the market gate, the one with the queue she never had time for.

“When did he—”

“On the way home. He made me stop.” Bao shut her door and went round to his. “She wasn’t open yet.”

“So how did you get—”

“He knocked.”

She pictured it. Her husband, at dawn, fresh out of whatever he’d done, hammering on a bakery shutter. The poor woman.

She held the bag on her knees. At the first lights she leaned forward between the seats and looked at his arm.

“How many stitches?”

“Some.”

“Bao.”

“A few.”

“Bao.”

“Fourteen, Mrs. Zhao.”

“FOURTEEN?”

“The doctor was slow.” He pulled away from the lights gently. “She kept stopping to look at the glass.”

“You should be lying down. With your feet up. With somebody bringing you soup!”
