“Boss said the same.”

“And?”

“And here I am.” He checked the mirror. Checked it again. “Eat a tart, Mrs. Zhao.”

She didn’t. All the way across the city, she didn’t open the bag. Her stomach was a fist.

✦ ✦ ✦

The house in the Walled City hadn’t changed at all. That was the worst part.

Same crack in the third step. Same New Year charm on the door, faded to pink. Same neighbour’s birds yelling in their cages like somebody owed them money. Up on the balcony, the empty patch where Mama’s lemon tree had stood for twenty years. The tree lived in her husband’s hall now.

Somebody in this house had sold her. And the birds were still yelling.

Her phone went.

Unknown: You left.

Already? He’d slept an hour. One.

Elowen: you were asleep

Unknown: Two hair ties.

Elowen: so you’d know i’m coming back

Nothing for a bit. She stood at the gate and watched the screen.

Unknown: Bao says the tarts are still in the bag.

She turned round. Bao was looking at the birds with enormous interest.

Elowen: why is bao reporting on PASTRY

Unknown: I asked.

Unknown: Eat one. Please.

Please. From him. She stood at her father’s gate with six strips of tape on her neck and a bag of cold egg tarts, and found she was smiling. Unbelievable.

She ate one standing up. Burnt edge. Perfect. She took a photo of the empty paper case and sent it.

Unknown: Good.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden opened the door before she could knock, his left arm still in plaster to the elbow.

Seven black stitches over one eyebrow. A bruise down that side of his face going green at the edges. He’d been at the window. Of course he had.

He looked at her neck.

His face crumpled. She’d seen it do that once before. He was ten, standing at this same gate, filthy, alone, with a road map drawn up his arm in biro.

He hugged her one-armed. The plaster stuck out sideways. She hugged him back and he squeaked.

“Ribs. Ribs, ribs, ribs—”

“Sorry!”

“S’fine. Don’t let go. Just… gentler.”

She held on gentler. He put his face in her hair. He smelled of hospital soap and the cheap shampoo he’d used since school.

“Jie. I’m sorry. I should’ve done the window. I only did the floor. I had the spec for the glass, it was on my desk, I was going to—”

“The floor held four people, Raiden.”

“I could’ve done laminated, I could’ve—”

“And Mimi’s sunflowers. Mostly.”

He laughed. It came out cracked and he had to hold his side and swear.

He let her go and looked at the strips again, close up. Squinted at them like a drawing he didn’t trust.

“Who did these?”

“Zhendong.”

“Zhao did these? With his hands?”

“What else would he use?”

“They’re very straight.” He sounded offended. “They’re straighter than mine.”

He let her into the hall. Same smell. Soy and floor polish and Baba’s cigarettes.

“Baba’s out. The office. He goes at six. Every day since Wednesday. Comes back at midnight and sits in the kitchen with the light off.”

“Doing what?”

“Nothing. That’s what’s creepy.” He dropped his voice. “He sent you lilies. Did you know? Xiao Pan rang me. White ones. To the shop. No card.”

Baba didn’t buy flowers. He hadn’t bought a single flower since Mama.

Raiden’s phone buzzed in his pocket. He had it out so fast he nearly threw it at the wall. He looked at it. His whole face dropped. He put it away.

“Who was that?”

“Nobody. Work.”

“You’re on sick leave.”

“Work’s very… keen.”

She looked at him. He looked at the ceiling. There was a crack in it. Apparently it was fascinating.

Oh, she was getting this out of him. Later. With a crowbar.

“Eliana’s upstairs. She hasn’t slept.” He rubbed the back of his neck with his good hand. “She’s got something. She wouldn’t tell me what. She said you first.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana’s room was dark. It was always dark.

Blackout curtains. Three screens on the desk, two on the wall. Cables taped along the skirting in coloured bundles. Her actual bed was covered in hard drives, so she slept on a camp bed in the corner like a soldier.

She was in her chair with her knees up under Raiden’s old hoodie. It came down to her shins. She didn’t get up when Elowen came in. She looked at the strips, one by one. Her face went flat.

“Six.”

“Six. Elara says it’s a paper cut with ambitions.”

“Elara says that about everything. She said it about Raiden’s face.”

Elowen sat on the camp bed. It creaked. Her phone buzzed in her hand. Eliana leaned over and read the screen upside down without even trying to hide it.

“Who’s Unknown?”

“Nobody.”

“Unknown says eat the other tart.” Eliana stared at her. “Jie. Is that HIM?”

“It’s none of your business.”

“It is. Who else would care about a tart?” Eliana’s mouth went flat. “You’ve got your husband saved as Unknown. You’re a florist. You name roses.”

“Eliana.”

“I could fix it. Two seconds.”

“Touch my phone and I tell Baba who rewired the doorbell.”

Eliana shut her mouth. Then she turned back to her screens. Her shoulders had come down a little.

“I found him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen didn’t move.

“They had to know when you’d be on your own at the counter.” Eliana pulled her sleeves over her hands. “And about Bao. Where he sits. When he looks up. So I made a list. Everyone who knows your week.”

“How long’s the list?”

“Short. Xiao Pan. Your husband’s people. Us.” A pause. “And Baba’s drivers. Because Baba knows where all of us are. Always.”

Elowen knew that. Eight o’clock every night, her phone. Have you eaten? She’d always thought it was love. It was love. It was also a list.

“I went through all of it.”

“All of what?”

“Phones. Bank accounts. Messages.” Eliana didn’t look round. “I’m not supposed to be able to see Baba’s staff accounts. I can.”

She clicked. A spreadsheet came up. Dates. Numbers.

“Someone who works for Baba got paid. Four times. Cash, each one small enough not to get noticed. Into an account in his mother’s name.” Click. “First one six weeks ago. Last one Tuesday.”

Tuesday. The day before the window.

Click. A face. A driving licence photo, flat and badly lit.

Square jaw. Forties. Elowen knew the face. Last spring, two in the morning, getting out of Baba’s car with a gun under his jacket. The week Old Tan was found in the alley with both legs broken.

Protection, Baba had said. Not looking at her. I hired him.

“Feng.”

“Feng Jun. He eats in the kitchen on Sundays.” Eliana’s voice wobbled. She stamped on it. “He was there when you told Baba Wednesdays are dead at four. He was there when you said Bao reads the paper and only looks up for the door. You said it over the fish, Jie. I passed you the vinegar.”

Elowen sat on the camp bed and looked at the face.

Every Sunday for a year. Lunch at the long table. Her week, out loud, all of it. Showing off, honestly. How quiet the shop was. How bored Bao looked in his corner. And a man in the kitchen doorway, eating rice. Listening.

Had she ever once looked at him? She couldn’t remember his voice.

✦ ✦ ✦

“There’s more.”

“Eliana.”

“I nearly deleted it.” Knees up tight. “But you’d find out. You always find out.” She clicked. A message thread. Two phones. “Baba knew.”

Nobody said anything. One of the fans in the computers whined.

“Not about the shooting. I don’t think he knew that. I don’t.” Too fast. “But he knew Feng was selling something. He found the account. Eight days before.” She pointed. “Look. The first. Baba sent this.”

Lin Jian: I know about your mother’s account. Come to the office tonight. We need to talk.

And under it, an hour later:

Feng: Talk all you like, old man. If I go, the story about the paper twins goes with me. To people who pay a lot more than Qiu Wen.

Then nothing.

No reply from Baba. No more messages. Eight days of nothing. And then a black car coming down her street on a slow Wednesday afternoon.

“What story about the paper twins?” Eliana’s whisper cracked. “Jie. What does that mean? Raiden and Ev? What story?”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen didn’t answer.

She’d known for as long as she could remember. And she’d been told never to know it.

She was two. She remembered it anyway. Or she remembered being told not to remember, which was nearly the same.

A night. Baba coming in with a baby in a blanket that wasn’t theirs. Silk. Foreign. Mama in the kitchen crying with the tap running so nobody would hear. Then Mama in hospital. Then Mama home again with Raiden, red and furious and tiny.

Then Raiden was gone. Sick, they said. Sent somewhere for his chest.

And the foreign baby stayed, and got called Evangeline, and everybody said twins. Twins, twins, twins.

When Raiden came back at ten, walking up to the gate filthy and alone, the whole family just carried on saying it. Like saying it enough would make it true.

Once, at New Year, very drunk, Baba said Evangeline was worth more than this house. Mama told him to be quiet. He was.

Eight days. If I go, the twins go with me. And Baba had chosen.

He’d picked Evangeline’s secret over Elowen’s Wednesdays.

Or he hadn’t known it was her Wednesdays. He’d told himself it was routes. Money. The usual. He hadn’t asked.

Which was worse? She honestly didn’t know.

Either way, eight days. Either way, a black car.

“Jie?” A tiny voice. “Are you okay?”

Elowen stood up. Her knees cracked.

“Print it. All of it. The money, the messages, his face. Two copies.”

“Where are you going?”

Elowen looked at her little sister. Eighteen. Curled up in a hoodie that could fit two of her. Eyes red from three days of screens, finding the man who’d sold her big sister to a shooter.

She pushed Eliana’s fringe off her forehead and kissed it. Energy drinks and Raiden’s laundry.

“Baba’s office.”

“Now? It’s Saturday—”

“He’s there. He’s been there since six.” The printer started up behind her, loud in the dark. She picked up the first warm page. “I think he’s waiting for me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden was at the bottom of the stairs. Obviously. Listening. He didn’t even pretend he wasn’t.

“I’m coming.”

“You’ve got one arm.”

“I’ve got one GOOD arm. And this face.” He pointed at the stitches. “Look at it. I can glare now. I’ve been practising in the mirror.”

“Stay here. Make Eliana sleep.”

“How?”

“Sit on her.”

“She bites!”

“Then sit on her carefully.”

He opened his mouth to argue. His phone buzzed again. He grabbed for it, looked, and his face did the same sad drop as before. He shoved it back in his pocket.

Elowen narrowed her eyes at him. He looked at the crack in the ceiling again.

Later. Crowbar.

The kitchen door was open a hand’s width. Evangeline was at the stove in an old cardigan, barefoot, watching a pan of water like it might do something interesting. She looked round when Elowen came past.

She looked at the strips. Then at the folder of warm pages against Elowen’s chest.

She didn’t say anything. She turned the gas off, filled a flask from the pan, screwed the lid on, and put it in Elowen’s free hand. Hot. Barley tea. Mama’s flask, the green one with the dent.

“Thank you.”

Evangeline nodded.

She went back to the stove. Then she stopped with her back to the room.

“Jie.”

Elowen waited. Evangeline said maybe ten words a day. You didn’t rush any of them.

“Is that about me?”

The flask burned her palm.

Why would she ask that? Why would she even think it? Elowen stood in the kitchen doorway and couldn’t think of one lie that would work on that back.

“Yes.”

Evangeline nodded. Slowly. Like somebody had told her it might rain later.

“Okay.”

She turned the gas back on.

chapters.title: The Man in Her Father’s Office
chapters.desc: Feng is in the outer office eating sunflower seeds. Inside, her father finally tells her what he was paid to do with a baby in a silk blanket, while her husband cuts her tulips at the wrecked shop.
chapters.epigraph: “He wanted to come. I told him no. I told him this was mine.”
chapters.content:
He woke because the bed was cold.

Not because of a sound. There wasn’t one. Just the cold, on his left, where she should have been. He was sitting up with his hand under the pillow before he’d decided to.

Then he saw his wrist.

Two hair ties now. The one he’d taken with him when he left, grey and stretched from the harbour. And next to it a new one. Black. Dry. Hers. She had about a hundred. She left them on the sink, on the dashboard, round the handle of the kettle. He’d found one in his gun case once and put it back exactly where it was.

He looked at them. Kept looking. He didn’t take either of them off.

She’d gone to her father’s. She’d said she would. Page three, paragraph two, in her handwriting. In everything that concerns my family, you answer to me. He’d signed under it.

So he didn’t go to the Walled City.

He went to the shop instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

The police tape was gone. Song Wei Long’s doing. The shutter was half up and the hole where the window had been was covered in board, and somebody had written OPEN SOON on the board in green marker. Xiao Pan. Nobody else wrote like a ransom note.

Inside, glass still sparkled in the corners. The sunflowers were dead on the floor. The ribbon shelf was hanging off one bracket.

The glazier from the Docks was back, measuring the frame again. He’d fixed windscreens on Zhao’s trucks for six years. He saw who’d come in and dropped his tape measure.

“Mr. Zhao. I didn’t… on Thursday nobody said it was yours.”

“It’s hers.”

“Right. Yes. Hers.” The man picked up the tape. His hands weren’t steady. “I’ve got standard on order, it’ll be—”

“No.”

“Laminated, then. The kind jewellers have.”

“Thicker.”

“Thicker than… Mr. Zhao, that’s bank glass.”

“Then bank glass.”

“For a flower shop?”

Zhao looked at him. The glazier wrote bank on his hand in biro.

Xiao Pan came out of the cooler with a broom. Bandages showed at the neck of his T-shirt. Glass in his back on Wednesday, and here he was on Saturday morning, sweeping. He stopped dead.

“Mr. Zhao! You’re supposed to be asleep! Miss Lin said—”

“She’s at her father’s.”

“Oh.” Xiao Pan looked at the floor. “Is she okay? Is her neck—”

“Six strips.”

“Six. Okay. Six is good. Six is fine.” He nodded too many times. “Is that fine?”

“Yes.”

Zhao took his coat off and hung it on the hook behind the counter, where hers went. Then he went to the tulips.

They were still standing. Pink and white. The bucket that had sat over Raiden’s floor. Everything else in the shop had been smashed and they hadn’t lost a petal. There was glass in the water, though. He could see it on the bottom. He rolled his sleeve up and started fishing it out.

“You can’t touch the buckets! Nobody touches the buckets. She’ll kill you.”

He kept going.

“Mr. Zhao. Please. She’ll kill me.”

“Get the knife.”

Xiao Pan got the knife. Zhao took the tulips out of the dirty water and laid them on the bench in a row. He cut the first stem.

“Not like that! On the angle! Under the—”

He’d already done it on the angle. Under the tap. An inch off the bottom. One clean pull towards himself, the way she did it, never a saw. He did the second. The third.

Xiao Pan watched with his mouth open.

“…How do you know how to do that?”

“I watch.”

He’d watched her do it a thousand times. More. Every morning from the egg stool. Every Sunday on the kitchen table at home. The little twist of her wrist at the end. The way she held her breath for the cut and let it out after. He could have done it with his eyes shut.

“That’s actually really good.”

“Hm.”

“That’s, like, scary good—”

His phone buzzed on the bench.

Bao: Walled City. Inside.

He cut another stem.

Bao: Upstairs. Little sister.

Bao: She ate one tart.

Good.

Bao: Leaving. Her father’s office.

He put the knife down.

Lin Jian’s office. The old building by the river, above the shop that sold fishing nets. Twenty minutes from here. He’d done it in fourteen once.

One stairwell. One door. A window at the back over the water, with the desk in front of it. Lin Jian had sat with his back to that window for twenty years.

He thought about it calmly. The stairs. The window. How long. Which hand.

A man who’d sold his daughter’s Wednesdays sat with his back to a window. And Zhao was standing in her shop with her knife, doing nothing about it.

“Mr. Zhao? You’re holding the knife weird.”

He looked down. He put it on the bench.

Bao: Stairs.

He picked the phone up instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

The stairwell smelled of damp concrete, old cigarettes and fish. It always had. She’d run up these stairs after school a hundred times, shouting for him before she got to the top.

Her phone went on the second flight.

Unknown: Bao says you’re on the stairs.

Unknown: I’m at the shop. Twenty minutes. Say the word to Bao and I’m there.

She stopped on the landing.

Elowen: the SHOP?

Unknown: The glazier came.

Unknown: Xiao Pan says I’m doing the tulips wrong.

Elowen: you’re CUTTING them??

Unknown: On the angle.

Elowen: you’re meant to be asleep

Unknown: Not till you’re home.

She was typing go back to bed when the next one came.

Unknown: Then you can put me to bed yourself.

She stood on the landing with a folder of her father’s secrets under her arm, and her face went hot. In this stairwell. Of all the places in the world.

She put the phone away and went up the last flight faster than she meant to.

✦ ✦ ✦

Feng was in the outer office.

She hadn’t expected that. He was in the secretary’s old chair, feet up on her empty desk, eating sunflower seeds out of a paper twist and spitting the shells on the floor.

What was it with men like this and sunflower seeds? Kang at the Docks. Now this one. She was going to have them banned. Citywide.

He looked up when she came in. His face didn’t change. Then he saw Bao behind her. He saw Bao’s arm. He saw the folder.

His feet came off the desk.

“Miss Lin. Your father’s busy.”

“I know. He’s been busy for eight days.”

Feng’s hand went inside his jacket.

“Don’t.”

Bao. Just the one word. His good hand was in his coat pocket. Whatever was in there made a shape.

Feng’s hand stopped.

“He’s been up for three days,” Elowen told Feng. “He’s got fourteen stitches in that arm. He’s in a mood. I wouldn’t.”

Feng took his hand out of his jacket. Slowly. Empty. Then he smiled at her. Wide. Ugly. A man with something in his pocket she couldn’t see.

“Your old man won’t do anything, Miss Lin. He can’t afford to.”

She looked at the shells on the floor. Then at him.

“Sit there. Eat your seeds.”

She walked past him and opened her father’s door without knocking.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lin Jian was at his desk.

He wasn’t working. There were papers everywhere and he wasn’t looking at any of them. His hands were folded on the blotter. He was staring at the door. Like he’d been staring at it since six.

When he saw her, he shut his eyes.

“Elowen.”

She shut the door behind her. She put the folder on his desk, on top of everything, and opened it. She laid the pages out one at a time, the way she laid out stems on the bench. The deposits. The dates. Feng’s face. And on top, the two messages.

He looked down at them.

No questions about how she’d got them. Not one word about Eliana. He just looked, and his face went.

“I didn’t know it was you.” Barely a voice. “I swear on your mother. I thought it was routes. Money. Men like Feng always sell something. I thought it was business.”

“You didn’t ask.”

“No.”

“You found out he was selling to Qiu Wen. And you didn’t ask what.”

“No.”

“Why?”

Nothing.

She put her finger on the second message. The paper twins.

“Because of this.”

He looked up at her. Red eyes. Wet. Old.

“…Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She sat down. She hadn’t meant to. Her legs went and there was a chair behind her. The visitor’s chair. Her feet used to not reach the floor from it.

“Tell me.”

“You know some of it.”

“I know a baby came home in a silk blanket when I was two. I know Mama cried. I know Raiden went away and Ev stayed and we all had to say twins.” She kept her voice flat. “I know you said once she was worth more than our house. That’s all. Nobody ever told me anything else.”

He unfolded his hands. Laid them flat. They were shaking.

“I was paid to make a baby disappear.”

She didn’t move. Her thumb found the ring on her middle finger and turned it. Round and round. Too big. Still. Fifteen months and she’d never had it fixed. Why not? She’d never once asked herself.

“A woman came to me. From a court. Foreign. You’d know the country if I said it. I won’t.” He swallowed. “The king had a child. Not with the queen.”

“And the child was a problem.”

“They wanted it moved. Far away. Permanently.” His mouth twisted. “They never say kill. Nobody ever says kill. They said permanently, and gave me more money than I’d ever seen.”

“And you didn’t.”

“She was in the back of the car in that blanket. A day old. She didn’t cry. She just looked at me.” He stopped. “And I thought about you, at home. Two years old. And your mother, any day now with Raiden.”

“So you kept her.”

“I kept her because I thought she’d be worth something.”

He made himself look at her. She watched him do it.

“A king’s daughter. Alive. Hidden. One day, leverage against a throne. That’s the truth. I want you to have the truth for once in your life. I wasn’t being kind, Elowen. I was doing business.”

“Baba…”

“Then your mother held her. And cried. And called her Evangeline.” His voice cracked straight down the middle. “It means bringer of good news. Did you know that? She found it in a book. And after that I couldn’t do anything with her. She was ours.”

“But the secret was still worth more than the house.”

“It still is. If the wrong people knew she was alive, and where—”

“Traffickers. Ransom. Her father’s enemies.”

“Yes.”

“So you hid Raiden.” She heard her voice climbing. She couldn’t stop it. “Your real son. You sent him to the borderland so nobody would ever count the babies and get two.”

He flinched.

“He was in a freezer, Baba. When he was nine. For eleven hours. Did you know that? Did he ever tell you? He counted to forty thousand in the dark because he thought men were coming for him.”

His face went grey.

“I didn’t know.”

“You didn’t ASK!”

She was on her feet. When had she stood up?

“You never ask! You didn’t ask Raiden what it was like. You didn’t ask Ev what it’s like to be worth more than a house. You didn’t ask Feng what he was selling.”

He had his hand over his mouth.

“You didn’t ask me if I was happy when I married Zhendong. You came to my table and told him I didn’t choose him, and you never once—”

She stopped.

Her father was crying.

Face in his hands at his desk. Shoulders going. No sound at all. Zhendong had cried like that on the bathroom floor. Men like these two had never learned to do it out loud.

She stood over him with the pages spread out between them, and she couldn’t finish the sentence.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a long time before he lifted his face. He looked beaten.

“Eight days.” Hoarse. “I sat in this chair eight days. I told myself it was routes. Money. That he was bluffing. That I’d sort him out after, quietly, when it was safe.”

He laughed. It came out wrong.

“I was scared. That’s it. That’s the whole thing. Scared for Evangeline. Scared of your husband finding out one of my men talked to Qiu Wen.”

“Baba.”

“Scared of losing all this.” He waved a hand at the office. The peeling wall. The calendar from four years ago. “And then on Wednesday Raiden rang me from the hospital. And said your name. And said glass.”

She didn’t say anything.

“I’ve sat here every day since. Waiting. I thought your husband would come up those stairs.” He wiped his face with the back of his hand. “I thought he’d kill me, and I’d let him. I thought that was fair. I didn’t think he’d send you.”

“He didn’t send me.”

She picked the pages up and squared the edges. Tap, tap, on the desk.

“He wanted to come. I told him no. I told him this was mine.”

He stared at her.

“He listened to you.”

“He always listens to me.”

“The arms dealer.” Slowly, like he was reading it off the wall. “Who made my hands shake for six years. Who put a knife through a man’s hand at dinner. Who I hear put Qiu Wen in his own fish pond last night.” His voice dropped. “He wanted to come. You said no. And he stayed home.”

“He’s not home. He’s at the shop.”

“The shop?”

“Cutting stems. My tulips.” She could see it. The egg stool. The knife. Xiao Pan having a breakdown. “On the angle, apparently. Xiao Pan’s supervising.”

Her father opened his mouth. Shut it again.

He looked at her like he hadn’t seen her properly in years. Maybe he hadn’t.

“I was wrong. At your table. What I said to him.” He swallowed. “Wasn’t I?”

She thought about the kitchen floor this morning. Her husband shaking, his fists in the back of her dressing gown. The bottom stair, and I’m sorry, from a man who didn’t say it. A square of paper taped to a wall under the tulips. I’ll come.

“Yes, Baba. You were.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Through the door, a chair scraped. Feng. Moving.

She turned round.

“What will you do?” her father said. “About Feng?”

She stood with her hand on the door handle.

She could open it now and tell Bao to ring her husband. One call. Feng would be gone by tonight and nobody would ever find him. Dead men don’t sell stories. Ev would be safe for good.

Easy. So easy her other hand was already on her phone.

She thought about the koi pond. About a man called Tian with a fish on his wrist. About Zhendong on the kitchen floor, saying he hadn’t felt anything, more frightened of that than of anything he’d done with his hands.

I don’t kill them first.

“Not that.”

“Then what?”

She scrolled. Unknown. Her thumb stopped on it for one second. Then it kept going. Down to a name Aurelia had typed in at the gala, laughing at her. For emergencies, darling. The real kind.

“I’m ringing somebody who can make a man disappear without anybody dying.”

It rang once.

“Mrs. Zhao.”

chapters.title: What a Daughter Owes
chapters.desc: Chen Si takes Feng away and nobody dies. At the kitchen table her father tells them all about the paper twins. Evangeline already knew.
chapters.epigraph: “I wasn’t being protected. I was being hidden.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
Chen Si came in a quarter of an hour.

Camel coat. Two men who stayed on the stairs. A lawyer who stayed in the car. He walked into the outer office and didn’t look at anybody. He held out his hand for the folder.

Elowen gave it to him.

He read it standing up. Every page. The deposits. The messages. Feng’s licence photo. He turned the pages slowly, like a man reading a menu in a restaurant he’d already decided he didn’t like.

Feng watched him from the secretary’s chair.

Feng’s face went through about four things. Confused. Annoyed. Then he worked out who the man in the camel coat was, and a sunflower seed fell out of his fingers and bounced off the desk.

Chen Si closed the folder.

“Go home to the Walled City, Mrs. Zhao. Have dinner with your family. I’ll take it from here.”

“I want to know what you’re going to do.”

“Talk to Mr. Feng.” Mild. Pleasant. A man discussing the weather. “About his mother’s bank account. And about where he was the night Old Tan’s legs got broken.”

Feng made a noise.

“Then I’ll ring your friend Detective Song. He’s been wanting a nice quiet arrest all week.” Chen Si looked at her properly. Finally. “Nobody dies. I promise. I keep my promises. Your husband can tell you.”

She looked at him. This man. Tidy hair. Clean hands. A voice you could fall asleep to.

“He told me you carried him through the sewers.”

For one second the calm face slipped.

“He was very heavy.” He put the folder under his arm. “Go home.”

Feng was on his feet. Sweating.

“You don’t know what I’ve got. Mr. Chen. Ask the old man. There’s a story, there’s two babies, there’s a—”

“Mr. Feng.”

Chen Si didn’t raise his voice. He didn’t even turn round. He was looking at the calendar of girls with beer bottles on the wall like it was a painting.

“I’m going to stop you there. For your sake.” A pause. “Every word you say in front of me is a word I have to do something about. And I’m having such a nice afternoon.”

Feng shut his mouth so fast his teeth clicked.

Chen Si looked at Elowen. Eyebrows up. Still here?

She went. At the door she heard him behind her, still mild.

“Bao. Get that arm seen to.”

“After, Mr. Chen.”

“Bao.”

“After.”

A sigh. A long-suffering one, from a man who ran half the city.

“Every single man he owns is exactly like him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At the shop, Zhao’s phone rang.

He was on the egg stool with the last of the tulips across his knees. Xiao Pan was tying them in bunches with string, very badly, with his tongue out.

“Si.”

“Your wife rang me.”

“I know.”

“Bao?”

“Hm.”

A car door on Chen Si’s end. Traffic. “She rang me so you wouldn’t have to do it.”

“I know.”

He picked up her knife off the bench. Put it down again. Lined it up with the edge.

“Is he alive?”

“He’s sitting on your father-in-law’s floor. Crying.” A pause. “Do you want him?”

Zhao looked at the two hair ties on his wrist.

“Yes.”

“…”

“She said no.”

“She did.”

“Then no.”

Chen Si was quiet. Zhao could hear him breathing down the line. Eleven years he’d heard that breathing. In a drain. In a back room. On the phone at three in the morning when one of them was bleeding.

“You married well, Zhendong.”

“I know.”

“No. I mean for me.” Dry. “Eleven years I’ve been waiting for somebody to say no to you. I’d given up.”

Zhao didn’t answer. He didn’t need to. Si was already laughing at him.

He hung up. Xiao Pan was staring.

“Was that Mr. Chen? Is everything okay? Did something happen to—”

“Your string’s wrong.”

“My string?”

“Double knot. She does a double knot.”

Xiao Pan looked down at the tulips. He looked at Zhao. He undid the knot and did it again.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went home. Not to the hill. The other home.

Baba came with her. He sat in the back of Bao’s car with his hands folded in his lap and didn’t say a word all the way. She didn’t either.

Raiden was in the kitchen, sitting on the counter, which wasn’t allowed. He saw Baba’s face and stayed where he was.

“Off the counter.”

“I’ve got one arm, Jie. I’m allowed.”

“That’s not how arms work.”

“That’s exactly how arms work.”

“Raiden.”

“…Getting down.”

He didn’t get down.

Evangeline was at the stove, which she always was. Eliana came down from the dark at the top of the house hugging her laptop to her chest like a shield. She looked at Baba’s face, and at Elowen’s, and sat down on the bottom stair.

Elara was on the phone, propped against the teapot. Speaker on.

“I’ve got twenty minutes. I’m on nights. I’m in a supply cupboard.” Something rattled. “Go. I’m listening. Go!”

Everybody looked at Elowen.

She looked at her father.

“You tell them. I’m not doing it for you this time.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He told them.

He sat at the head of the long table where he’d sat since before any of them could walk. He told them all of it. The woman from the foreign court. The silk blanket. Moved permanently. The money. Keeping her because she was worth something.

When he got to worth something, he looked straight at Evangeline. His voice broke. He kept going.

Then the other baby. His real son. Born two days later and sent to the borderland so nobody would ever count. The lie the whole family had told for twenty-three years.

Then he stopped. Nobody said anything.

Raiden had slid off the counter at some point and into a chair. He sat with his good hand flat on the table and the plaster arm in his lap. He looked about nine.

Eliana was crying on the stairs with her face pressed into the lid of her laptop. No noise. Just her shoulders.

“Oh, Baba,” Elara said, from the teapot.

And Evangeline—

Evangeline was at the far end of the table now, in her chair, with both hands round a cup of tea. She looked at their father. Perfectly calm.

“I know.”

Everyone turned.

“You WHAT?” Raiden. “You know? Since WHEN?”

“Fifteen.”

Barely there. They all leaned in. They always had, when Ev talked. You didn’t want to miss it.

“The blanket’s in the cedar chest. In the attic. There’s a crest on it.” She turned her cup a little. “Gold thread.”

“Ev…”

“I didn’t say. If I said it, I’d have to be it.” She looked up at their father. “I just wanted to be yours.”

Lin Jian made a sound like something tearing. He put his face down on his folded arms on the table, and his back shook.

“What’s happening?” Elara, from the teapot. “Somebody turn me round. I can only see the ceiling!”

Eliana got up off the stair, wiped her face on her sleeve and turned the phone. Elara saw the table. She stopped talking.

“…Oh, Ev.”

Evangeline got up.

She walked down the long table. Past Raiden. Past Elowen. She stopped next to her father’s chair and stood there a moment. Then she put her hand on his back, between his shoulder blades. Lightly. And left it there.

That was all. She didn’t say anything else. She’d said more in one minute than in most months.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden’s chair went over.

Everyone jumped. He didn’t pick it up. He stood in the middle of the kitchen with his good fist shut and his face white under the bruise.

“Eleven hours.”

Their father lifted his head.

“When I was nine.” Raiden’s voice was shaking. The silly voice had gone. The one he did for everybody. This was the real one under it, low and flat, like Baba’s. “There were men on the road. I thought they were coming for me.”

“Raiden—”

“I hid in the chest freezer in the yard. Eleven hours. I counted to forty thousand. I lost count. I wet myself.” He swallowed. “I didn’t come out till it was light.”

Nobody breathed.

“And all these years I thought it was because I mattered. That somebody wanted to hurt me. That I was being protected.”

He laughed. It was horrible.

“I wasn’t being protected. I was being hidden. So nobody would count. I was the spare.” He looked at his father. “I was the one you could lose.”

“Raiden, please—”

“Don’t. Not yet. I can’t…”

He stopped. He looked at Evangeline, standing by their father with her hand on his back. His twin. His not-twin. The girl he’d argued with their entire lives about who was older.

“You knew. Eight years. You knew and you never—”

“You’d have hated me.”

“I’d have—”

He didn’t finish. He came round the table and put his good arm round her.

Evangeline went still. She always did when somebody touched her. Then she put both arms round him. Careful of the plaster. Not careful of the ribs. Elowen saw him go white and not let go.

The two of them stood there beside their father’s chair. Raiden’s face in her hair. Ev’s eyes shut.

Elowen sat at the table and couldn’t see properly. Somebody pushed a tissue into her hand. Eliana. Who didn’t have one for herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went out into the yard after. The neighbour’s birds were asleep under their cloths. The air smelled of somebody else’s dinner.

Her phone had four messages on it.

Unknown: Si says Feng cried.

Unknown: On the floor.

Unknown: Good.

Unknown: Are you crying.

She sat down on the back step.

Elowen: no

Unknown: Elowen.

Elowen: a bit. everyone is. ev talked. a whole speech. like four sentences

Unknown: Do you want me to come.

She looked at that. Read it again.

Yes. Obviously yes. She wanted him in this yard right now with his big stupid coat and his hand on the back of her neck.

Elowen: no. stay. have you eaten

Unknown: Yes.

Elowen: what

Unknown: Xiao Pan’s pork bun.

Elowen: half or whole

Unknown: Bao isn’t here to tell on me.

She laughed out loud. A bird woke up under its cloth and complained about it.

Unknown: The window goes in on Monday. Bank glass.

Elowen: BANK glass??

Unknown: The glazier asked if it was for a flower shop. I said yes.

She sat on the back step of her father’s house with her face in her knees, laughing, crying a bit, both. Raiden came to the door, saw her, and went away again.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when the others had gone up, she sat at the table with Baba. Just the light over the stove. The kitchen she’d grown up in, dark round the edges.

He looked smaller than this morning. Like somebody had taken a heavy bag off him and he’d forgotten how to stand without it.

“What happens now?”

“Chen Si rang. Feng confessed. About Old Tan.” She watched his face. “He worked for the Qiu brothers the whole time, Baba. They put him with you. He broke Old Tan’s legs himself. Then he came to you the next week and said he could keep you safe.”

Her father shut his eyes.

“You hired the man who did it.”

“…Yes.”

“Wei Long arrested him an hour ago. Old Tan. The money. Helping plan a shooting.” She turned her cup. “Chen Si’s lawyer will make sure he doesn’t get bail. And Chen Si told him that if he ever says the word twins to anyone, his mother’s bank account will be the least of his problems.”

“Do you believe him?”

“Chen Si? Yes.” She shrugged. “Feng believed him too. Wei Long says he was shaking.”

“And your husband?”

“I’ll tell Zhendong everything. Tomorrow.” She turned the cup again. “I don’t lie to him. That was the deal.”

“Even about Evangeline?”

“He’ll keep it. He keeps everything I give him.”

He had a folded order slip in his wallet with one character of his own name on it, in her handwriting. She’d found it when she was looking for change. She’d never said.

Her father didn’t answer. The tap dripped.

“What do I owe you?”

She looked up.

“Tell me. Whatever it is. I’ve owed you since you were seven.” His voice was going. “Since your mother died and you put on her apron and made dinner for your sisters. And never once asked me for anything.”

“Baba—”

“You married a man you were afraid of. For me. And I sold your Wednesdays to keep a secret.” He leaned across the table. “What do I owe you, Elowen?”

She looked at him across the table she’d done her homework on, peeled garlic on, cried on.

“Ask us things.”

He blinked. “What?”

“That’s it. Ask Raiden about the freezer. Ask Eliana why she never sleeps. Ask Elara if she’s happy at the hospital.” She stood up. Her legs were tired. “Ask Ev anything. I think she’d tell you now.”

He didn’t say anything.

“And next time you see my husband, ask him something. Anything. Ask him how the lemon tree is.” Her voice wobbled. She let it. “Don’t tell him who I chose. Ask him.”

Her father didn’t move.

“And you?”

She stopped at the door.

“I won’t come to Sunday lunch. For a while. I’ll come back.” She held on to the frame. “Not yet.”

He nodded. No argument. Not one word about dramatic, or ungrateful, or any of the other things he’d once have said.

“All right.” Then, so low she nearly missed it: “Elowen. Are you happy? With him?”

He’d asked.

She stood in the doorway with her hand on the frame and looked back at him.

“Yes, Baba. I am.”

He nodded again. He looked at his hands. Then he looked up, and he was Lin Jian again, just for a second, the man who rang at eight.

“Have you eaten?”

She laughed. It came out wet.

“One egg tart.”

He got up and put the rice on.

chapters.title: Chen Si Makes a Phone Call
chapters.desc: She can’t go home tonight, so Aurelia takes her forty-four floors up, runs a bath and tells her about the boat. Her husband sits on the stairs till morning.
chapters.epigraph: “Those are wet jeans. In my bath. With my fig bubbles!” — Aurelia Chen
chapters.content:
She didn’t go home that night.

She meant to. She stood at the gate of the house in the Walled City at eleven, with Bao holding the car door open and her phone in her hand. Unknown, on the screen. All she had to do was press it.

She couldn’t.

She wasn’t angry. She was empty. Twelve hours of pulling the truth out of her family one thread at a time, and there was nothing left in her. If she saw his face tonight, she’d fall apart. All over him. And he’d only just stopped shaking on the kitchen floor this morning.

Was that fair? To walk in and fall on him? Tonight?

No.

So she texted instead.

Elowen: feng’s arrested. chen si did it. nobody’s dead. i’m safe

Elowen: i need one night. i’m not coming home. i’ll tell you everything tomorrow. promise. don’t come

The answer came in under ten seconds.

Unknown: Ok.

Then, a minute later.

Unknown: Where will you sleep.

She looked at it. Typed somewhere safe. Deleted it. Typed go to sleep. Deleted that too.

Behind her the front door opened. Baba, in his socks, with the kitchen light behind him.

“Ring me when you get there.”

“I’m always somewhere, Baba.”

“Ring anyway.” He held on to the door. “Please.”

That word again. Everybody was saying it today.

“Okay.”

Headlights came round the corner behind Bao’s car. A long black one. It stopped. The back window came down, and Aurelia Chen leaned out in a cashmere coat over silk pyjamas, hair in a knot, not a scrap of make-up.

“Get in, darling. You’re sleeping at ours.”

“Aurelia—”

“Chen Si’s already told your husband. He said ok to him too.” She rolled her eyes. “They’re both very articulate tonight.”

Bao cleared his throat.

“Mrs. Zhao, I have to—”

“You too, Bao. I have a sofa.” Aurelia was already sliding over on the seat. “It’s Venetian.”

Bao’s face did something complicated. He went to lock his own car.

In the doorway, Baba was staring at the long black car.

“Is that the Song girl?”

“Chen, Baba. She’s been Chen for two years.”

“In her pyjamas?”

“Good night, Mr. Lin!” Aurelia waved at him out of the window like a queen at a parade. He shut the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Chens lived forty-four floors up. Glass on every side. White marble. Paintings Elowen strongly suspected were real. From the living room you could see the whole city, every light of it, all the way to the dark edge of the sea and the cranes of the Iron Docks. Tiny. Like toys somebody had left out.

Aurelia walked straight through all of it, kicked her shoes off, and ran a bath.

“I don’t want a bath.”

“It’s not for you. It’s for me.” She was pouring something into the water. “You can sit on the edge. I’m not drinking alone.”

The bath was black stone, sunk into the floor in front of a window that went straight down forty-four floors. It was the size of a small swimming pool. Aurelia filled it with bubbles that smelled of fig, dropped the pyjamas on the floor without a flicker of shame, got in, and opened a bottle of champagne with a pop that echoed off the stone.

Two glasses. She held one out.

Elowen sat on the edge in her jeans, with six strips of tape on her neck, and took it.

“To Feng. Who’s going to spend a long time in a very small room thinking about his choices.”

They drank.

“What did Chen Si actually do?”

“The usual.” Aurelia put her head back on the stone. “Three phone calls. One to your detective, saying where to find Feng and what he’d find with him. One to a judge who owes us a great deal, about bail. And one to Feng’s lawyer.”

“Feng’s got a lawyer?”

“He does now. He works for us.” A sip. “Nobody shouted. Nobody bled. My husband is good at making things quiet.”

“That’s why I rang him.”

“I know.” Aurelia turned her head on the stone and looked at her. “Do you know what he said when he put the phone down? He was in the kitchen. He looked at me and he said, Zhendong’s wife just stopped him killing a man by ringing me instead.”

Elowen looked down into her glass.

“Then he said, That has never happened. Not once since Block C.” Aurelia smiled. “He was impressed. He’s never impressed. It was extremely attractive. I nearly—”

“Don’t.”

“—made him an omelette. God. What did you think I was going to say?”

✦ ✦ ✦

“You stayed with me.”

It came out of nowhere. Elowen hadn’t planned to say it. She was looking at the bubbles.

“Two days. When he was gone. You slept in the guest room with the door open.”

“Somebody had to.”

“You didn’t have to.” Elowen looked up. “We’ve hated each other since we were fifteen.”

“We have never hated each other.” Aurelia sounded offended. “We compete. It’s completely different. You only hate people you don’t rate.”

“…You rate me?”

“Don’t make it weird. And I’m ahead. Two nights in your guest room.”

“Minus the ice cream.”

“The ice cream was medicinal.”

“You ate the WHOLE tub! With a serving spoon!”

“I was keeping your strength up, darling. By keeping mine up.”

Elowen opened her mouth. Aurelia lifted one wet finger out of the water and pointed it at her.

“And I came because I know what it’s like. The waiting. The phone not ringing. A man going out of the door at six in the morning and you not knowing what comes back.”

Elowen waited.

Aurelia looked out of the window at the city. All of it lit up and none of it making a sound.

“You said he was poisoned. That morning. At the door.”

“I said intensive care. I didn’t say how.” Aurelia’s finger traced a line in the bubbles. “The winter after we married.”

Elowen went still.

“New Year’s Eve. On the Pearl, with the whole Syndicate on board.” Aurelia turned her glass. “I chose the wine. Every bottle. I watched them come off the van, I checked every seal. I opened them myself.”

“Then how—”

“At midnight he took my champagne out of my hand.”

Elowen stared at her.

“He doesn’t drink what people give him. Never. He only drinks what he takes.” Her mouth went crooked. “So somebody made sure it was in my hand.”

“Aurelia…”

“Twenty minutes later, his hand started to shake. His coffee cup rattled in the saucer.” Her voice was perfectly steady. That was the frightening part. “He looked at me across the room. Very calm. And I knew.”

“How long was he—”

“Two weeks in hospital. He couldn’t lift his head off the pillow.” A sip. “And the man who did it sat at our table and waited to see if he’d die.”

“What did you do?”

Aurelia turned her head and smiled. It was not a nice smile. It was a beautiful one.

“I ran everything. In his name. I told his men it was food poisoning. Oysters. And a filthy temper, and anybody who rang him directly would regret it.”

“They believed that?”

“They believed me.” She set the glass down on the stone. “I signed his name on forty documents. I sat in his chair. I knew who it was before he was out of intensive care.”

“And then?”

“I won’t tell you what I did to him. You’d think less of me.”

“I wouldn’t.”

Aurelia looked at her for a long moment.

“No. You wouldn’t. Not any more.” Her eyes narrowed. “Would you?”

Elowen thought about a koi pond she’d never seen. A boy called Tian with a fish tattooed on his wrist. The thing she’d felt on the kitchen floor this morning, with her husband’s head in her lap. Glad. She’d been glad.

She wasn’t ashamed of it. That was new.

“No.”

Aurelia nodded. Like something had just been signed.

✦ ✦ ✦

“His first night home, he woke at three.” Aurelia’s mouth twitched. “I was asleep in the chair next to the bed. Laptop on my knees. Gun on the table. I hadn’t lain down in two weeks. I looked like death.”

“You never look like death.”

“I looked like death, darling. Ask him.” She was smiling now. Properly. “In the morning he texted Qian that his co-ruler was asleep and nobody was to wake her.”

“His co-ruler?”

“That’s what I said! It’s not in the contract.”

“What did he say?”

“He’s putting it in when we renew. In ten years.” She flicked bubbles at the window. “He’s already drafting. He thinks I don’t know.”

Elowen laughed. She couldn’t help it. It surprised them both.

“That’s why I came. Not because I like you.” Aurelia paused. “I do. God help me.”

“You do?”

“Don’t. I’ll deny it in court.” She looked at the water. Her voice changed. “But the nights I sat by that bed with a gun, I was more alone than I’ve ever been in my life. I told you about the chair.”

“The plastic chair.”

“Has he mentioned it yet?”

“No.”

“He won’t. Ever.” Aurelia’s mouth twisted. “I fell asleep on his shoulder once. Four in the morning. I woke up at six and he hadn’t moved. Not an inch. I don’t think he breathed.”

Aurelia’s eyes had gone bright. She blinked at the window until they stopped.

“I’ll love him for that till the day I die. But he doesn’t talk, Elowen. Nobody slept in my guest room with the door open. My own mother didn’t ring.”

She turned her head.

“So. Not while I’m alive. Not to you. That’s all.”

Fourteen nights on a plastic chair, outside his brother’s door. A woman asleep on his shoulder, and him not moving for two hours so she wouldn’t wake. And not one word about it to his wife. Not once in fifteen months.

Why would he? What else was in there that he’d never said?

Elowen put her glass down on the stone.

She stood up. She took her shoes off. One. Two. Then she stepped down into the bath in her jeans and her shirt and all, and sat down in the warm water up to her chest.

Aurelia stared at her.

“You’re wearing JEANS.”

“I know.”

“Those are wet jeans. In my bath. With my fig bubbles!”

“I know.”

And then she was crying.

Three days of not. The window, the blood, the bolt she couldn’t let go of. Her husband’s hands shaking over six white strips. A man she’d never looked at, eating rice in the kitchen doorway. Ev’s calm little voice. I just wanted to be yours. It all came up at once. Ugly. Loud. She couldn’t breathe through it. She hiccupped. Her nose ran into the fig bubbles and she didn’t care.

Aurelia didn’t say anything. She put an arm round Elowen’s wet shoulders and pulled her in, and let her cry into her neck. With her other hand she poured more champagne. Steady as a surgeon.

“There,” she said, when the worst of it was through. “There. It’s all right.”

“It’s not.”

“It is a bit.” She rubbed Elowen’s arm. “It’s a bit all right.”

Somebody knocked on the bathroom door.

“Don’t come in,” Aurelia called. “There’s a florist in the bath.”

A pause on the other side.

“…Dressed?”

“Fully. Jeans, Si. In my fig.”

A longer pause. Elowen put her face in her hands and laughed into her wet palms. It came out half a sob.

“Feng’s in a cell.” Chen Si’s voice through the wood, mild as milk. “Song Wei Long says thank you, and he’ll deny he said it. And Mrs. Zhao—”

Elowen lifted her head.

“I rang the guardhouse at the house. Zhendong’s on your stairs. Since eleven. With the dogs.” Another pause. “He hasn’t moved.”

“On the stairs?”

“On the stairs. I’ll make tea.”

Footsteps going away.

“He’s supposed to be in bed. Zhendong. Not on the—”

“Tomorrow, darling.” Aurelia looked at the door with enormous fondness. “And mine is about to make terrible tea. He thinks you boil the leaves. Tonight you’re in my bath in your wet jeans. We’re going to talk about Miles Wei’s suit at the reunion.”

A laugh hiccupped out of her. “It didn’t fit.”

“It didn’t fit ANYWHERE. Then you’re going to sleep. And in the morning you’ll go home to the man on the stairs and tell him everything.” Aurelia pushed the wet hair off Elowen’s face. “And you’ll finally say it.”

“Say what?”

Aurelia gave her a long, pitying look.

“Elowen. I know when you’re holding something in your mouth. You’ve been holding it for months. Everyone can see it but him.”

Elowen didn’t answer. Her face was burning. It was the bath.

“And you’re still doing my peonies for the museum.”

“…White?”

“White.” Aurelia lifted her chin. “Nobody gets to have white peonies now but us.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the way to the guest room she went past the living room. Bao was on the Venetian sofa. It was gold and had lion feet, and his shoes hung off the end of it. He was sitting up, arms folded, eyes shut, facing the front door.

“Mrs. Zhao.”

His eyes didn’t open.

“Go to sleep, Bao.”

“After.”

“After what?”

“After.”

She gave up. She took the cashmere throw off the back of an armchair that probably cost more than her van, and put it over his knees. He didn’t move. His ears went red.

Aurelia’s guest bed was big enough to lose a person in. The T-shirt she’d lent her smelled of fig. Elowen’s jeans were hanging over the towel rail, dripping on Italian tiles. She’d rung Baba from the lift. He’d answered before it even rang. Have you eaten? Twice.

She lay in the dark and took out her phone.

Elowen: are you on the stairs

The answer came straight away.

Unknown: Yes.

He didn’t even pretend. Of course not. Page three, in his square blunt handwriting, on the first day. He didn’t make things up.

She typed. Deleted. Typed again. Then, before she could be sensible about it, she sent it.

Elowen: tomorrow when i come home don’t let me sleep

The dots came up. Went away. Came up again. She could see him on the bottom stair, Dumpling across his feet, typing with one thumb and deleting it.

Unknown: Ok.

She should have stopped there. She didn’t.

Elowen: page two. line six

Nothing. For a long, long minute, nothing at all. She pictured his face. She pulled the duvet over her head.

Unknown: Elowen.

Just her name. Full stop. She could hear exactly how he’d say it.

Her heart was going like she was seventeen.

Elowen: go to sleep

Read. No answer. He wasn’t going to sleep. She knew it. He knew she knew it.

She lay there grinning at the ceiling like an idiot, with her hand flat over the phone on her chest.

Through the wall, Aurelia’s voice.

“Elowen. I can hear you typing. Put your husband down and go to sleep.”

chapters.title: She Comes Back Through the Front Door
chapters.desc: He spends the whole night on the bottom stair with the dogs, sure she isn’t coming back. She comes home in Aurelia’s clothes, tells him everything, and he asks her to save the last thing for a boring day.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ve meant it for ages. You just have to wait for a boring day to hear it.” — Elowen
chapters.content:
The stair was cold by one in the morning. Zhao didn’t move off it.

Dumpling lay across his feet. Noodle had tried the step above him, then the hall floor, then his lap. Now she was back on the floor with her chin on his shoe, sighing every few minutes like he was the problem.

He was.

Go to sleep. That was the last thing she’d sent. He’d read it forty times. It didn’t get longer.

He knew where she was. Chen Si had sent one line. Ours. Guest room. Door open. So she was safe. Forty-four floors up, in a building with two guards in the lobby and Aurelia in the next room with a gun in her bedside drawer. Safer than here, probably.

That wasn’t the point.

The point was that she’d spent twelve hours in her father’s house finding out her father had sold her. And she hadn’t come home after.

Why would she?

He went through it again, slowly, the way he went through a route. She’d married him to keep Lin Jian alive. Lin Jian was alive. The man who’d put the circle round her face was in a koi pond. The man who’d sold her schedule was in a cell. Whatever she’d needed a wall for, it was gone.

So.

He thought about Feng. About the cell. About how long it would take a man who owed him money to get himself put in the next one. A week. Less. He thought about it in detail, calmly, the way he’d think about a crate.

Then he stopped. She’d chosen. She’d rung Chen Si, not him, so he wouldn’t be the one doing it. Fine. Feng would grow old. Feng could have that.

At three, Bao came down the corridor on his rounds and stopped at the top of the stairs.

“Boss.”

“Go to bed.”

Bao went. He came back ten minutes later with a blanket and dropped it on the step without a word. Zhao didn’t use it. Dumpling did.

At five the window by the door went grey. He was still there.

✦ ✦ ✦

Bao drove her home at seven. He looked almost human. He’d slept at the Chens’ too, on a sofa Aurelia said was Venetian. Whatever that meant for a sofa.

Elowen was in Aurelia’s trousers. They were too long. She’d rolled them twice and they still pooled over her shoes. The jumper was cream cashmere, soft as a cat, and probably worth more than her van.

“He hasn’t moved,” Bao said at the gate. “The guardhouse says. Since eleven.”

“Has he eaten?”

“No.”

“Slept?”

Bao drove halfway up the gravel without a word.

“Bao. Slept?”

“He had the dogs.”

“That’s not sleeping!”

“No, Mrs. Zhao.”

“The first month. When you slept with your door open.” He stopped the car at the steps. “I checked on him at three. Every night, on my rounds. He was awake. Every night. A month.”

She stared at the back of his head.

“Every night?”

“Every night…”

“Why didn’t you say?”

“He’d have shot me.”

A month? She’d thought he dozed out there. She’d thought it was a habit. A sort of guard-dog thing.

“He doesn’t sleep when he doesn’t know where you are.” Bao looked at her in the mirror for once. “He never has. I thought you should know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The dogs didn’t bark. They pressed against her legs, one each side, whining low in their throats.

She opened the front door.

He was on the bottom stair.

Elbows on his knees. Hands hanging between them. The grey sweatshirt from the office cupboard, the one that didn’t fit across the shoulders. Behind him, at the end of the hall, the lemon tree caught the first light.

He looked at her. He didn’t get up straight away. Then he did, slowly, one hand on the banister, like an old man.

“You came back.”

His voice was rough. Like he hadn’t used it all night. He probably hadn’t.

“You thought I wouldn’t?”

No answer. It was all over his face. A whole night on that step, working out that she didn’t need him any more.

Oh, you idiot.

“Zhendong.”

She crossed the hall. He let go of the banister and met her halfway, and she walked straight into him. Arms round his waist. Face in his chest. For one second his hands just hung there. Then his arms came round her so hard her ribs creaked.

He breathed in against her hair. Stopped. Breathed in again.

“All night? On the stairs?”

“Hm.”

“Zhendong!”

“The dogs were with me.”

“You smell of figs.”

“Aurelia’s bath.”

He leaned back enough to look at her. At the trousers. The jumper. Then her neck, the six white strips, one by one. Counting them back.

“I got in it. In my jeans.” She sniffed. “These are hers.”

He looked at her like that was intelligence he’d need to think about later. Alone. Then he pulled her back in and put his chin on top of her head.

“Don’t sleep somewhere I can’t sit outside the door.”

“Zhendong—”

“Not again.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She told him everything. On the bottom stair, side by side, with his hand in her lap and the dogs on their feet.

Feng. The bank deposits. Feng in the kitchen at every Sunday lunch, eating rice, listening. Her father knowing for eight days. The paper twins.

Evangeline. All of it. The foreign court, the silk blanket, moved permanently. The crest in gold thread in the cedar chest. Raiden in the freezer at nine. Baba at the head of the kitchen table, telling them with his face open.

She’d promised at the start that she’d never lie to him. So she didn’t. Not one bit of it.

He didn’t interrupt once. When she got to Evangeline, he went very still. When she ran out, he said one thing.

“She’s safe. Evangeline. Nobody hears it from me. Not Chen Si. Nobody.”

“I know. That’s why I told you.”

He nodded at their hands.

“And Feng.”

“Arrested. Wei Long took him. Chen Si did the calls. A judge, the lawyer.” She watched his face. “Nobody died. I chose that.”

Here it came. You should have called me. The cold flat look. The lecture about leaving men behind you.

“You chose it.”

“Yes.”

“Not me. You.”

“Yes!”

“Okay…”

He turned her hand over and laced his fingers through hers.

That was it? Okay?

“You’re not angry?”

“At Feng. At your father.” He looked at the floor. “Not at you. You made it your way. It worked. Nobody’s dead and he can’t touch you.” His jaw moved. “I put a man in a fish pond this week. I don’t get to tell you your way’s wrong.”

She put her head on his shoulder. Her eyes were stinging. Stupid. She’d cried in a bath all night. Where was it all coming from?

“Aurelia says Chen Si was impressed. That I stopped you by ringing him instead.” She sniffed again. “She says he’s never impressed.”

A breath came out of him. Nearly a laugh.

“Chen Si says a lot of things. He’s usually right.” A pause. “It’s annoying.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She took him upstairs. He was swaying on the step, grey with no sleep. So was she. All she wanted was something soft and his weight next to her.

In the big room at the end of the corridor she turned round. He put his hands on either side of her face. Gently. He bent his head and stopped, a breath from her mouth.

“You said don’t let you sleep.”

Oh. Right. She had said that. In writing.

“I did say that.”

He waited. Of course he waited. He’d sat on a stair for eight hours and now he was going to stand here and wait some more, until she said it.

She grabbed the neck of the ugly sweatshirt and pulled him down.

It wasn’t careful. It wasn’t anything. Two days of thinking she’d lost him, two days of him thinking the same, and it all came out in the worst, best kiss of her life. His teeth caught her lip. She didn’t care. She yanked the sweatshirt up and he had to let go of her face to get his arms out, and it got stuck on his head, and he swore into the cotton.

She laughed. She couldn’t stop. He got free and threw it across the room and kissed her again, laughing too, ragged, like he didn’t believe it.

Then he got hold of the cashmere.

“No—no, it’s Aurelia’s—”

“Let her.”

“She’ll kill me—”

“Let her try.”

He pulled it over her head and dropped it on the floor. Just dropped it. In a heap.

Then he stopped and looked at it.

He folded everything. Towels. Shirts. Her cardigan on the back of a chair, every night, for a year. And there was a cream jumper in a heap on his floor and he was staring at it like he’d found a body.

“I didn’t fold it.”

“No.”

He looked back at her. Chest going. Hair everywhere. That stare. Like something in him had been let off a lead and he’d just found out the ground didn’t open.

“Elowen.”

“Don’t you dare fold it now.”

He didn’t. He picked her up instead and put her on the bed.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was clumsy. So was she. They’d done this a hundred times and suddenly neither of them could do it at all. His belt jammed. Her hair pins went everywhere. He knelt on one and swore again, and she laughed into his shoulder until he shut her up with his mouth.

Then nobody laughed.

He kept stopping to look at her. Her face. Her neck. The strips. His hand hovered over them and wouldn’t land.

“They’re fine. You did them. They’re perfect.”

“Don’t move your head.”

“I’m not moving my—”

“Elowen.”

“Then you move.”

He did. Slowly at first, his forehead on hers, breathing like he’d run up the hill. He said her name. Then he said it into her shoulder, rough, over and over, like it was the only word he had left. His hand stayed spread at the back of her head the whole time, between her and the headboard.

She held on. She’d been holding things for two days. Her father’s file. Evangeline’s blanket. Her own face, still, in that kitchen. Now she let go of all of it and held on to him instead.

When his control went, it went all at once. She felt it. He made a sound like she’d hurt him and pulled her so tight against him she couldn’t breathe, and she didn’t want to.

After that it was just the window going from grey to white, and his heart, slowing down under her cheek.

✦ ✦ ✦

Day came properly. They lay facing each other with the sheet half off, legs tangled. His eyes were nearly shut. His thumb went back and forth on her hip.

She thought of Aurelia in the black stone bath. You’ve been holding it for months. Everyone can see it but him.

“Zhendong. I—”

His eyes opened. He saw it coming. Right there on her face.

He put two fingers on her lips.

“Don’t.”

She blinked at him over his fingers.

“Not today.” Low and rough. “Not after your father. And Feng. And the stairs. If you say it today, I’ll never know.” He swallowed. “If it was true. Or if it was because I looked tired. Because you came home and felt sorry for me.”

She glared at him. He didn’t move his fingers.

“I want to believe it. When you say it. I want it so much I—” He stopped. “So don’t say it on a day like this. Please.”

His thumb went once along her lower lip.

“Say it on a day when nothing’s happened.”

She took his hand off her mouth. She kissed his scarred knuckles, one at a time, all four, while he watched her do it with his jaw tight.

“Fine. A day when nothing’s happened.”

“A boring day.”

“The most boring day in the world.” She held up a finger. “No glass. No fathers. No men in grey jackets. I go to the market at four. You carry the buckets. Nobody orders anything with your name on it. I make fish. You sit down at the table like a person.” Another finger. “Then I tell you.”

He looked at her for a long time.

“And you’ll mean it.”

Same words as the morning after the typhoon. Two centimetres from her face. She’d known even then there was something under them.

“I already mean it. I’ve meant it for ages. You just have to wait for a boring day to hear it.”

His face did something. Not a smile. More like ice on a lake in spring. Not breaking. Just one long crack running all the way across.

He pulled her in against his chest.

“Okay. A boring day.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her phone went at noon. She reached for it over his arm. He didn’t let go, so she read it against his chest.

Aurelia: where is my jumper

Aurelia: elowen

Aurelia: that is italian cashmere

Elowen: it’s fine

Aurelia: WHERE IS IT

She looked over the edge of the bed. Cream heap. Floor. One sock of his on top of it.

Elowen: folded

He read it over her shoulder. He didn’t say anything. His chest started to shake under her.

“Don’t you laugh.”

“Hm.”

“You did that. That’s your fault.”

“Yes.”

He sounded extremely pleased about it.

Before she slept she reached across him for her phone. Thirty-one messages from Unknown. She typed four letters over it and pressed save.

“Took you long enough.”

She hadn’t known he was watching. One eye open. Smug. Unbearably smug.

They fell asleep at noon with the curtains open and the jumper on the floor. A boring day. Easy. Next week, probably.

It took two years.

chapters.title: A Shipment With Children’s Names on It
chapters.desc: Two years on, there’s a plant room with a tap at the height of her hip and a black card she can’t give back. Then he brings home the biggest deal he’s ever been offered and asks her to read it, every page.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t sell to good people, Elowen. Good people don’t need what I sell.” — Zhao Zhendong
chapters.content:
Two springs after the glass, the business came back. Most of it.

The Red Notice was still there. So was the UN report, page sixty, with his name in it. He still couldn’t leave the country. Two old buyers had gone to other brokers and didn’t pick up. But Qiu Wen was gone. His network had scattered like pigeons. And every man at the Docks who’d been waiting to see the wolf fall had heard about the koi pond, and thought about it, and decided to keep buying from him after all.

The house had changed too. Elowen couldn’t have said which day.

One afternoon she came home from the market and the builders were gone. Off the back of the kitchen there was a glass plant room. Stone sink. Slatted shelves. A tap at exactly the height of her hip. The key was on the counter. No note.

“Did you measure my hip?”

“Hm.”

“When?”

He went back to his newspaper.

“Zhendong. When did you measure my hip?”

“You lean on the sink at home. At your father’s.” He turned a page. “Your hip’s on the edge. Every time.”

“You measured me off my father’s sink?”

“Raiden measured the sink.”

“Oh my god. Raiden knew?”

“Raiden drew it.”

She went to look at the plant room again. The tap was perfect. That was the worst part.

Then the kitchen got gutted and put back with a range that took six pots at once, and a cold room for her stems. The woman from the village still came three mornings a week. She still made the lotus root soup better than Elowen did. She still never asked about the locks.

And there was a black card in her wallet with her name on it.

She’d used it once, for a stepladder, to see what would happen. Nothing happened. No bill came. Ever.

“Where do the bills go?”

“Mr. Yao.”

“Who’s Mr. Yao?”

“The accountant.” The newspaper went up again.

She was furious for a week.

“I don’t need a card.”

“I know.”

“I’ve paid for myself since I was fifteen!”

“I know.”

“Then take it back.”

“No.”

He said it the same way he said pass the salt. Then he ate his rice. She took the card out of her wallet and put it on the table between them like a dead fish. It stayed there three days. Then it was back in her wallet. She hadn’t put it there.

“Did you go in my bag?”

“Hm.”

“That’s not an answer…” Then the cooler at the shop died in August with two hundred lilies in it, and she stood in the heat with the card in her hand and argued with herself for ten minutes. She used it.

“It’s a loan.”

“Hm.”

“I mean it! I’m writing it down.”

He’d already forgotten the number. She could tell.

✦ ✦ ✦

She read his files now. Some of them.

At the start she’d told him she’d find his leaks. So she did. Shipping schedules. Warehouse ledgers. The dull paper bones of the thing. She found two small leaks the first year. A warehouse manager in the south who was skimming. An accountant rounding numbers his own way for six years.

She did it at the kitchen counter in the evenings, with a pencil and a cup of tea. He sat beside her and watched.

Like that. Like Granny Su watching a new girl cut a stem right first time.

“Stop it.”

“Stop what.”

“Watching me. Nobody sits that still unless they’re thinking about something.”

“I am.”

“About what?”

“You. And what I’m going to do when you finish that page.”

Her pencil stopped. He refilled her tea. He moved the lamp two centimetres closer to her ledger. He went on sitting exactly that still. She found the skimming warehouse manager twelve minutes later and her face was hot the whole time.

She shut the ledger.

“I’ve finished the page.”

He got up. He turned her stool round by the seat so she faced him, and put his hands on the counter either side of her. He bent his head and stopped. A breath from her mouth. The pencil was still in her fingers.

“Tell me to stop.”

Two years married. He still did this. Every time. Waited right there, an inch away, until she couldn’t stand it.

She didn’t tell him to stop. She dropped the pencil and grabbed his shirt.

He kissed her slowly. All the way. One hand came off the counter to the back of her neck. The other hooked the edge of the stool and dragged it, and her on it, the last bit into him. The warehouse manager in the south went straight out of her head. So did her own name, for a while. When he lifted his mouth to breathe she chased it. He laughed under his breath and gave it back.

The lamp got knocked crooked. Nobody fixed it.

The tea went cold.

She never read the buyer files, though. He never offered. It was the one door in the house nobody opened now.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d had the folder on his desk at the Docks for a week before he brought it home.

Grey cardboard. An elastic band round it. Every morning he took the band off and read it again. Every evening he put the band back on.

Maartens. Alive. In Rotterdam, with a scar through the back of his hand. Two years he’d been quiet. He’d never answered the photograph. And now his office sent this, polite and clean, like there’d never been a knife in a table or peonies or a pond.

Desperate? Or a trap?

He couldn’t tell. That was new. He’d always been able to tell. You read a man like you read a crate. What it weighed. What it said on the side. Whether the side was lying.

This one he couldn’t read.

There was one person who could. She did it at his counter with a pencil and the tip of her tongue between her teeth. She’d hate this one. She’d read it anyway. Every page. She couldn’t not.

For a whole day he thought about not asking. That door was the last clean thing he could keep shut for her.

On the eighth night he put it in his coat and drove home.

✦ ✦ ✦

He put it on the counter in front of her.

“I want you to read this.”

She looked at it. Then at him. He never brought those home.

“What is it?”

“The biggest deal I’ve ever been offered.” He sat on the stool beside her. “A militia in the Velde highlands. Fighting a government that’s also very bad. Enough for four thousand men. Two years. Rifles. Ammunition. Heavier things.”

Flat. No colour in it. The way he always talked about it.

“If I take it, I’m back. All the way. Nobody remembers the notice.” A pause. “Three hundred million.”

She didn’t touch it.

“Why do you want me to read it?”

“The broker’s Maartens.”

Cold went straight down her back.

“Maartens? The hand? He’s alive?”

“Rotterdam.” His jaw went tight. “Quiet for two years. Then this. Either he’s desperate or it’s a trap.” He looked at the folder. “I’ve been looking at it for a week. I can’t tell which.”

He turned his head.

“You see things in paper I don’t.”

She took the band off.

✦ ✦ ✦

She read it with a pencil. Every page. Of course she did.

The Highland Liberation Front. Maps. Lists, in the dry words she’d learned at that awful dinner: units, lots, the agricultural order. A proposed end-user certificate from a small third country she had to look up. Flight routes. A payment schedule in three parts, through banks in four countries.

All very professional. All exactly like the files in Baba’s bottom drawer.

Then, near the back, between the payments and a list of delivery coordinates, something else. A few photocopied pages. Crooked. An aid agency stamp in the corner. Like someone had stuck it in by mistake.

She nearly turned past it.

A children’s charity. A report on how the militia got its soldiers.

Schools. Villages. Refugee camps. Twelve, thirteen, fourteen. Rifles too big for them. Pills to make them brave. Front lines. Because children didn’t run. Because they were cheaper than men.

There was a photo. Five boys in a row in front of a mud wall. The tallest maybe fourteen. The smallest eleven, if that. All holding rifles. The rifles were nearly as tall as the smallest boy. All of them had the same flat empty eyes.

And on the next page, a list.

Names. Ages. Villages. Children the charity had managed to name. Some had a little cross beside them.

It went on for four pages.

She read every name.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she looked up, he was watching her.

Had he moved at all? Her tea had been refilled twice. She didn’t remember it. There was a cardigan round her shoulders that hadn’t been there when she started. The lamp sat exactly over the page.

“How long was I…”

“An hour and twenty minutes.”

“You moved the lamp.”

“Twice.”

“And this?” She touched the cardigan.

“You were cold. Your shoulders go up.” He didn’t look away from her face. “What is it.”

She turned the folder round and pushed it at him, open at the photo.

He looked at the five boys. He turned the page. He read the list. All four pages. She watched his eyes go down the names and not skip one.

He closed it.

“I didn’t see that.”

“It was at the back. Like somebody put it there by mistake.”

“Maybe somebody did.”

“Or somebody in his office wanted you to see it.” She folded her hands on the counter to keep them still. “Somebody who doesn’t want this to happen either.”

He didn’t say anything.

“Zhendong. No.”

The fridge hummed. One of the dogs sighed in the hall.

She could see him thinking. All of it, stacked up behind his eyes. Three hundred million. The notice. The buyers who’d stopped calling. A hundred men at the Docks who needed paying on Friday.

“They’re all bad.” Not arguing. Just telling her. “Every buyer I’ve ever had. The general Maartens bought for at that dinner? He burned villages. The south. The north. I don’t sell to good people, Elowen. Good people don’t need what I sell.”

He tapped the folder.

“If I don’t, someone else will. Russians. A man in Dubai. Those boys still stand in front of that wall.”

“I know.”

“So why this one?”

She looked at the corner of the photo, sticking out where he hadn’t pushed it in. Five pairs of feet in the dust. The smallest pair bare.

“Because I can see their names.”

He went very still.

“All the others, I never saw. The villages. The south. I knew. I married you knowing.” Her voice was going. She let it. “But I never saw a face. Now I have. I can’t un-see them. There’s a boy called Samuel. He was eleven. There’s a cross next to him.”

“Elowen—”

“I’m not asking you to be someone else. I married you knowing. I’d do it again.” She made herself hold his eyes. “But I can’t read the routes for this one. I can’t keep its books at this counter and go to the market at four and know those rifles went to the people who took Samuel. I’ve tried to think of a way. There isn’t one.”

She put her hand flat on the folder.

“So I’m saying no. For me. Not because it’s a trap. Because of the names.” She swallowed. “You decide for you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything for so long she got scared.

Not of him. Scared that this was it. That she’d walked up to the edge of what he was and pointed over it, and now he’d look at her, kind, and say Elowen. This is me. You knew.

He opened the folder again. The list. He ran his finger down the first page, slowly, until it stopped.

Samuel Okonjo. 11. Marisi village. ✝

“When I was eleven I was carrying steel. Old Zhao’s yard. Twelve hours a day.” He didn’t look up. “He didn’t pay me. He fed me, if the work was good. When I dropped something, he burned me.”

She put her hand over his on the page.

“Nobody came to the yard to see. Nobody wrote my name on a list.”

“Zhendong…”

“I’m not a good man. I won’t ever be. I don’t know how.” He shut the folder under her hand. “But I know what it’s like to be eleven and holding something too heavy because a man with a stove told you to.”

He got up. He walked to the kitchen bin and opened it. He dropped the grey folder in, on top of the onion skins and tonight’s fish bones, and let the lid fall.

Then he came back, sat on the stool, and put his face in his hands.

She put her arm round his back and leaned on him. She didn’t say anything. What was there?

“Three hundred million,” he said at last, through his fingers. “Chen Si’s going to be very angry. Maartens is going to be worse.”

“I’ll talk to Chen Si.”

He lifted his head. His eyes were red. He looked about nineteen. Like a boy in a steel yard who’d put something down for the first time and didn’t know what to do with his empty hands.

“You know what this means. Saying no to Maartens. After the pond.” He looked at her. “Something’s going to happen.”

“Yes.”

He took her hand off his back and pressed his mouth into her palm. Same as the night he left for forty-eight hours.

“Okay,” he said, into her skin. “Then something’s going to happen.”

chapters.title: He Cancels the Deal
chapters.desc: Chen Si says there are children in all of it, Bao tells her about his little brother, and Granny Su says soft men live longer. Then the man who runs the northern warehouses calls her husband a dog in front of her, and she turns a page.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ve worked for Mr. Zhao for eight years. I have never been proud of it until yesterday.” — Bao
chapters.content:
“No.”

Chen Si put his coffee cup down on the corner of Zhao’s desk. Click. Very small. Very neat.

Elowen had known him three years. That click was another man throwing a chair.

“It’s done,” Zhao said.

“It is not done. Nothing’s done until Maartens’ office hears. And they haven’t, because I told them you were ill.”

“You told them what?”

“Food poisoning. It’s always food poisoning.” Chen Si stood in the middle of the long bare office with his hands in the pockets of his camel coat. “Zhendong. Three hundred million. Every broker who stopped calling comes crawling back. You’d be where you were before the notice. You’d be—”

“There are children in it, Si.”

“There are children in all of it.”

He didn’t raise his voice. He never did.

“There have always been children in all of it. Every rifle you have ever sold ends up, sooner or later, in hands too small for it. That’s the business. You know that.” He turned. “Mrs. Zhao. With the greatest respect.”

Elowen was on the metal chair by the shelves. The same chair. The first day, with her three pages of terms, and Kang shouting downstairs.

“You married an arms dealer.”

“Si.”

Zhao didn’t even turn round from the whiteboard. Just the one word. Mild.

Chen Si stopped. Down in the warehouse a forklift beeped, backing up.

“I know what I married,” Elowen said.

“Then you know this is what he does.”

“Did. He’s allowed to stop.”
