Chen Si looked at her for a long moment. Then at his brother’s back.

“Is that true? Are you stopping?”

The whiteboard was covered in the Velde routes. Flights. Ports. Arrows. Zhao had been staring at it when Chen Si came in. He hadn’t wiped it.

“I don’t know.” He picked up the eraser. “I’m stopping this one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si was angry for exactly one day. Elowen knew because Aurelia rang that night.

“He came home and sat in his study in the dark for three hours. Three hours, darling. Not a word.”

“Oh no.”

“Then he came out and said, ‘Your friend has ruined my brother.’ And I said, ‘Good.’”

“You didn’t.”

“I did! And he looked at me like I’d shot him. And then he laughed.” A pause, for effect. “He never laughs. It was terrifying.”

“What’s he doing now?”

“Phone calls. Since ten. He’s working out how to do it without anyone getting killed.” A sniff. “He loves a puzzle. It’s disgusting.”

“Is he still angry?”

“Oh, furious. Not at you.” Aurelia’s voice went sly. “He said you were right. In the voice he uses when he hates that somebody else was right. And then he said, ‘Zhendong reads the numbers. She read the names.’”

Elowen didn’t say anything. She held the phone and looked out of the kitchen window at the dark garden.

“Elowen?”

“I’m here.”

“Are you crying?”

“No!”

“You’re crying. I can hear it. Oh, this is the best week of my life.”

The next morning Chen Si’s lawyer went to the Docks with a letter for Rotterdam. Very polite. Very professional. Regrets that, owing to unforeseen circumstances, Northgate Agricultural Holdings is unable to proceed.

He sent a second letter too. Privately. To the children’s charity whose pages had been in the back of the folder. Elowen never saw what was in it. She only knew that a month later the charity got an anonymous donation big enough to build a school.

✦ ✦ ✦

The men at the Docks were angrier than Chen Si.

Not Bao. Bao came into the shop at six the morning the letter went, with the buckets. He put the eucalyptus down carefully. Then he stood in the middle of the floor and looked at her like he was making up his mind.

“Mrs. Zhao.”

She looked up from the roses.

“My younger brother. When I was twelve.” He looked at the eucalyptus, not her. “A man came to our village. He was paying money for boys. My father said no. The man came back with a truck.”

She put the knife down.

“I was at the market in town. My brother wasn’t.” He picked up the empty boxes. “I never saw him again. He was nine.”

“Bao…”

“I’ve worked for Mr. Zhao for eight years. I have never been proud of it until yesterday.”

He went out to the van before she could say a thing.

Xiao Pan was standing in the back doorway with a bucket of water, frozen.

“Miss Lin. Did Bao just… talk? Like, a lot?”

“Fill the buckets, Xiao Pan.”

“That’s the most words I’ve ever heard him say! That was like forty words!”

“Buckets.”

She stood at the counter for a while with her hand flat on the wood. Then she wrapped the roses.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the second morning it had got to the market.

Elowen could tell before she reached stall forty-two. Two of the rose men stopped talking when she walked past. A woman with lilies looked at Zhao, three steps behind her with the buckets, and then very hard at her own feet.

Granny Su was waiting with her cigarette.

“They say your man’s gone soft.”

“Do they.”

“They say he threw money in the rubbish. A lot of money. For a girl.” Granny Su looked past her at Zhao. He was holding four buckets of eucalyptus exactly right. He looked back at her. “That one. Soft.”

“Apparently.”

The old woman squinted at him for a long time. What was she seeing? Elowen honestly didn’t know. A man with a Red Notice and good arms, probably.

“Hm.”

That was Granny Su.

“Hm.”

That was Zhao.

Was that a conversation? Had they just had a whole conversation?

Granny Su stubbed out her cigarette and counted Elowen’s bunches. Every one. Then she leaned across the boxes.

“Soft men live longer,” she said, very low. “Tell him I said. Don’t tell him I said.”

“Which one?”

“Both.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Wu was different.

Wu ran the warehouses in the north. Broad, heavy, in his fifties. He’d known Zhao since Zhao was twenty and carrying boxes for Kang. Wife. Three children. A big house with a big mortgage. A gambling habit he thought was a secret. A third of his money came from the big deals. The Velde would have paid off the house.

He came into the office on the third day without knocking.

It was a Thursday. Elowen was at the desk with the warehouse ledgers and a pencil, the way she was every Thursday now. Zhao was at the whiteboard, finally wiping the Velde off it.

Wu looked at her. Then at him.

“So it’s true. You turned down the Velde. Because of her.”

Zhao kept wiping.

“I turned it down.”

“Because your wife read a charity pamphlet!” Wu’s face had gone dark red. “Three hundred million. My share was six. Six, Zhendong! I carried boxes beside you. And you throw it in a bin because a florist cried over some photos.”

Elowen kept her pencil on the ledger.

Zhao put the eraser down. He turned round. He didn’t come any closer. He just stood by the clean whiteboard with his hands at his sides and looked at Wu. And the whole office went quiet. The way the market did when he walked in.

“She didn’t cry.”

Wu laughed. Short and ugly.

“Oh, sorry. She didn’t cry. She just told you what to do and you did it. Like a dog.”

Zhao didn’t move.

Wu took a step forward. “Everyone’s saying it. All down the Docks. The wolf’s got a muzzle on. He sits in a flower shop in an apron. He lets his wife pick the buyers.” Another step. “And now he’s scared of a bit of blood. The great Zhao Zhendong, who put Qiu Wen in his fishpond—”

“Mr. Wu.”

Both men turned.

She hadn’t looked up. She turned a page. Ran the pencil down a column.

“Warehouse seven. In the north. Yours.” Another page. “Last March you logged eight hundred cases in. The port has six hundred. The two hundred went to a buyer in the south for cash. Again in June. Again in September.”

Wu’s mouth opened. Nothing came out.

“I found it the first time. I wrote it down.” Now she looked up. “I didn’t tell my husband. I thought, he’s got three children and a gambling problem. He’ll stop on his own.” She closed the ledger. “You didn’t.”

His face went from red to grey. Like someone had pulled a plug.

“You’ve worked for him eight years. You’ve been stealing for one of them.” She put the pencil down. “If anyone in this room should be worried about a bit of blood, Mr. Wu, it isn’t my husband.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Wu didn’t look at her. He looked at Zhao.

Zhao was looking at his wife.

Surprise went all the way through him. She watched it. Then something after it, warmer, a lot more dangerous.

“Is it true?”

He said it to Wu. His eyes didn’t leave her.

Wu said nothing.

Zhao turned his head, finally.

“Get out.”

“Zhendong, I—”

“You have three children. That’s the only reason you’re walking out of this room.” Flat. He could have been reading a delivery note. “Take your family. Leave the city tonight. Don’t come back. If I see you again, at the Docks or anywhere, I won’t remember your children.”

Wu stood there breathing hard for one more second. Then he went. Fast down the stairs. The door at the bottom banged.

Zhao looked at her.

She looked back at him over the closed ledger.

“A year. You knew for a year.”

“I said I’d find your leaks.” She stood up and slid the ledger back on its shelf. “I never said I’d hand you all of them. Some I was saving.”

“For what?”

“For a day when somebody called you a dog in front of me.”

He stared at her.

Then he laughed. Out loud. Head back. It filled the whole bare office. Down in the warehouse two men on the forklift looked up.

He crossed the room in three steps and took her face in both hands and kissed her. Hard. In the middle of the office, door wide open, forklift men gawping. No asking. No stopping an inch away. She laughed into his mouth and hung on to his shirt.

“You’re terrifying.”

“Terrifying isn’t the same as afraid.”

She pulled back. Her lips were tingling. So was the rest of her.

“Zhendong. He’s going to talk. Everywhere. The muzzle. The apron.”

“Let him.”

“People will think you’ve gone weak.”

He touched her cheek with one knuckle.

“Weak men don’t throw three hundred million in the bin.” His voice dropped. “And anyone who thinks I’m weak will find out.”

There it was again. Under the words. The thing from the kitchen, when the folder went in on top of the fish bones.

Something’s going to happen.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she’d gone to the shop, he sat at the desk where she’d been sitting. The chair was still warm.

Wu would talk. Good. Let him. A dog with a muzzle on was the kind of dog men walked right up to. He wanted to see who walked up.

He took a pad and wrote three names. The three men who’d laughed loudest at Wu’s jokes about the apron, last month, by the gate. He’d heard them. He’d said nothing. He’d remembered.

Then Maartens.

The letter would reach Rotterdam on Monday. A week to be angry. Another to be sure. Then he’d do something, and it would be loud, because of the knife. The knife had made it about faces. About her face, across a table, telling him to sign with the other hand.

He wasn’t frightened. He checked. He went through himself like a crate, and there was nothing in there about Maartens but a date he didn’t know yet.

What was in there was a Thursday. Fifty-one Thursdays. She’d sat in that chair with Wu’s ledger every one of them, and found it, and said nothing. Saved it up. For him.

He tore off the page with the three names, folded it, and put it in his wallet. Behind the other thing he kept there.

✦ ✦ ✦

Bao followed Wu to the station that night. Zhao didn’t ask him to. He didn’t have to.

He rang at ten. Zhao listened. He said “Hm” twice and hung up.

“Well?”

They were in the kitchen. She was at the counter. He was making her tea. Badly. She’d said once that she liked it when he made it. Now she wasn’t allowed near the kettle.

“The night train north. Wife. Three children. Eleven suitcases.” He put the cup down in front of her. “He cried on the platform.”

“Good.”

He looked at her.

“What?”

“Nothing.” His mouth did the thing at the corner. “You said good.”

“He called you a dog.”

“He called me a dog in front of you.” He leaned on the counter beside her. Close. Shoulder to shoulder. “That’s different.”

“Is it?”

“Hm.”

He picked up her left hand off the counter and turned it over. Looked at the ring. Too big still. It had slid round so the green stone was on the inside of her finger. He turned it back. Stone on top. Where it went.

“What else are you saving?”

“Wouldn’t you like to know.”

“Yes.”

“Tough.”

He bent his head and stopped. An inch away. Of course. Right back to it. Earlier in the office he’d just grabbed her, and now he was going to stand there and be polite?

“Elowen—”

He was going to say something. A report. A plan. She could see it coming. Something about Wu’s men, or the Docks, or what Maartens would do next.

She pulled him down by the collar and kissed it out of his mouth.

When she let go he’d forgotten whatever it was. She could tell. He stood there blinking.

“What was I saying?”

“Nothing important.”

“Hm.”

He left the tea. Neither of them drank it.

chapters.title: The Buyer Does Not Take No Well
chapters.desc: A warehouse burns with a florist’s card left on the gate, and Maartens flies in to ask for a meeting at the old shipyard. She can’t tell her husband not to go, so she moves the fish to the front of the fridge.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ll be home for dinner tomorrow. Will you make the fish?” — Zhao Zhendong
chapters.content:
Nine days after the letter went to Rotterdam, warehouse four went up at three in the morning.

Elowen didn’t hear the bang. Just a thud, far off. Like a door slammed in some other building. Then the dogs. Both of them, howling. Then his phone, buzzing on the bedside table.

By the time she sat up he was dressed.

From the window she could see it. Down at the Docks, past the dark cranes, a column of orange going straight up into the sky. Blue lights crawling toward it along the harbour road.

“Two men.” He was at the door with the phone still in his hand. “The night guards. Old Ming and his nephew.” A beat. “Ming’s dead. The boy’s going to the burns unit.”

“Will he—”

“They don’t know.”

She shut her eyes.

Old Ming was sixty-three. Last summer he’d brought her a bag of lychees from his garden. He’d held them out at arm’s length, shy as a boy. For the lady of the house. His nephew was twenty. He wanted to be a chef.

When she opened her eyes, Zhao was watching her.

“It’s Maartens. He left a card on the gate.” Nothing in his voice moved. “A florist’s card. For the widow.”

Her stomach turned over.

He crossed the room and crouched by the bed. He put his hand on the back of her neck, under her hair. Right where the six strips had been, two years ago. Did he even know he did that? Every time?

“You don’t go to the shop today.”

“I’ve got a wedding at noon.”

“Then Bao takes you. Peng stands at the door. You don’t stand at the window.” His thumb moved once on her neck. “Please.”

He never said please. Not like that.

“I won’t stand at the window.”

He kissed her forehead, hard, and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t stand at the window. It nearly killed her.

Peng stood in the shop doorway all day in a jacket too big for him, glaring at the street. He was twenty-two. He glared at a schoolgirl. He glared at the man who delivered the water. He glared at a pigeon.

“Peng. It’s a pigeon.”

“Yes, Mrs. Zhao.”

“You can stop glaring at it.”

“Boss said nobody.”

Xiao Pan leaned on the counter with his chin in his hands, delighted.

“Miss Lin. Is he going to shoot the pigeon?”

“Nobody is shooting anything!”

She did the wedding. Thirty tables. White and green. She did not go near the window once. At three she went to the shelf beside it for a roll of tape. Her phone buzzed before she’d picked it up.

Zhao: Window.

She stared at it. Then at Peng. Peng looked at the ceiling.

Elowen: I’m getting TAPE

Zhao: Get it from the other side.

Elowen: there isn’t another side

Zhao: Then Peng gets it.

“Peng. Did you just text my husband?”

“…No, Mrs. Zhao.”

“Peng.”

“He said every hour!”

She got the tape herself. From the other side. She went round the long way, behind the cooler, to do it. Then she wrapped thirty tables’ worth of ribbon. Halfway through she thought about Old Ming holding out the lychees. She had to stop. She went into the back and put her face in a bucket of eucalyptus where Xiao Pan couldn’t see.

He saw.

He didn’t say anything. He just started sweeping the floor, very loudly.

✦ ✦ ✦

Maartens came to the city a week later.

He didn’t hide. Commercial flight. Dutch passport. Two lawyers and six men who didn’t look like lawyers. He checked into the hotel on the harbour. The one with the restaurant on the top floor. He booked the same private room.

Then he sent a message through Chen Si. Very polite.

Mr. Maartens believes there has been a misunderstanding. He would like to meet Mr. Zhao in person, at the old Hengli shipyard, Thursday, midnight, so both parties can move on. Mr. Zhao may bring two men. Mr. Maartens will bring two.

“It’s a trap,” Chen Si said.

“Of course it’s a trap.”

They were in the kitchen on the hill. Chen Si had driven up at eleven at night, which he never did. He stood by the counter and didn’t take his coat off. Aurelia had come too. She was on the stool beside Elowen and she hadn’t said a word.

Aurelia. Silent. That was the scariest thing in the room.

“Then don’t go.”

“If I don’t go, he burns another warehouse. Then another. Then the shop.” Zhao leaned on the sink with his arms folded. “He came here. On a plane. With his own face. He knows I can’t go to him, so he came to me.” A pause. “He wants it finished. So do I.”

“He wants you finished.” Chen Si’s voice stayed level. It cost him. Elowen could see it in his hands. “Six men. Two lawyers. And a country that wants you extradited. If anything happens to him here, the whole world watches. Song Wei Long won’t be able to look away even if he wants to.”

“I know.”

“Then let me do it. Calls. His visa. The hotel. I can have him on a plane by—”

“And he goes home and waits.” Zhao shook his head. “A year. Two. And one day a car comes down her street again.” His eyes went to Elowen and away. “I left him behind me once. At that table. With his hand. I’m not doing it twice.”

Chen Si looked at him for a long time. Then at Elowen.

She had her hands round a cup of tea she hadn’t touched. She’d heard every word.

“Mrs. Zhao. Tell him not to go.”

Everyone looked at her.

She looked at her husband. Arms folded. Face gone flat and far away. She’d seen that face once before, crouched by the bed in the dark, saying forty-eight hours.

Old Ming’s lychees. A boy who wanted to be a chef. For the widow.

A boring day. A word she’d been carrying in her mouth for two years.

“Will you come back?”

“Yes.”

“You promised you’d never make anything up.”

His jaw moved.

“I’ll come back. I promise.”

She held his eyes for a long moment. Then she turned to Chen Si.

“I can’t.”

“Elowen—”

“I can’t tell him not to! He’s right. Maartens won’t ever stop. Not after the pond. Not after the Velde.” Her voice held. Somehow. “I said no to the deal. This is what happens when you say no. I knew that.”

Chen Si shut his eyes.

Aurelia reached over without a word and took Elowen’s hand. She held it so tight her rings dug in. Elowen let them.

✦ ✦ ✦

Wednesday night he made her say the code.

They were in bed. Lights off. His arm under her neck. She’d thought he was asleep.

“The basement.”

“I know the code.”

“Say it.”

She said it. Six numbers, into his shoulder.

“Again.”

“Zhendong. I know it.”

“Again.”

She said it again. He was quiet for a bit.

“Your key. The red tag.”

“On my ring. With the shop keys.”

“Keep it on you tomorrow. In your pocket. Not your bag.”

“Why not my bag?”

“Bags get left.”

“Zhendong. I’m going to work. I’m not going to war.”

“The phone on the wall down there. It only rings Chen Si.”

“I know. You showed me. Twice.”

“Hm.”

Was he going to make her say the phone number too? He was. She could feel him thinking about it.

She lay there and counted the scars on his chest with one finger in the dark. She knew them by heart. Block C. The knife at the Docks. The little round one she’d never asked about. She went down the line and back up.

“You’re coming back.”

“Yes.”

“Say it again.”

“I’m coming back.”

“Again.”

He caught her hand flat on his chest and held it there.

“Elowen. Go to sleep.”

She didn’t. Neither did he. She could tell by his breathing. Neither of them said so.

✦ ✦ ✦

He left at eleven on Thursday night.

She walked him to the door. Black coat. Black gloves. Bao was waiting in the car with his arm healed to a long pink scar. A man she didn’t know well, Deng, was in the passenger seat, chewing gum.

At the door, by the lemon tree, he stopped.

“I’ll be home for dinner tomorrow. Will you make the fish?”

“Last time you came home washed.”

He looked at her.

“I’ll come home.”

She reached up and straightened his collar. It didn’t need it. Mama used to do it for Baba every morning, at the door, whether it needed it or not. She smoothed it flat with both hands. Then she left her hands there, on his chest.

She opened her mouth.

He saw it coming. Of course he did. He put two gloved fingers on her lips.

“Not today.”

She glared at him over the leather.

“Today isn’t boring.”

“Zhendong—”

“Tell me tomorrow. At dinner. Over the fish.”

He took his fingers away. He bent and kissed her. Once. Then again, harder, his gloved hand at the back of her head, all of him bent over her in the doorway. Like he was taking the taste of her out into the dark and coming back for the rest.

“Then I’ll know it’s true. Because I’ll be home. And nothing will be happening. And you’ll still say it.”

He went down the steps. The dogs went after him, to the car, and then stood on the gravel side by side, stiff, watching it go. Down the drive. Out of the gate. Down the hill.

She stood in the doorway until the tail lights were gone.

Then she went to the kitchen and opened the fridge. The fish was on the bottom shelf. She moved it to the front. Ready.

✦ ✦ ✦

Bao drove. Nobody talked. Deng had stopped chewing.

Zhao looked out at the harbour. Black water. The shipyard cranes coming up ahead, rusted, against a sky with no stars.

Maartens would be early. Men like Maartens were always early. They liked to stand in a place first and feel it was theirs. He’d have more than two men. He’d have the six. Whoever he’d bought here. Somebody up a crane with a rifle, probably. He’d have seen it in a film.

Fine.

He went through it. The yard. The dock edge. The old slipway. Where he’d put a man, if he were Maartens. Where he’d put two.

Not the house. Not her in the doorway, with her hands flat on his chest and her mouth open on a word.

He thought about it the whole way.

“Boss.” Bao, at the gate. “Lights. Three cars. Not two.”

“Hm.”

“Boss…”

“I know.”

He took off one glove and put his hand in his coat pocket. His wallet was there. He touched it once, through the leather, the way some men touched a cross. Then he put the glove back on.

“Let’s go.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before one, her phone rang.

Not his number. Chen Si’s.

She was on the bottom stair in the hall by the lemon tree. In her coat. She hadn’t been able to take it off. She answered before it rang twice.

“Elowen. Listen to me.”

He didn’t sound calm. She’d known him three years and he had never once not sounded calm.

“Something happened at the shipyard. There was shooting. A lot. My people are there. Maartens is dead. Two of his men are dead.”

“Zhendong.”

“Bao’s alive. He’s hurt. My people have him, they’re taking him to Elara. Deng is…” He stopped. “Deng’s dead.”

“Zhendong.”

A gap on the line. Short. Horrible.

“We can’t find him.”

She couldn’t say anything. Her body had gone somewhere ahead of her. Her hands were cold to the wrist. A high thin ringing started in her ears. The hall went far away and bright. Her heart was thudding slow and stupid, like it hadn’t heard yet.

Her free hand was flat on the stair beside her. On the worn place. Where he always sat.

Was it still warm? Was he? Somewhere?

“Bao says he was hit. In the side. He saw him go down by the water. Then Maartens’ other men came round the cranes and Bao was hit too, and when he looked again—” A breath. “Gone. There’s blood on the edge of the dock. A lot. Then nothing.”

“The water.”

“We’re searching the water. The yard. Every boat in the harbour. Forty men. Song Wei Long has the police out, unofficially. Eliana’s in the traffic cameras.”

“He can’t swim far. His side—”

“I know.” He stopped. “Elowen. I need you to go to the basement. Put in the code. Lock it. Stay there until I ring. Maartens had more than six men. We don’t know where the rest are. We don’t know if they’re coming to the house.”

She looked down the hall. The lemon tree. The dark window. The kitchen door, and the fridge, and the fish at the front of the shelf.

“Elowen?”

“I heard you.”

She stood up.

She went through the kitchen and opened the door to the basement stairs. At the bottom, the steel door. Six numbers, or one small key with a red tag.

She went back up first.

His old coat was on the hook in the hall. Black wool. The one he’d worn the night it rained in her shop, three years ago. He’d kept wearing it till the elbows went thin. She took it down and held it against her chest.

Then she went down and put in the code and locked herself in.

She turned on the lamp over the workbench. She sat on the armory floor with her back against the wall and his coat in her arms.

In the drawer was the small black pistol. The one he’d taught her on, on a wet terrace on a mountain. She took it out. She checked it the way he’d shown her. Hands steady. Why were her hands steady? She put it on the floor by her knee.

Then she waited. Like he’d told her to, the very first night.

For how long?

For me.

chapters.title: Three Days
chapters.desc: Three days in the armory with his coat and a gun. Everyone who loves her comes to the steel door, and she won’t open it for any of them.
chapters.epigraph: “Tell the girl her husband carries better than anyone I’ve ever had, so he has to come back.” — Granny Su
chapters.content:
She’d done her teeth first. That was the stupid part.

Husband gone to a shipyard to meet a man who wanted him dead, and she’d done her teeth and put on her nightdress like any wife on any Thursday. Then she’d put her coat back on over it and gone and sat on the stairs.

Now she was on the armory floor. Nightdress. Her coat. His old coat on top of that. Bare feet, because the slippers had come off somewhere by the bench and she couldn’t be bothered to find them.

The little pistol sat by her knee. The lamp over the workbench hummed.

Thick walls. Air hissing through the vent he’d built from somewhere up the hill. Her own heart. Nothing else.

No signal, either. Except, she found out, if she stood on the bench and held her phone up to the vent like an idiot. One bar. If she didn’t breathe.

His last message was still at the bottom of the screen.

Zhao: Hall light.

Elowen: it’s on

Ten minutes before Chen Si rang. He’d been standing in a shipyard with men waiting to shoot him, and he’d texted about the hall light. So he’d see it from the gate when he came up the drive.

She typed with one thumb, wobbling on the bench.

Elowen: still on

Elowen: i’m in the basement. i said the code twice. you’d be so smug

One grey tick each. They didn’t go blue.

She got down before she fell off.

✦ ✦ ✦

The wall phone rang at three. She had it before the first ring finished.

“Nothing yet.”

Chen Si. Wind behind him. An engine.

“Divers are in. The coastguard. Eliana has every camera within five kilometres of the shipyard. Nothing.”

“Is he—”

“I don’t know.”

Chen Si didn’t say that. Chen Si always knew.

“He texted me. About the hall light.”

A gap on the line.

“When?”

“Ten minutes before you rang.”

“Then he was thinking about coming home.” Something scraped at his end. A hull, maybe. “Are you safe?”

“I’m in a steel box under a hill. Yes.”

“Don’t open the door for anyone.”

“I can’t see anyone. It’s steel.”

“Then don’t open it.”

He rang off. She kept her hand on the receiver after she’d hung it up. Warm plastic. Stupid.

The coat smelled of him. Soap. Gun oil. Cold air off the sea. Something crackled in the inside pocket. A page, folded tight, over and over, gone soft at the creases.

Gravitational lensing of light by low-mass compact objects: a perturbative approach. M. Wei.

The last page of Miles’s paper. His square blunt writing in the margin. He made her feel calm. I make her feel afraid. I should let her go to the reunion alone.

Under it, in hers. No. You come with me. Plus one. And for the record, I said terrifying. That isn’t the same as afraid.

Two years and a bit. In the pocket of his oldest coat.

Who keeps that? Who carries round a page of somebody else’s physics?

Him. Obviously. She knew why, too. That was the problem.

She sat with it in her lap and didn’t fold it up again. When she next looked at her watch, it said morning. Nothing else down here did.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia came at nine. Heels on the concrete steps. Then knuckles on the steel, which must have hurt.

“Darling. It’s me. Open the door.”

“No.”

“I brought coffee. Mine. You know how terrible it is, so you know I mean it.”

“No.”

“Elowen. I sat with you last time. You let me.”

Elowen put her forehead on her knees.

“Last time I knew he was coming back.”

“You don’t know he isn’t.”

“Last time he gave me a number! Forty-eight hours. He came back in forty-eight hours, washed.” Her voice cracked right down the middle. “This time he gave me dinner. Dinner was yesterday.”

Nothing from the other side.

“If I open the door, I have to come out. If I come out, I’m in a house he isn’t in.”

“Elowen…”

“This is where he wants me. So I’m here. I’m being good, Aurelia. For once in my life.”

A coat rustled. A thump. A swear in Italian, under her breath.

Aurelia Chen was sitting on a concrete step. In whatever that coat had cost.

“Fine. Then I’ll wait out here.”

“You’ll ruin your coat.”

“I have four.”

She stayed six hours. Phone calls in Italian, sharp and low. The click of her lighter, once. Then the snap of it shutting again, when she remembered what was racked up on the other side of the door.

At three she knocked.

“I’m leaving a sandwich on the step. Eat it, or I tell everyone you cried in my bath in your jeans.”

“Everyone knows.”

“Then I’ll tell them what you think of my sofa.”

Elowen had never once mentioned her sofa. She nearly smiled. It hurt her face.

The heels went up the stairs. The sandwich stayed where it was.

✦ ✦ ✦

Other feet came down after the heels. Heavy. Uneven. Like one side of the man didn’t want to come.

They stopped. Nobody knocked.

“Bao?”

“Mrs. Zhao.”

She was at the door before she knew she’d got up. Both palms flat on the steel.

“You’re hurt. Chen Si says you were hit.”

“Shoulder. Your sister sewed it up.” A pause. “She was rude to me the whole time.”

“Good.”

“Lucky, she kept saying. Lucky, lucky. I’m not lucky.”

She could hear him breathing on the other side. Slow. Through his nose. Like he was trying to do it properly.

“Tell me.”

“Mrs. Zhao—”

“You were there. Chen Si wasn’t. Tell me, Bao.”

“Three cars. He knew. He went in anyway.” The steel creaked. He’d leaned on it. “The Dutchman talked a lot. Boss didn’t. Then the Dutchman had a gun in his good hand. Boss saw it late.”

She shut her eyes.

“And Maartens?”

“Boss.”

Just that. Good. She waited to feel anything else about it. Nothing came.

“Then the men on the cranes. He pushed me down behind the car. He was already hit. Here.” A thump, low on the steel. A fist. Left side. “He went back two steps and over the edge. Into the water. Then they got me, and when I could look—”

“Gone.”

“I lost him.” Bao’s voice went up. She’d never heard it go up. “Eight years I drive him. I never lost him once. Not once, Mrs. Zhao!”

“You didn’t lose him. He went in the sea.”

“I should have gone in after.”

“With a hole in your shoulder? You’d have drowned, you idiot.”

He breathed for a bit.

“His orders. If anything happens, I drive you to the market. Every day. Four o’clock. Same as him.”

“Nothing’s happened.”

“No, Mrs. Zhao.”

“Nothing’s happened, Bao.”

“No.”

He sat down out there. She heard him do it, slow, careful of the shoulder. Then a rustle of paper.

“Bao. Are you eating Aurelia’s sandwich?”

“…You weren’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father came at five. She knew his feet. Slow. Heavy. He didn’t knock either.

“Baba.”

“Elowen.” Rough. “Chen Si rang me. I came.” A long breath against the steel. “I don’t know what to say.”

She didn’t either. She put her cheek on the door.

“I was wrong. At your table. I sat there over your fish and called him the price. To his face. In his own house.”

“Baba, don’t—”

“And after that. At the Docks. Every time I went in with a file, he got in first. Before I could open my mouth.”

“Got in with what?”

“Mr. Lin, how is your back.” His voice went flat and low. Doing Zhao. Badly. “Mr. Lin, did Eliana get her exam results. Mr. Lin, I heard Raiden won a prize.”

Oh. Oh, Zhendong.

“A year of that. I thought it was a trick. Some way to make me owe him.” The door creaked again. Everyone leaned on this door. “Then you, in my kitchen. Ask him something, Baba. And I understood. A year he’d been doing it. For you.”

“So what did you…”

“The next week I went in with a file, and I got in first. How is the lemon tree?”

His voice broke on tree.

“And him?”

“That look. That long look of his. Then: Seven lemons. The most it’s ever had.” A breath. “And he smiled. At me. I didn’t know his face could.”

She was crying. No sound. Straight into the wool of his coat.

“He’ll come back. You hear me? He’s too stubborn to die in a harbour.” A laugh with no air in it. “He hasn’t had his dinner.”

She laughed too. Wet and horrible, into the coat.

“Go home, Baba. Ring Raiden. He’ll be pretending he’s fine.”

“And you?”

“I’m not pretending anything. I’m in a basement.”

He stood there a while longer. Then his feet went back up, one at a time. Bao’s didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second night, she cleaned a gun.

She hadn’t planned to. Some time after midnight she got up off the floor, stiff all over, and went to the bench. Not the little pistol. The heavy one. The one he cleaned at two in the morning when he thought she was asleep.

Cloth. Brushes. Oil. She laid them out how he did.

She’d watched him a hundred times. She’d never once done it.

First go, wrong. Second go, a spring shot across the floor and she had to crawl under the rack after it, swearing. Third go, the pieces lay in a straight line on the cloth. She picked them up one at a time.

When I was sixteen, nothing in my life did what it was supposed to. Except this. You clean it, you put it back, it works. Every time.

People don’t.

An hour to put back. The last piece clicked in. She sat there holding it under the lamp. Heavy. Done. Exactly what it was.

So that was it. Two in the morning, down here, he got an hour of holding something that wouldn’t break on him.

She climbed on the bench with her phone.

Elowen: i cleaned your gun. the heavy one

Elowen: a spring went under the rack. i found it

Elowen: you’d have done it in ten minutes. shut up

Grey. Grey. Grey.

The wall phone rang at four.

“They found his phone.”

Chen Si. No wind this time. Indoors.

“In the harbour. A diver. On the bottom by the dock edge.” A pause. “Nothing else.”

She looked at her own phone. Three grey ticks. That was where they’d been going all night. Into the mud. Into the black.

All those nights it had buzzed on the bedside table, and he’d grabbed it before the second buzz so it wouldn’t wake her.

When had she slid down the wall? She was on the floor. Knees up. His coat jammed against her mouth so hard she could taste wool, so the noise wouldn’t go down the line.

“Elowen. I’m not stopping.”

She couldn’t answer.

“Do you hear me? I carried him through a sewer. I am not stopping.”

“I know…”

“Say it back.”

“You’re not stopping.”

“Good. Now drink some water. Bao says he hasn’t heard a bottle open since yesterday.”

Bao. Sitting on the step. Listening for bottles. Reporting her. Unbelievable.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second day, Raiden came.

He sat on the step and said nothing for an hour. Raiden. Saying nothing. For an hour.

“Rai?”

“Mm.”

“Say something stupid.”

“Can’t think of anything.”

That was worse than the phone.

Then paper slid under the door. A floor plan of the house on the hill. Every room. Every door, every window. In the corner, in his neat draftsman’s hand: Every way back in. He knows all of them. I built three of them.

“Which three?”

“Not telling. He’d kill me.” A pause. “So he has to come back and kill me, Jie. That’s the rule.”

She held the plan till the edges went soft.

Evangeline came after him. She didn’t say a word. Elowen only knew it was her because nobody else alive could be that quiet and still be breathing. Three hours. Then the feet went away.

“Mrs. Zhao.” Bao. “She left tea. And a flower. In a glass.”

“What flower?”

“…Purple.”

An orchid. Of course. From the stalls at five in the morning, where Ev always went.

“Drink the tea, Bao.”

“It’s yours.”

“Drink it.”

A long slurp through the steel.

“It’s very good tea.”

Eliana didn’t come. Eliana sent messages through Chen Si, every hour, and made him promise to read them out at the end of every call. Word for word. He did, in his flat careful voice, like a man reading out a share price.

Eliana: still looking. still looking. camera 112 has nothing. still looking. jie im not sleeping either

“Tell her to sleep.”

“I have. She sent back a word I won’t repeat.”

At six, an engine buzzed up the drive. Xiao Pan’s motorbike. The small red one Jinx had built him. She’d know that rattle anywhere.

“MISS LIN!” From the top of the stairs. Miles up. “Peng won’t let me come down! He says it’s Boss’s rule!”

“Peng’s right!”

“I opened the shop!”

“You what?”

“I did the market with Granny Su! I’m sending a note down with Bao!”

Paper came under the door, damp from Bao’s hand. Careful schoolboy writing.

Miss Lin, the shop is open. Granny Su counted every bunch. She says to tell you, “Tell the girl her husband carries better than anyone I’ve ever had, so he has to come back.”

She read it lying flat on the floor by the gap. She laughed and cried at once. She couldn’t tell which one was winning.

“Is she laughing?” Xiao Pan, faint, from the top. “Bao. Is that laughing or the other one?”

“Go home, boy.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The third night, she stopped crying. Nothing left.

She sat with his coat round her shoulders, Miles’s page in her lap, the gun by her knee. Calm. Empty. And she thought about the thing she hadn’t said.

She’d said happy. On the mountain, in the rain. Not the other one.

Two years she’d had it in her mouth. The morning she came home from Aurelia’s, and his fingers on her lips. The front door, by the lemon tree. His gloves. Tell me tomorrow. At dinner. Over the fish.

The fish was still in the fridge upstairs. Front of the shelf. Going off. She couldn’t throw it out.

What if he didn’t come back?

Then he’d never know. He’d die thinking she married him for her father and stayed because she was polite. Her. Polite.

He’d sat outside her door every night for a month so she’d never have to wonder where he was. And she’d let him wonder about her for three years.

She pushed her face into the coat. It smelled of her now. Her shampoo. Her crying. The floor. She had to dig her nose into the seam under the collar to find him. Soap. Oil. The sea. Fainter every hour. She took tiny breaths of it, like water she was making last.

Then that ran out too. So she remembered.

This room, the first night. His hand stopped in the air by her cheek. Say yes. Or go upstairs. The cooler at one degree. Cold water off the roses running down her neck, and his warm hand catching it. The mountain. His mouth on the back of her neck while the rain came down.

How he nearly always stopped first. Waited for her to say it.

And the office, last week. No asking. Forklift men gawping. She hadn’t minded at all.

If he came back, she’d never make him wait for anything again.

If.

She climbed on the bench one last time.

Elowen: the fish has gone off

Elowen: i’ll buy another one

Elowen: come home and eat it

✦ ✦ ✦

At 3:10 in the morning on the third night, the dogs started barking.

Not fox barking. Not car barking. High. Wild. Both of them, far off, up through all that concrete. On and on. Then something that was nearly a scream.

She was on her feet with the pistol in her hand. When had she stood up?

The wall phone went.

“Mrs. Zhao—Miss Lin—”

Not Chen Si. Peng, from the gatehouse. Young and shaking.

“The gate! Somebody’s at the gate, on the ground, the dogs got there first, they won’t let us near—” He was nearly crying. “It’s him. It’s Mr. Zhao. He crawled. From the sea road. There’s a trail all the way up the hill—”

She dropped the phone.

She didn’t remember the code. Or Bao flattening himself against the wall as the steel swung out. Or the stairs, or the kitchen. She remembered the hall light, still on. The front door. Cold. Gravel under her bare feet, running, his coat flapping off her shoulders, the pistol still in her hand.

The floodlights at the gate. Two dogs standing over something dark on the ground. Barking. Nobody could get near.

Then the dogs saw her. They stopped. They stepped aside.

chapters.title: He Crawled the Last Mile
chapters.desc: He crawls home up the hill with a bullet in his side. Elara brings two bags of stolen hospital supplies, and Elowen holds his face on the kitchen table for two hours.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m late. For dinner.”
chapters.content:
The hold smelled of fish. Diesel. Him, by the second day.

Maartens had brought a gun. In the hand Zhao hadn’t put a knife through. Zhao hadn’t expected him to be any use with it. Wrong. The bullet went in low on his left side, under the old Block C scar, and came out round the back.

He shot Maartens twice. The second one to be sure. The man had come a long way, and Zhao didn’t want him making the trip again.

Then the cranes opened up, like he’d known they would. He pushed Bao down behind the car. Two steps back. The dock edge. Black water. He came up under the pilings with his mouth full of the harbour.

There was a fishing boat tied at the end of the old slipway. Nets in the stern. A hatch. A hold nobody had washed since spring. He got in. He tied what was left of his shirt round his middle and pushed the rest into the holes, front and back. He’d seen it done in Block C. It wasn’t clever. It would do.

He pulled the nets back over the hatch from underneath. Then he lay down on the fish scales in the dark. At dawn the boat went out. Nobody looked under the nets. Why would they?

He heard the search go past. Engines. A coastguard horn. Chen Si, once, far off across the water, shouting his name. He didn’t shout back. Maartens had bought men in this city. A man shouting from a hold with a hole in him got found by whoever was closest. He didn’t know who was closest.

So he lay there and looked at her.

There was nothing to look at. Slats. Dark. But she was there anyway. At the market at four with the van keys in her teeth. In the cooler, cross, with rose water running down her neck. On the bottom stair in Aurelia’s trousers. At the door, with her hands flat on his chest and her mouth open on a word.

When he looked away from her, the dark came up. So he didn’t look away. The fever came on the second day. He noted it. He noted the smell from his side, too. Sweet. Wrong. Then he went back to her.

The boat came in on the third night, to the little harbour under the sea road. The crew went up to the noodle stall. He climbed out. That took a long time.

The sea road was flat. The hill road wasn’t. He’d driven it a thousand times and never counted the bends. Eleven. He counted them now. On his elbows. Then on his hands, when his elbows went.

Somewhere around the seventh bend he worked out, in plain words, what he was doing this for. It was so stupid he’d have laughed if he’d had the air. I said I’d be home for dinner.

The dogs heard him at the gate. They’d been listening for three days.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was curled on his side at the foot of the gate. Soaked. Salt water and something darker. His shirt was mostly gone. What was left was knotted round his middle, black with blood. His face was grey. His lips were blue. His palms were torn open from the road.

Behind him, out through the gate and down the hill toward the sea, a long dark broken line shone under the floodlights.

She went down on her knees in the gravel.

“Zhendong.”

“Mrs. Zhao, don’t move him, don’t—”

“I’m not moving him!”

His eyes were half open. They didn’t move.

“Zhendong. Look at me. Look at me!”

She put her hands on his face. Cold and wet, and burning under the cold. She felt for the pulse in his neck, in the place Elara had shown her at Sunday lunch for a joke. Fast. Thin. A moth in a jar.

But there.

His eyes came round slowly and found her. He kept looking. Like he’d seen her too often in the dark to trust this one.

“I’m late. For dinner.”

His lips split when he said it.

A noise came out of her. Not a word. She grabbed his face and kissed him. His cracked blue mouth. Salt and blood and cold. Hard, like she could shove the heat back into him by force.

His lips moved under hers. Barely. It was enough.

She put her forehead down on his wet shoulder and breathed.

“Mrs. Zhao.” Peng, crouching beside her, hands going. “We have to move him, he’s—”

She lifted her head. Something in her went cold and clear. Same as the day the glass came in.

“Ring Elara. My sister. Her number’s on the gatehouse wall.”

“Yes, yes—”

“Tell her gunshot, left side, three days, fever, he’s lost a lot of blood, he’s been in the sea. Tell her to bring everything. Tell her to steal it if she has to.”

Peng stared at her.

“No hospital. Tell her that. Tell her come.”

“Mrs. Zhao, he needs a hospital—”

“He has a Red Notice and a dead Dutchman at the shipyard. In a hospital he wakes up in handcuffs.” She looked down at him. “If he wakes up. Go! Then Chen Si. Then nobody.”

Peng ran.

She pulled his old coat off her shoulders and put it over him. It was his. He could have it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

They put him on the kitchen table. Biggest surface in the house. Best light. Next to the sink.

She swept it clear with her arm. Fruit bowl. The post. Bao’s mandarins, rolling everywhere. Bao and the other guard carried him in, Bao one-armed and grey in the face.

“His head. Mind his head!”

“I’ve got him, Mrs. Zhao.”

“You’ve got one arm!”

“I’ve got him.”

When they put him down he made a sound, low and awful. Then no sound at all.

She went for the knot of shirt with her florist’s knife.

His hand shot up and closed on her wrist. Where did that come from? Three days in a hold and he still had that grip.

“Leave it.”

“It’s filthy, Zhendong—”

“It’s holding.” His eyes rolled shut. “Leave it for her.”

She put the knife down. Bao folded a clean towel one-handed and pressed it over the knot. The smell came up through it anyway. Sweet and wrong. Lilies a week in old water.

She went round to the head of the table. His hands were ice. She took one and pushed it inside the neck of her nightdress, flat on her collarbone, and held it there under her own.

He hissed. His fingers twitched on her skin.

“Cold.”

“I know you’re cold.”

“You. Your feet.”

She looked down. Blood on the floor tiles. Hers. The gravel. She hadn’t felt a thing.

“Don’t you dare worry about my feet.”

“Hm.”

Half dead on her kitchen table and he could still do that. She could have hit him.

“Elara’s coming. She’s good. She practises on bananas. Best in her year.”

Nothing.

“Peng says you crawled from the sea road. That’s two kilometres. You won’t even carry the buckets past the van.”

Nothing.

“The fish has gone off. I didn’t throw it out.” Her voice wobbled. She made it stop. “I’ll buy another one. You promised you’d eat it. You don’t make things up. Page three.”

His fingers moved on her collarbone. Once.

At the foot of the table Bao was still pressing the towel down one-handed. His face was wet. He kept wiping it on his good shoulder.

“Boss.”

Zhao’s eyes opened a crack. Went down the table. Found him.

“Shoulder.”

“It’s fine, Boss.”

“Liar.”

“Boss, I’m sorry, I lost you, I looked and you were—”

“You were down. I put you down.” A long breath. “Stay down next time.”

“There isn’t going to be a next time!”

That was Elowen. Both men looked at her. Then Zhao shut his eyes again, and Bao went back to the towel, and neither argued.

✦ ✦ ✦

Gravel spat at the front of the house. A car door. Peng, out in the hall, gasping.

“Miss Lin! Kitchen! Go, GO!”

Eight minutes to four. Elowen saw it on the oven clock later and didn’t believe it.

Elara came through the doorway at a run and stopped.

She was twenty-three now, in her final year of medicine. Scrubs. Hair falling out of its clip. A big blue bag over each shoulder, both of them clinking.

She looked at the man on the table. Elowen watched her sister’s face go white. Then still. Then it turned into somebody else’s.

“Elara.”

Her own voice. Calm. Too calm. Where was it even coming from?

“I’m here. I’m here, Jie.”

“Okay. Okay. Okay.”

Elara dumped the bags on the counter and ripped them open. Bags of fluid. Tubing. Needles in paper. Gauze. A green drape. An instrument case in blue wrap.

“I stole all of this. From the hospital. From the supply room. If anyone ever finds out, I will never be a doctor, and I’ll go to prison, and I don’t care, Jie, I don’t care, move his arm, I need a vein.”

Elowen moved his arm.

First try, nothing. Elara swore and blew on her fingers. Second try, inside the elbow. Tape. She looked round for somewhere to hang the bag. Nowhere. She ran out into the hall and came back with a coat hanger off the back of the door, and hooked it on the cupboard above the table.

A second line in the other arm. Then two boxes from the bottom of the bag.

“Antibiotics. The strongest I could find. Into the drip. He needs fluids, he needs these, and he needs—”

She stopped. She looked at the towel.

“Show me.”

Elowen lifted the towel.

Elara looked at the wound and didn’t say anything.

Elara. Not talking. Twenty years Elowen had known her and never once got her to shut up.

“Elara.”

“It went through. In and out. Low, on the side.” Her fingers hovered over it and didn’t land. “I don’t think it’s in his belly. If it was in his belly, three days… he’d be dead already.”

“But.”

“But it’s infected. Badly. He packed it with his shirt. That kept him alive.” Her voice wobbled. “Now it’s killing him. It all has to come out. Everything that’s dead. Washed out. Left open.”

“Then do it.”

“Jie, I can’t put him under! I don’t have the drugs, I don’t know how. I’ve got local. It won’t be enough. It’s going to hurt him like—”

“Elara. Do it.”

Elowen took his face in both her hands.

“I’ll hold him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Two hours.

Afterwards she couldn’t put it in order. The light, long and bright over the table. She’d picked that light. For cooking. Black strips of shirt coming out of him one at a time, stiff as card. The noise he made. Elara didn’t stop.

Saline running off the edge of the table onto the tiles. Bao and the guards on their knees with towels. Pink. Red. Pink. Elara cutting away what was dead in tiny snips, biting her lip, sweat running off her chin. She didn’t talk. Not once. Only under her breath, over and over.

“Okay. Okay. There. Okay.”

So Elowen talked for both of them. She stood at the head of the table with his face between her hands and talked for two hours straight. Half of it she didn’t know she was saying. The flower market. The soy milk man. The lemon tree.

“The soy milk man’s son passed his exams. Did I tell you? He brought a cake to the shop.”

He arched off the table. His scream went straight through her teeth. She put her forehead on his and kept going.

“Granny Su counted every bunch again on Tuesday. Every single one.”

He’d got hold of her hand somewhere in it. When Elara pulled the deepest strip free, he crushed her fingers together till the heavy ring bit into the bone. She didn’t let go. His jaw worked under her palm. The cords in his neck stood out like wire. Sweat ran back into his hair.

“Zhendong. Seven lemons. You have to come and see.”

His eyes slid toward Elara’s hands. Toward the snips.

“Look at me. Don’t look at her. Look at me…”

He looked at her. For a while he did nothing else.

Then his eyes cleared. Just for a second. He knew exactly where he was. Who was holding his face. What she was looking at.

“Elowen.”

His eyes were open.

“Go upstairs.”

“No.”

“Don’t… watch—”

“I married you. I wanted all of it, remember? It’s in the terms.” She held his face harder. “I’m watching. You look at me.”

He looked at her. He didn’t look away again until he passed out.

She kept talking after that too. Just in case.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six, the kitchen window went grey.

Elara stripped her gloves. Red to the wrist. She dropped them on the floor and stood with her hands braced on the counter, head down, breathing.

“That’s all I can do. It’s clean. It’s open. The antibiotics are going in. Now it’s his body. If the fever breaks in the next two days, he lives. If it doesn’t—”

She stopped.

“If it doesn’t, we take him to a hospital, Jie, Red Notice or no Red Notice. I won’t let him die on a kitchen table because of a piece of paper.”

“Neither will I.”

Elara lifted her head. She looked at the blood on her sister’s hands. The nightdress. The bare cut feet. Whatever Elowen’s face was doing. Nothing, probably.

“You held him for two hours. You didn’t look away once. You didn’t even cry.”

“I’ll cry later.”

Chen Si was in the doorway.

When had he come? Soaked to the knees. The camel coat ruined. Three nights on the water, all over his face.

“Is he—”

“Alive. For now.”

Elara didn’t even turn round to say it.

Chen Si looked at his brother on the table. Grey. A drip in each arm. White gauze where his side should be. Breathing.

Then he turned and walked out into the hall. Elowen heard him stop by the lemon tree. She heard him take a long breath. It broke in the middle.

Chen Si. Who talked about bodies on the phone like they were weather.

✦ ✦ ✦

They carried him upstairs at seven, on a door Raiden had taken off its hinges.

Nobody saw Raiden arrive. He was just there, in a coat over his pyjamas, white as paper, with a screwdriver. He had the door off the cupboard under the stairs in about a minute.

“Where?”

“Big room. End of the corridor.”

“Can he feel this?”

“Not much. Lift on three.”

“Okay.”

On the landing Raiden looked down at the floor behind her. Then at her.

“Jie. Your feet.”

“Leave it.”

“You’re leaving footprints. Red ones.”

“Raiden. Walk.”

Raiden didn’t make one joke the whole way up. Not about the door. Not about the stairs. Not about anything. Elowen kept waiting for one. It never came.

Elara hung the drips from the curtain rail. Checked the lines. The dressing. His breathing. She wrote numbers on the back of an envelope off the dressing table, with the time beside each one, in tiny neat writing. Since when did Elara have neat writing?

Elowen sat down on the floor by the bed and took his hand.

“Go and sleep, Elara.”

“In a minute.”

“Now.”

“In a MINUTE, Jie.”

Elara went out. A door shut at the far end of the corridor. Then a tap went on full and roared.

Elowen looked at the hand in hers. Hot now. Too hot. Torn and scabbed from the hill. She held it against her cheek.

“You’re home. Do you hear me? You’re home now. So you don’t get to go anywhere.”

His fingers moved against her face.

“Hm.”

That was all he had. She’d take it.

chapters.title: “I Stained Your Life”
chapters.desc: Two days of fever. He wakes once, says sorry for everything, and falls asleep on the question he’s been carrying for three years.
chapters.epigraph: “You walk into my office tomorrow, I say yes again.” — Zhao Zhendong
chapters.content:
The fever didn’t break on Sunday.

He burned. She’d never touched anything alive that was that hot. Dry skin, tight as a drum. Short fast breaths. He shook under the blankets in long hard waves with his teeth going, and the room was warm. Elara had turned the heating up herself.

Elara came and went. Drips every four hours. Packing morning and evening. She’d written the times on the inside of her own wrist in blue biro.

“That’ll come off in the shower.”

“I’ll write it again.”

“Where do you even go? You vanish for two hours and come back with wet hair.”

“Somewhere with a shower, Jie.”

“We have six showers.”

“Somewhere with a different shower.”

Elowen looked at her. Elara studied the drip like it owed her money.

A phone charger was poking out of the side pocket of her bag. Black cable. Big square plug. Elara’s chargers were all pink, and all broken.

“That’s not your charger.”

“It is now.”

“Elara Lin.”

“Hold his arm, please.”

Fine. Later. There’d be a later. There had to be, so she could get it out of her.

At six Aurelia came up with a tray, a carrier bag and her sleeves rolled to the elbow. She looked at the bed. She looked at Elowen on the floor. Her mouth went thin.

“You’re still in that nightdress.”

“It’s fine.”

“It has his blood on it. And yours. And I think a mandarin.” She put the bag down. “Clothes. Mine. Don’t argue.”

“The last lot of your clothes ended up on his floor.”

“I know. I’ve been told. Folded.” Aurelia sniffed. “If he folds these, I’ll know he’s dying.”

Elowen laughed. It came out cracked. Aurelia knelt down on the floor in her good trousers and put a bowl of soup into her hands.

“Eat that.”

“I’m not hungry.”

“I didn’t ask if you were hungry. I asked my cook to make it, and she cried the whole time, so you’re eating it.”

She ate it. Aurelia watched every spoonful like a prison guard. Then she brushed Elowen’s hair, which nobody had done since Mama. Long slow strokes. She didn’t say anything about it. Neither did Elowen.

On the bed he turned his head toward the sound of their voices. His mouth moved.

“What’s he saying?”

Elowen leaned in. Listened.

“…He says you’re loud.”

“He’s delirious.” But Aurelia’s eyes had gone wet, and she brushed harder.

✦ ✦ ✦

He talked, sometimes. Not to her. To people she couldn’t see.

Once in a boy’s voice, high and scared. I didn’t drop it. I didn’t. It fell.

“It fell. It’s all right. It wasn’t you.”

Once low and fierce. Si. Si. Get down. Behind me.

“Si’s fine. He’s downstairs on the sofa in his coat. He won’t go home.”

Once in the middle of the night, so low she had to put her ear by his mouth. My wife’s at the counter. She’s alone at the counter. Bao. Drive faster.

“I’m not at the counter. I’m here.” She put her mouth by his ear. “You came. You already came.”

In between, she did what Elara had shown her. A cloth wrung out in cool water. His face. His neck. The dips above his collarbones. His chest. It came away hot every time, like she’d laid it on the stove. She wet his cracked lips with the tip of a spoon and wiped the corner of his mouth with her thumb when it ran.

When his breathing went too fast she counted out loud. Like she’d counted for Xiao Pan with his hands under the cold tap.

“In. Two. Three. Out. Two. Three.”

Some time before dawn his breathing came down to her counting. She had to put the spoon down. Her hands had started going.

His hand came up off the sheet. Clumsy. It knocked her cheek. Then it found a bit of her hair that had come loose over her eye, and pushed it back behind her ear.

His eyes never opened.

She sat there with her hand over her mouth.

Half dead. Out of his head. Still fixing her hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

It didn’t break on Monday either.

Elara read the thermometer at noon and didn’t say anything. She went out into the corridor with her phone.

Elowen could hear her through the door. Crying with her hand over her mouth, trying to do it so nobody in the house would hear. Then a while of nothing. Then, loud—

“That’s what I said! That’s EXACTLY what I said to them!”

Them? Elowen and Chen Si. That was them. So who was on the other end, agreeing with her about fevers, at noon on a Monday?

Elara came back with red eyes and a face like nothing had happened.

“Who was that?”

“Nobody.”

“Nobody knows a lot about fevers.”

“Jie. Hold his arm.”

At two, Chen Si came up and stood at the foot of the bed. He’d shaved. Changed. He looked nearly like himself, except round the eyes.

“The search is over. Officially.”

“And unofficially?”

“Unofficially he was on your kitchen table.” He put his hands in his pockets. “The police found Maartens and two of his men at the shipyard. And Deng. Song Wei Long is calling it a dispute between foreign criminals. His report says the man known as Zhao Zhendong was not present. Whereabouts unknown.”

“He wrote that?”

“He brought it to me at six this morning. Before he filed it.” A frown. “Then he gave me a message. Tell her this is the cat. I don’t know what it means.”

“It means he owed me. Now we’re even.”

Chen Si waited for more. She didn’t give him any. He looked faintly offended. Good.

“Elara wants him in a hospital if it isn’t down by morning. I’ve found somewhere. Private. A surgeon who owes me. No records.”

“He’d hate it.”

“He made me promise once. In Block C. Fifteen, and bleeding into the snow.” Chen Si looked at his brother. “If I’m dying, don’t take me to a hospital. Hospitals have records. They’ll send me back. Take me somewhere quiet. Let me go.”

“And?”

“I carried him to a back room behind a clinic in the next town and lied about our name.” A breath. “I didn’t listen then. I’m not listening now.”

“Neither am I.”

“Good.”

He went to the door. He stopped there with his hand on the frame, and turned round.

“Elowen. I never asked you this. I should have, at the registry. I didn’t, because I thought I knew. Your father.” His face didn’t move at all. “Do you love him?”

She looked up from the floor.

“I haven’t told him.”

“That’s not the question.”

She looked at the hand in hers. Torn. Scabbed. Burning.

“Yes.”

Chen Si shut his eyes. When he opened them, something in his face had let go.

“Then why haven’t you—”

“He won’t let me! Every time I open my mouth he puts his fingers on it. He wants a boring day. No fathers. No glass. No Dutchmen. A boring day, Chen Si!”

Chen Si looked at the drips. The gauze. The bloody sheets in a heap by the door.

“Then you’d better make him one.”

He went out and shut the door without a sound.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elara did the evening packing at nine. She was swaying on her feet.

“I’m lying down in the end room. Wake me the second anything changes. The second, Jie.”

“And if nothing does?”

“Then he goes to Chen Si’s surgeon in the morning, and I don’t care what he promised anybody in the snow.”

She went. Elowen got up onto the bed beside him at last, on top of the covers. Her back had given up on the floor hours ago.

At eleven, he woke.

Not all the way. His eyes opened in the light off the Docks. Glassy. Too bright. They went round the room and didn’t catch on anything. Then they found her face on the pillow next to his.

“Elowen.”

A cracked thread of a voice.

“I’m here.”

“Are you real?”

“Yes. Unfortunately for you. I’m furious.”

His eyes went down the bed. To her feet. Wrapped in white, where Elara had picked the gravel out that morning and made her sit still for it.

“Feet.”

“They’re fine.”

“Who.”

“The drive, Zhendong. I ran down the drive. Who do you think?”

Something went across his face. Pure, stupid outrage. At gravel.

“It’s coming up.”

“You are not digging up the drive from your deathbed.”

“Hm.”

She could see him planning it.

Then his eyes wandered off, and came back.

“I saw you. On the boat.”

“What boat?”

“In the hold. In the dark. Two days.” He swallowed. It looked like it hurt. “At the market at four. In the cooler. On the mountain. I thought if I stopped looking at you, I’d die. So I didn’t stop.”

She took his hand. She didn’t trust her voice.

“I don’t remember the hill. I remember the dogs. I remember thinking, I said dinner.” Nearly a smile. Gone. “Three days late.”

“You came home. That counts. That’s on time.”

He shut his eyes. She thought he’d gone under again.

Then they opened, and his face was terrible. Wide open. Nothing held back in it anywhere.

“I’m sorry.”

“Don’t—”

“Let me. I might not get—” He stopped. Started again. “I’m sorry. Your father. The van. Xiao Pan’s hands.”

“Zhendong, stop it—”

“The glass. The man in the grey jacket at your counter. The circle round your face.” His voice was going more with every word. “Old Ming. The kitchen floor. Your nightdress. Your sister cutting me open on the table where you eat.”

He was crying. No sound. Tears running sideways across his face into the pillow.

“You had a shop with your name on it. A lemon tree. One day you were going to get on a train and go somewhere nobody knew your father.”

“I never said that!”

“You did. The first month. To the dogs.”

Oh god. She had. On the back step, with a cup of tea, thinking nobody was listening. Of course somebody was listening.

“Then you walked into my office. And I said yes.” He breathed. “I stained your life.”

“You did not—”

“Everything I touch. I knew. I said yes anyway. I wanted something clean, once. I took it. And look.” His torn hand twitched toward the drips. The gauze. The bloody sheets in the corner. “Look what I did to it.”

Then he gripped her hand. Harder than he had any right to.

“And I’d do it again.” Lower. Like that was the worst thing he’d ever owned up to. “You walk into my office tomorrow, I say yes again. I can’t be sorry for that bit. I tried. Three days in the dark, I tried.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She looked at him. Grey. Wet. Burning. Two inches away.

Then she kissed him.

Not carefully. Not like a question. She took his face in her hand and kissed him like an answer. Hard. On his cracked mouth. He made a noise against her lips. Then he got his torn hand into her hair and gripped, scabs and all.

When she pulled back he was staring at her.

“Listen to me. Are you listening?”

He nodded. Barely.

“You didn’t stain my life. You’ve spent three years keeping things off it.”

He stopped breathing for a second.

“It was always there. All of it. When I was seven and Mama died and I put on her apron. In Baba’s garage when I was eight, in long boxes I wasn’t allowed to open.”

“Elowen—”

“Men like Feng at our kitchen table. Men like Kang. Maartens. They were always there. I just never had anybody standing in between.”

His eyes were wide.

“Then you sat outside my door. Every night. A month. Bao says you never slept once.”

“Bao talks too much.”

“Bao’s managed about forty words in eight years and they’re all about you!”

Her voice cracked. She let it.

“You put a room under my shop with a light that stays on. You went to the shipyard so a car would never come down my street again. And when they shot you, you crawled up a hill on your hands. For dinner.”

She put her forehead on his.

“You’re the wall. You keep it out. You always have. Since the first night, in the rain.”

He was crying again. She kissed his eyelids. One. Then the other. Salt.

“I don’t believe you.” Hardly any voice left. “I want to.”

“I know.”

She kept her forehead where it was. He was going again. She could feel the heat dragging him under.

“Elowen. I need to ask you something.”

Oh.

She knew what it was. She’d felt it in him for three years. In the dark on the night of the typhoon. On the mountain, like a stone under a quilt. In the car home from the gala. When you married me—

“Ask me.”

Nothing.

“Zhendong. Ask me.”

His eyes had shut. His breathing went long and slow. His hand slid out of her hair onto the pillow.

Asleep. He’d fallen asleep. On the question.

She could have strangled him. She held his hand instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

Some time after two, something changed under her palm.

She’d left it on his forehead. For two days that forehead had been a stove. Now it was damp. Then wet. Sweat broke out all over him. The pillow. The sheet. Her sleeve. His breathing slowed. The shaking stopped. In the light off the Docks his face lost that awful flush and went pale and ordinary.

Was she dreaming? She’d dreamed it twice already.

She put two fingers on his neck and counted against her watch. Then again, because she didn’t believe the first time.

Ninety-six.

She ran down the corridor on her bandaged feet and shook the lump on the bed in the end room.

“Elara. Elara! It’s broken. He’s sweating through everything. Ninety-six.”

“It… what?”

“It’s broken.”

Elara was out of the bed and past her before she’d finished. Elowen found her in the big room with her fingers on his neck and her lips moving. Counting. Then she sat down hard on the floor and laughed with her hands over her face.

“It broke. Jie, it broke!”

“I know. I said.”

Elara got her phone out. She typed with both thumbs, fast, sniffing.

“Who are you texting at this time?”

“Nobody. Go back to him.”

Nobody. Again. Nobody got a lot of texts.

Elowen got back on the bed. The sheets were soaked. She didn’t care. She lay down on her side against him, careful of the gauze, and put her face in his shoulder.

Then she cried. Properly. Three days in the armory and two on the floor, all at once, with no sound, the way he did it. Her whole body shook with it.

His hand moved. Up off the sheet. Heavy. It landed on the back of her head and stayed there.

“You’re crying.”

Barely a breath. He wasn’t even awake.

“I said later.” She wiped her face on his shoulder. “This is later. Go back to sleep.”

chapters.title: The Question He Never Asked
chapters.desc: Two weeks after the shipyard, on the most boring day there has ever been, he finally asks why she married him. She tells him the truth, and makes him wait for the rest.
chapters.epigraph: “Did you marry me to control your father’s boss?”
chapters.content:
He hated the drips.

He hated the tablets that came with them. Big white ones, twice a day, with food. Elowen read the label every single time. Twice. He watched her do it and kept his mouth shut, because the one time he’d said something she’d read it out loud to him. Slowly. Like he was five.

Most of all he hated Elara.

Not Elara. What Elara did. Morning and evening she put on her gloves and a kindergarten-teacher voice. Then she changed the packing in his side.

“Big breath for me, Zhendong!”

He did not take a big breath for her. He lay on his back with his jaw locked and his eyes on the ceiling and let her get on with it.

And he hated the stick.

Raiden had brought it on the fourth day. Black wood. A silver dog’s head for a handle.

“It belonged to a general.”

“Which general?”

“A general, Jie! Does it matter? He was very brave. He had a limp.”

Zhao looked at the dog’s head for four seconds. Raiden backed out of the room.

Elowen sat on the bed for every dressing. She held his hand. On the fourth morning he spoke through his teeth.

“You don’t have to watch.”

“I’m not watching. I’m holding your hand. It’s different.”

“Hm.”

Elara snapped her gloves off and left. He didn’t let go for an hour. Elowen read an entire seed catalogue one-handed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first morning she went back to the market, he was awake before her alarm.

Of course he was.

“Who’s driving you?”

“Bao.”

“Bao has one arm.”

Bao had one arm in a sling, and another one Elara had told him not to use, and he was downstairs in the kitchen anyway, jangling the van keys.

“Then Peng.”

He was sitting up against the pillows. Grey. Thinner. Too much bone in his face. He watched her pull her jeans on like he was learning it for an exam.

“Peng brakes too hard on the corner by the old Qiu warehouse. There’s a pothole.”

“I know about the pothole.”

“He forgets.”

Peng did not forget. Last winter Zhao had made him drive that corner forty times with Zhao in the passenger seat saying again. Peng would remember that pothole on his deathbed.

She took his old grey sweatshirt off the chair and pulled it over her head. It came down to her knees. He watched her roll the sleeves up four times, and something went soft and stupid in his face.

“That’s mine.”

“It’s cold at the market.”

“Hm.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao: Corner?

Elowen: he slowed down. he slowed down so much a bicycle overtook us

Zhao: Good.

Zhao: Where are you now.

Elowen: roses

Zhao: Which stall.

Elowen: GO TO SLEEP

Granny Su squinted at the phone over her cigarette.

“Him?”

“Him.”

“Tell him I counted.” She counted the bunches again anyway, every one, her lips moving. “Tell him the boy did it for three days and got it wrong twice and I hit him.”

“I’m not telling him that.”

“Tell him.” She pushed the last bucket across. “He’ll like it.”

Bao met her at the door at seven with his good hand out for the eggs.

“Light’s been on the whole time, Mrs. Zhao.”

She went up in her market boots, smelling of wet stems and diesel. He was sitting exactly where she’d left him. Looking at the door.

“You didn’t sleep.”

“You weren’t here.”

She climbed onto the bed without taking her boots off. She slid both cold hands up under his T-shirt and laid them flat on his ribs, well clear of the dressing. He hissed. He didn’t move away.

“There. I’m here. Sleep.”

He was gone in under a minute. Unbelievable! Three hours awake staring at a door, and then out, like somebody had pulled his plug.

She lay there with her boots on the duvet and her hands on him and didn’t move until ten. Xiao Pan sent her a photo of the locked shop door with one question mark.

She didn’t answer it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fifteenth morning he walked to the bathroom on his own.

She knew because she heard him swear. Three times. Once at the bed. Once at the doorframe. Once at the general’s stick, which he’d tried not to use and then had to.

“Do you need—”

“No.”

He came back the same way. He sat down on the edge of the bed sweating like he’d carried a crate up from the Docks. Then he looked up at her.

Very pleased with himself. Ridiculous man.

“Did you see?”

“I saw.”

“On my own.”

“You swore at a door, Zhendong.”

“The door was in the way.” He held his hand out for his tablets. “Read it twice.”

“I always read it twice.”

“I know. I like watching.”

She went to work.

And then nothing happened.

She noticed it at noon, wrapping a birthday bouquet for a schoolteacher. Nobody came in with a strange order. No car crawled past the window. The new glass Raiden had put in, which he swore would stop a missile, let in plain grey spring light. Xiao Pan sang along to the radio, flat, and nobody shot him for it.

A woman bought tulips for her mother. The old man came in for his chrysanthemums, the way he did every Sunday, for his wife’s grave.

Her phone buzzed.

Raiden: ah sim made TWO cakes

Raiden: ev won’t blow her candles out she just looks at them

Raiden: are you coming tonight?? baba keeps asking

Elowen: can’t. happy birthday. both of you. he walked to the bathroom today

Raiden: ON HIS OWN??

Raiden: tell him the general is very proud

She put the phone down. She looked round the shop. Tulips. Radio. Xiao Pan, flat as a board on the high notes.

Wait.

Was this it? This?

It was. It was the most boring day there had ever been.

She put the scissors down. She picked her phone back up and rang a number in the Greenstone hills.

“Mrs. Zhao?” Mr. Wen’s grandson sounded like she’d woken him. “Is everything… Grandpa heard there was trouble.”

“Everything’s fine. Everything’s really, really boring.” She was holding the phone too tight. “Is the camellia still flowering?”

A pause. Then, away from the phone, at the top of his voice: “GRANDPA! It’s the wife!”

When she hung up, Xiao Pan was staring at her over a bucket of stock.

“Miss Lin. Why are you smiling like that?”

“Like what?”

“Like…” He thought about it. “Like Mr. Zhao when he’s being scary.”

“Fill the buckets, Xiao Pan.”

He filled the buckets. He kept looking at her. Twice he walked into the cooler door.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elara was on the stairs with her bag when Elowen got in with the fish.

“Perfect. You can do it.”

“Do what?”

“The dressing. Last one. He’s on tablets now. You do it morning and night from tomorrow, so I’m watching you do it tonight.” Elara was already pulling her up the stairs by the wrist. “He walked to the bathroom on his own this morning and hated every step. Did you know that?”

“I heard him.”

“Everybody heard him.”

He was propped up on the pillows. He saw the gloves in Elowen’s hands and his face did absolutely nothing.

She was terrible at it. Her fingers were too slow and she said “sorry” every time she touched the edge. Elara stood at her shoulder going tape, no, the other way, yes. And he lay there and watched his wife’s face the whole time. No locked jaw. No ceiling. Just breathing. In. Out.

Elara stared at him.

“Oh, so for HER you breathe.”

“Hm.”

“Unbelievable. Two weeks. Two weeks I’ve been saying big breath!”

Her phone buzzed in her pocket. She looked at it. Her whole face went pink and silly.

“Who’s that?”

“Nobody.”

“Nobody again?”

“The hospital! It’s the hospital.”

“You’re smiling at the hospital?”

“I love the hospital.” She was already at the door with her bag. “Bye! Peng’s taking me down. Don’t let him lift anything!”

Elowen looked at the empty doorway.

“Nobody texts her a lot.”

“Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She cooked the fish the way her mother had. Ginger, spring onion, a little soy, steamed whole. Rice. Green beans with garlic. No soup. Soup was better on the second day, and she was planning on there being one.

She carried it up on a tray, because the stairs were still beyond him without the general, and set it on the bed between them. She sat cross-legged on the other side.

“You made fish.”

“You asked for fish. At the door. You said tomorrow. That was sixteen days ago.” She picked up her chopsticks. “It’s a different fish. The first one went off. I threw it out and cried. Don’t look at me like that.”

He picked the bones out of her half first. Slowly, one by one, with his scabbed fingers. Then he took the belly, the best bit, and put it in her bowl.

She put it in his.

He put it back in hers.

They looked at each other across the tray.

“Baba gave it back to Mama. Every night.”

“I know.”

“So one of us has to eat it. Or we’ll be them.”

He looked at the belly in her bowl. Then he reached over with his chopsticks, took it, and ate it himself.

She laughed so hard the rice bowls rattled.

✦ ✦ ✦

He ate everything. He put his chopsticks down across his bowl, neat, the way she’d taught him.

Fifteen days he’d had, lying here. Fifteen days of ceiling. He’d gone through it the way he went through a yard before a meeting. Where she’d be sitting. What her hands would do. What he’d do with his face when she said it, so she wouldn’t have to watch. He’d planned it to the inch.

He couldn’t remember any of it now.

She waited. She was good at it now. Three years of practice.

“Elowen.”

He wasn’t looking at her. He was looking at the fish bones.

“The night of the fever. I said I needed to ask you something.”

“And then you fell asleep. Mid-sentence. Very rude.”

He didn’t smile. His hands closed on the blanket and opened again.

“It’s a boring day.”

“The most boring day there’s ever been.”

He nodded. Like he’d checked the numbers himself and they were right.

Then he looked up.

There it was. The thing he’d been carrying since the night she walked into his office with three pages of terms. She’d felt the shape of it in the dark in the typhoon. Under the quilt on the mountain. In the car home from the gala, when you married me—. Three years. Was he really going to do it now? Over fish bones?

“Did you marry me to control your father’s boss?”

✦ ✦ ✦

She could lie.

She’d promised she wouldn’t. Page three, in his blunt square handwriting. Lie to everyone else. Not to me. Ever. She could see exactly what the truth would do to his face. She gave herself one second.

“Yes.”

It went straight into him. No sound. Like the knife into the table at the Maartens dinner.

“Yes. I married you for Baba.” She made herself keep looking at him. “I wasn’t thinking about you at all. I was thinking about Old Tan with his legs in plaster. A hired gun in Baba’s car who’d run the first time anyone shot at him.”

“Elowen—”

“Raiden. Ev. Elara. Yu-er. All asleep upstairs.” Her voice wobbled. She didn’t let it go anywhere. “You weren’t a man to me that night. You were a wall. I wanted to stand you between them and everything else. That’s the truth.”

He nodded.

“Thank you.”

Calm. The voice he used for I know. She hated that voice.

“For not lying. I knew. I always knew. I just…” He looked down at his hands. “I wanted to hear it once. So I could stop wondering.”

“Zhendong—”

“It’s fine. I said yes anyway. I signed. It’s fine, Elowen, you don’t have to—”

“That was one question.”

He stopped.

“You asked why I married you. I told you. Now ask me the other one.”

“What other one?”

“Why I stayed.”

He stared at her.

He opened his mouth. Nothing. He shut it. Opened it again. Was he going to manage it? No. Three years to get one question out of him, and it had nearly killed him, and there wasn’t a second one in there. She watched him look for it and come up empty.

She reached across the tray and took his hand. Scabs and all.

“It’s okay. You don’t have to ask. I’m telling you anyway.”

“Then tell—”

“Not here.”

“Elowen.”
