“Not in bed! Not with a tray! Not after I sat on the floor two days watching you burn.” Her eyes had gone hot. Stupid eyes. “You said a boring day. With nothing in the way. Your rule. So.”

“So?”

“So tomorrow you get up. You put on a real shirt. With buttons. You take the general’s stick, and Bao drives you, one arm or not, and you come to the shop at closing time.”

“The shop.”

“Where it started.” She looked at the window. “The forecast says rain.”

He looked at her like she’d stopped speaking his language.

“And then?”

“And then you never have to wonder again.”

He caught her wrist. He pulled her across the tray, fish bones and all, and stopped with his mouth a breath from hers.

And waited.

Even now. Even after this. She could feel him shaking with it.

“Yes,” she said. “Obviously yes. You idiot.”

He kissed her like he was signing his name to something before anyone could take it off the table. A rice bowl went over. Nobody picked it up.

“What if it doesn’t rain?” she said, a long time later, into his shoulder.

“It’ll rain.”

“You can’t make it rain, Zhendong.”

He didn’t answer that. She checked the forecast four times before she fell asleep.

He didn’t check it once.

chapters.title: The Flower in His Lapel
chapters.desc: Closing time, rain, and a camellia from the mountain in his lapel. She tells him why she stayed, and he finally says it back.
chapters.epigraph: “I kept choosing you, Zhendong, and you never once asked.” — Elowen
chapters.content:
The box came at three, on the back of a courier’s motorbike.

Small. White. Wrapped in a plastic bag against the weather. There was a note taped to the lid in a shaky old hand.

For the wife. From the idiot’s mountain. Don’t let him touch it, he’ll crush it. — Wen.

She took it into the back and opened it on the workbench.

Damp moss. And on the moss, one camellia.

Deep pink. So full it looked fake. Petal over petal over petal, every one exactly where it should be. Picked that morning off the dark shrub against the mossy wall, and flown up on somebody’s lap. She’d stood in front of that bush on the mountain in the rain and cried at it like an idiot.

She was not going to cry at it again. In her own shop. On a Monday.

She cut the stem short with her knife. At an angle. The way you cut something so it heals.

“Miss Lin? What’s in the box?”

“Nothing.”

“It’s from the mountain! It says Wen on the—”

“Go home, Xiao Pan.”

“It’s five o’clock!”

“I know what time it is. Go home.”

He looked at her face. Then at the box. The tips of his ears went bright red, and he went without another word. Outside it was spitting.

She swept the floor. She re-cut the roses that didn’t need it. She moved the delphiniums away from the door. Then back. Then away again.

What was wrong with her? Three years married. She was moving buckets round like a schoolgirl waiting for a date.

At six it started to rain properly.

Good. Fine. She’d said it would rain.

✦ ✦ ✦

The shirt was the problem.

Zhao stood in front of the wardrobe for a long time. White. Buttons. She’d said buttons.

His hands were still bad. Scabs across both palms. Two fingers on the left that didn’t bend right yet. The buttons were tiny and stupid. There were a lot of them. It took him ten minutes. He didn’t look in the mirror after. If he looked, he’d do them again, and then he’d be late.

He wasn’t going to be late twice.

The black suit, the one from the reunion. The old coat over it. Then the wallet, inside pocket, left side. He touched it once through the cloth.

Bao was in the hall by the lemon tree with the car keys in his good hand and an umbrella under the sling.

“Boss.”

“Not tonight.”

Bao looked at the umbrella. Then at him. He put it back in the stand without a word.

He drove one-handed, very slowly. He took the pothole by the Qiu warehouse like it was a landmine.

Zhao watched the wipers.

He’d done this before. Not this. The other thing. A yard, a meeting, the place every man would stand. He’d gone through Maartens like that the whole way to the shipyard.

He couldn’t go through this. He didn’t know where anything would stand. She’d said you’ll never have to wonder, and that could mean a lot of things, and he had spent three years not letting himself want any of them.

Three years, one month and eight days since he’d stood on her mat.

He knew the number. He always knew the number.

“Boss. We’re here.”

“I know.”

He didn’t move.

“Boss. You’re getting wet sitting still.”

He got out.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bell went at seven.

She didn’t look up. She was wiring a stem of eucalyptus that did not need wiring.

“We’re closed.”

The sign said OPEN. Nobody answered.

She looked up.

He was in the doorway. Soaked to the skin. Black coat gone darker with water, hair flat on his forehead, leaning on the general’s ridiculous silver dog. Thinner. Greyer. Water ran off him onto her clean floor.

Under the coat, a white shirt. Buttoned one off. All the way down.

She almost laughed. She didn’t.

“You’re dripping on my floor.”

He looked at the puddle round his shoes. Then he took the coat off, folded it over his arm, and stood on the mat.

Exactly where he’d stood three years ago. She could have drawn round his feet.

She didn’t throw a towel this time.

She came round the counter. Past the buckets. Past the tulips over Raiden’s floor. She stopped in front of him on the mat, close enough to smell the rain on him. Then she reached up and started undoing his shirt.

His breathing changed.

“You did them wrong.”

“I know.”

“You knew?”

“I didn’t look.”

She did every button up again. Properly. Top to bottom. Then she smoothed the front of the shirt flat with both hands, the way Mama used to smooth Baba’s collar at the door.

She took the camellia out of her apron pocket.

He saw it. All of him went still.

She tucked the short stem into the buttonhole of his lapel and settled it. Deep pink on black. She left her hand flat over it. Over his heart. It was going like a hammer.

“Zhendong.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“I married you for Baba. I told you last night.”

“You did.”

“Shh. I didn’t stay for him.”

The rain hammered on the glass.

“The first night. You bought every flower in here so you could wait for Baba without scaring my customers. Then you scared a woman off my window anyway.”

“She was—”

“She wanted tulips for her mother. I told you. And you walked out in the rain and gave her the whole bucket.” Her chin was going. “And I stood behind that counter thinking, that isn’t what a monster does. All night. I didn’t tell anyone. I didn’t even tell me.”

His eyes had gone very wide.

“You sat outside my door for a month. You carried Mama’s lemon tree up the steps like it was glass. You set an alarm to water it.”

“Thursdays.”

“I know it’s Thursdays! Let me finish!”

He shut his mouth.

“Sorry.”

“Don’t be sorry, just… let me…” She’d lost her place. Of course she had. “Where was I?”

“The alarm.”

“You read about light bending round a star eleven times, because you thought that was what I wanted. You bled on two hundred roses. You’ve driven me to the market at four every morning for three years and never once let me carry a bucket.”

“I like carrying—”

“I KNOW you like it!” She was crying now. Fine. Let her. “You bought a mountain so nobody could dig up a flower. You threw three hundred million in a bin with the fish bones because I read four pages of names.”

She pressed her hand flat on the camellia. On him.

“I don’t want a train to the end of the line. I don’t want a quiet library and a man who talks about light.”

“Elowen—”

“I want you. I chose you. Not in your office. After. Every morning at four, with two coffees on the counter. Every night you sat outside that door. I kept choosing you, Zhendong, and you never once asked.”

He looked like she’d hit him.

“It’s a boring day. Nothing happened. Granny Su counted every bunch. Xiao Pan asked about a box and I sent him home.” She took a breath. It came in wet. “And I love you.”

His face didn’t move.

Was he even breathing? She couldn’t tell. She said it louder.

“I love you. I’ve loved you so long I can’t remember not. I’d mean it if you were nobody and owned nothing and had never carried a bucket in your life.”

✦ ✦ ✦

For a second he stood there on the mat with her hand on his chest, and nothing happened at all.

Then his face broke.

She’d seen him cry before. On the bathroom floor, with his hands over his eyes. In the fever, tears running sideways into the pillow. This wasn’t that. This was the ice going on the lake. All of it, at once.

The general’s stick hit the floor.

He got one hand into her hair at the back of her head. It was shaking.

“Say it again.”

His voice was nearly gone.

“I love you.”

“Again.”

“I love you, Zhendong.”

He didn’t wait. No inch. No asking. He hauled her up into him with one arm, wound or no wound, until her toes were barely on the mat, and kissed her.

It wasn’t careful. It wasn’t anything like careful. His face was wet and hers was wet and he was making a noise into her mouth like something tearing, and she got both fists in the shirt she’d just fixed and hung on. The camellia was crushed flat between them. She could smell it. She didn’t care.

When he finally lifted his head he didn’t go far. Forehead on hers. Breathing like he’d run up the hill again.

“I love you,” she said into his collar. Just because she could now.

She flattened her hand on his chest, on the inside pocket. Left side. His wallet was in there. And behind his identity card, a tiny blue flower gone nearly grey, which she’d found last spring looking for change.

She’d never said. She didn’t say now.

“I loved you first.” Rough. Into her hair. “Before the office.”

“When?”

He didn’t answer.

“Zhendong. When?”

“Another day.”

“You can’t say that and then just—”

“I love you.”

He said it like he was putting something down he’d carried a very long way.

“I love you. I didn’t think I’d ever be allowed to say it.”

He reached behind him without letting go of her, felt for the sign on the door, and turned it to CLOSED.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took him into the back. Behind the cooler, to the workbench.

She cleared it with one sweep of her arm. Wire. Ribbon. Eucalyptus. A bucket of offcuts tipped over and went everywhere across Raiden’s warm floor. He laughed, low and wet and amazed.

“Your side.”

“I don’t care about my side.”

“I care! You crawled up a hill with a hole in you!”

“Then be careful with me.” He was very close. “You always are.”

She started on the buttons again.

“I just did these.”

“Hm.”

She was careful. He let her. She pushed the shirt off his shoulders and kissed the scars she knew by heart, in order. Block C. The knife at the Docks. The little round one she’d never asked about. Then the new one. The dressing low on his left side, and the skin all the way round it, very gently.

He put his head back and shut his eyes and said her name. Once. Under his breath.

Then he opened them, and she saw careful wasn’t going to last.

He pulled the pins out of her hair, every one, and they went skittering across the bench among the petals. He kissed her like he’d been dead a week and come back to find her, which, honestly, wasn’t far off. Hard. Salt and rain. She grabbed his shoulders and made a sound that should have embarrassed her.

He stopped. Lifted his head an inch.

“Tell me to stop.”

The oldest words they had.

“Don’t you dare.”

He kissed her throat, her collarbone, the hollow at the bottom of her neck, hard enough to leave a mark. She wanted it. She wanted to walk into the shop tomorrow with him written all over her. Her blouse button stuck. He swore at it. Actually swore! She laughed, pulled the whole thing off over her head and threw it somewhere behind the cooler.

He looked at her in the yellow light from the shop. Her knees went.

“I thought about this. In the water. Going down.” He put his hand flat over her heart. “I thought, I never told her.”

“You told me.” She put her hand over his. “You’re here. Touch me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d thought, three years ago, it would always be him asking.

Not tonight.

Tonight she laid him back on her coat on the bench, slowly, minding his side, and climbed up over him. She took her time. She kissed everywhere she could reach until he had the edge of the bench in both fists.

“Elowen—”

“Say it.”

“I love you.”

“Again.”

He said it again. And again. Then he didn’t need asking. He said it into her hair. Into her shoulder. Into her mouth, over and over, his voice breaking on it every time, like three years of it were coming out all at once. She kissed it out of him. She said it back into his mouth.

“I love you.”

Then nobody was saying anything. Rain on the window. The cooler fan humming. Petals stuck to their skin. His hands on her hips, holding on, and she watched his face the whole time. Every night outside her door was in it. The water. All of it, open, for her.

“Slow,” she managed, when he started to lose it.

“I can’t.”

“Then don’t.”

He didn’t. He swore into her shoulder. He held her so tight she could barely breathe. He said her name like something breaking.

She said it right against his ear. Twice, because once wasn’t enough.

“I love you. I love you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The bench turned out to be too narrow for two people to lie on for more than about four minutes.

They ended up on the floor under her coat. Among the petals.

He’d found the camellia. Crushed flat, half its petals gone. He was turning it in his fingers.

“Mr. Wen said not to let you touch it. He said you’d crush it.”

“I did crush it.”

He said it like he was confessing to a murder.

“In about a minute.”

“Less.”

He tucked it, crushed, behind her ear.

“I don’t have to wonder.” Like he was testing a floor to see if it held. “Anymore.”

“No.”

“You chose me.”

“Every day.” She put her chin on his chest so she could see him. “I love you.”

He went quiet so long she thought he’d fallen asleep. He hadn’t. He was looking at her ceiling. Her lights. The rain on her window. Like a man with nowhere to be and nobody coming.

Later, when they finally got up, she took the flower out of her hair and put it in a glass of water by the till. She left the sign on CLOSED. Xiao Pan could turn it round in the morning.

At the door he stopped with his hand on the switch.

“Nine.”

“Nine what?”

“Nothing.”

He switched the lights off and held the door for her.

Out in the car, Bao took one look at his boss’s face and forgot to start the engine.

chapters.title: Closing Half an Empire
chapters.desc: He starts shutting down the worst of the business, slowly. Chen Si lies for him, Elowen keeps the books, one man finds out what happens if he cheats, and Wei Long gets a list.
chapters.epigraph: “You can’t stop being what you are overnight, Zhendong.” “I know. I’m going to do it slowly.”
chapters.content:
“A hundred and forty people.”

He put the ledger down on the kitchen counter between them. A month after the shop. Her tea was going cold at her elbow. His was gone, because he’d drunk hers first by mistake and then his own to cover it up.

“Bao. The men at the Docks. The warehouses in the north. The drivers. Old Ming’s widow.” He turned a page. “They get paid because of what I do. If I shut it all tomorrow, they don’t.”

“So they go and work for someone worse.”

“Or get killed by someone who thinks I’ve gone soft and wants what’s left.”

“And the rifles don’t stop.”

“Somebody else sells them.”

“You can’t stop being what you are overnight, Zhendong.”

“I know.”

He put one finger on a column.

“I’m going to do it slowly.”

She looked at the column. Buyers. Not names, codes, the way he wrote everything. She could read them now. Beside each code, in his square blunt hand, one letter.

K. K. S. K. S. S. S.

“K is keep. For now. Governments. Licensed buyers. Paperwork that’s real, or near enough.”

“And people who’ll buy anyway.”

“From somebody. Might as well be somebody who checks.” He moved his finger. “S is stop. Militias. Anyone the UN has a report on. Anyone who uses children. Anyone Maartens sold to.” A pause. “Anyone I wouldn’t want you reading about.”

She counted.

More S’s than K’s.

“Your S’s look like fives.”

He looked at the column. Then at her. Sideways. From very close. He’d leaned in to read over her shoulder about ten minutes ago, and somewhere in there he’d stopped pretending to read.

“Then you’ll have to read them for Mr. Yao.”

“Is that a job offer?”

“Hm.” He put his chin on her shoulder. “It doesn’t pay.”

“You pay for everything else. I’ve noticed.”

She let him stay there anyway. His breath was warm on her ear. She started counting again.

She lost it at seven. He’d turned his head and put his mouth on her neck, just under her ear, and left it there.

“You’re doing that on purpose.”

“Yes.” He didn’t move. “Count again.”

She turned round on the stool and kissed him instead. Pencil still in her hand. The ledger slid off her elbow and hit the floor. Nobody went after it. When she turned back she had to start the whole column from the top, and he sat next to her looking very pleased with himself and didn’t say sorry.

He took the pencil out of her fingers. He drew a neat little K on the back of her hand.

“What’s that for?”

“Keep.”

Her ears went hot. She looked at the ledger very hard.

“That’s sixty per cent. Zhendong, that’s…”

“I know what it is.” He shut the book. “Chen Si says it’s insane. He says I’ll lose half my men and all my name, and someone will put me in a koi pond.” The corner of his mouth went up. “He also says he’ll help.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si helped by lying.

“It’s what I’m best at.”

He was cutting his steak into exact squares at the long table on the forty-fourth floor.

“The world thinks Zhao Zhendong nearly died at the Hengli shipyard. The world thinks the Dutchman shot him and he hasn’t been right since. He’s scaling back because he’s frightened. Because his health is poor. Because of the Red Notice.”

“All of which is true,” Elowen said.

“All of which is true. None of which is the reason.” He ate a square. “I make sure everyone believes the true things. Then nobody goes looking for the real one.”

“And the men who think he’s gone soft?”

“Will be told, by people they trust, that the last man who thought so is at the bottom of a fishpond on the coast.” He smiled, faintly. “Fear lasts much longer than money.”

Aurelia rolled her eyes so hard it was nearly audible.

“He’s enjoying this. Look at him. He was up till four drawing diagrams on my good paper.”

“It’s an interesting problem.”

“It’s a hobby. He’s got a hobby. I’m going to have it framed.”

Zhao didn’t say a word all dinner. He ate. He had his arm along the back of Elowen’s chair the whole time, from the soup to the coffee, and never once took it off.

Aurelia noticed. Aurelia noticed everything.

“Darling. Does he ever move that arm?”

“No.”

“Not even to cut his meat?”

“He cuts it one-handed.”

Aurelia looked at the arm. Then at her own husband’s two hands, folded neatly beside his plate. Then back.

“I want that arm,” she said, to nobody. “Si. I want an arm.”

Chen Si cut another square and didn’t look up.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were three names on a folded page in his wallet. They’d been there since March.

Two of the three took what he offered. Money. A ticket north. They shook his hand at the gate and went without a fuss, because they’d heard about Wu on the platform with his eleven suitcases.

The third was Tsang.

Tsang was clever. Tsang had waited three weeks after the S column went round, until everyone was busy being relieved. Then he’d sold forty crates to one of the S buyers off a north warehouse, down one of Zhao’s own routes, and logged them in the books as damaged and returned.

Elowen found it on a Tuesday.

She hadn’t said anything. She’d just left the ledger open on his desk at the page, with one pencil line under the number and a question in the margin in her neat little hand. Who is Tsang selling to?

So on Thursday night Zhao drove north.

Tsang was in the warehouse office with his feet on the desk. He took them off fast.

“Boss! I didn’t… I didn’t know you were coming—”

“Sit down.”

Tsang sat. Zhao didn’t. He stood by the door and looked at him. Four seconds. Five. Tsang started talking at six.

He talked for a while. The buyer’s name. The route. Where the money was. Who else knew, which was nobody, which was a pity for Tsang. He talked until there was nothing left in him to say. Then he said sorry. Several times.

Zhao looked at his watch. Eleven. Elowen went to bed at eleven on market nights. She’d be lying on his side, because she did that when he wasn’t home and thought he didn’t know.

There was tea spilled on the desk. Tsang’s. It was running towards the ledger. Zhao moved the ledger.

Then he nodded to Bao.

Bao’s arm was out of the sling by then. He used both.

It didn’t take long. Zhao didn’t watch the whole of it. He’d seen it. Afterwards, Bao took Tsang out to the car. Zhao didn’t ask where. Bao didn’t tell him. Nobody at the Docks ever saw Tsang again, and nobody at the Docks asked, either.

On the way down the stairs he took his phone out.

Zhao: Eaten?

Elowen: yes

Zhao: What.

Elowen: noodles. the leftover ones

Zhao: Cold?

Elowen: i’m a grown woman

Zhao: Cold.

Elowen: …a bit cold

Zhao: Heat the soup. It’s in the blue pot.

He’d split two knuckles somewhere. He couldn’t remember on what. He looked at them under the stairwell light and thought, she’ll get the peas out. And she would. And she wouldn’t ask.

He was right on both.

She was at the kitchen counter in his sweatshirt when he got in, with the ledger. She looked at his hand. She got up without a word, got the frozen peas out of the freezer, wrapped them in a tea towel and pressed them on his knuckles. She held them there.

“Tsang?”

“Tsang.”

She sat down again, picked up her pencil, and drew one neat line through Tsang’s code.

“Which column?”

“Neither.”

She nodded. Then she took a clean sheet of paper and wrote the buyer’s name on it. Just the name. She folded it and put it under the ledger.

“For later,” she said.

He looked at the folded paper. Then at her.

“Is the soup still hot?”

“I didn’t heat the soup.”

“Elowen.”

“I’m heating it! Look! I’m walking to the pot!”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Yao came up the hill on a Wednesday with forty S accounts in a box.

He sat at the dining table with Elowen for three hours. He came out into the hall by the lemon tree looking like a man who’d been through a car wash with the windows down.

“Mr. Zhao.”

“Mr. Yao.”

“Mrs. Zhao would like all forty closed. By the end of the month.” He took his glasses off. He put them back on. “All forty, sir. With paperwork. She’s written the paperwork. She’s written it for me.”

“Then close them.”

“Sir, I said to you last year that I might be afraid of your wife.”

“You did.”

“I was wrong. I’m not might.” Mr. Yao gripped his box. “I am.”

Zhao looked down the hall at his wife. She was still at the table, frowning at a ledger, chewing the end of her pencil, with a K on the back of her hand in pencil, fading.

“Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Song Wei Long got the name.

Elowen took it to him herself. A noodle shop near the police station in the old town, on a Tuesday afternoon. He was in the corner with a bowl of beef noodles in his plain dark coat. He looked up when she sat down. He didn’t say anything.

She put an envelope on the table.

“What is it?”

“Names. People my husband used to do business with. People he’s stopped.” She kept her voice down. “Men who move people as well as guns. Some of them have offices you can walk into.”

He looked at the envelope. He didn’t touch it.

“Why?”

“Because he can’t do anything about them without killing them.” She held his eyes. “He would, if I asked. I thought you might do it quieter.”

“And in return?”

“Nothing. No deal. He isn’t asking you to look away from anything.” She stood up. “He said, ‘Tell the detective I owe him a cat.’ I told him that was your line. He didn’t care.”

The carved face moved. On anyone else it might have been a smile.

“The report I wrote. In March.”

“I know.”

“I don’t write things I don’t believe, Mrs. Zhao.” He turned his spoon over. “The man known as Zhao Zhendong was not present at the shipyard.”

“No. He wasn’t.”

“Good.” He looked at the envelope again. “I’d hate to have been wrong. I’ll read it.”

He put it inside his coat.

Six weeks later it was on the evening news. A warehouse by the railway in the east of the city. Fourteen men arrested. A shipping container with people in it, alive. Nine of them children. A detective with a carved face stood behind the reporter, not looking at the camera.

She watched it at the kitchen counter. He was on the stool beside her.

When it finished he reached over and took her hand. He didn’t let go of it to eat. He ate the rest of his dinner left-handed, badly, dropping rice all over the counter.

She laughed at him.

“Hm,” he said, and dropped some more.

✦ ✦ ✦

Was he a good man now?

Don’t be stupid.

He still sold to governments and licensed buyers and people who’d buy anyway. He still had a Red Notice. Some nights he came home smelling of other people’s cigarettes. Some nights he went down to the basement at two in the morning to clean something that didn’t need it. She went down after him in his old sweatshirt and sat on the end of the workbench with her feet tucked under her. She handed him the little brushes in the right order before he reached for them. She’d learned the order in three days in the armory, and she’d never forgotten it.

But the S column got longer every month. The K column got shorter.

By August he’d sold the warehouse in the north. Tsang’s warehouse, Wu’s before that. He gave the money to Old Ming’s widow and the nephew who wanted to be a chef. All of it.

They opened a noodle restaurant near the Docks.

It was very good. They ate there every Friday. Every Friday the widow said no, no, on the house, and every Friday Zhao paid anyway, and left twice as much under the soy sauce bottle when she wasn’t looking. She’d stopped arguing by the third week. She just lifted the bottle now and sighed at it.

One Friday they sat watching the nephew through the kitchen hatch, chopping spring onions with a cleaver and singing to himself. Zhao reached over and wiped a bit of chilli oil off the corner of her mouth with his thumb. Then he licked his thumb. She went red to the hairline. The widow, at the till, pretended she hadn’t seen.

He put his chopsticks down.

“I could keep going. One day. All of it.”

“You could. Or not.” She stole a piece of beef out of his bowl. “I’ll keep the books either way.”

He looked at her for a long time. Like he’d been ready for an argument and didn’t know what to do with his hands now.

“I don’t know who I am if I’m not this.” He turned his bowl a little on the table. “Since I was nineteen. Since before. Since the yard.” He looked up. “I don’t know what else I’m for.”

She took his scarred hand across the table.

“You carry buckets very well. Granny Su says you’re the best she’s ever seen.”

He looked at her.

Then the corner of his mouth went up. It stayed up. Rusty and crooked.

“That’s not a job.”

“It could be.” She pinched the last dumpling off his plate. “I’m very short-staffed.”

chapters.title: The Wedding They Eloped From
chapters.desc: Three and a half years after the registry, they have the wedding in the flower shop. Raiden walks in with a wife nobody knew about, and Baba asks about the lemon tree.
chapters.epigraph: “You never had a wedding.” “We had a registry office on a Tuesday.” “That isn’t a wedding, darling. That’s an appointment.” — Aurelia Chen
chapters.content:
It was Aurelia’s idea.

Of course it was. She announced it at the penthouse in June, over dessert, with the air of a general announcing an invasion.

“You’re having a wedding.”

Elowen put her spoon down. “We’re married.”

“You never had a wedding.”

“We had a registry office on a Tuesday.”

“With soil under your nails. And a ring two sizes too big. And Chen Si as a witness nobody needed.” Aurelia pointed her fork across the table. “That isn’t a wedding, darling. That’s an appointment.”

“It was a very good appointment.”

Everyone turned. Zhao was eating his cake with his fingers. He looked up, mild as milk, and met his wife’s eyes.

“Nine forty-one. I remember the time.”

Aurelia looked from one of them to the other. Then she put her fork down.

“Oh, for heaven’s sake. You’re having a wedding. September. I’m organising it. Nobody argues. Si, write it down.”

Chen Si took out a pen.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia wanted the Harbour Hotel. No. The penthouse. No. A garden, a yacht, a temple, a castle in the hills belonging to a man who owed Chen Si money.

“The shop.”

“It holds thirty people, Elowen. Standing.”

“Then thirty people. Standing.”

Aurelia opened her mouth to fight. Then she looked at Elowen’s face and shut it.

“Where it started.”

“Where it started.”

So: the shop.

Raiden built an arch over the door out of old Hengli shipyard timber, bolt holes and all. He said it was poetic. Chen Si said it was in very poor taste. Zhao said nothing. But the night it went up, he stood under it with one hand flat on the wood until Raiden turned the lights off on him.

Eliana strung lights. Thousands, all over the ceiling. She set them for nine forty-one and wouldn’t say why.

“Why not nine?”

“Spreadsheet.”

“Why not ten?”

“SPREADSHEET.”

Elara did the cake. Four tiers. Sugar camellias, deep pink, every petal done with tweezers at three in the morning. “It’s relaxing,” she said. Nobody believed her.

Evangeline did nothing anyone could see.

✦ ✦ ✦

Four in the morning. He drove. At the red light by the Docks he didn’t look at her.

“What are you wearing?”

“You’ll see.”

“Hm.” The light went green. He didn’t move.

“Zhendong. It’s green.”

“I’m thinking about it.”

The van behind them leaned on its horn. He drove on with the corner of his mouth up.

He carried the buckets. Granny Su was waiting at stall forty-two with a cigarette and a box.

“For the bride.”

Five stems of lily of the valley in damp moss. Out of season. Stupidly expensive. The same as the morning of the registry.

“How do you even get these?”

“Trade secret.” Granny Su squinted at the hand holding the box. “Still too big?”

Elowen held it up. The heavy gold ring with the square green stone sat on her fourth finger, where it belonged. It had been there three weeks. It fitted.

Granny Su looked at it. Then at Zhao, with the eucalyptus held exactly right.

“Hm.”

That was all. But when Elowen looked back from the end of the row, the old woman was wiping her eyes with the back of her wrist and glaring at her cigarette, like it had done it.

At six she let herself in the back of the shop and nearly trod on her sister.

Eliana was asleep on the floor under a ladder with her laptop on her chest and a grey jacket that wasn’t hers tucked round her shoulders.

“Yu-er? Why are you on the FLOOR?”

“Spreadsheet.”

On the counter was a dented flask, lined up square to the edge. Elowen looked at the jacket. At the flask. At her little sister, going pink.

She put the buckets down.

“There’s tea on the counter. In his flask.” Over her shoulder. Not turning round. “He left it. For when you woke up.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mid-morning, Evangeline came in with an orchid.

White, in a little pot. She put it on the counter by the till. Elowen looked at it and burst into tears. It was a cutting. From the orchid Ev had given her the week she moved up the hill. The one she’d thought had died.

“I kept a piece. Before you moved. In case.”

Elowen held on to her until she could breathe. Ev let her. Ev even patted her back, twice, very stiffly, like she’d read about it.

In the afternoon she found the coat.

It was hanging in the back beside the dress. Dark green wool, lined with silk, cut to go over it. The forecast said rain by evening. No note. There was never a note.

He’d paid for everything else too. Every bill Aurelia sent came back settled, from an account with no name on it.

She’d said nothing new but the dress. Very clearly.

She was furious with him. Then with herself, for liking it this much.

She left it on the hook. For later.

✦ ✦ ✦

By eight the shop was full, and she was by the arch in green with her mother’s pearls in her ears, when she saw her brother through the window.

Raiden. On the step. Silver waistcoat. Next to a tall woman in a dark red dress and an old black leather jacket, who was doing something to her own hand. Raiden was staring at it.

Then he hooked his finger into a black string round his own neck, yanked it out of his collar and snapped it. Just snapped it. Something dropped into his palm and went onto his finger. His hand was shaking so badly it took two goes.

He walked her in with his arm round her waist.

“Everyone!”

Thirty heads turned.

“Jinx, my wife, she built Xiao Pan’s bike, don’t touch her tools.”

Nobody made a sound. Aurelia’s pen stopped. Elowen kept her face perfectly still. Years of practice.

By the cooler, Baba went still too. He was looking at the woman’s left hand. A thick plain ring, like a washer. Then at his son’s. Then he walked out. Straight past them, onto the step, and stood there with his back to the shop.

“Oh no,” Raiden breathed. “Oh no, no. Baba—”

“Leave him.”

Ice. Her own voice.

Raiden looked at her. Then he steered his wife straight to the arch, like it was the safest place in the room.

Zhao looked at Jinx for four seconds.

“Hm.”

“Hm.”

Raiden turned a laugh into a cough so badly that Zhao looked at him for four more. Then somebody grabbed Raiden’s hand, and he was off round the room like a lit firework. “This is my wife. This is my WIFE. Have you met my wife?”

Elowen waited until the crowd shifted. Then she went to the corner by the cooler, where they’d backed the wife in.

Raiden saw her coming. He opened his mouth. She looked at him once. He shut it and went to find a drink.

“Your wife.”

“Yes.”

“How long?”

“Two years. Next week.”

“Two years.” Perfectly level. “He came to Sunday lunch every week. He brought me a shelf. I used to lie awake at night thinking he was lonely.”

“He wanted to tell you. I made him not.” She didn’t look away. Hardly anyone managed that. “My terms. I wrote them on a napkin.”

“Why?”

So Jinx told her. Low and flat. A chop shop under the flyover. Buyers who bought from Baba’s people. A black car down the lane when she was nine, and every man in the shop standing up.

Elowen turned her head and looked across the room. Zhao was under the arch in black, with one of Elara’s sugar camellias in his lapel. He felt her looking. His shoulders moved.

“Zhendong knew.”

“Since the hospital. He took my jacket off the chair before you turned round.” A pause. “And there’s a photo on the wall at the noodle shop. From the registry.”

Elowen shut her eyes.

When she opened them she knew exactly what was on her face. Fury. Love. The fury losing.

“I’m going to kill him.” Very calm. “After the wedding.” She looked back at Jinx. “Thank you for Xiao Pan’s bike. He cried the first time he rode it. He made me promise not to tell you.”

“I know. I saw.”

The collar of the old jacket had turned under at the back. Elowen reached out and fixed it.

“It suits you. Don’t let Aurelia buy you a new one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine o’clock that night, thirty people stood in a flower shop.

Lin Jian, in his funeral suit, the only suit he owned, back in off the step. Hands clasped in front of him by the cooler. Trying not to cry and failing.

Raiden, in a silver waistcoat he had designed himself, beside a tall, quiet, broad-shouldered woman with grease under her nails. Jinx, my wife, she built Xiao Pan’s bike, don’t touch her tools. He’d said it to an old man from the tea shop and both dogs.

Evangeline, at the back, alone, in pale blue, watching the door. Her husband, whom nobody in the shop knew she had, was on a roof across the street.

Elara, flushed and proud beside her cake, with a tall, serious young doctor in glasses standing very close beside her whom nobody had been introduced to yet and everyone noticed. Her husband, it would turn out, of six weeks.

Eliana, in a hoodie, with a laptop. And beside her a lanky boy from next door with a medical textbook under his arm, who had apparently come because Eliana told him to. Elowen did not ask where his grey jacket was. She was very good.

Chen Si in grey, by the counter. Aurelia in gold, at the front, in charge of absolutely everything. Bao in a new suit that didn’t fit across the shoulders, by the door, because Bao stood by doors. Xiao Pan with his helmet under his arm. Old Ming’s widow and the nephew. Mr. Yao, as far from Elowen as the shop allowed.

Mr. Wen’s grandson, who’d flown up from the Greenstone hills with a box of oolong, and delivered his grandfather’s message to the whole room before he’d got his coat off.

“Grandpa says: Tell the idiot I was right.”

Detective Song Wei Long, at the very back, in his plain dark coat. He’d told Bao he wasn’t there officially. Then he stood through the whole thing with his carved face perfectly still and his eyes suspiciously bright.

A card from Miles, from a conference somewhere cold. Light bends around heavy things. I hope you’re very happy. I think you are. — M.

And two dogs in white ribbons, lying on the mat. Exactly where a man had once stood, dripping.

✦ ✦ ✦

Baba walked her down the aisle.

Four metres, between the buckets of white roses. It should have taken five seconds. His arm was shaking. Halfway, past the tulips over Raiden’s floor, he stopped.

Everyone waited.

He looked at Zhao, at the far end under the shipyard arch. Zhao looked back. Steady. Waiting.

“Zhendong.”

The shop went quiet.

“How is the lemon tree?”

For a second Zhao didn’t say anything at all.

Then his face opened, slowly, like a door.

“Nine lemons. The most it’s ever had.”

Baba nodded. His eyes were wet. He walked the last two metres and put her hand into the hand of the man who’d made his own shake for six years. He held them both together for a moment between his.

“Look after her.”

“She looks after me.”

Baba looked at him. Then his whole face crumpled up into a smile. He stepped back beside Raiden, and Raiden put an arm round him without even looking.

No priest. No official. The little red book was in the drawer under the till where it always was. Chen Si stepped up beside the arch and said exactly four sentences, which was how many he’d prepared.

“Thirteen years ago, I carried this man through a sewer. He was very heavy. He has been carrying people ever since, and nobody has ever carried him. I am very glad to see that somebody finally does.”

He stepped back. Aurelia looked up at him with a face that made Elowen look somewhere else, to give them a minute.

Nobody had written the vows down.

“I don’t run.” She was holding both his hands. Hers were cold. His weren’t. “I cut things cleanly. And then I keep them. I keep you. Every day. At four in the morning. I keep choosing you.”

His jaw moved.

“I’ll sit outside your door. Every night. For as long as I live. So you’ll always know where I am.” He swallowed. “So you’ll never have to wonder.”

“You sleep in my bed now. You don’t have to sit outside the door.”

“I know. I’ll still be there.”

In the corner, Eliana pressed one key on her laptop and shut it.

Nine forty-one. Every light came on at once. Gold. Warm. The whole ceiling turned into a sky, and thirty people went oh.

He didn’t wait for anyone to tell him he could.

He took her face in both hands and kissed her under it. In her shop. In front of everyone she loved. Long and deep and not polite at all. Aurelia started counting out loud. Raiden whistled through his fingers. Baba found something very interesting to look at inside the cooler.

Lin Elowen kept her face still for a living. She didn’t keep it still at all.

When he lifted his head he didn’t step back. Forehead on hers. Low enough that nobody else could hear.

“Green. I thought about it all morning. I was right to.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The cake went in ten minutes. Zhao ate his off a paper plate with his fingers, Elara’s camellia still in his lapel. He went over to Elara’s doctor with the plate.

The doctor looked straight back at him. “How’s the side?”

Zhao looked at the doctor’s left hand. Up again.

“Hm.”

What was that? Elowen filed it. Later. Everything was later.

Aurelia gave a speech about Elowen being wrong about everything for ten years. Elowen gave one back. It was shorter and better. Then their husbands stood up at the same moment, said the same word, mine, and sat down again. Aurelia threw a napkin at hers.

Near midnight Chen Si danced with her. Correctly.

“He’s happy,” he said, very low, like it was classified.

Over his shoulder she saw Aurelia at the little bar by the cooler, standing beside Ev. A whole minute. Not a word. Then Ev’s lips moved, and Aurelia went absolutely still.

Ev had talked to Aurelia?

Then the front door went. Baba came in off the street with a very strange face. He picked Elara’s bag up off the counter, took it out, and came back without it.

She didn’t ask. It was her wedding. Everything was later.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before two she found Zhao by the cooler and grabbed him by the tie.

He came. He always came. She pulled him inside, among the roses, and shut the glass door, and the cold hit them both at once.

“It’s after the wedding.”

“Hm?”

“I said I’d kill you after the wedding. It’s after.” She kept hold of the tie. “Two years. You knew about Raiden for two years.”

“Since the hospital.”

“Zhendong!”

“You’d have gone to the Docks road and shouted at him.”

“I would NOT have—” She stopped. She would have. “That’s not the point!”

“It was his.”

“His what?”

“His to tell.” His breath came out white. “I keep things for people. You know that.”

She did know that. That was the worst part.

“I’m still going to kill you.”

“Tomorrow.”

“Tomorrow?”

“I’m busy tonight.”

“Doing WHAT?”

He took her hand off his tie and held it. “Hm.”

She pulled him down by the tie anyway and kissed him. Cold mouth. Warm hands. A bucket of white roses went over against her heel. Through the glass, Xiao Pan walked past with a plate of cake, saw them, turned round and walked straight back the other way.

When they came out, the lights were going off one string at a time. Baba was asleep in a chair by the door with his funeral jacket over his knees. Raiden was carrying both dogs out to Zhao’s car, one under each arm, because they were asleep and Elowen had said so. At the back, Ev was cutting two slices of Elara’s cake onto a paper plate. She put her coat on over the pale blue and went out the back door into the lane.

Elowen didn’t ask about that either.

Rain on the window. Of course.

Zhao went into the back. He came out with the green coat. He put it round her shoulders over the dress and did up the top button under her chin. Then he crouched and took her shoes off, because he’d seen her wince.

He stood up with her heels hooked on two fingers.

“No note,” she said.

“There’s never a note.”

“I said nothing new.”

“You said nothing new but the dress.” He held the door open on the rain. “The coat goes with the dress.”

“That isn’t how it—”

“Elowen.”

“What.”

He didn’t answer. He’d gone back to just looking at her, standing in his coat in the door of her shop.

“I’m still killing you tomorrow,” she said, and walked out barefoot into the rain before he could see her face.

chapters.title: Every Flower in the Shop
chapters.desc: Five years on, it starts to rain over the Docks and he walks out of a meeting without his umbrella. He’s on her mat at closing time, and a girl outside is looking at the tulips in the window.
chapters.epigraph: “How much, for everything?”
chapters.content:
Hou was late again.

Not with the money. Hou was never late with money now. He was late in the way men got late after a while, when they stopped being scared. He talked. He sat across the desk at the Iron Docks with his round face shining and talked. Diesel. His wife’s knee. A nephew who wanted to study abroad. And every few sentences he slid the price down a little. Like nobody would notice.

“…so if we said eleven, instead of twelve, just for this quarter, with things the way they are—”

Zhao looked at the window.

The sky over the cranes had gone low and yellow-grey. The flags on the container stacks were standing straight out. Rain. Not yet. Soon.

“Twelve.”

“Mr. Zhao, with respect, everybody knows you’re… you’re selling things off. Half the north. People are saying—”

Zhao put his hand flat on the desk. That was all. He didn’t lean forward. Hou stopped talking anyway, mid-word, and his eyes went to the hand and stayed there. Was he thinking about the knife in Maartens? Everyone at the Docks had heard about that table. Five years, and they still told it wrong. Some of them said it was a fork.

“What are they saying?”

“Nothing. Nothing at all.”

“Twelve.”

“Twelve. Of course. Twelve is fine. I only meant—”

Something tapped the glass. One drop. Then three. Then the whole window went grey and loud, and the cranes disappeared.

Zhao stood up.

Hou half stood too, confused, his folder clutched to his chest. “Are we… is that it?”

“Tuesday. All of it.”

He was already at the door. Bao was in the corridor with the car keys in one hand and a big black umbrella in the other. He held the umbrella out.

“No.”

“Boss. It’s pouring.”

“I know.”

Bao looked at him. Then at the rain. Then at the calendar on the wall, the free one from the tyre place, with nothing written on it. Something happened in his face. A small private grin, swallowed fast.

“It’s the second.”

“I know what day it is.”

Bao put the umbrella back in the stand. Not another word all the way to the Walled City. He didn’t need one. He hummed.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Miss Lin. You’ve looked at the sky eleven times.”

“I have not.”

“Twelve now.”

Xiao Pan was leaning on the cooler with his helmet under his arm, red bike outside, last delivery done. Twenty-four now. Taller. Still went red when anyone looked at him. The scars on his palms had gone white and shiny, and he didn’t hide them any more.

Elowen went back to her stock. Strip the lower leaves. Cut. Into the bucket. Next. She was twenty-nine. The shop was ten. The sign over the door still said Elowen’s in white paint. She’d repainted it twice. Both times she’d stood on the ladder with the brush and couldn’t think of anything better.

“Is it raining yet?”

“You just looked!”

“Go home, Xiao Pan.”

“It’s only six.” He squinted out at the street. A drop hit the glass. Then lots. “Oh. Now it is.”

“Have you got a raincoat?”

“I’m a professional.” He put his helmet on. Then he took it off again, because he’d remembered something, and his ears went pink. “Is it… is it a special day? You keep touching your ring.”

She looked down. She had the ring off for work, as always. It was in the little wooden dish beside the till. And her thumb was rubbing the bare place on her finger where it usually sat.

“Go. Home.”

He went. Grinning. Idiot.

She checked her phone. Nothing. She sent one message, very casual.

Elowen: it’s raining here

Three dots. Gone. Nothing.

She stared at the screen. Five years. Five years, and he couldn’t manage one word? Not even hm? She put the phone face down on the counter, harder than she needed to, and picked the knife back up.

Fine. She didn’t care.

She cared a bit.

✦ ✦ ✦

Rain killed the last hour. It always did. Nobody in the Walled City bought flowers with water running down their collar. Radio on. Old songs. A bucket of white stock.

The bell rang.

“We close in ten minutes.” She didn’t look up. “If it’s an apology, get the peonies. They look expensive.”

Nobody answered. She looked up.

He was soaked. Black coat dark with rain, hair flat on his forehead, water pouring off him onto her clean floor. Same coat. The old black wool. The elbows went through in the second year. A tailor in the old town patched them with leather and shook his head the whole time.

Across the street, under the noodle shop awning, Bao sat on the stool the owner kept for him. Eating noodles. Very loudly not looking this way.

“You’re dripping on my floor.”

He looked down at the puddle. Took his coat off. Folded it over his arm and stood on the mat. Exactly where he’d stood the first time. She could have drawn round his shoes.

“Where’s your umbrella?”

“It was raining the first time.”

That wasn’t an answer. It was, though. She grabbed the towel off the workbench and threw it at his head. He caught it without looking. Some things you didn’t lose.

“You didn’t answer my message.”

“I was driving here.”

“Bao was driving.”

“I was thinking about driving here.”

She tried not to smile. She failed. Disaster.

He dried his face. Then he came round the counter. Straight round. No asking. She pointed the knife at him.

“Rule two.”

He didn’t stop. He opened the drawer under the till, which he had no business knowing about, and took out the sign. Five years old. Soft as cloth at the folds. 2. The husband is not allowed behind the counter. A line through it. His square capitals beside it: EXCEPT WHEN SHE SAYS SO. And under that, in her own small writing, from some night she didn’t remember deciding: She always says so.

He held it up next to her face. Like evidence.

“…I hate you.”

“Hm.”

He put the sign back. Then he stood behind her and wrapped both arms round her, wet shirt and all. Chin on top of her head. She was cold all down her back at once. She didn’t move away. She should have. Her good blouse.

“You’re tired.” His chin moved on her hair when he talked. “You were at the market at four.”

“I’m always at the market at four.”

“Let me go alone tomorrow. Granny Su will count for me.”

“Granny Su is eighty-three. She can barely see the bunches.”

“She counts by feel now. She told me.” His hands slid under her apron to her waist, thumbs on the bones of her hips. Checking she was all there. He’d done that for five years and she still didn’t know if he knew he did it. “She said, tell the girl I was counting before she was born.”

Elowen laughed and leaned back into him and shut her eyes. Just for a second. Rain on the glass. The cooler humming. His heart going under her shoulder blade, slow and stupid and hers.

Somebody knocked on the window.

✦ ✦ ✦

A girl. Twenty, maybe. Backpack, cheap umbrella blown inside out on one side. She was pointing at the bucket of red tulips in the window, with the face people make at things they know they can’t afford.

Elowen knew that face. Not the girl. The face. There was a woman with a green umbrella who came every year in the rain for tulips. Every year. For her mother.

Behind her, Zhao had gone still. Not the old stillness. The new one. The one that meant he’d had an idea.

“Wait.”

He let go of her. He took his wallet out of his wet trousers, counted a stack of notes onto the counter beside her scissors, and looked at her.

“How much, for everything?”

She stared at him.

Five years ago, on that mat, with a holster under his arm. Same words. She’d done the sum without meaning to. She did it again now. She couldn’t help it. She always did the sum. The roses. The stock. The lilies in the cooler. The delphiniums, nowhere near the door. The tulips.

“Six thousand eight hundred.” Her voice did something funny. “Prices went up.”

He counted seven thousand. Picked up the whole bucket of tulips, twenty stems, dripping. Opened the door into the rain.

“Hey.”

Not loud. The girl stopped dead on the wet pavement. He held the tulips out.

She looked at them. At him, enormous and soaked, with rain running into his collar. At Elowen behind the glass. She took them in both arms and nearly dropped her umbrella.

“I can’t… I only wanted one, it’s my mum’s birthday, she normally comes herself but she did her hip, and I can’t pay for—”

“They’re paid for.”

“Is your mum the lady with the green umbrella?” Elowen had come to the door without deciding to.

The girl’s mouth fell open. “How do you know that?”

“Tell her the florist says get well.”

The girl looked from her to him. Her eyes went shiny. She said thank you about four times, the last one already running. The tulips bounced off down the alley in the rain like a fire somebody was carrying.

He came back in. Shut the door. Stood on the mat. Wet to the elbows.

“Those were my tulips.”

“They were my tulips. I paid.”

She opened her mouth. Shut it. Five years and he still won that one. And nobody had asked him. Nobody had been watching except her. He’d just done it, again, because a girl in the rain had looked at the window.

She came round the counter and grabbed his wet shirt in both fists and kissed him.

He made a noise against her mouth. Surprise, then not. His hands came up into her hair and he kissed her back like the first night, like he’d finally been let off the doormat. He walked her backwards. One step. Two. The counter hit the small of her back. The scissors rattled. The till gave a tiny ping. She laughed into his mouth. He didn’t stop. He was cold everywhere. His mouth wasn’t. She was getting soaked through her blouse and she didn’t care at all.

When he finally lifted his head, he stayed close. Forehead on hers. Breathing like he’d run there.

“Rule one.” She could barely get it out. “No frightening the customers.”

“She wasn’t frightened.”

“I’m frightened. Look at my blouse!”

He looked at her blouse. For far too long.

“Hm.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They closed at eight.

He swept. He did the corners with his fingers. Every corner. Xiao Pan said nobody in the history of the shop had ever done the corners. She re-cut the roses that hadn’t sold. All of them, because he’d bought them. Into the cooler for the morning. She’d sell them again tomorrow. He’d pretend not to notice he’d paid for them twice.

At the door she stopped with her hand on the light switch and looked back.

The buckets. The cooler. The second row of tulips, over a room under the floor where a light came on if you needed it. The dish by the till with her ring in it. She went back for that, obviously. Evangeline’s orchid on the windowsill. A narrow glass frame on the wall with a camellia pressed flat inside it, from a lapel, on a night it rained. And on the mat, two wet shoeprints.

“Elowen.”

He had his wallet open. Behind his identity card, flat and faded nearly to grey, was the ghost of a tiny blue flower. One delphinium floret. Smaller than a fingernail.

She’d found it three years ago, looking for change. She’d never said. He knew she knew. They’d never said that either.

“Five years. Today.”

“I know what day it is.”

He nearly smiled. He put the wallet away. Inside pocket. Left side. “That night. When you threw the towel. Do you know what I thought?”

“That I was rude.”

“That I’d pay four thousand two hundred every night. For the rest of my life. To stand on that mat.”

She looked at the shoeprints. At him. She had absolutely nothing to say to that. Fine. She turned the lights off instead, so he couldn’t see her face, and took his hand in the dark.

He held the coat over both their heads all the way to the car. Half of it. The other half was over her. His left shoulder got drenched and he didn’t seem to notice. Behind them, Bao finished his noodles, paid, and followed at a distance. Humming.

✦ ✦ ✦

At home she pushed him into the bathroom and made him sit on the edge of the bath.

“You’ll get a cold.”

“I don’t get colds.”

“Everyone gets colds!” She had the big towel. She put it over his head and rubbed. Hard. Like the dogs after the beach. He let her. He sat there with his eyes shut, hands on his knees, and let himself be dried like a wet animal. The corner of his mouth went up. It stayed up.

She threw the towel at him in the shop once. Now she was doing this. When had that happened? She honestly couldn’t say. Some Tuesday.

She pushed the towel back off his face. His hair stuck up everywhere. The piece at the back that never lay flat was standing straight up. Of course it was.

“There. Human again.”

He didn’t answer. He was looking at her blouse again. Still damp. Still see-through in places, thanks to him. He reached out and undid the top button. Then he stopped. Hand flat on her collarbone. Looking up at her.

“Elowen.”

Just her name. Like a question. Five years, and he still stopped there. A breath away. Every time. It still did something terrible to her knees.

“You don’t have to ask. You haven’t had to ask for years.”

“I know.” His thumb moved on her collarbone. “I like the answer.”

So she gave it to him. “Yes.” And then, because he was still sitting there like a statue, she got hold of his ears and kissed him.

The buttons were hopeless. His fingers were cold and clumsy. She was laughing. He swore at the third one, actually swore. She pushed his hands away and did them herself. He stood up off the bath and picked her up and didn’t make it to the bed the first time. The wall was closer. He said her name against her neck like he was reading it off something. She said his, and he stopped breathing for a second, the way he always did. Five years. Still.

Then the bed. Cold sheets, hot skin. Rain on the window. He was slow, deliberately, infuriatingly slow, until she bit his shoulder and told him to stop showing off, and he laughed into her hair. Then he wasn’t slow at all. Then nobody was laughing. She held on to his back, where the long scar ran. He held her face in both hands like he had to check it was her. He said things into her mouth she would never repeat to anyone. Ever.

After, she lay with her head on his chest. Hair everywhere. His hand moved in it, slow, the way he cut stems now, like she’d taught him.

She heard the drawer before she saw it. His bedside drawer. He was reaching for it with his free hand.

She lifted her head.

“Zhendong. Don’t you dare write this down.”

He already had the pen.

chapters.title: Zhao Zhendong Tries to Arrange Flowers
chapters.desc: The florist has a fever on Mother’s Day, so her husband takes her forty-three orders. He measures every bow with a ruler, and then he gets to the one that says use your judgment.
chapters.epigraph: “How hard can it be?” — Zhao Zhendong
chapters.content:
“No.”

It came out as a croak. Elowen tried again, louder, and her throat felt like she’d swallowed a cactus.

“No, Zhendong.”

Her husband stood at the end of the bed. Fully dressed. Five in the morning. Van keys in one hand, her order book in the other, open to Mother’s Day. Forty-three orders. Somebody had stuck little yellow notes all down the margins in square blunt capitals.

“Xiao Pan is coming at seven. Bao drives. Granny Su has your flowers boxed. I rang her at three.”

“You rang Granny Su at three?”

“She was up.”

“You can’t arrange flowers!”

He looked at her. Calm. Totally sure of himself. It was the face he wore into rooms full of men with guns, and it was the most worrying thing she’d seen all year.

“How hard can it be?”

She tried to get up. The room tipped. He put the book down, picked her up by the shoulders, laid her back on the pillow and pulled the duvet up to her chin. Then he read the paracetamol box. Both sides. Then the first side again.

He held up the thermometer. He’d already used it on her while she was asleep, apparently. Unbelievable.

“Thirty-eight point nine. You stay.”

“It’s Mother’s Day. It’s the second biggest day of the—”

He was gone. She heard the van start.

She lay there and stared at the ceiling. Forty-three orders. Her husband. Her knives. Oh god.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first hour was fine.

Zhao did the wrapped ones. They were easy. She wrote them down like orders. 12 red roses, gypsophila, brown paper, red ribbon. He did exactly that. Twelve. He counted twice. He measured the ribbon with a steel ruler from the drawer.

Xiao Pan watched him from the cooler. Twenty years old. Hands healed. Red bike outside. He had the look of a boy who was going to tell this story for the rest of his life.

“Mr. Zhao… you don’t have to measure. Miss Lin never measures.”

“Eleven centimetres. Each side.”

“How do you know that?”

Zhao didn’t answer. He tied the bow. Eleven. Xiao Pan checked it with the ruler when he wasn’t looking. Eleven. He put the ruler back very slowly.

Then they got to order nineteen.

Not wrapped. A bowl. A low round ceramic bowl full of wet foam. And her writing, in the margin, in that small neat hand like a wedding card:

Something soft, for a mother who has everything. Use your judgment.

Zhao read it three times.

Judgment. Whose?

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d watched her do this a hundred times. More. He’d stood behind this counter and watched her hands go in and out of the buckets like she was picking things up off a table. One stem. Another. Done. It always looked right. He’d never once seen her think about it.

He picked up a pink rose. He put it in the foam. He looked at it.

Wrong.

He moved it a centimetre to the left. Still wrong. He put three more round it. Then four at the top and four at the bottom and four on each side. Same distance apart. He filled the gaps with gypsophila. Neat little rows. He stepped back.

Xiao Pan made a noise.

“What.”

“Nothing! It’s very… it’s very straight, Mr. Zhao.”

It was. It looked like a parade. It looked like the roses were about to march somewhere and shoot someone. It looked like a crate of rifles laid out on a cloth before a buyer arrived, which was the only kind of arranging he’d ever done.

He took it all out and started again.

And again.

By the fifth time Xiao Pan had stopped making noises and started praying. By the seventh the roses were finished. Not dead. Just beaten. Bruised all down the petals from being pushed in and pulled out. Two had lost their heads completely. The gypsophila had gone flat. There were petals on the bench, on the floor, on his sleeves. He had one stuck in his hair and didn’t know.

Half eleven. The customer was coming at twelve.

“Mr. Zhao.” Very carefully, from a safe distance. “Maybe I could ring Miss Lin and just ask—”

“No.”

“Just one quick—”

“She has a fever. She can’t talk.” He didn’t look away from the bowl. “She went to the market the morning she married me. With soil under her nails. I’m not ringing her because I can’t put flowers in a pot.”

Xiao Pan shut his mouth.

Zhao stood there with his arms folded. What did she do? Really. He knew what her hands did. He’d memorised her hands. The bows were eleven centimetres because her hands were eleven centimetres from wrist to fingertip, give or take, and he knew that too. But what was she thinking?

“How does she know?”

Xiao Pan blinked. “Know what?”

“Where it goes. She doesn’t plan. She doesn’t measure. She picks things up and it’s right.”

Xiao Pan thought about it. He scratched the white scar on his palm.

“She says… you have to stop trying to make it look like flowers. You make it look like the person.”

Zhao turned his head.

“A mother who has everything. Miss Lin would think about her. What she’s like. What she’d actually want. Not what looks nice.”

Zhao looked at the bowl for a while.

He didn’t know what mothers wanted. He’d never had one long enough to find out. The orphanage had a woman who cut everyone’s hair in a row on Thursdays. Old Zhao had a cough and a truck. That was the whole list.

But he knew what one woman kept. A lemon tree, twenty years on a balcony. A coat with a torn pocket. The bent stems nobody would buy, which she put in a jar by the till instead of throwing out.

He walked into the cooler and shut the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiao Pan told her all of this that evening. Standing at the end of the bed. Still slightly pale. Like a soldier back from somewhere.

“He was in there for ages, Miss Lin. In the cold. Just standing. I thought he’d died.”

“And?”

“And he came out with weird stuff.”

Small white sweet peas. Three stems of pale blue scabious, the messy wild ones. A sprig of rosemary off the pot on the windowsill. And the peach rose she’d put aside on Friday, because its head was bent.

“He didn’t measure. He just shoved it all in. Fast. Like packing a bag when you’re late.” Xiao Pan’s hands flapped. “And then he stopped. And it was… Miss Lin, it was a mess. The scabious was leaning. The sweet peas were all in one corner. The bent one was off to the side.”

“And?”

“And it looked like someone’s garden. In the morning. Before anyone’s tidied it.”

Elowen put her hand over her mouth.

“I told him it was very good. He said it was a mess. I said it looked like a mum. A nice one. The kind who’d keep the crooked rose because nobody else would.” Xiao Pan went pink. “And he said, ‘Yes. That’s what I was thinking about.’”

The customer had come at twelve. A woman in an expensive coat, collecting for her own mother. She’d looked at the bowl on the counter for a long time without saying anything. Then she’d looked up at the huge silent man behind the counter, with a pink petal in his hair.

“She said, ‘Did you make this?’ And he said yes. And she said her mum had a garden when she was little. Before she got ill. Sweet peas. Rosemary by the door.” Xiao Pan swallowed. “She said, ‘How did you know?’ And he said, ‘I didn’t. I thought about what she’d keep.’ And then she cried. In the shop. And left a tip so big I made a sound.”

Elowen didn’t say anything. She couldn’t. Her throat was bad. That was all.

“And the roses?” she croaked eventually.

Xiao Pan looked past her at the doorway. Zhao was standing there with a tray and a very stiff face.

“The roses,” Xiao Pan said solemnly, “did not survive.”

He fled.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao put the tray on the bed. Congee. Bao’s wife had made it, thank god. There was still a pink petal in his hair.

Elowen reached up and picked it out. Held it between two fingers.

“You made a mother cry.”

“I made a bowl look like a garden. By accident.”

“That’s not an accident. That’s the whole job.” She laid the petal on the tray. “I’m proud of you.”

He looked at the petal instead of her. The back of his neck went red. All the way up to his ears. She watched it happen and felt about a hundred times better than paracetamol had ever made her feel.

“Xiao Pan says you measured my bows. With a ruler.”

“Eleven centimetres.”

“I’ve never measured a bow in my life.”

“I know.” He sat on the edge of the bed and pulled the duvet back up to her chin, where it had been before she started laughing. “They’re always eleven. I’ve watched your hands for a year. The number was just there.”

She looked at him over the duvet. Her face was hot and it wasn’t the fever. What did you even say to that?

He picked up the spoon. He blew on it. Twice. Then held it out. Like she was five.

“I can feed myself.”

“Hm.”

She ate it off the spoon. He watched her swallow. He blew on the next one.

“Finish it. Then water. Bao’s wife says two litres.” He topped her glass up. It was already full. He topped it up anyway. “And you don’t get up tomorrow. I told Granny Su. If you go near the shop I’ll take the van keys and I’ll take your knives and I’ll lock the—”

She took a fistful of his petal-covered shirt and pulled him down and kissed him. Fever and all. Mostly so he’d stop talking.

It worked. He stopped. For about a second he was completely still against her mouth. Then he made a low sound in his throat and kissed her back, one hand braced on the pillow by her head, the other holding the tray level. Of course. Even now. She laughed into it and had to break off and cough for ages. He sat back. He looked at her like she’d cheated at something and he’d let her.

“You’ll catch it.”

“Then I stay home too.” He put the spoon back in her hand. Like that had been his plan all along. “I’m never doing that again. I mean it.”

“I know you do.”

When the bowl was empty he put the tray on the floor. He lay down on top of the duvet in his ruined shirt and pulled her against his chest, duvet and all. She was boiling. He didn’t move away.

“Get better.” Into her hair. Rough. “The shop’s wrong without you in it.”

She was nearly asleep. “Wrong how?”

He thought about it so long she thought he’d gone to sleep first.

“Too straight.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next Mother’s Day she had a fever again.

Or said she did. She lay in bed with the duvet up to her nose and coughed, once, not very well.

He stood at the end of the bed with the van keys and looked at her for four whole seconds. He picked up the thermometer. He looked at her. He put it down again without using it.

Then he went to the shop.

chapters.title: The Delivery Boy Who Saw Too Much
chapters.desc: Xiao Pan has worked at Elowen’s for five years and would like it on the record that he never wanted to see any of it. A numbered list, the cooler not included, and the best tip he ever got.
chapters.epigraph: “Please don’t make me say more, Miss Lin. I have to live.” — Xiao Pan
chapters.content:
My name is Pan Xiaodong. Everybody calls me Xiao Pan. I’m twenty-two. I’ve worked at Elowen’s for five years. I deliver flowers. I’m very good at it.

I would like it on the record that I did not want to see any of this.

✦ ✦ ✦

1. The night of the rain. I wasn’t there. I want that written down. I went home early with a cold. Next morning there was five thousand in cash under the till. And a wet shoeprint on the doormat that Miss Lin wouldn’t let me mop.

“Leave it.”

“It’s mud, Miss Lin.”

“Leave it, Xiao Pan.”

She kept looking at the delphiniums and smiling at nothing. I was nineteen. I thought she’d met a nice man.

I was wrong about the nice.

2. The first time I saw him. He didn’t buy anything. He stood in the doorway and looked at Miss Lin. Miss Lin looked at him. I was sweeping. I stopped sweeping. The whole shop went like the sky before a typhoon, when the birds shut up.

“Xiao Pan. Go and get lunch.”

“It’s ten o’clock—”

“Go and get lunch.”

I went. I didn’t come back for two hours. I’m not stupid.

When I did come back he was gone and she was cutting stems really, really fast.

“Who was that, Miss Lin?”

“Nobody.”

“He looked like—”

“Nobody. Ribbon.”

I passed her the ribbon. Nobody. Sure.

3. The van. I don’t want to talk about the van.

My hands are fine now. I can hold a spoon. I can hold a cleaver. Old Ming’s nephew taught me, at the noodle place. I can ride a motorbike. A small red one. A woman called Jinx built it. She has tattoos on both arms. She made me sit on it in her garage for an hour before she let me start it.

“Helmet.”

“I’ve got it, it’s right—”

“If I ever see you on this without a helmet, I take the engine out. With my hands. While you watch.”

I believe her. I wear the helmet.

He paid for everything. The hospital. The grafts I didn’t need in the end. The squeezy ball. My wages every month I couldn’t work. My mum’s hotel room across the road from the hospital, with the big breakfast she still talks about. The bike. He never said one word about it. I tried to thank him once.

“Mr. Zhao, I just wanted to say, for the hospital and my mum and the—”

“Hm.”

He picked up a newspaper. Upside down. I didn’t tell him.

4. The house rules. Miss Lin put a sign on the back wall. No frightening the customers. The husband is not allowed behind the counter. So he swept. He did the corners. With his fingers.

Once he stopped sweeping in the middle of the floor because Miss Lin pushed her hair back with her wrist while she was cutting. That’s all she did. He stood there holding the broom for about a minute. Then he saw me looking. He went red. He did the same corner twice.

She didn’t even turn round.

“You missed a bit.”

“Where.”

She pointed with the knife without looking. He got down on his knees. On my floor. In a suit. The most frightening man at the Docks, on his knees, doing a corner. Who does that? Who does corners?

Five years I’ve worked here. Nobody has ever done the corners. Not even her.

4½. The van again. Not that van. The new ones. The white ones with her name on.

Every morning he carries the buckets in. He goes back out to the van. She follows him to the door. He kisses her goodbye on the pavement. Every morning. I’ve seen it about a thousand times. I always look at something else.

But I can hear it. The door’s open. And here’s the thing. He asks. Every time. He stops right in front of her face and says her name like it’s a question.

“Elowen.”

And waits. And she says yes. Or she just grabs his collar. And the bus stop across the road goes really quiet.

He’s only once not asked. The week after the glass. He came round the back of the van and took her face in both hands and didn’t say anything at all. She grabbed his coat with both fists. She didn’t seem to mind.

I don’t know why that’s the bit that makes my ears go red. It is, though.

5. The cooler. I’m not describing the cooler.

I’ll say she went in for lilies for a funeral order. He followed her. The door shut. Nine minutes. It’s one degree in there. I timed it. When they came out her face was pink and she’d forgotten the lilies, and he was carrying the bucket.

When they came out I said nothing. She looked at me anyway.

“Did you hear anything?”

“NO, Miss Lin!”

Too loud. Way too loud.

I wrapped the same bouquet four times while they were in there. The customer pointed out it had four ribbons.

“Is that… a style?”

“Yes,” I said. “It’s new.”

6. The apron. The morning of the four hundred roses, she made him wear the green apron. ELOWEN’S on the front. It came up to his ribs.

Then Mr. Chen walked in. Camel coat. Coffee. He stopped dead in the doorway.

“Good morning.”

Like a man watching a dog walk on its back legs. Mr. Zhao didn’t even look up from his rose.

“Si.”

“Is that… Zhendong, is that an apron?”

“Yes.”

Later they stood out on the pavement and Mr. Zhao laughed. Out loud. Two old ladies with shopping stopped to stare. One of them crossed herself.

I’ve never told anyone about the apron. Who would believe me?

7. The hoodie. He asked to borrow my hoodie. The grey one. I said yes, because you say yes. As he was going out the door I said, “Mr. Zhao, it says ‘FLOWER POWER’ on the back.” He said, “I know.” And left anyway.

I found out later he wore it to a physics lecture. To look at a man Miss Lin liked at school.

When she asked where my hoodie was, I tried to lie. I can’t lie. My ears go red. I said a man had borrowed it for an important mission. She just looked at me.

“Please don’t make me say more, Miss Lin. I have to live.”

She laughed so hard she had to sit on the floor.

He gave it back washed and folded. With a note in the pocket. Thank you. You were right about the back. I still have the note. It’s in my wallet. Don’t tell him.

8. The glass. I don’t want to talk about the glass either.

There was a little girl called Mimi, buying sunflowers for her grandma. The window went white. I didn’t think. I just went. I was lying on top of her and her mum with my hands over my head. Glass came down on my back like hail. It didn’t hurt then. It hurt later. A nurse at City Hospital took forty-one bits out of me with tweezers. I counted. She told me to stop counting.

Later Miss Lin told me what he said on the phone, driving too fast to get to her.

“Tell him his motorbike is going to be a very good one.”

It is. It’s a very good one.

Mimi came to the shop with her mum a month after. She was six. She stood in front of me and looked at my back like she could still see the glass in it.

“Does it hurt?”

“Nah.”

“Liar.”

Six! Mimi sends me a drawing every New Year. Last year it was me on the red bike, with a helmet on, and about a hundred sunflowers. They’re all on my wall.

9. The three days. I wasn’t there for the bad part. I did the market every morning with Granny Su, because somebody had to. Miss Lin was down under the shop and wouldn’t come up.

Granny Su made me count every bunch. Every single one.

“Get it wrong and the girl’s husband will know when he’s back. And he’ll look at you.”

“What if… what if he doesn’t come back?”

She hit me on the back of the head with a bunch of eucalyptus.

“OW!”

“Count.”

“He comes back. He carries too well not to.”

On the fourth morning Miss Lin sent me one word.

Elowen: Home.

I cried on my bike at a red light. A taxi driver wound his window down and asked if I was okay. I said yes. He gave me a tissue. He was crying a bit too and he didn’t even know why.

10. The camellia. Sixteen days after, she sent me home at five. There was a little white box on the workbench. She wouldn’t tell me what was in it. She had a face on her I’d never seen before.

“Go home, Xiao Pan.”

“It’s five o’clock!”

“I know what time it is. Go home.”

Outside it had started to rain. What was in the box? I didn’t ask that either. I’m learning.

Next morning I came in at six. The bench was cleared. Petals everywhere. Stems everywhere. And one crushed pink flower in a glass of water by the till. Like it was the most important thing in the shop.

The sign still said CLOSED. I turned it to OPEN. I swept up. I didn’t ask.

Not stupid.

✦ ✦ ✦

11. The tip. Here’s the thing nobody gets.

Five years of flowers. Weddings. Funerals. Hospitals. Offices. Once, terrifyingly, a prison. I’ve been tipped well and badly and not at all.

The best tip I ever got was tonight.

Their real wedding. In the shop. Thirty people standing up, the little gold lights all over the ceiling, Mr. Yao hiding behind me because he’s scared of her. I’d put my helmet by the door. I was eating cake.

Mr. Zhao came over. He didn’t say anything for a while. He stood next to me with his hands in his pockets and looked across the room at her. She was laughing with her sisters. She never laughs like that. Well. She does now.

“The night of the van. You went for the roses.”

“Yes, Mr. Zhao.”

“Why?”

I had cake in my mouth. I swallowed it. Was I in trouble? Five years later? For roses?

“I… I’m sorry about the roses, Mr. Zhao.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“They were for a wedding. Two hundred people. She’d worked on them till her eyes went red. I didn’t want her to have to start again.”

He didn’t say anything. Then he put his hand on my shoulder. One second. Heavy. Warm.

“Thank you. For looking after her. Before I knew how.”

That was it. That was the tip.

I know. It doesn’t sound like much. But I’ve worked at Elowen’s for five years, and I’ve seen everything, and I’m telling you. Best one I ever got.

I’m still not telling anyone about the cooler.

chapters.title: Chen Si, Please Tell Your Wife to Stop
chapters.desc: Chen Si rings in the middle of the night because Aurelia has been pacing the living room in her silk robe for two hours. Elowen has bought the building next door, he gave Aurelia sapphires, and somehow he’s losing.
chapters.epigraph: “And somehow, Zhendong, I am losing. I don’t understand how. I gave her sapphires.” — Chen Si, 2 a.m.
chapters.content:
The phone buzzed just after two.

Zhao was awake. He was usually awake around two. He had it before the second buzz, looked at the name, and slid out from under his wife’s arm without waking her. That took a while. She slept like she worked. Total commitment. One leg over his.

Out in the corridor, in the dark, he leaned on the wall by the bedroom door.

“Si.”

“Zhendong.” Calm. Much too calm. “Are you awake?”

“You rang me.”

“I need you to do something for me.”

Zhao waited. He had one of Elowen’s hair ties round his wrist. Black. He didn’t remember putting it there. He turned it with his thumb.

“I need you to tell your wife to stop.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Stop what.”

“Don’t. You know what.” Something rustled on Chen Si’s end. A door, maybe. A man going into another room so his wife wouldn’t hear. “Aurelia has been walking up and down the living room since midnight. In the silk robe. Talking to herself in Italian.”

“Hm.”

“She’s holding a printout. She’s been holding it for two hours. Every so often she stops. Looks at it. Says incredibile. Starts walking again.”

“What’s on it?”

“A property registration. From this afternoon.” A pause. “The building next door to your wife’s shop. The empty one. Old tailor’s on the ground floor.”

Zhao said nothing.
