“Your wife bought it. With her own money. From the shop and the tea and, apparently, a very good wedding season.” Chen Si breathed out through his nose. “She’s knocking through at the back. A proper workroom. A cold room. She told Aurelia at lunch. Over salad. Like it was nothing.”

“I know.”

“You… know.”

“She showed me the drawings last week. Raiden did them.” He looked down the dark corridor. “It’s a good building. Roof’s sound.”

“The roof—Zhendong. Do you understand what this means?”

He did, actually. But Si explaining things at two in the morning was one of maybe four things in the world he enjoyed, so he said:

“Explain.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Three weeks ago I gave Aurelia a necklace. For no reason. Sapphires. An estate sale in Geneva. It was in a magazine.”

“Hm.”

“The same day, you took your wife up a mountain and stood in a garden in the rain looking at a shrub.”

“It was the anniversary of the mountain. We go every year.”

“I know. She knows. She saw the photo.” Chen Si’s voice went very level. “Your wife posted one picture. One. The two of you under an umbrella, looking at a camellia. It got more likes than the necklace.”

Zhao shut his eyes. In the dark it didn’t make much difference.

“She didn’t speak to me for a day. Then she bought a jewellery workshop. In Milan. As a treat. For herself. Because she deserves it.” A tiny pause. “And she told your wife. At lunch. Over—”

“Salad.”

“Over salad. And today your wife bought a building.”

“They’re competing.”

“They have been competing since they were fifteen and somebody pinned a list on a noticeboard. They will compete in the nursing home. They will compete about whose funeral has better flowers.” Chen Si stopped. When he went on, he sounded honestly confused, which Zhao had heard maybe three times in fifteen years. “And somehow, Zhendong, I am losing. I don’t understand how. I gave her sapphires.”

Zhao looked at the bedroom door. Open a hand’s width. Through the gap he could see her. Asleep under the window, one arm flung across his side of the bed, where he’d just been. Like she was keeping it.

“You gave her something expensive.”

“Yes, I’m aware—”

“Elowen bought something herself.”

Nothing on the line.

“…Go on.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He wasn’t good at going on. He tried anyway.

“The necklace is good. Aurelia wears it, everyone looks at her. She likes that. But you picked it. You paid. It’s a present.”

“That’s what a present—”

“The building, Elowen picked. Elowen paid. Money she made. For a shop with her name on the front. Nobody gave it to her.” He turned the hair tie. “Aurelia isn’t angry the building’s bigger. She’s angry she didn’t buy the workshop first.”

Long silence. Long enough that Zhao checked the screen to see if it had dropped.

“How do you know that?”

“Elowen told me. The year she came first. Aurelia didn’t mind losing. She minded that Elowen made it look like she wasn’t trying.” He shrugged at the wall. “She doesn’t want the best present, Si. She wants to win something.”

“When did you start understanding women?”

“I don’t. I understand one. She talks in her sleep.”

Chen Si made a noise that, in another man, would have been a laugh.

“So what do I do?”

“Don’t buy her anything.”

“That sounds like a terrible idea.”

“Give her a problem. A real one. One nobody else can fix. Ask her. Then get out of the way.”

He could hear Si thinking. Si thought loudly, for a man who didn’t move his face.

“The port authority. The new deputy director. He’s been sitting on our permits for four months. I was going to deal with him myself next week.”

“Give him to Aurelia.”

“She’ll be terrifying.”

“She’ll be happy.”

“She’ll be terrifying and happy. The poor man won’t sleep for a month.” But his voice had gone lighter. Almost fond. “Thank you.”

“Thank me by telling her to stop ringing my wife at midnight about planning permission.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He nearly hung up.

“Zhendong.”

“What.”

“When I met you, you couldn’t read. You had no front tooth. You hit people for looking at you.” A pause. “And now you’re standing in a corridor at two in the morning explaining my own wife to me.”

Zhao didn’t answer. What was there to say? It was true. All of it. The tooth, too. It was a good fake tooth. Si had paid for it, the first year they had money. He’d sat in the dentist’s waiting room the whole time reading a book about ships, and when Zhao came out numb and drooling he’d looked up and said, Smile. Zhao hadn’t. Not for years. Si never asked again.

“I’m proud of you. I never said. I should have. So. There.”

Zhao stood in the dark with the phone against his ear. His throat did something stupid. He waited for it to stop.

“Go to bed, Si.” It came out rough. Fine.

“Yes.” Chen Si sounded like he was smiling, which was worse. “Tell Elowen congratulations on the building. And tell her Aurelia is going to buy the one on the other side.”

“She already did.”

“…What?”

“Last week. In Raiden’s name. Aurelia won’t find out until the permits come through.”

The silence on the line went on for a very long time.

“God help us all.”

Click.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was awake.

Lying on her side with her eyes open, in the light off the Docks. Looking extremely pleased with herself.

“Was that Chen Si? About the building?”

“Yes.”

“Did he ask you to tell me to stop?”

He got back into bed and pulled her onto his chest before she could move over on her own. One arm locked round her. He always did that when he’d been out of the bed for more than a minute. She’d stopped teasing him about it in the second year. She’d started timing it instead.

“Yes.”

“And are you going to?”

He thought about it. He put his hand on her hair.

“No.”

She smiled against his chest. Then she lifted her head and narrowed her eyes at him.

“And I do not talk in my sleep.”

So she’d heard that bit too. Of course she had. Door open a hand’s width. She heard everything. He looked at the ceiling, where the light from the Docks moved, and decided she might as well know.

“Prices, mostly.”

“Prices?”

“Lilies went up. You were very upset.” A pause. “And my name. Every night. Since the typhoon.”

She stared at him. Then she put her face in his chest and groaned, a long mortified noise, and he felt her laughing through it. Every night? Since then? He could see her doing the maths. Four and a half years of him lying there listening.

She climbed up him. Her hair fell round both their faces like a curtain.

“Say mine, then. So I can hear what it sounds like.”

“Elowen.”

Low. Into her mouth. She kissed it straight back out of him. Then again. She didn’t wait for him to roll her over and do his careful stopping. She knew all about his careful stopping. She pinned his wrists to the pillow, hair tie and all. She kissed him slow and warm and very smug. He let her. He’d have let her do anything. After a while he forgot Si. He forgot Aurelia. He forgot the deputy director of the port authority, who had no idea what was coming.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nine days later, at lunch, his phone went four times.

Chen Si: He signed everything.

Chen Si: He thanked her. In writing.

Chen Si: She is wearing the sapphires. She says they are her lucky sapphires now.

Chen Si: She has asked me what else I have.

Zhao showed the screen to his wife across the table. She read it. She put down her chopsticks.

“Oh, no. Now she’s going to be unbearable!”

She was already reaching for her own phone. To find a bigger building, probably.

chapters.title: Anniversary Math
chapters.desc: She goes looking for a pen and finds two notebooks in his drawer: every date since the night it rained, and a number in the corner of every page.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m very bad at forgetting things.”
chapters.content:
Elowen was married on two dates. The seventeenth of March, at a registry office, with soil under her nails. The twenty-third of September, in her own shop, under a ceiling full of lights. Two. She’d checked.

So why was there a box of egg tarts on her workbench?

Six of them. Still warm. From the bakery by the old town gate, the one with the queue round the corner, the one she’d mentioned exactly once, years ago, with her mouth full.

Bao had brought them. He’d put the box down on the bench at seven, said “From the boss,” and tried to leave.

“What for?”

“He said you’d ask that.”

“And?”

“And he said don’t tell her.” Bao looked at the door like it might save him. “So I can’t, Miss Lin. Sorry. They’re very good tarts.”

Then he’d fled. Bao. Who had once put a man face down on gravel at four in the morning without blinking. Fled from a florist.

“Is it your birthday?” Xiao Pan was looking at the box like the dogs looked at the fridge.

“No.”

“His?”

“No.”

“Is it… the wedding?”

“That was September.”

“The other wedding.”

“Last week. He took me to dinner.” She frowned at the tarts. “Today’s the twenty-second. Nothing happened on the twenty-second.”

Xiao Pan took one. Nobody stopped him. He chewed and thought about it.

“Maybe he just likes you, Miss Lin.”

“He likes me every day. He doesn’t buy tarts every day.”

Did he, though? Now she thought about it. A pot of jasmine on the till one spring morning. Hot soy milk on the van seat on some random Thursday, no sugar. New market boots the week before her old ones split. She’d never once worked out why. She’d assumed he was just like that.

She texted him.

Elowen: why are there egg tarts

Zhao: Eat them.

Elowen: that’s not an answer

Zhao: Eat them while they’re warm.

Elowen: what day is it

Zhao: Friday.

She showed Xiao Pan the screen. He read it, put the rest of his tart in his mouth whole, and backed into the cooler.

She tried Aurelia instead.

Elowen: what happened on the 22nd of march

Aurelia: which year darling

Aurelia: wait

Aurelia: is this an ANNIVERSARY. does he do anniversaries. of WHAT

Aurelia: si has never once

Aurelia: i hate you

Elowen ate a tart. It was perfect. That was the worst part.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven that night Xiao Pan texted an order. A birthday, tomorrow, pink, nothing that smells too strong her mum gets headaches. Her pens were downstairs. Zhendong was in the shower. His bedside drawer was right there.

She’d never opened it. Not a rule. She just hadn’t.

A pistol. Fine. Expected.

A box of the paracetamol she always forgot to buy. Not expected.

A whole packet of black hair ties. Hers. So that was where they went.

And two notebooks. The cheap black kind with an elastic band, from the stationery shop by the Docks. One was soft and fat and finished. The other was half full. She took the soft one out to check for a pen in the band.

It fell open in her hand.

March 2. 7:00 p.m. Rain started at six. Bought every flower in the shop. 4,200. She threw a towel.

Delphiniums. Not near the door.

She sat down on the bed. Hard.

March 5. Docks. She found Kang. Moved my rice to put her paper down. Didn’t look at him once.

March 14. Three pages. “You don’t touch me unless I ask.” Coat buttoned one off. All the way down.

“Oh no. Oh, no no no…”

March 17. Registry. 9:41. Soil under her nails. Ring too big. Head on my shoulder in the photo. On the steps she said “not here.” Not no.

Not no. He’d stood on those steps in his good suit, and gone home, and written not no. What kind of man did that? What kind of man did that and then never said a word for four years?

She turned the page faster.

March 22. Basement. Six numbers. I asked. She said yes.

Said her name after. Not before.

March 22. She named the dogs.

She looked at her phone. The date sat there at the top of the screen.

Twenty-second of March. Egg tarts.

“You absolute…”

✦ ✦ ✦

The shower went off. He came out in a towel with his hair dripping, saw her on his side of the bed with the drawer open, and stopped dead.

She held the notebook up.

“You found it.”

“I was looking for a pen.”

“Hm.”

He didn’t come any closer. Water ran off his shoulders onto the floor. He had the face from the registry steps. Waiting to find out what she’d say.

“The egg tarts.”

“Yes.”

“Are for the basement.”

“Yes.”

“You bought me egg tarts because four years ago you kissed me next to a gun bench!”

“You kissed back.”

“That is not the—” She flipped pages. “April third. ‘She left the door open a hand’s width.’ You wrote down my door?”

“It was open.”

“April eleventh. ‘Cold tap. I didn’t ask. Didn’t take my arm out.’”

“You said twenty minutes.”

“May eleventh. ‘Bled on two hundred. She kissed the plaster.’ Zhendong. How many of these are there?”

He looked at the notebook in her hands. He looked at the second one in the drawer. He didn’t answer. That was an answer.

She turned another page, still half laughing, and read the next one out loud before she’d looked at it properly.

“September nineteenth. Mountain. ‘I’m happy.’ She did not say the…”

Her voice ran out.

She did not say the other word.

The night of the candles. The camphor quilt. She’d fallen asleep on his chest feeling like the luckiest woman alive, and he’d lain there in the dark and written down what she hadn’t said.

He sat down next to her. The mattress dipped. He smelled of soap and he was still wet and he didn’t touch her.

She kept going. Out loud wasn’t working any more, so she read with her finger, like a child.

March 17. One year. Fourteenth key. She almost said something after. Said happy anniversary instead.

“I did almost say it.”

“I know.”

June 9. Glass. Six strips. I did them. My hands would not stop.

Forty-eight hours.

Nothing under that. Half a page of nothing.

“There’s nothing here.”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Nothing I wanted to keep.”

Flat. Like the weather. She looked at the blank half page and thought about a man on a landing with a rifle case, and Qiu Wen in a silk dressing gown, and didn’t ask the next thing. She’d asked it once already, years ago. He hadn’t lied.

She came back through the front door. Tried to say it. I stopped her. “A boring day.”

Velde. Four pages. Samuel, 11. Bin.

Then a page with one line on it, so shaky she had to tilt it to the lamp.

I came up the hill.

“I can hardly read this.”

“My hands were bad.”

“You wrote it with your hands like that?”

“Elara was asleep. I had to write it before I forgot.”

“You never forget anything!”

“I thought I might be dying.”

Her eyes had gone. She wiped them with her wrist and kept going.

Day 15. Fish. I asked one. She said “now ask me the other one.” I couldn’t.

Day 16. Rain started at six. Camellia. Lapel. She said it. Nine times. I counted.

I don’t have to wonder any more.

That was the last page. The rest of the book was empty.

She was crying properly now. Ugly. Nose and everything. He reached over and got a tissue from the box on her side. Held it out. She snatched it and blew her nose like a trumpet. She was furious. He was an idiot. She loved him so much she could have bitten him.

“Why?”

“I’m very bad at forgetting things.”

“That’s not why.”

He looked at his hands on his knees.

“At the registry I looked at the clock.”

“I know. Nine forty-one.”

“In case it was the only one.” A breath. “Then there was another one. And another. I thought, if it ends, I’ll have them.”

“Ends?”

“You married me for your father.”

“Zhendong—”

“I know. Now I know.” He took the soft notebook out of her hands and held it on his knee. Closed. Thumb on the elastic. “I didn’t think I’d get to keep you. I thought I could keep the dates.”

She couldn’t say anything to that. Nobody could have. So she grabbed the other notebook out of the drawer instead, before he could stop her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second one started the day after the camellia. Same square capitals. Smaller entries.

Day 17. She said it in the van. Four in the morning. Bao heard. Bao hit a bollard.

Sept 23. Lights. Nine lemons. Green. I was right.

Oct 2. Fell asleep on the sofa during the news. Left her. Wrong. Her neck.

Nov 30. Sneezed four times at the market. Granny Su says chrysanthemums. It’s always chrysanthemums.

Jan 9. Laughed at Bao’s joke. The bad one.

And in the top corner of every page, in pencil, a number. Going up.

Forty. One hundred and six. Three hundred and something. On the last page with writing, small and neat in the corner: 1,209.

“What’s this number?”

He looked at the ceiling.

“Zhendong. What is the number.”

“How many times.”

“How many times what?”

He didn’t say. Didn’t have to. She watched it land on her own face in the mirror on the wardrobe. Hot. Red. Up to the hairline.

“You’re COUNTING?”

“I don’t count. I just know.”

“That’s counting!”

Twelve hundred and nine times. Since April. In the van. At the gate. Into his back at four in the morning when she didn’t think he was awake. He’d been awake. He was always awake. Fine. Fine.

“I love you.”

He went still.

“I love you. I love you, I love you, I love you, I love—”

“Elowen.”

“—you, I love you, what number is that? What number?”

His mouth moved. He was actually doing it. She watched him do it.

“…Twelve hundred and sixteen.”

She hit him in the chest with the notebook. He let her. She hit him again. He caught her wrist, took the notebook off her, and put both of them back in the drawer on top of the paracetamol. Very neatly. Then he shut it.

Then he looked at her. Still wet. Still in a towel. A breath away from her face, and stopping there, because he always stopped there.

“Say yes.”

Four years ago to the night. Same words. Did he know? Of course he knew. He had it written down.

“Or what? Go upstairs?”

“We’re upstairs.”

“Then you’ve run out of options.”

She took his face in both hands and kissed him first. He made a noise into her mouth like she’d knocked the air out of him. Then he wasn’t careful at all. He pushed her back into the pillows. His wet hair dripped on her cheeks. She was laughing, so he kissed the laugh. Then her jaw. Her neck. The spot under her ear he’d found in a basement and had apparently been keeping a record of ever since.

“Your towel—”

“Hm.”

“The sheets, Zhendong, you’re soaking the—”

He didn’t care about the sheets. Eventually she didn’t either. He undid her shirt one button at a time, slowly, with his eyes on her face the whole way down, and when she pulled at him to hurry up he said no against her collarbone and kept going at exactly the same speed. Unbearable. She told him so. He said her name into her stomach like it was the answer to that. Her hands were in his hair. His were everywhere. The lamp was still on. Nobody could reach it. Then she stopped caring about the lamp too.

Afterwards he took her earrings out. The green ones. One, then the other, slow, his big fingers careful on the little hooks, and put them in the glass vase on her side. Click. Click.

She was nearly asleep on his chest.

“Love you.” Mumbled. Into his skin.

His hand stopped in her hair.

“Twelve hundred and seventeen.”

“Stop counting.”

“No.”

chapters.title: Fifteen Years Ago, Block C
chapters.desc: January, fifteen years ago. A riot in Block C, a sharpened bed slat, and Chen Si dragging him half a kilometre through the drains into the snow. Then his wife finds him awake at two.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t leave them behind you, Zhendong. Not ever. Everything you leave behind you comes back.” — Chen Si, aged sixteen
chapters.content:
“You fold them first.”

The new boy was in the laundry doorway with a basket on his hip. Small. Thin. Clean hands. He talked like the television. Zhao didn’t answer. He folded the next shirt corner to corner and fed it into the press.

“Nobody else does. They just throw them in. Why do you?”

Because if you dropped something, it cost. Old Zhao’s yard. The stove. Zhao didn’t say that either. He’d been at the centre since the autumn, and he hadn’t said much to anyone. He was fifteen. He had no front tooth. He couldn’t read much past his own name. He’d stolen a truck full of copper wire and driven it into a wall, because he didn’t really know how to drive. And he hit people who looked at him too long. So nobody looked at him. Nobody sat with him. In Block C that was the same as being safe.

The new boy looked at him anyway.

“I’m Chen. You’re Zhao. They told me not to stand near you.”

Zhao folded another shirt.

“I’m standing near you.”

So? Zhao didn’t look up. After a while the new boy picked up his basket and went.

Chen Si arrived in November.

✦ ✦ ✦

The older boys hated him by the second night. It wasn’t hard to see why. He said please to the guards. He held his chopsticks properly. He read on his bunk with his back straight, like a boy in a library. They started waiting for him. The showers. The laundry corridor. The corner of the yard where the camera didn’t reach.

Zhao watched from his top bunk. He watched Si come back from the showers with a split lip, sit down, open his book, and keep reading. Who did that?

The next day Si sat down at the end of Zhao’s table in the canteen. Tray. Book. Nothing else.

“Oi. Reader.” One of Gao’s boys, two tables over. “Found yourself a guard dog?”

Zhao looked at him. Just looked. The boy found something interesting in his soup. Nobody came near Si the whole meal. He did it again the next day. And the next.

On the seventh day, Zhao said it to his rice.

“What’s the book?”

Si turned it round so he could see. Zhao looked at the cover. Black marks. Nothing. His face got hot. Was the rich boy going to laugh? He didn’t laugh.

“It’s about a war. Two generals. One wins because he’s stronger.” Si shut the book. “The other one wins because he knows where the river goes. I’ll read it to you, if you want.”

Zhao said nothing. He didn’t say no. That night Si read from the bunk underneath, in a whisper. Zhao lay on his back with his eyes open and listened to a general who knew where the river went. After the war book there was a library one. A monkey king for little kids, with pictures.

“What are the pictures?”

Si held it up to the light from the corridor. A stone monkey. A mountain. Five hundred years under it, by himself. The third night, Si stopped at the end. Zhao lay there in the dark.

“Again.”

Si read it again.

✦ ✦ ✦

In December a guard stopped by their table at breakfast. Between the rice and the tea.

“Chen. Your mother died. Tuesday. Heart.” He looked at the tray. “Pass the salt.”

Si passed the salt. His hand didn’t shake. His face didn’t move. He ate his rice. Zhao watched him eat every grain, and then he did a thing he hadn’t done since the orphanage. He pushed his own bread across the table.

Si looked at it for a long time. He ate that too.

✦ ✦ ✦

The riot was in January.

It started in Block A, over the heating. By night they could hear it through the walls. Banging. Screaming. Then smoke, coming under the door in a grey line. Somebody had lit the mattresses in Block B. The guards locked the blocks and walked out. Zhao saw them through the high window, standing in the yard in the snow. Smoking. Waiting for the boys inside to finish whatever they were going to do to each other. Sixty boys in Block C worked it out at once. Nobody was coming.

Three of them came down the aisle through the smoke. Gao in front. Seventeen. A slat off a bed frame in his fist, sharpened on the concrete for weeks. Si was on his bunk with a book. Not the library one. The old one. Blue cloth, gone grey. He slept on it. Nobody was allowed to touch it. He looked up. Saw them coming. He closed it and set it down on the blanket. Careful. Like he meant to pick it up again.

Zhao came down off the top bunk. He didn’t decide to. He was against the wall, and then he was in the aisle, in the smoke, in front of Si.

“Move.”

He didn’t move.

“This isn’t your business, dog.”

It wasn’t. He stood there with his fists shut anyway.

“Zhendong.” Si, behind him. Very calm. “Don’t.”

Too late for that.

Gao came at him. Zhao hit him once and felt something crack. He threw the second boy into the bunks. The frame screamed. Then there was something cold under his left arm. It went in and kept going. Down. Ribs to hip. He looked at it. Gao was holding the end. The rest was in him.

He looked up at Gao. Gao saw his face and let go and backed away. Zhao pulled it out himself.

After that it went in pieces. Gao on the floor. His own fists. Somebody’s arms round him from behind, thin arms, holding on, and a voice in his ear. Zhendong. Zhendong, stop. He’s down. You’re bleeding. STOP. He stopped.

He sat down in the aisle. Everything was red. His shirt. His trousers. The floor. He felt tired. Calm. Si was on his knees in front of him with his own shirt balled up against the hole, both hands, pressing so hard it hurt more than the slat had.

“Si.” First time he’d said it. “You should go.”

“Go where? The doors are locked.”

“Go anyway.”

Si laughed. Short and shaking and completely mad.

“Zhendong. I know where the river goes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Si held the shirt there for an hour. Maybe. Then he got Zhao up and half carried him to the shower block, where the floor was warm under their feet. Too warm. Something was burning underneath. There was an iron grate in the floor. Si jammed a bit of bed slat under it. It wouldn’t come.

“Come on. Come on… I gave a guard my father’s watch for this drain. MOVE.”

Zhao was lying against the wall. His eyes kept closing. He heard a hiss. Smelled something like meat on Old Zhao’s stove. Heard Si make a noise through his teeth. High. Thin. Not a word. Then the grate scraped and moved, and Si was dragging him by the collar into black water.

Cold. Up to his chest. So cold it stopped his breath. It stank. Si was in front of him the whole time with Zhao’s arm over his shoulder, and Si was counting.

“Forty. Forty-one. Forty-two. Keep going, Zhendong. Keep going.”

He kept going. He fell. Si pulled him up.

“Talk to me.”

He didn’t have anything.

“Zhendong! Say something!”

“…Hm.”

“That’s not a word. Fifty. Fifty-one…”

He fell again. This time his legs stopped. He sat down in the water and couldn’t get up.

“Leave me. Go.”

“No.”

“You can make it on your own.”

Hands found his face in the dark. Thin cold hands. One of them wrapped in something wet.

“You don’t leave them behind you. Not ever. Everything you leave behind you comes back.” The hands squeezed. “And you are not something I am leaving behind. Get up.”

He got up.

Later Si wasn’t holding him up any more. Si was carrying him. Fifty kilos carrying eighty. He had no voice left for counting, so he told the monkey king instead. From memory. All of it. The stone. The mountain. Five hundred years. Then he got to the end and started again.

They came out in a ditch by the road. It was snowing. Straight down out of a black sky. No wind at all. Si laid him in it. Zhao lay on his back and felt snowflakes land on his face, one at a time.

“Si. If I’m dying, no hospital. They’ll send me back. Just let me go.”

Si looked down at him. Teeth chattering. Covered in blood. All of it Zhao’s.

“No.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next town. A back room behind a clinic. A doctor in a cardigan who looked at them both and asked nothing at all.

“On the table. You, hold the lamp. Higher. Don’t you faint on me, boy.”

“Brothers,” Si said. “Our name is Wang.”

Zhao heard it through the fog. He heard the doctor name a price. A plastic bag rustled. He turned his head on the table. The blue cloth came out of a shirt and went into the doctor’s hands.

“This is worth more than the clinic.”

“I know.”

“Are you sure?”

“I’ve paid for something better with it.”

Zhao tried to say no. Nothing came out.

He woke on the third day. Si was asleep in the chair with his head against the wall. His left arm was bandaged from the wrist to the elbow. When Si woke up, Zhao was looking at it.

“Your arm.”

“The road. When I got you out of the ditch.”

Zhao had heard the hiss. He’d smelled it. He looked at Si for a long time, and Si looked back with his rich-boy face, and Zhao let him have it.

“Gao?”

Si’s face didn’t change.

“You don’t leave them behind you, Zhendong. Not ever. Everything you leave behind you comes back.”

Same words as the drain. They didn’t mean the same thing this time. Zhao understood both.

On the fourth day he could sit up. There was a knife on the doctor’s tray, for the stitches. He picked it up. He looked at Si. He held out his left hand, palm up. Si took the knife and did his own first. Then Zhao did his. They put them together. Neither said a word. There wasn’t one.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fifteen years later, at two in the morning, his wife woke up and found him on his back with his eyes open. She didn’t ask. His hand was on his side, under his arm, where the ridge started. That told her.

“Block C?”

“It’s January.”

“It’s been January for two weeks.” She took his hand off the scar and put her own there instead. Warm. His was freezing. “Why are you cold? You’re never cold.”

“I was thinking about the water.”

She lifted the duvet and put her feet on his shins, which was a war crime, and he let her. She knew the story. He’d told her the night of the typhoon, in the dark, holding her hand. She knew Si dragged him. She knew about the snow. She didn’t know about the hiss.

“Si’s arm.”

“What about it?”

“He says it was the road.”

She came up on one elbow. Her hair fell on his chest.

“And it wasn’t.”

“No.”

“Does he know you know?”

“No.”

“Are you going to tell him?”

He thought about it. Fifteen years of Si saying the road with that face.

“No.”

“You two are impossible.” Her voice wobbled. Was she crying? She was crying. Furious about it, too. “You’re both completely… fifteen years!”

He tucked her hair back behind her ear so he could see her face. She let him. Then she bent and put her mouth on the top of the scar, under his arm, and stayed there. He breathed out hard. She went down it a little at a time. Ribs. Lower. All the way to where it stopped above his hip. Then back up.

By the time she got to his mouth he wasn’t cold. He rolled her under him and stopped a breath away, weight on his arms, like he always stopped.

“Elowen.”

She grabbed a fistful of his hair and pulled him down.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning there was a text. Sent at six, like every year.

Chen Si: Fifteen.

Zhao looked at it for a while. Then at his left palm, the thin white line.

Zhao: Hm.

Chen Si: Elowen says to tell you you’re both impossible.

He looked up. His wife was at the kettle with her back to him, and her phone was face down on the counter, and she was humming.

chapters.title: The Ring Was Too Heavy
chapters.desc: Three weeks before the real wedding her ring vanishes from the dish by the till, and Bao is a terrible liar. Then she reads the inside.
chapters.epigraph: “I told him I wanted something that wouldn’t break.”
chapters.content:
“Bao. Get up.”

Bao did not get up. He had been on his hands and knees behind her counter for twenty minutes, looking under the till with a torch, very seriously, like a man looking for a bomb.

Three weeks before the real wedding, on a Monday, her ring had gone.

She’d put it in the dish by the till at nine. Same as every morning for three and a half years. The little wooden dish Raiden had made her out of a bit of old shipyard timber. At six she went to put it back on, and the dish was empty.

She’d looked everywhere. The floor. The cooler. The offcut bucket, with her arm in it to the elbow. Every drawer. She’d made Xiao Pan look. Xiao Pan had looked so hard he’d found a coin from about 2019 and a pen she’d been blaming on Raiden.

No ring.

“Miss Lin.” Bao finally sat back on his heels. “I don’t think it’s here.”

Careful voice. Very careful. Far too careful.

“Bao. Where is my ring?”

Bao looked at the ceiling.

“I couldn’t say, Miss Lin.”

Oh, she knew that voice. That was the voice of a man who’d been told not to say something by the person who paid him, and was going to obey, and wanted her to know he was obeying. She’d heard it a hundred times. Usually about where her husband had gone at two in the morning.

“He took it.”

“I couldn’t say.”

“Why would he take my ring?”

Bao got up, dusted his knees, and left without his torch. What had he done with it? Pawned it? Lost it at cards? Zhendong didn’t play cards. Zhendong didn’t lose things. That was the whole problem with him.

She texted the only other suspect.

Elowen: did you take my ring

Aurelia: darling

Aurelia: i would never steal something that ugly

Aurelia: wait is it LOST

Aurelia: i have sketches. i have had sketches since 2020. say the word

Elowen: no

Aurelia: three weeks before the wedding. this is a sign from god

She put the phone face down. Her middle finger felt wrong. Bare. There was a pale stripe round it where the sun never got.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d made fish. He’d been making fish a lot since spring.

She sat down. She picked out the belly, the best piece, and didn’t put it in his bowl. She put it in her own. He watched it go.

“Where’s my ring?”

“Which ring.”

“I have one ring!”

“You have the earrings.”

“The earrings are not a ring, Zhendong.”

“Hm.”

“If you’ve sold it—”

“I haven’t sold it.”

“So you know where it is.”

He ate his rice. He said the lemon tree had nine lemons now. He said a broker in the south had rung about cement, and he’d told him no. He said nothing at all about the ring.

She ate the whole fish belly, slowly, looking at him the entire time. It didn’t work. Nothing ever worked.

That night she slept with her back to him. Pointedly. With a pillow between them, like a wall.

Some time after three she rolled over in her sleep, shoved the pillow on the floor, and grabbed a fistful of his shirt.

He didn’t move until morning, so she’d never know.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Bao’s across the road again.” Xiao Pan was at the window. “Eating noodles. He won’t look at the shop. It’s his third bowl.”

Elowen put down her knife.

She crossed the road in her apron. Bao saw her coming and tried to hide behind the menu. He was a very big man. It was a very small menu.

“Bao.”

“Miss Lin.”

“Is it safe?”

He looked at his noodles for a long time.

“…It’s safe, Miss Lin.”

“Is it coming back?”

“Thursd—” He choked. Actually choked, on a noodle, and had to be hit on the back by the owner. “I couldn’t say.”

“BAO.”

He paid for three bowls and fled up the alley. She went back to her shop and stood at the counter and smiled at a bucket of stock until Xiao Pan asked if she was feeling all right.

✦ ✦ ✦

The jeweller in the old town was older than he’d been three and a half years ago, which was saying something. He had a loupe screwed into one eye and a cough that came up from his shoes.

“You.”

Zhao put the ring on the glass.

“Something that won’t break.” The old man picked it up. “That’s what you said. Did it break?”

“No.”

“Too big. I told you it was too big. You said you didn’t know her size.”

Zhao took a piece of string out of his pocket and laid it beside the ring. Four knots in it. Close together.

The jeweller looked at the string. Then up at him.

“You measured four times.”

“She moved.”

He’d done it at two in the morning, on four different nights, with her hand open on his chest. Every time, her fingers curled up in her sleep, and he waited till they uncurled. Ten minutes, once. He hadn’t breathed.

“While I’m in there, I can thin it. Lighter. Ladies like lighter.”

“No.”

“It’s very heavy, young man.”

“She likes heavy.”

She’d never said so. She’d never had to. Three and a half years, and she’d turned down every offer to swap it. Aurelia’s. Her sisters’. Granny Su’s, every single week. She went for the heavy buckets at the market before he could get to them. Same thing.

He wrote on the back of a receipt and pushed it across. The jeweller read it out loud, slow.

“Nine forty-one. Seven p.m. Rain.” He looked up. “Inside?”

“Inside.”

“People put names. Dates. Nobody puts times.”

“Hm.”

“What happened at seven?”

“It rained.”

The old man looked at him for a long moment. Then he decided he didn’t want to know, which was the smartest thing anyone in the old town had done all week.

“Thursday.”

Thursday. Fine.

He could have done it in the first year. The jeweller had offered. He hadn’t, because back then it was a ring she might take off one day. You didn’t put your times inside something somebody was going to give back.

Then a camellia. A boring day. Her voice on the mat in the rain, saying it nine times.

In three weeks her father would walk her four metres across her own shop floor and put her hand in his, and thirty people would look at that hand. It was going on the right finger.

✦ ✦ ✦

Thursday dinner. A small box beside her bowl.

The same box from the registry steps. Worn at the corners now. Had he kept the empty box all this time? Of course he had.

She looked at it. Then at him.

“You took it.”

“Bao took it.”

“Bao was on his knees for twenty minutes!”

“He said it was the worst thing I’ve ever asked him to do.”

“You’ve asked him to do some terrible things.”

“He said this was worse.”

She opened the box.

Same ring. Same heavy yellow gold. Same square green stone, sunk deep and old-fashioned and nothing she’d ever have picked herself.

But smaller.

“You had it resized.”

“For the wedding.”

“I said leave it.”

“You said that three and a half years ago. I left it.” He wasn’t looking at her. He was looking at the fish. “Your father’s putting your hand in mine. Everybody will look at it.”

She waited. Was that it? Was he going to just sit there and look at the fish? He didn’t say the rest. She could hear it anyway. I don’t want them to see I got it wrong.

She held out her left hand.

He looked at it. The pale stripe on the middle finger. The bare one beside it. Then he reached across the table, took the ring out of the box, took her hand, and slid it on.

Over the knuckle. And stopped. Right where it should.

“How did you know the size?” Her voice had gone funny.

“String. While you were asleep.”

“…How many times?”

“Four.”

“Four?”

“You kept moving.”

She laughed. It came out wet. There was soy sauce on her lip from the fish, and before she could get to it he leaned over and wiped it off with his thumb. Then licked his thumb. Like that was normal. Like he did it every day.

He did, actually.

She got up, came round the table, took him by the collar and kissed him. Hard. He made a noise into her mouth. His chair scraped back. His hand went to her waist. Hers was on his jaw, ring and all. Right finger.

✦ ✦ ✦

In bed she took it off again. Just to look. She turned it in the light from the Docks.

That was when she saw the inside.

Writing. Cut into the gold. Tiny and neat.

9:41.

And beside it, smaller still: 7:00 p.m. Rain.

The red book at the registry. The night he walked into her shop dripping on the floor.

“Zhendong.”

He was on his back with an arm behind his head, watching her. He’d been watching her look at it. Of course he had.

“When did you do this?”

“Tuesday.”

“Why not before? You’ve had it for three and a half years.”

He was quiet so long she thought he wouldn’t answer.

“Before, it was something you might take off.”

Oh. Oh, that idiot.

“And now?”

“Now you won’t.”

“That’s very arrogant.”

“Hm.”

She put it back on. Fourth finger. It fitted like it had been waiting. She held her hand up between them in the dark so he could see it there.

“It’s still too heavy.”

“I know.”

“Aurelia is going to cry.”

“Good.”

He took her hand out of the air and kissed the knuckle under the ring. Then the inside of her wrist, where her pulse was going like a bird. She forgot whatever she’d been about to say next. Something about Aurelia. Gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

Four in the morning. The market. Granny Su was counting ranunculus with a cigarette in her mouth.

Elowen kept her left hand in her coat pocket.

“Hand.”

“What hand?”

“You’re hiding a hand, girl. I’m old. I’m not dead.”

“It’s cold.”

“It’s September!”

Elowen paid with her right hand. She took her change with her right hand. Behind her, Zhendong picked up all twenty boxes before she could get to the heavy ones, and said nothing, and his mouth was doing something at the corner.

“Why?” he asked, in the van.

“She’s said ‘too big’ every week for three and a half years. She’s not seeing it till the wedding.” Elowen did her seatbelt one-handed. “I want to see her face.”

He looked at her. Then he started the van, and from the back of the market, over all the trolleys, Granny Su’s voice came after them like a thrown shoe.

“STILL TOO BIG, IS IT?”

chapters.title: Eliana Sleeps Over at the Big House
chapters.desc: The heating breaks in the Walled City, so Eliana spends a weekend at the house on the hill. She takes Zhao’s security apart in thirty-eight minutes, and he has never been happier.
chapters.epigraph: “Your cameras have a blind spot by the lemon tree. I’m telling you because I like you.” — Eliana Lin, 18
chapters.content:
Her father rang the shop on Friday afternoon. Not her phone. The shop. Like it was business.

“Elowen.”

“Baba.”

She had a knife in one hand and a stem of eucalyptus in the other. Xiao Pan, at the cooler, froze. Phone calls from the Walled City never went well.

“The heating’s broken.”

“Since when?”

He didn’t answer that.

“Elara’s on nights. She’ll sleep at the hospital. Evangeline says she’ll be fine with the electric heater.”

“And you?”

“I have a coat. I’m not asking about me.”

She waited.

She could have helped him. She’d been helping him since she was seven. One word from her and he’d never have to say the rest. She cut the eucalyptus and didn’t say it.

“There’s the question of Eliana.”

Then he stopped. She could hear him breathing down the line. Heavy. Annoyed with himself.

“Would your husband mind. Two nights.”

Your husband. Asking. Her father, asking that man for something. She’d take it.

“I’ll ask him.”

She put the phone down. Xiao Pan was staring at her.

“Miss Lin… you went all cold-room.”

“Bucket.”

“Yes, Miss Lin.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was in the back, doing the corners. Of course he was. She stood over him with her arms folded.

“My father wants to know if you’d mind.”

“Mind what?”

“My little sister. Sleeping at ours. Two nights.”

He sat back on his heels and thought about it. Properly. Like it was a shipment.

“Does she eat fish?”

“She eats instant noodles and energy drinks. That’s it. That’s the whole list.”

“Then she can stay. And eat fish.”

He went back to the corner. She didn’t move.

“He asked if my husband would mind.”

The brush stopped.

“On the phone. Just now. Would your husband mind.” She nudged his knee with her boot. “He’s never asked you for anything. Not once. He’d rather freeze.”

“Hm.”

He did the same corner twice. The back of his neck had gone red. She went back to the counter grinning like an idiot and cut the next stem far too short.

✦ ✦ ✦

Uncle Mok dropped Eliana at the gate a bit after five. One small bag of clothes. One enormous bag of everything else. She was eighteen and swimming in a grey hoodie, hood up, and she came into the hall like a cat into a new flat. Slowly. Looking at corners.

She stopped by the lemon tree. She looked up.

“That camera’s pointing at the wrong place.”

Zhao had come out of the kitchen to say hello. He stopped.

“It’s pointing at the door.”

“It’s pointing at where the door used to be.” She tipped her head. “You moved it. There’s a patch in the plaster. It sees the frame and half a person. Come in on the left and it doesn’t see you at all.”

Zhao looked up at the camera. Then at the patch. Four years he’d walked past that patch.

Eliana didn’t even look round. Very casual.

“Also. Your cameras have a blind spot by the lemon tree. I’m telling you because I like you.”

Elowen nearly dropped the coats. Like? Her sister didn’t like anyone. Her sister liked Wi-Fi.

Zhao looked at Eliana like she’d handed him a puppy. Elowen knew that look. She’d had it once herself, in his office, the day she walked in and told him who’d sold his route.

“What else?”

Eliana smiled. Slow and wicked and delighted.

“Can I have the Wi-Fi password?”

He went to the kitchen, wrote it on the back of an envelope and gave it to her. Just like that.

“Excuse me.” Elowen held up a hand. “I’ve lived here two years. I’ve never had the password.”

“You never asked.”

“I shouldn’t have to ASK! I’m your wife—”

“You use your data. Every month. You go over.” He took Eliana’s enormous bag. “I pay it.”

Eliana snorted so hard her hood fell off.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took her thirty-eight minutes.

She sat cross-legged on the living-room rug with three laptops round her like a fort. The floor was warm under her. Zhao’s house had heating in the floors. She’d put her socks flat on the boards and made a noise like a happy dog.

Zhao sat on the floor beside her. Not the sofa. The floor. In his good trousers.

“Thirty-eight minutes.” She held up a hand and counted. “Five holes. The door camera. The lemon tree. All your east wall cameras run through one box in the guardhouse. Cut that and you’re blind for ninety seconds.” Fourth finger. “Your dog camera still has the password it came with. It’s password.”

“And five?”

“One of them is the garage.” She turned a laptop round to show him. “I could open your garage from the road.”

He stared at the screen.

“From the road.”

He said it the way other men said I do. Elowen, in the doorway with a tea towel, had to go back in the kitchen and hold the counter for a second.

She made fish. Ginger, spring onion, rice. She brought it through because nobody was coming to the table, and found them exactly where she’d left them. Heads together. Red pen.

“Eat.”

“In a minute…”

Zhao took the bowl off her. He picked the bones out of Eliana’s fish with his chopsticks, every one, without looking up from the screen, and put it in front of her.

“Eat it.”

“I don’t really like fish…”

“All of it.”

Eliana looked at Elowen for help. Elowen looked at the ceiling. He did that to her fish too. Every night for two years. She wasn’t about to stop him.

Eliana ate most of it. He watched every mouthful.

At eleven Elowen went up.

“Don’t keep her up.”

“She’s keeping me up.”

“Zhendong.”

He looked up from the floor. He actually looked guilty. She went to bed and lay there smiling at the ceiling. What was wrong with her?

✦ ✦ ✦

Past midnight. The rug. Her red ink all over a printed plan of his own house.

He’d had men walk through this house before. Men paid to find the holes. None of them had noticed the door. None of them had found the garage. This one had done it in a hoodie with a can of energy drink, and then said I like you, and gone back to typing.

He read the plan slowly. Every red circle. He was going to have it framed.

Her phone buzzed by her knee. It had been buzzing all night. Every time, she picked it up, typed with both thumbs, put it face down. This time she laughed. Into her sleeve. Like she didn’t want the room to hear.

He looked at her for four seconds. Then went back to the plan.

“Who’s that?”

She nearly dropped the phone.

“Nobody! Ah Sim. It’s Ah Sim. She texts in full sentences.”

“Hm.”

He turned a page.

Ah Sim was nearly eighty. Ah Sim went to bed at nine with the radio on. He knew that because he knew the name of everyone with a key to the red door, and what time they slept, and which of them owed money.

He could have a name by breakfast. One call to Bao. Maybe two.

“Ah Sim,” he said. “Hm.”

He didn’t make the call. She’d broken his house in thirty-eight minutes. If whoever it was had been a problem, she’d have broken him first. He was sure of that the way he was sure of his own hands.

He was never going to mention it. Not tonight. Not ever.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen woke at one. His side was cold.

She went down in her socks. The living-room lamp was on. Laptops. Cans. The plan of the house. Her husband and her baby sister sitting on the floor, side by side, looking up at her with exactly the same guilty face.

“It’s one in the morning.”

“She found—”

“He’s learning firewalls!” Eliana beamed. “He’s not bad!”

Elowen looked at them for a while. Then she went back upstairs, got the duvet off the bed and came down and lay on the sofa behind them.

“Don’t mind me.”

Zhao got up. He tucked the duvet round her feet. One side, then the other, folded under, so no cold could get in. Then he sat back down on the floor with his back against the sofa, right under her hand.

“Traitor,” she mumbled.

“Hm.”

She fell asleep with her fingers in his hair, listening to them argue about routers.

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday night she made congee. Eliana was at the back door with her phone, her forehead on the cold glass, talking low.

Elowen didn’t ask. Her sister had a right to one thing in this house that wasn’t on a camera.

“Eliana. Congee. Now.”

Behind her, Zhao put the lid back on the pot she’d forgotten and moved her hand off the hot handle without a word.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday morning Baba’s car came up the hill. Zhao carried the enormous bag out to the top of the steps and put it down, and looked at her.

“The guardhouse box. I had it moved this morning. Split in two. One on each side of the house.”

“Good.”

“And the garage.”

“I saw. New code. Eight digits.” She paused. “It’s my birthday backwards, isn’t it.”

Zhao looked faintly embarrassed.

“I needed a number I’d remember.”

Eliana looked at him from under her hood. Then she stepped forward and hugged him, as far as her arms went, which wasn’t far. Her face against his chest. One second.

Then she let go, grabbed the bag and went down the steps without looking back. At the car, she turned round.

“Brother-in-law.”

He waited.

“The lemon tree blind spot. Don’t fix that one.”

“Why not?”

She looked past him into the hall, where Elowen was standing by the long window, watering the lemon tree.

“Because that’s where you two always stand, when you think nobody’s looking.”

She got in. The car went down the hill.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came back down the hall. Elowen kept watering. Very hard. The pot was going to drown.

He took the can out of her hands and put it on the floor. Then he stood in front of her. Close. In the exact spot. And waited, the way he always waited. A breath away.

Elowen kept her eyes on the leaves.

“She’ll check the footage.”

“There isn’t any. Here.”

“My birthday would have been easier to remember.”

“Yours is the first one anyone tries.” He looked at her mouth. “Anyone who wants to hurt me starts with you.”

That should have frightened her. Sunday morning. Light off the Docks. It didn’t frighten her at all.

She grabbed his jumper and pulled. He came down the last inch like he’d been waiting two years for it. Which he had. His hand went round the back of her head. She kissed him slow, then not slow, up on her toes in the blind spot, until her back hit the window and the lemon tree shook and a leaf came down in her hair.

The dogs came to see what had happened to the watering. Dumpling put his nose in the can.

“Leave it.” Against her mouth. Elowen honestly wasn’t sure which of them he meant.

He never fixed that blind spot.

chapters.title: Elowen Does the Armory’s Accounts
chapters.desc: From the private diary of Mr. Yao, Zhao’s accountant, the year the boss’s wife starts keeping the books. She finds his four-year-old mistake with a pencil, and he never quite recovers.
chapters.epigraph: “She found an error from four years ago. With a pencil. In twenty minutes.” — Mr. Yao
chapters.content:
From the private diary of Yao Jianguo, accountant. Kept in a locked drawer. Not to be read by anyone. Especially her.

Monday.

Mr. Zhao called me into the office at the Docks.

“My wife is keeping the books.”

“The warehouse ledgers, sir? She already does the—”

“All of them. The side that stays.”

“…All of them?”

“Tuesday. The house.”

“Shall I bring the summaries?”

“Bring everything.”

“Everything is eleven ledgers, sir.”

“Then eleven.”

I have been an accountant for twenty-six years. I have done the books for a man who sells rifles to generals. I have lied to tax inspectors in three ports. I know she reads the warehouse ledgers on Thursdays. Warehouse men are thieves. Of course she caught one. Bao told me about Wu and the dog and the train north. I assumed Bao was exaggerating.

Bao has never exaggerated anything in his life. I am only now thinking about that.

My books are not warehouse books. My books are mine. I am not afraid of a florist.

Tuesday.

I am afraid of the florist.

The house on the hill has a lemon tree in the hall. I don’t know why I am writing that down. It’s the last thing I remember being calm about.

She sat at the dining table with a pencil, a cup of jasmine tea and a calculator. She never touched the calculator. Not once. Why have it there? To frighten me? It worked.

“Third quarter. Four years ago, please.”

“That’s… quite an old one, Mrs. Zhao.”

“Your north warehouse has never balanced. I’ve been looking at the summaries on Thursdays.” She held out her hand. “Please.”

I gave it to her. She turned the pages slowly. Twenty minutes. I counted, because the clock was the only thing in the room I could look at.

Then she put the pencil down on page forty-one.

“Mr. Yao. This should be one thousand two hundred and six. You’ve written one thousand two hundred and sixty.” She tapped it. “And then you carried it.”

I looked. She was right.

Four years. I have dreamed about that warehouse. A six where there should have been nothing.

Mr. Zhao refilled her tea twice. He came in from the garden without a sound, filled her cup, and stood behind her chair reading over her shoulder.

“You’re in my light.”

He moved. About two centimetres. Then he put one hand on the back of her chair and stayed there for three hours.

I have seen this man walk into a room full of armed men. I did not know he could stand behind a chair like that.

When I was packing up, she tipped her head back against him. He bent down. He said her name, low, and stopped. Right there. Waiting.

She didn’t even open her eyes.

“Yes.”

Then he kissed her. Upside down. Not on the cheek.

I put the third quarter in the box twice.

In the hall, by the lemon tree, I made myself say it.

“Mr. Zhao. Your wife found an error in the third quarter accounts from four years ago. I made that error.”

“Yes.”

“Nobody ever found it. I didn’t find it. I’ve been looking for four years.” I took my glasses off. My hands were shaking. Disgraceful. “She found it in twenty minutes. With a pencil.”

He looked down the hall. She was frowning at a ledger, chewing the end of the pencil.

“Yes. She does that.”

“I think I might be afraid of her.”

“Good.”

What does good mean? I have been awake since four thinking about it.

Wednesday.

She writes in the margins. Small, neat handwriting, like a wedding card. Every question is polite. Every question makes me feel like an onion.

Mr. Yao, is this a five or an S?

It was an S. I would rather not write here what it stands for.

Mr. Yao, who is Mr. Lam, and why is he paid every month to consult on nothing?

I don’t know who Mr. Lam is. I have paid him for nine years. I decided long ago that I would live longer not knowing.

Wednesday, later.

She rang me at home. At night. My wife answered and handed me the phone like it was hot.

“Mr. Yao? Sorry. Is it late?”

“No! No, Mrs. Zhao. Not at all.”

I was in my pyjamas.

“Page nine. The second column. Is that freight or storage?”

“Freight.”

“Then why’s it in storage?”

“…I’ll look in the morning.”

“Thank you.” A pencil, scratching. Then a man’s voice, further off. Low.

“Come to bed.”

“One minute.”

“You said that an hour ago.”

“I said one more page. That’s different.” Her voice went away from the phone. Not far enough. “Zhendong. Zhendong, I’m on the phone… stop it…”

Then she was back. Very crisp.

“Goodnight, Mr. Yao.”

“Goodnight, Mrs. Zhao.”

I lay awake until two. It was freight. It was in storage. I don’t know how.

The following Thursday.

At the Docks. She found her own loan.

I should explain. I knew her handwriting before she ever wrote in my margins. It was on a note that came with a bill, two summers ago. A cooler for the shop. This is a loan. Mr. Zhao read it twice, folded it up and put it in his wallet. He did not tell me to record a loan. I did not record a loan.

She has now found the cooler.

“Mr. Yao. August, two years ago. Where’s my loan?”

“There… isn’t one, Mrs. Zhao.”

“Why not?”

I looked at the door of the inner office. She looked at it too. Then she got up and went in, and didn’t shut it, so I heard everything. I was not listening. The walls are thin.

“You didn’t record it.”

“No.”

“It’s a LOAN, Zhendong!”

“It’s a cooler.”

“I wrote it down! I gave you a note!”

“I kept the note.”

Then nothing. For quite a while.

I took my ledgers out into the yard and checked a column I had already checked. Bao was there, peeling an orange.

“Mr. Yao. You’re learning.”

“I don’t want to be learning, Bao.”

“Nobody does.”

The same afternoon.

She asked him about Mr. Lam. In front of me. I wished hard to be somewhere else, for example dead.

“Who’s Mr. Lam?”

“A man who doesn’t open a container.”

“For nine years?”

“He has a good memory.”

She thought about it. Then she wrote something next to Mr. Lam’s name and turned the page.

“Then pay him on time. You were late in March.”

Mr. Zhao looked at me.

I have worked for this man for nine years. I have never once seen him look at me like a man who has just been told off. He looked at me like I should do something about it.

Since that day, whenever I take him a question, he says the same two words.

“Ask her.”

I asked him about the port fees. Ask her. I asked him about Bao’s new van. Ask her. I asked him if he would like his tea.

“Ask her.”

I went home that night and bought my wife a necklace. She asked why. I couldn’t explain. She made me sit down and try.

I couldn’t. She kept the necklace.

Saturday. September.

The wedding. In the flower shop. Little gold lights all over the ceiling, thirty people, two dogs in white ribbons.

I stood as far from her as the shop allowed. Behind the delivery boy. He is not a big boy. I did my best.

She came over anyway. Champagne in one hand. Her husband one step behind her, the way he always is.

“Mr. Yao. You came!”

“Yes, Mrs. Zhao. Congratulations, Mrs. Zhao.”

“Page forty-one is still perfect, by the way.”

I didn’t know what to do with that. The delivery boy gave me some of his cake.

A Thursday in winter.

A meeting at the Docks. Port fees, the quarter, the new route. Mr. Zhao, Mrs. Zhao, Bao, me. I was reading my report out loud.

He took her hand under the edge of the table. I saw because I was looking at the table instead of at anyone’s face. He lifted it and kissed her knuckles. Then put it back on the ledger. Kept reading over her shoulder like nothing had happened.

She turned a page with the other hand.

I lost my place in my own report. Bao had to tell me which line I was on.

“Twelve, Mr. Yao.”

“Thank you, Bao.”

“You’re welcome, Mr. Yao.”

He was grinning. Bao. Grinning.

One year later.

Mrs. Zhao reviews all the books on Thursdays now.

My mistakes are down ninety-one per cent. I worked it out. I do every sum twice. Sometimes three times. Before I send anything, I read it out loud in an empty room, to hear whether it sounds like something she’d put a pencil next to.

My wife says I’m a better man. My children say I’m very boring at dinner.

Last Thursday she looked up from page twelve.

“Mr. Yao… this is perfect.”

I had to go and stand outside by the water for a while.

Mr. Zhao came out and stood next to me. He didn’t say anything for a long time. Gulls. Cranes. Somebody shouting about a forklift.

“She said you were good. Before she started.”

“Sir?”

“He’s careful. He’s just got nobody to check him.”

I couldn’t say anything. I took my glasses off and cleaned them on my tie, which doesn’t work.

“Does it get easier, sir? Being checked?”

He thought about it. He watched the office window. She was in there with her pencil, and her tea, and the calculator she doesn’t use.

“No.”

Then he went back inside. Straight to her desk. He stood in her light, and she didn’t tell him to move.

I have kept this diary in a locked drawer for a year. If anyone ever finds it, I would like it known that I am not afraid of the florist.

That’s a lie. I’m writing it down anyway.

She’d find it in twenty minutes.

chapters.title: The Language of Flowers, Studied in Secret
chapters.desc: He buys her yellow roses, and she tells him what yellow means. So he buys a very old book and starts again, one stem at a time.
chapters.epigraph: “Yellow roses mean jealousy, Zhendong. Or the end of a friendship.” “…Oh.”
chapters.content:
The first morning of the second spring, Elowen came down to the kitchen in the dark and found roses on the counter.

Yellow ones. A dozen, long-stemmed, next to the two coffees. Wrapped in brown paper and tied with string. The knot was so tight she’d need a knife.

Her husband was at the window with his cup. Not looking at them. Really, really not looking at them.

“You bought me roses?”

“A stall by the Docks. The man opens at three.”

“You went to the Docks at three?”

He drank his coffee.

“You buy everyone else roses. Nobody buys you any.”

She picked them up. Good ones. Tight heads, straight stems. Somebody had taken the thorns off with a knife and gone in too deep, so every stem had little torn places down it. She ran her thumb over them. He’d done it himself. In the dark. Probably swearing.

“They’re beautiful.”

“Hm.”

She’d always liked the yellow ones. Since she was tiny, holding Old Tan’s hand at the market. Did he know that? How would he know that?

He put his cup down and zipped her coat up to her chin, the way he did every market morning now. Like she couldn’t do it herself. She let him. The roses crackled between them.

“I’ll get the van.”

She took the roses to the shop and put them by the till, where she’d see them all day.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven an old lady came in for carnations. She looked at the till. Her eyebrows went up.

“Oh dear. Who’s jealous?”

“Sorry?”

“Yellow roses, love! On the counter. Somebody’s jealous or somebody’s sorry.” She patted Elowen’s hand. “Or both. It’s usually both.”

She left with her carnations. Xiao Pan came out of the cooler like a tortoise.

“Miss Lin… is Mr. Zhao jealous?”

“Of what?”

Xiao Pan thought about it. You could see him thinking. It was painful.

“…The physics man?”

“Go and load the van.”

“I’m just saying, at the reunion he—”

“Van, Xiao Pan!”

✦ ✦ ✦

At dinner she put her chopsticks down.

“The roses.”

He looked up from his fish.

“Do you know what yellow roses mean?”

“Mean?”

“Flowers have meanings. The Victorians wrote whole dictionaries. Red for love. White for innocence.” She turned her cup round. “Yellow roses mean jealousy, Zhendong. Or the end of a friendship. Or I’m sorry, I did something I shouldn’t have.”

He put his chopsticks down too.

“…Oh.”

“It doesn’t matter. Nobody uses it any more. Most people think yellow just means happy.” She picked hers back up. “Only florists know. And old ladies. And the old lady in the shop this morning.”

“What did she say?”

“She asked me who was jealous.”

He didn’t answer. He picked up a piece of fish and put it in her bowl. Then another one.

“Zhendong.”

“No.”

“You’re feeding me. You do that when you’re guilty.”

“…A bit.”

“A bit what?”

“Jealous.” He said it to the fish. “The physics man. At the reunion. He asked if you were happy. Why would he ask that?”

“Because he’s polite!”

“Hm.”

She laughed so hard she had to put her face in her hands. When she came up he was still looking at her, dead serious, with his ears gone red. She took a piece of fish off her own plate and held it out to him. He looked at it. He ate it off her chopsticks.

“I’m happy. Idiot.”

He finished his rice. He washed his bowl. She thought that was the end of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The antique shop on Bell Lane opened at ten. He was outside at nine.

The owner saw who it was through the glass and dropped his keys twice getting the door open.

“Mr. Zhao. Sir. Anything. Is it the jade? I can—”

“A book. About what flowers mean.”

The man blinked.

“…For a lady, sir?”

“My wife.”

It took the man an hour. He went up a ladder, down to a cellar, onto the phone to his brother. Zhao stood in the middle of the shop with his hands in his pockets and didn’t touch anything. He didn’t need to. Everyone who came to the door saw him and walked on.

He paid what the man asked. The man nearly cried.

That night he sat on the narrow bed in the little room with a pencil and read it from the first page. Yellow. Jealousy. He’d stood in the dark at the Docks and picked them out because they were the colour she went soft over at the market. Every time. He’d watched her do it for a year. He’d been sure.

He wrote NO in the margin. Pressed hard.

Then he turned the page. He had a lot to get through.

✦ ✦ ✦

A week later she found the book.

She was changing the sheets in the little room at the top of the stairs. His old room. The narrow bed. He still went there some nights when he couldn’t sleep and didn’t want to wake her. She lifted the mattress to tuck the corner, and there it was. Flat on the slats.

A small cloth book with gold letters on the spine, rubbed almost away.

The Language of Flowers. With Illustrations. 1884.

It smelled like an antique shop. There was a price inside the cover in pencil. She sat down on the bed.

How much? For a book?

Every page had a little painted flower and a meaning underneath. And all down the margins, in pencil, in square blunt capitals, there were notes.

Next to Yellow Rose: Jealousy, decrease of love, he’d written: NO.

Next to Red Rose: Love: TOO OBVIOUS? SHE SELLS 400 A WEEK.

Next to Lily of the Valley: Return of happiness: GRANNY SU. REGISTRY MORNING. ANNIVERSARY. DOES GRANNY SU KNOW THIS BOOK?

She put her hand over her mouth.

Next to Ranunculus: You are radiant with charms: TUESDAYS. DOES SHE KNOW?

Next to Gardenia: Secret love: TOO LATE.

Next to Delphinium: Ardent attachment there was no note. Only a line under the words, gone over and over until the pencil had shone. The night of the rain, the whole shop full of delphiniums. He’d bought every one.

Next to Camellia: My destiny is in your hands, nothing at all. Just a box round the words. Drawn with a ruler.

She sat there a long time.

Then she put it back under the mattress exactly where it had been, tucked the corner in and went downstairs. She said nothing. If he knew she’d seen it, he’d stop. She knew him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flowers started a week after that.

One at a time. Never a bunch. One stem on the counter by her coffee, every market morning, in the dark.

A sprig of rosemary. Remembrance.

One white tulip, the morning after they’d fought about him coming to the market with a cold. Forgiveness. She’d been the one who shouted. She knew what it meant.

A stem of honeysuckle. No florist in the city had honeysuckle in April. He’d cut it off somebody’s wall. Bonds of love.

Forget-me-nots, so small and so badly tied she knew he’d picked them on the hill with his own hands. She didn’t need the book for that one.

She put each one in a glass on the kitchen windowsill. A row of glasses that didn’t match, getting longer every week. He stood at the window every morning drinking his coffee and not looking at it.

Bao came into the kitchen one morning with the car keys and a face.

“Boss. The old man on Pottery Lane wants to know who’s been cutting his wall.”

Zhao didn’t turn round.

“Pay him.”

“He doesn’t want money.”

“Then what does he want?”

“He wants to know if it worked.”

Elowen had her back to them, filling the kettle. She stopped breathing.

Zhao drank his coffee.

“…Not yet.”

Bao went out. Elowen let the kettle overflow all over her hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

It went on for two months.

Then, one Tuesday in May, there was a single ranunculus next to her coffee. Pale apricot. Perfect.

You are radiant with charms.

She picked it up. He was at the window.

“I buy these every Tuesday.”

He didn’t move.

“Do you know why? My mother. When I was small.” Her voice did something. She kept going. “She said buy yourself ranunculus once a week, so you remember somebody thinks you’re lovely. Even if it’s only you.”

He turned round.

“I’ve bought them every Tuesday since she died.” She held the stem up. Her hand was shaking. Stupid. It was a flower. She sold a thousand a month. “So somebody would.”

Her eyes were going. She hated that. She hated crying in front of anyone, and she was going to, right here, in her market boots, over one stem.

He came across the kitchen. He took the ranunculus out of her hand and tucked it behind her ear. Then he kissed her eyelids. One. Then the other. Where the wet was.

“You found the book.”

“Under the mattress.” She sniffed. Very attractive. “In the small room.”

“I was keeping the camellia for last.”

“For when?”

“When I ran out.”

“Of flowers?”

“Of things to say.”

She laughed, and it came out wet and ugly.

“You don’t say anything! You’ve said about forty words since March!”

“Hm.”

“That’s forty-one!”

He bent his head. He stopped a breath from her mouth, the way he always stopped. She could feel him waiting. Wanting it so much his hand was tight on the back of her coat.

“Tell me to stop.”

“Don’t you dare.”

He didn’t stop. He wasn’t careful about it either. He backed her into the counter and kissed her until the ranunculus fell out of her hair and the coffee went cold and she was going to be late for Granny Su. She was never late for Granny Su.

She was. Granny Su took one look at her mouth.

“Hm!”

“Don’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t run out.

The glasses went all along the windowsill, then round the corner onto the next one. At the end of the summer Raiden came over to fix a hinge, saw the windowsills and stood there with his screwdriver.

“What’s all this?”

“Nothing,” they said. Both of them. At the same time.

Raiden looked at his sister. Then at her husband. Then he went and got his tape measure and built them a shelf.

chapters.title: Valentine’s Day in a Flower Shop
chapters.desc: Nine hundred roses, one till, and an arms dealer saying “Next.” The customers have never been so polite.
chapters.epigraph: “Next.” — Zhao Zhendong, four hundred and twelve times
chapters.content:
“I’ll work the till.”

“No.”

“Xiao Pan’s on deliveries all day. His cousin’s banned.”

“His cousin is banned for life, Zhendong, and you’ll be worse. You’ll frighten everyone.”

He thought about it.

“They’ll be fast.”

She pointed her pen at the back wall. The sign. HOUSE RULES. 2. The husband is not allowed behind the counter. With the line through it, and his four words in square capitals beside it.

He read them out anyway.

“Except when she says so.”

She looked at the order book. Nine hundred roses. Three hundred and eleven orders. A queue from seven in the morning to nine at night, and every man in it had remembered that morning and wanted twelve red right now. She’d done seven Valentine’s Days. Last year she’d cried in the cooler at four and come out and smiled at a man who called her sweetheart.

“…Fine. I say so.”

He was already tying the apron.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was behind the counter before seven.

The green apron. ELOWEN’S across his chest. It still came to his ribs. He’d pushed his egg stool to the back. He stood with his feet apart and his hands flat on the counter and looked at the door. Like the door owed him money.

She turned the sign at seven.

The first man in was about twenty-five, suit, phone at his ear. Talking before he’d reached the counter.

“Hi, yeah, I need a dozen red, the nice ones, can you do it fast because I’m late for—”

He looked up. He stopped talking.

“Twelve red. Wrapped or a box?”

The man’s mouth opened. Closed.

“…Wrapped. Please.”

“Card?”

“Yes. Please. Sir.”

Zhao slid a card and a pen across. The man wrote so fast the pen skidded. Elowen wrapped twelve red in brown paper and ribbon and passed them forward. Zhao took the money. Counted the change twice.

“Next.”

The man left. He didn’t run. It was close.

✦ ✦ ✦

By ten word had got round.

She didn’t notice at first. She was wrapping like a machine. Then she looked up and the queue was out the door and down the street and nobody in it was making a sound.

Valentine’s Day was loud. It was always loud. Men on phones. Men arguing about pink. Men asking if she could do something special for no extra. Not today. Forty men stood in a line looking straight ahead with their wallets out. Like they were waiting to see a doctor.

“Good morning, sir. Twelve red, if it’s no trouble.”

“Whichever ones you think are best. Thank you. Thank you so much.”

“I don’t mind what colour! Honestly! Whatever’s easiest!”

She’d put the price up a third, same as every year. Normally she spent the whole day defending it. Nobody said a word. Was that wrong? Probably. She tied another bow and didn’t care.

An older man in a good coat reached the front, looked up at Zhao, and went pale.

“Twenty-four. And the lilies. And… what are those? Those too.”

“Those are for a funeral.”

“…I’ll take them anyway.”

At eleven a young man in a leather jacket got to the front. He looked past Zhao at the workbench and smiled.

“And one for the florist. Since she’s working so hard. Maybe she’s free later—”

Zhao looked at him. That was all. Two seconds. The young man’s smile went out like a match.

“She’s married.”

“Right! Yes. Sorry. To… to who?”

Zhao kept looking at him.

Elowen didn’t look up from the ribbon.

“To him. Twelve red, was it?”

“…Yes. Please.”

“Next.”

She cut the ribbon. It was a perfect bow. She smiled at it for about twenty minutes.

✦ ✦ ✦

At noon she brought him noodles from across the road. He didn’t stop serving. So she stood beside him and fed him. One mouthful between each customer, off her own chopsticks.

The queue watched this happen. Nobody said anything. A boy near the front looked like he wanted to take notes.

“Next.” With his mouth full.

At one, Chen Si joined the queue.

Camel coat. Takeaway coffee. He stood about twelfth from the front, perfectly calm, and the men either side of him edged away without knowing why. When he got to the counter he looked at his brother for a long moment. At the apron.

“Good afternoon, Zhendong.”

“Twelve red?”

“I thought, as family—”

“Back of the queue.”

Chen Si looked at Elowen. Elowen tied a bow.

“You heard him.”

He went to the back of the queue. He actually went. Forty minutes later he reached the front again, and his face hadn’t moved once, and he had his phone out.

“Forty, please. Red. Aurelia counts them.”

“Forty.” Zhao didn’t blink. “Card?”

“No card. She’ll know.” He held up the phone. “Smile.”

“Next.”

The photo went to Aurelia anyway. Elowen’s phone buzzed under the ribbon ten seconds later.

Aurelia: IS THAT AN APRON

Aurelia: this is a point for me. I SAW it

Elowen: it’s my till. it’s my point

Where had he learned to say card like a threat? She’d never once heard anyone do that.

At two a girl came in. The only girl all day. Sixteen, maybe, in a school blazer, with a fistful of coins.

The line behind her shuffled.

She got to the counter and looked up at Zhao and flinched. Elowen saw it. Then she saw the girl lift her chin.

“I want one rose. One. Red.” She put the coins down. “For a boy in my class. I don’t know if he likes me. I’m going to put it on his desk.” Her voice wobbled. “That’s all I’ve got.”

It was about a third of a rose. On Valentine’s Day, less.

The whole queue had stopped breathing.

Zhao looked at the coins. Then at her. He took a rose out of the bucket by the till. Looked at it. Put it back. Took another. Held it to the light. Checked the head. Ran his thumb down the stem, the way Elowen had shown him on the morning of the four hundred roses, and found a thorn, and took it off with his nail.

He held it out.

She took it. She looked at the coins.

“That’s not enough. I know it’s not enough.”

“A boy in your class. And you’re putting it on his desk without saying who it’s from.”

She nodded. Her eyes were huge.

“That’s brave.” He swept the coins into the till. No change. “Next.”

She stared at him. Then she held the rose against her blazer and ran, and the queue moved apart for her without anyone telling it to.

Elowen had to turn round and face the wall for a second. Her face hurt.

✦ ✦ ✦

They closed at nine.

Nine hundred roses, gone. Three hundred and eleven orders. Four hundred and twelve customers on the till roll, every one served by a man in an apron that came to his ribs. Not one complaint. Not one.

He sat down on the egg stool when the last man had gone. Elbows on his knees. Head down. He didn’t move.

“Zhendong? Are you okay?”

“I said next four hundred and twelve times.” To the floor. “I’ve never said any word that many times. In my life.”

She came round the counter and knelt in front of him. He’d stood for fourteen hours in his good shoes. She undid the laces.

“Elowen. Don’t—”

“Stay there. I mean it.”

She pulled one shoe off, then the other, and rubbed his feet through his socks with both thumbs. He made a noise she’d only ever heard from him in bed. She looked up at him. He looked at the ceiling.

“Every single one of them was polite. Do you know how rare that is? Seven years! Nobody has ever been polite on Valentine’s Day.”

“They were frightened.”

“They were polite because they were frightened.” She sat back on her heels. “I’m hiring you. Every year. Forever. You’re the best till I’ve ever had.”

He laughed. Properly. It came out of him tired and surprised.

Then he leaned down and reached under the counter. Something he’d put there that morning, before seven, while she was in the cooler.

One red rose. Not a good one. The head bent over. The stem curved like it had grown round a corner. Out of nine hundred, the one nobody would ever have bought.

“I kept it back. Before anyone came.” He turned it in his fingers. “Worst one in the bucket.”

“Why?”

“Everyone else was getting the perfect ones.” He held it out to her. “I wanted this one for you.”

She took it. She looked at it for a while. At the bent head. At him, in his socks on her stool, in a green apron, after four hundred and twelve nexts so she wouldn’t have to say one.

She got up. She opened the till and lifted the tray where the notes went, and laid the crooked rose underneath. Flat. Safe. Then she shut it.

“That’s where I keep the important things.”

He looked at the till. Then at her. His face did the slow thing it did. The thing that still made her knees go.

She sat herself up on the counter. Took him by the apron straps. Pulled.

He stood up off the stool and came. No waiting this time. She didn’t give him the chance. She kissed him with her hands knotted in ELOWEN’S, the sign on CLOSED, the buckets all empty round them, until he was laughing into her mouth and she’d forgotten what day it was.

“Happy Valentine’s,” he said. Rough. Against her neck.

“Shut up. Kiss me.”

He did.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiao Pan came back from the last delivery a bit after half nine. He saw the shop window. He turned the red bike round and went round the block. Then he went round again. Just to be safe.

Next February, he was tying the apron on before she’d found the shop keys.
